ABANDONMENT A. DEFINITIONS ABANDONMENT 

An abandonment is a total withdrawal of a person from an object; to lay aside all care for an object; to leave it altogether to itself. 

Pidge v. Pidge, 3 Met. 257, at 265

An abandonment is the intentional relinquishment of a known right-the giving up of something to which one is entitled, whether with or without legal consideration. 

Saxlehner v. Eisner & Mendelsohn Co., 179, U. S. 19, at 31

B. DISTINCTIONS 

To establish the defense of abandonment it is necessary to show not only acts indicating a practical abandonment but an actual intent to abandon. Acts which unexplained would be sufficient to establish an abandonment may be answered by showing that there never was an intention to give up and relinquish the right claimed. 

Saxlehner v. Eisner & Mendelsohn Co., 179, U. S. 19, at 31 

Singer Mfg. Co. v. June Mfg. Co., 163 U. S. 169, at 186

Property is abandoned when it is thrown away or its possession voluntarily forsaken by the owner, in which case it becomes the property of the first possessor or occupant. 

In most cases abandonment is a question of fact and not of law.

The essentials of abandonment are: 

1. An intention to abandon. 2. 

N. E. Structural Co. v. Everett D. Co., 189 Mass. 145, at 154 

Dyer v. Sanford, 9 Met. 395 

An act carrying out the intention. 

Nelson v. Blinn, 197 Mass. 279 

N. E. Structural Co. v. Everett D. Co., 189 Mass. 145 

Dyer v. Sanford, 9 Met. 395

C. CLASSES 

1. Children a. Parents' Liabilities for 

Gen. Laws, c. 273, ss. 1-10 

Gen: Laws, c. 119, ss. 31-40 

2. Contract 

Upon his abandonment of the contract the contractor loses all right to recover from the owner any sums which otherwise might be due him under the contract. 1

ABANDONMENT 

Dobben v. Duncan Con. Co., 191 A.S. 1575, at 1585

Smedley v. Walden, 246 Mass. 393, at 400 (Intentional departure or willful default of building contract) When the contractor has abandoned the contract an intention by the owner to complete the contract for the contractor's benefit will not be inferred, unless it clearly appears. 

Dobben v. Duncan Con. Co., 1931 A.S. 1575, at 1585

Bernz v. Marcus Sayre Co., 52 N. J. Eq. 275 

3. Personalty

Personalty which is abandoned becomes the property of no one. 

The former owner gives up his title and right to it and the finder may successfully assert his ownership of it. 

So personalty which has been abandoned is not the subject of larceny. 

36 C. J. 757, Sec. 75 

4. Real Estate 

17 R. C. L. 36, Sec. 40 

It was said in N. E. Structural Co. v. Everett D. Co., 189 Mass. 

145, as to an easement, that: "Abandonment is a question of intent. In some cases, where acts of the owner of the dominant estate have seemed to be entirely inconsistent with an intention to make any further use of the easement, especially where a change in circumstances has rendered the easement no longer of any benefit, such acts have been regarded as showing conclusively as matter of law an intention to abandon, and the consequent extinguishment of the easement. 

Canny v. Andrews, 123 Mass. 155 

Corning v. Gould, 16 Wend (U. S.) 531 

Dillman v. Hoffman, 38 Wis. 559 "Since the abandonment however is a question of intent, any act relied upon either must be accompanied by evidence of intention, or be in its nature such as necessarily to show an intention, to abandon. As a rule mere encroachments upon a common right of way do not of themselves necessarily show an intention to abandon the way, and in most of such cases the question of abandonment is one of fact and not of law." 2

ABANDONMENT 

In King v. Murphy, 140 Mass.

254, the general rule is thus stated by Morton, C. J.: 

"Mere non-user, even for twenty years, will not conclusively show an abandonment of a right of way; but when the owner of a dominant estate, to which a right of way over a servient estate is appurtenant, does some acts inconsistent with the continued existence of the way, with the intention to abandon and extinguish his easement, it operates as a present abandonment; and it is a question for the jury to determine whether such intention existed."

An easement may be lost by abandonment and whether there is an abandonment is ordinarily a question of intention. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 158

Moreover to show abandonment there must be evidence of a present intent to relinquish the easement or a purpose inconsistent with its further existence. 

Parsons v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 216 Mass. 269, at 272 

Willets v. Langhaar, 212 Mass. 573, at 575

Whether there is an abandonment is a question of fact. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 158 

Willets v. Langhaar, 212 Mass. 573, at 575 a. As Extinguishing Easement

If the extinguishment of an easement by the execution by the. owner of the servient estate of a license which prevents the further enjoyment of the easement rests on the ground that the ownr of the easment intentionally abandons it, and where there is a complete extinguishment it may well rest upon that ground,his intention is conclusively presumed in favor of the owner of the servient tenement who executed the license, because between these parties, when one acts upon the license of the other, the manifest and apparent intention which is acted upon must control their rights, whatever the secret intention of the licensor may be.

Les v. 

Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 159 

Boston etc. R. R. v. Doherty, 154 Mass. 314, at 317 

In Boston etc. R. R. v. Doherty, 154 Mass. 314, at 317, the 

Court held: "When, pursuant to a parol agreement of the dominent and servient owners for the substitution of a new way for an old one, and the servient owner had constructed the new way, and so altered the servient estate that the old way could

ABANDONMENT 

no longer be used as before, the old way had been extinguished by the executed license; and further, that it had been abandoned since the change in the old way was consistent only with an intent of the dominant owner to abandon his old right.” 

Byrne v. Savoie, 225 Mass. 338, at 340

But the acts in the construction of the new way must be solely under the agreement, and the acts of the servient owner in dealing with the old way must be inconsistent with the continued existence of the old way. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 159 

Dyer v. Sanford, 9 Met. 395, at 401 

b. What is Not 

1. A temporary suspension of use is not enough. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 159 

Willard v. Stone, 253 Mass. 555 at 561 and 562 (Water rights.) 

Howe v. Johnson, 236 Mass. 379 (Railroad did not abandon location.) 

Hartt v. Rueter, 223 Mass. 207 (Non-user.) 

Tinker v. Bessel, 213 Mass. 74 (Non-user.) 

N.Y. etc. R. R. v. Chelsea, 213 Mass. 40 (Non-user)

Willets v. Langhaar, 212 Mass. 573 (Non-user for 23. years.) 

Amee v. B. & A. R. R., 212 Mass. 421 (Non-user) 

N. E. Structural Co. v. Everett, 189 Mass. 145, at 154 

Barnes v. Lloyd, 112 Mass. 224, at 232 

Pope v. Devereux, 5 Gray 409 

2. Plowing up servient estate and putting new road elsewhere are not enough to show abandonment of a right of way. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 159

ABATEMENT 

A. 

DEFINITIONS ABATEMENT 

1. At Law an abatement is an active overthrow or destruction of the action, so that the particular action is quashed and ended. 

2. But in Equity an abatement signifies only a present suspension of the suit for want of parties capable of proceeding therein.

At Law an action, when abated, is absolutely dead; but in 

Equity a suit when abated is merely in a state of suspended animation and may be revived. B. 1. 

Putman v. Putman, 4 Pick. 139, at 140 and 141

DISTINCTIONS Between ABATEMENT and BAR 

A plea in abatement goes to the form of the writ; a plea in bar goes to the cause of action. 

White v. E. T. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28, at 30 

Whiton v. Balch, 203 Mass. 576, at 578 A plea which sets out enough to show, not only that the present action can not be maintained, but that there is no cause of action whatever, is not in abatement but in bar. 

Davis v. Carpenter, 172 Mass. 167, at 172

Allin v. Conn. R. L. Co., 150 Mass. 560 

Grant v. Barry, 9 Allen 459

The question whether a matter is in abatement or in bar is to be decided, not by the form in which it is presented, but by its substance. If it is essentially in bar of the action, it will be so treated and considered even though cast in the form of a plea in abatement. 

White v. E. T. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28, at 31 

Merriman v. Currier, 191 Mass. 133, at 141

Cases just cited above 

But it was said in Guild v. Richardson, 6 Pick. 364, at 368: "Whether a plea is a plea in abatement, or in bar, or whether it is to the writ, or to the jurisdiction of the court, must be determined by the form of the plea, particularly by the conclusion or prayer of it; and not by the subject matter of the plea," 

2. Between ABATEMENT and DISMISSAL 

Dismissal of an action can be sustained only when founded on matters of law apparent on the record;

ABATEMENT 

Roberts v. Anheuser Busch B. Assoc. 215 Mass. 341, at 343 

Johnson v. Carr, 210 Mass. 1, at 5, lines 14-16 

Morton v. Sweetser, 12 Allen 134 

Hobbs v. Dane Co., 5 Allen 581 

Brown v. Webber, 6 Cush. 560, at 569 

Amidown v. Peck, 11 Met. 467, at 468 

Guild v. Richardson, 6 Pick. 369

Tingley v. Baterman, 10 Mass. 343 

But matters of fact, which do not appear on the face of the record, can be asserted only in abatement, and not by dismissal. 

Comm. v. Fredericks, 119 Mass. 199, at 204 and 205 

Crosby v. Harrison, 116 Mass. 114 

Haynes v. Saunders, 11 Cush. 537 

Belknap v. Gibbens, 13 Met. 471, at 474 

Simonds v. Parker, 1 Met. 508, at 511

Rathbone v. Rathbone, 4 Pick. 89, at 90 

Jacobs v. Mellen, 14 Mass. 135

In Nye v. Liscombe, 21 Pick. 263, Chief Justice Shaw said, at pages 265 and 266: "Where the matter, on which the defendant relies to abate the suit, is a fact not appearing upon the record or the return of the officer, it must be pleaded in abatement, so as to give the other party an opportunity to traverse and try it. But where all the facts upon which the claim to have the process abated is founded appear by the record including the return of the officer, of which the court will take notice without plea, there the action may be dismissed on motion. In that case the motion is not intended to state new facts, but merely to bring to the attention of the court, and also to furnish notice to the other party, of those facts appearing on the record and return, which of themselves are sufficient to show that the action cannot be properly proceeded in for want of due service, or other defect in the proceedings." 

In Paraboschi v. Shaw, 258 Mass. 531, Chief Justice Rugg said, at page 532: "The defendant appeared specially and filed a motion to dismiss and a plea in abatement, setting up want of proper service. A motion to dismiss for want of service is proper pleading [in an action at law]. It relates to a matter apparent on the record. It raises purely a question of law. A plea in abatement is appropriate when reliance is placed upon some fact not appearing upon the

ABATEMENT 

face of the record which the opposite party may deny and as to which there may be a trial. 

United Drug Co. v. Cordley & Hayes, 239 Mass. 334 

Oliver Ditson Co. v. Testa, 216 Mass. 123, at 124 

Lowrie v. Castle, 198 Mass. 82

Richmond v. Whittlesey, 2 Allen 230 "The practice is different in equity, where a motion to dismiss is irregular." 

Rothstein v. Comm. of Banks, 258 Mass. 196, at 197 

Wickwire Corp'n. v. U. S. Co., 247 Mass. 565, at 568 

Nelson Theatre Co. v. Nelson, 216 Mass. 30, at 32 

Noyes v. Bragg, 200 Mass. 106, at 110

Matters of dismissal are disposed of by the Court upon the state of the record without evidence from any other source. 

Matters in abatement may be determined upon demurrer, or trial with or without a jury with the introduction of evidence concerning facts outside of the record. 

Crosby v. Harrison, 116 Mass. 114, at 117 

Amidown v. Peck, 11 Met. 467, at 468

The question of dismissal is raised upon a motion, while the right to abatement is brought forward upon a plea or allegations in an answer.

C. PRESENTATION or WAIVER 

1. Appearance a. Must be Special

Pleas and answers in abatement are dilatory pleadings of defence.

To preserve his right to present matters in abatement, as well as dismissal, the defendant must (1) appear specially, and (2) in all his pleadings expressly, clearly and consistently indicate his intention to rely upon, and not waive such matters. 

Cheshire Nat. Bank v. Jaynes, 224 Mass. 14, at 15 (Non-resident defendant could appear specially and protect its attached property without submitting generally to court's jurisdiction.) 

Currier v. Beard, 216 Mass. 113, at 114 ("In order to prevail the party must appear specially and confine his pleading to the specific point of want of service.") 

Porter v. City of Newton, 133 Mass. 56, at 57

Hastings v. Inhabitants of Bolton, 1 Allen 529 

Hollis v. Richardson, 13 Gray 392, at 393

Barry v. Page, 10 Gray 398

ABATEMENT 

Wilson v. Coffin, 2 Cush. 316 

Smith v. Cleveland, 6 Met. 332, at 335

Carlisle v. Weston, 1 Met. 26 

Barnes v. Hurd, 11 Mass. 57 

Stevenson v. Hayden, 2 Mass. 405 

In Brown v. Webber, 6 Cush. 560, at 564 the court said: "If the defendant would object to the irregularity, or want of due service, he may do so, by plea in abatement, where it is necessary to plead any matter of fact, on which his objection is founded, or by motion to dismiss, where the objection is apparent on the face of the proceedings, or the return of the officer; and in either case, before pleading generally to the merits. And to enable him to do this, he may appear specially for purpose of stating such objection, without thereby waiving it. But if he will enter a general appearance, or plead to the merits, or lie by after he is aware of the matter of objection to the jurisdiction, he thereby submits himself to the jurisdiction of the court; and the court, then, having jurisdiction of the subject, and jurisdiction of the persons of the parties, may proceed, and the exception, that the suit is brought in the wrong county, cannot be made in arrest of judgment.' 

Gleason v. Dodd, 4 Met. 333, at 339 

2. Mode of Presentation 

Matters in abatement may be raised in three ways: a, by a plea; b, by an answer solely in abatement alleging the specific facts upon which reliance is placed; or c, by joining such answer in abatement with an answer to the merits, either in one document or in separate documents filed simultaneously. 

General Laws, Chapter 231 provides that: 

Sec. 20. A defence to a real, personal or mixed action, which formerly might have been made by plea in abatement, may be made by answer in abatement. 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262

Young v. Providence Co., 150 Mass. 550 

Moore Co. v. Speigel, 143 Mass. 413 

O'Laughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass. 600 

Smith v. Dexter, 121 Mass. 597 

Jaha v. Billey, 105 Mass. 208 

Morton v. Sweetser, 12 Allen 134

Hastings v. Bolton, 1 Allen 529 

Whipple v. Rogerson, 12 Gray 347 36

ABATEMENT 

Greenwood v. Lake Shore R. R., 10 Gray 373 

Hayden v. Inhabitants of Attleborough, 7 Gray 338 

Cole v. Ackerman, 7 Gray 38 

Benthall v. Hildreth, 2 Gray 288 

Seagrave v Erickson, 11 Cush. 89 

Bliss v. Bliss, 12 Met. 266

When the answer filed contains both an answer in abatement and an answer to the merits, the validity of either is not affected by their being pleaded together. 

Fisher v. Fraprie, 125 Mass. 472 

Claflin v. Thayer, 13 Gray 459 

In Parks v. Smith, 155 Mass. 26, the court said at page 30: "If the answer in abatement was overruled as matter of law, the defendant had the right to answer over; if as matter of fact, he might do so at the discretion of the judge." 

3. Time for Filing a. Civil Cases 

Common Law Rule 5 of the Supreme Judicial Court provides in part: “Answers and pleas in abatement, and motions to dismiss, shall be filed within the time allowed by law for entering an appearance, unless otherwise specially ordered by the court for good cause shown.” 

Superior Court Rule 25, (1931) provides that: "A defendant shall, within twenty-one days, or such other period as may be prescribed by statute, or in equity cases by the terms of the subpoena, after the return day of the writ, subpoena, notice or other process by which he or his property is brought before the court to answer in the action, suit or libel, enter his appearance in writing and also within the same time or such other time, greater or less. file. motion to dismiss, answer in abatement, demurrer, plea or answer, and in a suit in equity, his demurrer, plea or answer.' .... ... · 99 Answers and pleas in abatement must be filed within the time allowed by law for entering an appearance, unless otherwise shown specially ordered by the court for good cause shown. 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262, at 268

But after an answer to the merits, the court has no power, at a term subsequent to the return term, to allow matters in

ABATEMENT 

abatement to be set up, even though those matters were unknown to the defendant when he filed his answer to the merits. 

Silver v. Graves, 210 Mass. 26, at 32

Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 136

In Hastings v. Inhabitants of Bolton, 1 Allen 529, Chief Jus tice Bigelow said, at page 530: "The court has no power to allow the answer in abatement to be filed. It was not merely the exercise of an authority to permit the defendants to amend their pleadings. It went much farther. It set aside the well established rule of law that a dilatory plea must be filed within a certain period of time after the entry of an action, and it also deprived the plaintiff of the benefit of the waiver of such a plea by an answer to the merits. These were legal rights on which the plaintiff had a right to insist, and which the court, in the exercise of a judicial discretion, could not take away. The power to allow amendments, though very broad and comprehensive, does not authorize courts to disregard or abrogate the fixed and settled rules of law regulating judicial proceedings; and indeed, upon the broadest interpretation of the words of the statute by which the power to allow amendments is given, [Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 51] the action of the court in the present case was clearly unauthorized, because in the stage to which the cause had arrived, all matters of abatement had ceased to be a 'legal defence.'

It was suggested that the facts on which the answer in abatement was founded were not known to the defendants until after the case had been in court for more than one term, and after an answer to the merits had been filed. 

But this is wholly immaterial. The defendants were bound seasonably to make inquiry and ascertain whether the plaintiff had brought his action in the proper county. 

By omitting to do so they were guilty of laches, and the law will not relieve them from the consequences of such negligence."

WAIVER Matters for abatement are waived by a general appearance, pleading to the merits or delay in interposing objections. 

Gen. Laws, c. 231 s. 136 in part provides: 66 ....

After the defendant has appeared and answered to the merits of the action, no defect in the writ or other process by which he has been brought before the court, or in the service thereof, shall be considered to affect the jurisdiction of the court." 

Paige v. Sinclair, 237 Mass. 482, at 484 (Action in wrong county waived by general appearance) 

Riley v. Brusendorf, 226 Mass. 310, at 312 ("A general appearance waives formal defects as to the getting of the defendant before the court.") 

McManus v. Thing, 208 Mass. 55, at 58 

Pierce v. Equitable L. A. Society, 145 Mass. 56, at 57 (Both parties were residents of another State) 

In Simonds v. Parker, 1 Met. 508, at 511 and 512, the court said: "If a party takes no notice of any matter of exception to the form or service of the process, in an early stage

ABATEMENT 

of the proceedings, it affords reasonable ground to conclude that he considers them of no importance, and is willing to proceed to the trial of his rights upon the substantial merits of the controversy. By referring any question to the court, other than that of the jurisdiction itself, he acknowledges jurisdiction." 

In Carlisle v. Weston, 21 Pick. 535, at 536, 537 and 538, the court said: "The general rule upon this subject is, that irregularities and defects may be waived, but mere nullities cannot be cured, or restored to life, inasmuch as they never possessed any legal vitality. Jurisdiction cannot be given by consent of parties. "The defendant, by appearing and pleading to the action, admits the jurisdiction, that is, in this case, admits the fact which is necessary to make the service valid. "It is an elementary rule of pleading, that a plea to the jurisdiction is the first in the order of pleading; and that any plea which refers to the court any other question, is a tacit admission that the court has a right to judge in the cause, and is a waiver of all exception to the jurisdiction. "Wherever it appears upon the record, that the court has no jurisdiction, nothing which the parties may do or omit to do will give it; but where the want of jurisdiction must be shown by proof aliunde, or where the particular facts giving the jurisdiction may exist consistently with the record, a plea to the action is a waiver of any exception to the jurisdiction. "C . this was an irregularity which the defendant might waive, and that by appearing and pleading to the action, he has cured the defect in the service." 

The court said in Sturman v. McCarthy, 232 Mass. 44, at 48: "Any defect of service or of jurisdiction, so far as the person of the defendant was concerned, had been waived by his appearance and answer. If the want of jurisdiction had been of the subject matter, it could not have been cured by the appearance of the defendant. The want of jurisdiction as to the person was cured by the defendant's voluntary submission." 

Riley v. Brusendorff, 226 Mass. 310, at 312 

Andrews v. Knowlton, 121 Mass. 316 

Lawrence v. Bassett, 5 Allen 140 

Loomis v. Wadhams, 8 Gray 557, at 561 10

ABATEMENT 

In O'Laughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass. 600, Chief Justice Gray said, at page 601: "If a defendant pleads in abatement of the writ, and to the merits of the action in the proper order, the fact that both pleas are filed at the same time, and even upon the same paper, does not, in this Commonwealth, operate as a waiver of the plea in abatement, if seasonably filed. 

This mode of pleading is often convenient to both parties; to the defendant by stating, and to the plaintiff by giving him notice of, all the defences on which the defendant intends successively to rely, if the trial and judgment upon the first shall not dispose of the whole case; and it is sanctioned by a usage of more than a century.'

The original answer, if seasonably filed, may contain matters in abatement and matters on the merits; but after an answer solely on the merits it is too late for an answer in abatement."

(I) Venue 

There is a distinction between jurisdiction and venue. 

Potter v. Lapointe M. T. Co., 201 Mass. 557 at 560 and 563 

In Paige v. Sinclair, 237 Mass. 482, Chief Justice Rugg said at page 483: “Jurisdiction is a term of comprehensive import. It concerns and defines the power of judicatories and courts. 

It embraces every kind of judicial action touching the subject of the action, suit, petition, complaint, indictment or other proceeding. It includes power to inquire into facts, to apply the law, to make decision and to declare judgment. 

Dinan v. Swig, 223 Mass. 516, at 520 

Hopkins v. Commonwealth, 3 Met. 460, at 462 "Venue in its modern and municipal sense relates to and defines the particular county or territorial area within the State or district in which the cause or prosecution must be brought or tried. It commonly has to do with geographical subdivisions, relates to practice or procedure, may be waived, and does not refer to jurisdiction at all." 

United States v. Hvoslef, 237 U. S. 1, at 12

Parties a. Death

At common law all personal actions abated with the death of one of the parties.

Survival of actions is now largely the creature of statute. 

E. S. Parks Shellac Co. v. Jones, 265 Mass. 108, at 113 (Statutory liability of corporation director survives) 

Putnam v. Savage, 244 Mass. 83 

Electric W. Co. v. Prince, 195 Mass. 242, at 260 

Putnam v. Putnam, 4 Pick. 139, at 140 

Mellen v. Baldwin, 4 Mass. 480 

As was said in Putnam v. Savage, 244 Mass. 83, at page 85: "At common law a right of action for tort did not survive the death either of the person injured or of the wrong doer. 16

ABATEMENT 

Wilbur v. Gilmore, 21 Pick. 250 

Michigan R. R. v. Vreeland, 227 U. S. 59, at 67 "Resort therefore must be had to the general provisions of the statutes as to survival of actions to ascertain whether this action survives the death of the wrongdoer. 

If no survival is wrought by statute, the action must abate."

So, whether an action will abate on account of the death of one of the parties depends upon the existence of a statute creating its survival for or against such party. 

Gen. Laws, c 70, s. 21 

(Eminent Domain) 

Gen. Laws, c. 80, s. 8 (Petitions to abate betterments) 

Gen. Laws, c. 156, ss. 36-39 (Actions against corporate officers)

Gen. Laws, c. 228, ss. 1-14 (Actions generally) 

Gen. Laws, c. 237 s. 36 (Awards in writs of entry) 

Gen. Laws, c. 256, ss. 5-7 (Recognizance for debt) 

Gen. Laws, c. 228, s. 1, provides that: "In addition to the actions which survive by the common law, the following shall survive; actions of replevin, tort for assault, battery, imprisonment or other damage to the person, for goods taken and carried away or converted, or for damage to real or personal property, and actions against sheriffs for the misconduct or negligence of themselves or their deputies." "This statute is general in terms and manifestly designed to include all classes of cases within its scope. It comprehends all such cases whether then existing or thereafter created, unless excepted from its terms." 

Putnam v. Savage, 244 Mass. 83, at 85 (Death and conscious suffering survive) 17

ABANDONMENT A. DEFINITIONS ABANDONMENT 

An abandonment is a total withdrawal of a person from an object; to lay aside all care for an object; to leave it altogether to itself. 

Pidge v. Pidge, 3 Met. 257, at 265

An abandonment is the intentional relinquishment of a known right-the giving up of something to which one is entitled, whether with or without legal consideration. B. 

Saxlehner v. Eisner & Mendelsohn Co., 179, U. S. 19, at 31

DISTINCTIONS 

To establish the defense of abandonment it is necessary to show not only acts indicating a practical abandonment but an actual intent to abandon. Acts which unexplained would be sufficient to establish an abandonment may be answered by showing that there never was an intention to give up and relinquish the right claimed. 

Saxlehner v. Eisner & Mendelsohn Co., 179, U. S. 19, at 31 

Singer Mfg. Co. v. June Mfg. Co., 163 U. S. 169, at 186

Property is abandoned when it is thrown away or its possession voluntarily forsaken by the owner, in which case it becomes the property of the first possessor or occupant. 

In most cases abandonment is a question of fact and not of law. 

The essentials of abandonment are: 

1. An intention to abandon. 

N. E. Structural Co. v. Everett D. Co., 189 Mass. 145, at 154 

Dyer v. Sanford, 9 Met. 395 

2. An act carrying out the intention. 

Nelson v. Blinn, 197 Mass. 279 

N. E. Structural Co. v. Everett D. Co., 189 Mass. 145 

Dyer v. Sanford, 9 Met. 395

C. CLASSES 

1. Children a. Parents' Liabilities for 

Gen. Laws, c. 273, ss. 1-10 

Gen. Laws, c. 119, ss. 31-40 

2. Contract 

Upon his abandonment of the contract the contractor loses all right to recover from the owner any sums which otherwise might be due him under the contract. 1

ABANDONMENT 

Dobben v. Duncan Con. Co., 191 A.S. 1575, at 1585

Smedley v. Walden, 246 Mass. 393, at 400 (Intentional departure or willful default of building contract) When the contractor has abandoned the contract an intention by the owner to complete the contract for the contractor's benefit will not be inferred, unless it clearly appears. 

Dobben v. Duncan Con. Co., 1931 A.S. 1575, at 1585

Bernz v. Marcus Sayre Co., 52 N. J. Eq. 275 

3. Personalty

Personalty which is abandoned becomes the property of no one. 

The former owner gives up his title and right to it and the finder may successfully assert his ownership of it. 

So personalty which has been abandoned is not the subject of larceny. 1 

36 C. J. 757, Sec. 75 

4. Real Estate 

17 R. C. L. 36, Sec. 40

In some cases, where acts of the wner of the dominant estate have seemed to be entirely incosistent with an intention to make any further use of the easement, specially where a change in circumstances has rendered the easennt no longer of any benefit, such acts have been regarded as showng conclusively as matter of law an Intention to abanon, and tu.consequent extinguishment of the easement. 

Canny v. Andrews, 123 Mass. 15% 

Corning v. Gold, 16 Wend (US) 531 

Dillman v. Hoffman, 38 Wis. 559 "Since the abandonment however is a question of intent, any act relied upon either must be accompanied by evidence of intention, or be in its nature such as necessarily to show an intention, abandon. As rule mere encroachments upon a common right of way do not of themselves necessarily show an intention to abandon the way, and in most of such cases the question of abandonment is one of fact and not of law." 2

ABANDONMENT 

In King v. Murphy, 140 Mass. 254, the general rule is thus stated by Morton, C. J.: "Mere non-user, even for twenty years, will not conclusively show an abandonment of a right of way; but when the owner of a dominant estate, to which a right of way over a servient estate is appurtenant, does some acts inconsistent with the continued existence of the way, with the intention to abandon and extinguish his easement, it operates as a present abandonment; and it is a question for the jury to determine whether such intention existed."

An easement may be lost by abandonment and whether there is an abandonment is ordinarily a question of intention. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 158

Moreover to show abandonment there must be evidence of a present intent to relinquish the easement or a purpose inconsistent with its further existence. 

Parsons v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 216 Mass. 269, at 272 

Willets v. Langhaar, 212 Mass. 573, at 575

Whether there is an abandonment is a question of fact. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 158 

Willets v. Langhaar, 212 Mass. 573, at 575 a. As Extinguishing Easement

If the extinguishment of an easement by the execution by the. owner of the servient estate of a license which prevents the further enjoyment of the easement rests on the ground that the ownr of the easment intentionally abandons it, and where there is a complete extinguishment it may well rest upon that ground,his intention is conclusively presumed in favor of the owner of the servient tenement who executed the license, because between these parties, when one acts upon the license of the other, the manifest and apparent intention which is acted upon must control their rights, whatever the secret intention of the licensor may be. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 159 

Boston etc. R. R. v. Doherty, 154 Mass. 314, at 317 

In Boston etc. R. R. v. Doherty, 154 Mass. 314, at 317, Court held: "When, pursuant to a parol agreement of the dominent and servient owners for the substitution of a new way for an old one, and the servient owner had constructed the new way, and so altered the servient estate that the old way could the

ABANDONMENT 

no longer be used as before, the old way had been extinguished by the executed license; and further, that it had been abandoned since the change in the old way was consistent only with an intent of the dominant owner to abandon his old right." 

Byrne v. Savoie, 225 Mass. 338, at 340

But the acts in the construction of the new way must be solely under the agreement, and the acts of the servient owner in dealing with the old way must be inconsistent with the continued existence of the old way. 1. 2. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 159 

Dyer v. Sanford, 9 Met. 395, at 401 

b. What is Not 

A temporary suspension of use is not enough. 

Les v. Alibozek, 269 Mass. 153, at 159 

Willard v. Stone, 253 Mass. 555 at 561 and 562 (Water rights.) 

Howe v. Johnson, 236 Mass. 379 (Railroad did not abandon location.) 

Hartt v. Rueter, 223 Mass. 207 (Non-user.)

ABATEMENT 

A. 

DEFINITIONS ABATEMENT 

1. At Law an abatement is an active overthrow or destruction of the action, so that the particular action is quashed and ended. 

2. But in Equity an abatement signifies only a present suspension of the suit for want of parties capable of proceeding therein.

At Law an action, when abated, is absolutely dead; but in 

Equity a suit when abated is merely in a state of suspended animation and may be revived. B. 1. 

Putman v. Putman, 4 Pick. 139, at 140 and 141

DISTINCTIONS Between ABATEMENT and BAR 

A plea in abatement goes to the form of the writ; a plea in bar goes to the cause of action. 

White v. E. T. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28, at 30 

Whiton v. Balch, 203 Mass. 576, at 578

A plea which sets out enough to show, not only that the present action can not be maintained, but that there is no cause of action whatever, is not in abatement but in bar. 

Davis v. Carpenter, 172 Mass. 167, at 172

Allin v. Conn. R. L. Co., 150 Mass. 560 

Grant v. Barry, 9 Allen 459

The question whether a matter is in abatement or in bar is to be decided, not by the form in which it is presented, but by its substance. If it is essentially in bar of the action, it will be so treated and considered even though cast in the form of a plea in abatement. 

White v. E. T. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28, at 31 

Merriman v. Currier, 191 Mass. 133, at 141

Cases just cited above 

But it was said in Guild v. Richardson, 6 Pick. 364, at 368: "Whether a plea is a plea in abatement, or in bar, or whether it is to the writ, or to the jurisdiction of the court, must be determined by the form of the plea, particularly by the conclusion or prayer of it; and not by the subject matter of the plea," 

2. Between ABATEMENT and DISMISSAL 

... Dismissal of an action can be sustained only when founded on matters of law apparent on the record;

ABATEMENT 

Roberts v. Anheuser Busch B. Assoc. 215 Mass. 341, at 343 

Johnson v. Carr, 210 Mass. 1, at 5, lines 14-16 

Morton v. Sweetser, 12 Allen 134 

Hobbs v. Dane Co., 5 Allen 581 

Brown v. Webber, 6 Cush. 560, at 569 

Amidown v. Peck, 11 Met. 467, at 468 

Guild v. Richardson, 6 Pick. 369

Tingley v. Baterman, 10 Mass. 343 

But matters of fact, which do not appear on the face of the record, can be asserted only in abatement, and not by dismissal. 

Comm. v. Fredericks, 119 Mass. 199, at 204 and 205 

Crosby v. Harrison, 116 Mass. 114 

Haynes v. Saunders, 11 Cush. 537 

Belknap v. Gibbens, 13 Met. 471, at 474 

Simonds v. Parker, 1 Met. 508, at 511

Rathbone v. Rathbone, 4 Pick. 89, at 90 

Jacobs v. Mellen, 14 Mass. 135 

In Nye v. Liscombe, 21 Pick. 263, Chief Justice Shaw said, at pages 265 and 266: "Where the matter, on which the defendant relies to abate the suit, is a fact not appearing upon the record or the return of the officer, it must be pleaded in abatement, so as to give the other party an opportunity to traverse and try it. But where all the facts upon which the claim to have the process abated is founded appear by the record including the return of the officer, of which the court will take notice without plea, there the action may be dismissed on motion. In that case the motion is not intended to state new facts, but merely to bring to the attention of the court, and also to furnish notice to the other party, of those facts appearing on the record and return, which of themselves are sufficient to show that the action cannot be properly proceeded in for want of due service, or other defect in the proceedings." 

In Paraboschi v. Shaw, 258 Mass. 531, Chief Justice Rugg said, at page 532: "The defendant appeared specially and filed a motion to dismiss and a plea in abatement, setting up want of proper service. A motion to dismiss for want of service is proper pleading [in an action at law]. It relates to a matter apparent on the record. It raises purely a question of law. A plea in abatement is appropriate when reliance is placed upon some fact not appearing upon the

ABATEMENT 

face of the record which the opposite party may deny and as to which there may be a trial. 

United Drug Co. v. Cordley & Hayes, 239 Mass. 334 

Oliver Ditson Co. v. Testa, 216 Mass. 123, at 124 

Lowrie v. Castle, 198 Mass. 82 

Richmond v. Whittlesey, 2 Allen 230 "The practice is different in equity, where a motion to dismiss is irregular." 

Rothstein v. Comm. of Banks, 258 Mass. 196, at 197 

Wickwire Corp'n. v. U. S. Co., 247 Mass. 565, at 568 

Nelson Theatre Co. v. Nelson, 216 Mass. 30, at 32 

Noyes v. Bragg, 200 Mass. 106, at 110

Matters of dismissal are disposed of by the Court upon the state of the record without evidence from any other source. 

Matters in abatement may be determined upon demurrer, or trial with or without a jury with the introduction of evidence concerning facts outside of the record. 

Crosby v. Harrison, 116 Mass. 114, at 117 

Amidown v. Peck, 11 Met. 467, at 468

The question of dismissal is raised upon a motion, while the right to abatement is brought forward upon a plea or allegations in an answer.

C. 1. 

PRESENTATION or WAIVER 

Appearance a. Must be Special

Pleas and answers in abatement are dilatory pleadings of defence.

To preserve his right to present matters in abatement, as well as dismissal, the defendant must (1) appear specially, and (2) in all his pleadings expressly, clearly and consistently indicate his intention to rely upon, and not waive such matters. 

Cheshire Nat. Bank v. Jaynes, 224 Mass. 14, at 15 (Non-resident defendant could appear specially and protect its attached property without submitting generally to court's jurisdiction.) 

Currier v. Beard, 216 Mass. 113, at 114 ("In order to prevail the party must appear specially and confine his pleading to the specific point of want of service.") 

Porter v. City of Newton, 133 Mass. 56, at 57

Hastings v. Inhabitants of Bolton, 1 Allen 529 

Hollis v. Richardson, 13 Gray 392, at 393

Barry v. Page, 10 Gray 398

ABATEMENT 

Wilson v. Coffin, 2 Cush. 316 

Smith v. Cleveland, 6 Met. 332, at 335

Carlisle v. Weston, 1 Met. 26 

Barnes v. Hurd, 11 Mass. 57 

Stevenson v. Hayden, 2 Mass. 405 

In Brown v. Webber, 6 Cush. 560, at 564 the court said: "If the defendant would object to the irregularity, or want of due service, he may do so, by plea in abatement, where it is necessary to plead any matter of fact, on which his objection is founded, or by motion to dismiss, where the objection is apparent on the face of the proceedings, or the return of the officer; and in either case, before pleading generally to the merits. And to enable him to do this, he may appear specially for purpose of stating such objection, without thereby waiving it. But if he will enter a general appearance, or plead to the merits, or lie by after he is aware of the matter of objection to the jurisdiction, he thereby submits himself to the jurisdiction. of the court; and the court, then, having jurisdiction of the subject, and jurisdiction of the persons of the parties, may proceed, and the exception, that the suit is brought in the wrong county, cannot be made in arrest of judgment." 

Gleason v. Dodd, 4 Met. 333, at 339 

2. Mode of Presentation 

Matters in abatement may be raised in three ways: a, by a plea; b, by an answer solely in abatement alleging the specific facts upon which reliance is placed; or c, by joining such answer in abatement with an answer to the merits, either in one document or in separate documents filed simultaneously. 

General Laws, Chapter 231 provides that: 

Sec. 20. A defence to a real, personal or mixed action, which formerly might have been made by plea in abatement, may be made by answer in abatement. 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262

ABATEMENT 

Greenwood v. Lake Shore R. R., 10 Gray 373

Cole v. Ackerman, 7 Gray 38 

Benthall v. Hildreth, 2 Gray 288 

Seagrave v Erickson, 11 Cush. 89 

Bliss v. Bliss, 12 Met. 266

When the answer filed contains both an answer in abatement and an answer to the merits, the validity of either is not affected by their being pleaded together. 

Fisher v. Fraprie, 125 Mass. 472 

Claflin v. Thayer, 13 Gray 459 

In Parks v. Smith, 155 Mass. 26, the court said at page 30: "If the answer in abatement was overruled as matter of law, the defendant had the right to answer over; if as matter of fact, he might do so at the discretion of the judge." 

3. Time for Filing a. Civil Cases 

Common Law Rule 5 of the Supreme Judicial Court provides in part: "Answers and pleas in abatement, and motions to dismiss, shall be filed within the time allowed by law for entering an appearance, unless otherwise specially ordered by the court for good cause shown.”

Superior Court Rule 25, (1931) provides that: "A defendant. . . . shall, within twenty-one days, or such other period as may be prescribed by statute, or in equity cases by the terms of the subpoena, after the return day of the writ, subpoena, notice or other process by which he or his property is brought before the court to answer in the action, suit or libel, enter his appearance in writing and also within the same time or such other time, greater or less.... file . . . . motion to dismiss, answer in abatement, demurrer, plea or answer, and in a suit in equity, his demurrer, plea or answer."

Answers and pleas in abatement must be filed within the time allowed by law for entering an appearance, unless otherwise shown specially ordered by the court for good cause shown. 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262, at 268

But after an answer to the merits, the court has no power, at a term subsequent to the return term, to allow matters in

ABATEMENT 

abatement to be set up, even though those matters were unknown to the defendant when he filed his answer to the merits. 

Silver v. Graves, 210 Mass. 26, at 32 

Chamberlayne v. Nazro, 188 Mass. 454, at 456 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262, at 268 

Morton v. Sweetser, 12 Allen 134, at 137

Hastings v. Inhabitants of Bolton, 1 Allen 529 

Cole v. Ackerman, 7 Gray 38 

Seagrave v. Erickson, 11 Cush. 89 

Boynton v. Willard, 10 Pick. 166, at 169 

Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 136

In Hastings v. Inhabitants of Bolton, 1 Allen 529, Chief Jus tice Bigelow said, at page 530: "The court has no power to allow the answer in abatement to be filed. It was not merely the exercise of an authority to permit the defendants to amend their pleadings. It went much farther. It set aside the well established rule of law that a dilatory plea must be filed within a certain period of time after the entry of an action, and it also deprived the plaintiff of the benefit of the waiver of such a plea by an answer to the merits. These were legal rights on which the plaintiff had a right to insist, and which the court, in the exercise of a judicial discretion, could not take away. The power to allow amendments, though very broad and comprehensive, does not authorize courts to disregard or abrogate the fixed and settled rules of law regulating judicial proceedings; and indeed, upon the broadest interpretation of the words of the statute by which the power to allow amendments is given, [Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 51] the action of the court in the present case was clearly unauthorized, because in the stage to which the cause had arrived, all matters of abatement had ceased to be a 'legal defence.'

It was suggested that the facts on which the answer in abatement was founded were not known to the defendants until after the case had been in court for more than one term, and after an answer to the merits had been filed. 

But this is wholly immaterial. The defendants were bound seasonably to make inquiry and ascertain whether the plaintiff had brought his action in the proper county. 

By omitting to do so they were guilty of laches, and the law will not relieve them from the consequences of such negligence." 744

But before the time required for appearance the court may extend the time for filing matters in abatement or dismissal. 

Lowrie v. Castle, 198 Mass. 82, at 90

However, the defendant cannot file a plea or answer in abatement after the removal of a default.

WAIVER Matters for abatement are waived by a general appearance, pleading to the merits or delay in interposing objections. 

Gen. Laws, c. 231 s. 136 in part provides: 66 ...

After the defendant has appeared and answered to the merits of the action, no defect in the writ or other process by which he has been brought before the court, or in the service thereof, shall be considered to affect the jurisdiction of the court." 

Paige v. Sinclair, 237 Mass. 482, at 484 (Action in wrong county waived by general appearance) 

Riley v. Brusendorf, 226 Mass. 310, at 312 ("A general appearance waives formal defects as to the getting of the defendant before the court.") 

McManus v. Thing, 208 Mass. 55, at 58 

Pierce v. Equitable L. A. Society, 145 Mass. 56, at 57 (Both parties were residents of another State) 

In Simonds v. Parker, 1 Met. 508, at 511 and 512, the court said: "If a party takes no notice of any matter of exception to the form or service of the process, in an early stage

ABATEMENT 

of the proceedings, it affords reasonable ground to conclude that he considers them of no importance, and is willing to proceed to the trial of his rights upon the substantial merits of the controversy. By referring any question to the court, other than that of the jurisdiction itself, he acknowledges jurisdiction." 

In Carlisle v. Weston, 21 Pick. 535, at 536, 537 and 538, the court said: "The general rule upon this subject is, that irregularities and defects may be waived, but mere nullities cannot be cured, or restored to life, inasmuch as they never possessed any legal vitality. Jurisdiction cannot be given. by consent of parties. “The defendant, by appearing and pleading to the action, admits the jurisdiction, that is, in this case, admits the fact which is necessary to make the service valid. "It is an elementary rule of pleading, that a plea to the jurisdiction is the first in the order of pleading; and that any plea which refers to the court any other question, is a tacit admission that the court has a right to judge in the cause, and is a waiver of all exception to the jurisdiction. "Wherever it appears upon the record, that the court has no jurisdiction, nothing which the parties may do or omit to do will give it; but where the want of jurisdiction must be shown by proof aliunde, or where the particular facts giving the jurisdiction may exist consistently with the record, a plea to the action is a waiver of any exception to the jurisdiction. this was an irregularity which the defendant might waive, and that by appearing and pleading to the action, he has cured the defect in the service." 

The court said in Sturman v. McCarthy, 232 Mass. 44, at 48: "Any defect of service or of jurisdiction, so far as the person of the defendant was concerned, had been waived by his appearance and answer. If the want of jurisdiction had been of the subject matter, it could not have been cured by the appearance of the defendant. The want of jurisdiction as to the person was cured by the defendant's voluntary submission." 

Riley v. Brusendorff, 226 Mass. 310, at 312 

Andrews v. Knowlton, 121 Mass. 316 

Lawrence v. Bassett, 5 Allen 140 

Loomis v. Wadhams, 8 Gray 557, at 561 10

ABATEMENT 

In O'Laughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass. 600, Chief Justice Gray said, at page 601: "If a defendant pleads in abatement of the writ, and to the merits of the action in the proper order, the fact that both pleas are filed at the same time, and even upon the same paper, does not, in this Commonwealth, operate as a waiver of the plea in abatement, if seasonably filed. 

This mode of pleading is often convenient to both parties; to the defendant by stating, and to the plaintiff by giving him notice of, all the defences on which the defendant intends successively to rely, if the trial and judgment upon the first shall not dispose of the whole case; and it is sanctioned by a usage of more than a century." 

See: Stratton v. Davis, 222 Mass. 549 

Voss v. Sylvester, 203 Mass. 233 

Fisher v. Fraprie, 125 Mass. 472 

Claflin v. Thayer, 13 Gray 359 

In Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262, the court said at page 268: "By general rule of law an answer or plea in abatement cannot be filed after an answer to the merits; the latter waives all matters in abatement. The original answer, if seasonably filed, may contain matters in abatement and matters on the merits; but after an answer solely on the merits it is too late for an answer in abatement." 

Feigenspan v. McDonnell, 201 Mass. 341, at 345 

O'Laughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass. 600, at 602

If the defendant fails to object to the reference of a case to an auditor and appears at the hearing before the auditor on the merits, he waives any right to set up matter in abatement.

Jurisdiction

The plea or answer in abatement to the jurisdiction should deny the power of the particular court to entertain the action or suit and allege that some other court of this Commonwealth or nation has jurisdiction;

a. Persons (Page 12)

Instances where the court lacks jurisdiction over a person in this connection do not involve the infirmities or incapacities of the person but relate to the court's want of power to make the person amenable to its process. Such instances are: 

Assignee. Assignee can not maintain action on claim of foreign corporation which has not complied with Gen Laws, c. 181, ss. 3 and 5.

A non-resident must aver in his plea, not only that the property attached is not his, but also that he has no other property within the jurisdiction of the court. 

Guild v. Richardson, 6 Pick. 364, at 368 

Allin v. Conn. River Co., 150 Mass. 560, at 561

In Walling v. Beers, 120 Mass. 584, a bill in equity was filed in this Commonwealth against a New York resident seeking relief against him personally, service on him was made by leaving a subpoena at his last and usual place of abode in New York. He appeared specially and contested the jurisdiction. The motion was overruled and he filed an answer, not waiving the objection to the jurisdiction.

Later, an injunction was dissolved upon the defendant's filing a written stipulation to comply with the court's decree, which thereafter was entered against him. 

Held, the court had not acquired jurisdiction over the defendant and the defendant's acts in proceeding to trial and signing the stipulation did not amount to a waiver of the objection of the want of jurisdiction.

If a non resident corporation appears originally it can show only by plea in abatement, or by writ of error if judgment has been obtained by default, that it had no place of business in this Commonwealth, or if it had a place of business, that the person named in the officer's return was not in charge thereof as its agent.

(I) Venue 

There is a distinction between jurisdiction and venue. 

Potter v. Lapointe M. T. Co., 201 Mass. 557 at 560 and 563 

In Paige v. Sinclair, 237 Mass. 482, Chief Justice Rugg said at page 483: "Jurisdiction is a term of comprehensive import. It concerns and defines the power of judicatories and courts. 

It embraces every kind of judicial action touching the subject of the action, suit, petition, complaint, indictment or other proceeding. It includes power to inquire into facts, to apply the law, to make decision and to declare judgment. 

Dinan v. Swig, 223 Mass. 516, at 520 

Hopkins v. Commonwealth, 3 Met. 460, at 462 "Venue in its modern and municipal sense relates to and defines the particular county or territorial area within the State or district in which the cause or prosecution must be brought or tried. It commonly has to do with geographical subdivisions, relates to practice or procedure, may be waived, and does not refer to jurisdiction at all."

United States v. Hvoslef, 237 U. S. 1, at 12 

A plea that the action is brought in the wrong county or wrong district is commonly matter of abatement and does not go to the jurisdiction of the court.

Parties a. Death

At common law all personal actions abated with the death of one of the parties.

Survival of actions is now largely the creature of statute.

As was said in Putnam v. Savage, 244 Mass. 83, at page 85: "At common law a right of action for tort did not survive the death either of the person injured or of the wrong doer. 16 444777

Wilbur v. Gilmore, 21 Pick. 250 

Michigan R. R. v. Vreeland, 227 U. S. 59, at 67 "Resort therefore must be had to the general provisions of the statutes as to survival of actions to ascertain whether this action survives the death of the wrongdoer. 

If no survival is wrought by statute, the action must abate."

So, whether an action will abate on account of the death of one of the parties depends upon the existence of a statute creating its survival for or against such party. 

Gen. Laws, c 70, s. 21 

(Eminent Domain)

(C) Public Officers. 

A plea in abatement may be granted to a respondent public officer where, during the pendency of a petition for mandamus, his term of office expires. 

Tymon v. Comm. of Public Works, 258 Mass. 370, at 371 

Knights v. Treas. and Rec. Gen., 236 Mass. 336, at 338, 339 and 340 24

ABATEMENT 

But such a plea cannot be granted where the original respondent is a board which has a continuous existence as a body irrespective of the identity of its members. 

Andrews v. Board, 246 Mass. 572

In the last cited case the court said, at pages 574 and 575: "A writ of mandamus against a single public officer or the head of department or bureau to enforce the performance of official duty is a personal action founded on the fact that the defendant has failed to discharge a personal obligation in connection with his office. Therefore such action, in the absence of a statute to the contrary, commonly must abate upon the death or retirement from office of the original defendant. It cannot be amended by the substitution of his successor, who is not his personal representative and cannot be held responsible for his delinquencies. 'Where, however, the writ is directed against a continuing municipal board, with a constant official duty, with respect to a delinquency in the execution of such official duty, then, since the power to perform persists in the board, a change of one or more of the persons composing the board does not work abatement of the petition but it may be prosecuted against those who are its members, those newly chosen being brought in by amendment in place of those who have vacated office." Misjoinder 

Misjoinder is the improper uniting of parties to a suit as plaintiffs or defendants.

Misjoinder may be asserted in: 

1. Abatement, where the fact does not appear on the face of the record. 

2. Dismissal, where the fact does appear on the face of the record. 

Adams v. Richardson, 268 Mass. 78, at 83 

3. Demurrer, when the fact appears on the declaration. 

Lee v. Blodget, 214 Mass. 374, at 377 

Livermore v. County of Norfolk, 186 Mass. 133 at 135 (Not available to defendant against whom record shows good cause of action on the several liability.) 

Gerry v. Gerry, 11 Gray 381, at 382 

4. Bar. 25

47246 

5. General issue at the trial. 

Lee v. Blodget, 214 Mass. 374, at 377

In Lee v. Blodget, 214 Mass. 374, at 377, it was said: "The cause of action having been severed by death of S, his executors, although sued with them, were not jointly liable with the survivors. The misjoinder could have been availed of by demurrer, but, as this defense also could be raised under a request made after the plaintiff's opening and before any evidence had been introduced, the judge properly directed a verdict for the defendants [the executors]. "But if under [Gen. Laws, c. 197, s. 8], the executors in a separate action would be liable as if the contract of the testator had been joint and several, yet at common law, as well as by [Gen. Laws, c. 235, s. 6], the living defendants and promisors, although neither is bound by himself, are bound jointly to the full extent of the promise. "It was open to the plaintiff as soon as the defense of misjoinder had been raised to have moved to discontinue and no amendment to the declaration would have been necessary. "The verdict for the executors, however, insofar as the defendants were concerned operated only as a discontinuance and the action remained joint as to the survivors. "The plaintiff [was] entitled to a trial on the merits [as to the surviving contractors]." 

However, the right to claim misjoinder is waived unless asserted before or during the trial. That is, misjoinder cannot be asserted for the first time in an appellate court upon the review of errors of law. 

Dodge v. Wilkinson, 3 Met. 292, at 296 (I) Plaintiffs

Persons cannot be united as plaintiffs in one action, whether in contract or tort, unless their claims are joint. Plaintiffs are misjoined when their causes of action are several. 

Adams v. Richardson, 268 Mass. 78, at 83 (Plaintiffs having separate claims could not unite by virtue of their membership in a voluntary trade organization) 

Spear v. H. V. Greene Co., 246 Mass. 259, at 267 

Worthington v. Waring, 157 Mass. 421, at 422 and 423 26

ABATEMENT 

Cofran v. Shepard 148 Mass. 582, at 583 (Tenant in common and lessee cannot join to recover rent from tenant at sufferance)

Bullock v. Haywood, 10 Allen 460, at 462 (Misjoinder waived where no objection made at the trial) 

Whiting v. Cook, 8 Allen 63, at 64 (Legatees who were to divide a bequest of a certain sum of money cannot join but have distinct and separate claims and causes of action) 

Gazynski v. Colburn, 11 Cush. 10 

In Gerry v. Gerry, 11 Gray 381, at 382, it was said: "....Misjoinder of plaintiffs is fatal, both in actions of tort and in actions of contract. When the misjoinder appears on the declaration, it is fatal on demurrer... 

When it appears only in evidence at the trial, it is ground of nonsuit or requires a verdict for the defendant. In actions of tort, there is a distinction between non-joinder and misjoinder of plaintiffs. Non-joinder is matter of abatement only." 

Phillips v. Cummings, 11 Cush. 469 

Thompson v. Hoskins, 11 Mass. 419 

Chief Justice Shaw said in Dodge v. Wilkinson, 3 Met. 292, at 296: "The exception of misjoinder of plaintiffs not having been made at the trial, we think it now comes too late. 

It is an exception which, if taken at the trial, might have been obviated by an amendment. The ample power, now given to courts, to allow amendments without costs, renders this objection comparatively unimportant, when it does not affect the merits of the case. When therefore any of the plaintiffs may recover, the exception of misjoinder should regularly be made at the trial. If not made then, it is waived." 

Vinton v. Welsh, 9 Pick. 87, at 91 (Statutory penalty could not be recovered by several persons joining in one action) 

Glover v. Hunnewell, 6 Pick. 222 (Joinder as party plaintiff of person other than one who made contract alone was improper) 27

But General Laws, c. 231, s. 2, provides that: "In actions of contract for the recovery of money due for manual labor, two or more persons may join in one action against the same defendant, although the claims are not joint, if the claim of no one of such plaintiff's exceeds twenty dollars; and each plaintiff joining may recover the amount found to be due to him solely. The claim of each plaintiff shall be stated in a separate count, and the court may make such order for trial of the issues as may be most convenient, may enter separate judgments, issue one or more executions and make such order relative to costs as the case requires."

The court may permit a plaintiff to eliminate by striking from the record, such persons as are improperly joined and thus cure the misjoinder.

Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 51, in part provides: "The court may, at any time before final judgment, allow any other amendment in matter of form or substance in any process, pleading or proceeding, which may enable the plaintiff to sustain the action for the cause for which it was intended to be brought."

Before, during or after the trial, or even after rescript from the Supreme Judicial Court, a person misjoined as the plaintiff may be stricken out with the trial court's permission.

(II) Defendants (A) Contracts 

In the early case of Tuttle v. Cooper, 10 Pick. 281, Chief 

Justice Shaw stated the common law to be that: (page 282) 28

ABATEMENT 

"In covenant, debt or other action in form ex contractu a verdict or judgment cannot in general be given in an action against one defendant, without the other. 

And at page 291. "In an action of contract, against two or more, the contract must be proved as laid, and .... in a trial upon the general merits, the plaintiff cannot have a judgment against one or more, where all are not liable."

But soon after the decision in Tuttle v. Cooper, supra, the 

Legislature passed a statute, which, with occasional modification has since continued in force, authorizing the plaintiff in an action of contract against two or more defendants, to take judgment against those, though less than all sued, who should appear upon the trial to be liable. 

Johnstone v. Cochrane, 231 Mass. 472, at 479 

Monk v. Parker, 180 Mass. 246 

Leonard v. Robbins, 13 Allen 217

That statute is now General Laws, c. 235, s. 6, and provides that: "In an action against two or more defendants upon a contract, express or implied, the plaintiff shall be entitled to judgment against such defendant as are defaulted and against those who upon trial are found liable although it is found that all the defendants are not jointly liable."

The legal effect of this statute is, that a discrepancy between the contract declared on, and that proved, [because all defendants are not found liable] shall be deemed no variance. 

Zilli v. Rome, 240 Mass. 368 

Britton v. Goodman, 235 Mass. 471, at 475 (Three partners as defendants, no service on one nonresident partner, verdict against remaining two partners) 

Taft v. Church, 162 Mass. 527, at 533; S. C. 164 Mass. 

504, at 505

If the plaintiff makes out a case against some of the defendants jointly, or one alone, he has a right to go to the jury against such defendants. 

Monk v. Parker, 180 Mass. 246, at 249

In actions against two persons as partners, if one only is held liable judgment may be entered against him alone; and no amendment of the declaration is necessary. 

Wiggin v. Lewis, 12 Cush. 486

Where one of several persons is sued jointly in an action of contract and alone is found liable and appeals, the sole issue of the appeal is his own liability to the plaintiff, regardless of whether his liability on the contract was joint or several. 

Downing v. Coyne, 121 Mass. 347 

In Leonard v. Robbins, 13 Allen 217, at 220 and 221, the court said: "These statutes have not authorized the joinder in one action of one count on a joint contract of all the defendants, and another count on a separate contract of one of them; or allowed judgment or execution against one defendant for one debt, and against the other defendants or all the defendants for a different debt. If they had, a plaintiff might join in one action against two defendants counts upon two contracts, alleging them to be joint, one of which was in fact made by each severally; and recover judgment against each defendant upon his several contract, with which the other defendant had nothing to do. These statutes were intended to enable the plaintiff to recover one judgment upon a contract against such of the defendants as should appear to be actually liable thereon, but not different judgments in one action upon independent contracts which by the rules of the common law could not be joined in one action. "In other words, they have cured the objection of variance in the proof of the parties contracting, but have not touched that of misjoinder or causes of action in the declaration.

The difficulty in this has been occasioned by the plaintiff's suing in one action upon three ..... 30

ABATEMENT 

promissory notes which have proved to be entirely distinct in their nature, one note being the several contract of one of the defendants, and the others the joint contracts of all.

As the misjoinder in this case did not appear upon the record until the return of the verdict, it may be taken advantage of at this stage. The plaintiff may therefore amend his declaration as he may elect, either by striking out the counts upon the joint notes,... or by striking out the count upon the note on which the one defendant alone has been found liable; and according to his election the verdict may be amended so as to stand for the plaintiff on the count or counts which he elects to retain.'

So, the plaintiff cannot have separate judgments against different defendants. If the verdict on all counts is not against all defendants, the plaintiff must elect either as to which counts or defendants he will retain his case so that the ultimate judgment must be based upon uniformity in the defendants to enable a joint judgment against them. 

Leonard v. Robbins, 13 Allen, 217, at 220 and 221

As was said in Wheeler v. City of Worcester, 10 Allen 591, at 601: 31

ABATEMENT 

"If the injury is produced by the joint action of several parties, and especially if it is the result of the independent action of several parties contributing thereto, though not in combination or by concert it is no defense that all are not made defendants; for when the injury does not arise from privity of contract, but is a mere misfeasance, misjoinder of defendants cannot be availed of to defeat the action."

In an action of tort against several alleged joint wrongdoers, it is not legally possible to obtain a joint judgment against some of the defendants and a several judgment against others. Gen. Laws, c. 235, s. 6 is not applicable to joint tortfeasors when sued jointly. 

Contakis v. Flavio, 221 Mass. 259 

Cameron v. Kanrich, 201 Mass. 451

But the technical rule that a joint judgment is entire, and if bad against one is bad against all, has no application to the proceedings before judgment. 

Munroe v. Carlisle, 176 Mass. 199, at 201

So, before or after a verdict against all defendants the plaintiff by leave of court may discontinue against defendants improperly joined and the verdict as to the others will stand. 

Munroe v. Carlisle, 176 Mass. 199, at 201

In Parsons v. Winchell, 5 Cush. 592, it was said at 593: "The question to be decided is, whether this action on the case, brought against the owners of horses .... and their servant the driver, jointly, can be maintained for an injury done by the negligent driving of the servant, in the absence of the owners. And we are of opinion that it cannot. "To maintain an action against two or more jointly, the plaintiff must show a joint cause of action. In an action ex delicto, the act complained of must be the joint act of all the defendants, either in fact, or in legal intendment and effect. In trespass, all are principals, and he who commands a trespass to be committed, though absent when it is committed, is regarded as a trespasser, and may be sued alone, or jointly with him who obeyed his command." 32

ABATEMENT 

In Brown v. Thayer, 212 Mass. 392, where two owners of two automobiles were improperly joined the court said at page 400: "The plaintiff, however, is not remediless, he can apply to the Superior Court for leave to amend by discontinuance against one of the defendants." 

Under Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 51, the court may allow a person to discontinue. 

A plaintiff at his election may sue one or two or all tortfeasors. The discontinuance against any of them leaves the remaining defendants in the same position as if no suit had ever been brought against those defendants as to whom the action was discontinued. 

Matheson v. O'Kane, 211 Mass. 91, at 96

The plaintiff's discontinuance of the action as against some defendants does not affect the liability of those remaining.

d. Misnomer or Misdescription 

Misnomer is the using of a wrong name in describing one of the parties to the proceedings.

If a defendant cares to take any advantage of any misnomer or misdescription in the writ he should do so by plea or answer in abatement, and if he does not so plead or answer he waives any objection which might be raised against him in the name by which he or the plaintiff is described in the writ. 

Liddell v. Middlesex Motor Co., 1931 A. S. 1041, at 1046 

Dindio v. Meshaka, 1931 A. S.

793, at 794 

White v. E. T. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28

Grannis v. Ordean, 234 U, S. 385, at 395 

Gen. Laws, c. 221, s. 49, provides that: "No writ, process, action, declaration or other proceeding in the courts or course of justice shall be abated, arrested, quashed or reversed for any circumstantial errors or mistakes if by it the person and case may be rightly understood by the court; or for defect or want of form only.” 

In Wight v. Hale, 2 Cush. 486, where an amendment was allowed substituting a correct name, the court said at 493: "The misnomer was a mere mistake; the name of one of the plaintiffs was written Wright, instead of Wight, as it should have been; but the other plaintiff, B, was rightly named and described, and they sued as co-partners on a note payable to Wight and B."

A writ against Charles L, actually served upon Chase L. may be amended after default of the defendant, and without notice to Chase, by substituting Chase for Charles, and judgment may be given against Chase. 

Langmaid v. Puffer, 7 Gray 378 

Gen. Laws, c. 223, s. 19, provides: "If the name of a defendant is not known to the plaintiff, the writ may be issued against him by a fictitious name, and, if duly served, shall not be abated for that cause, but may be amended, and terms may be imposed." 

In Baxter v. Doe, 142 Mass. 558, at 562, the court said: "Under this statute when a fictitious name is inserted in a writ, it should be alleged, in some form, that the name is fictitious, and so used because the real name of the defendant is unknown. The statutory requirement would thus appear upon the record, and the allegation under the statute would be a sufficient answer to a plea in abatement. No such pleas were filed in these cases. We need not inquire whether the writs were duly served, because the defendants voluntarily appeared in court, submitted to its jurisdiction, and filed answers to the plaintiffs' declarations." 34

ABATEMENT Chief Justice Rugg said in Dindio v. Meshaka, 1931 A. S. 

793, at 794: "If the person upon whom the writ was served thought he was misdescribed in the writ, his remedy was by a plea in abatement. Advantage of such a matter cannot be taken after a general appearance." 

White v. E. T.. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28, at 31, and cases there collected 

Langmaid v. Puffer, 7 Gray 378

But misnomer need not be pleaded and a judgment is not valid against a person who is misnamed or misdescribed in the writ, not personally served with process and who does not appear and answer. 

Fitzgerald v. Salentine, 10 Met. 436, at 438

In the last cited case it was said: it is essential to the plaintiff's recovery, that it should be proved not only that the real person was sued, but that he was duly served with process, though under a mistaken name. "Where a party is sued by a wrong name, (S. F. 

Leonard, instead of Leonard Salentine), and a summons is left at a boarding house, without other service, we cannot hold it to be such a service as is contemplated by the law. The mere fact that the summons is left under the same roof where a person lives, does not make it a service at his last and usual place of abode. There may be different families residing there, and the summons may have been left in the apartment of the family not sued. There may be different apartments for different boarders to assemble in, and the summons may be left where the party sued never comes. "To make such a service valid, it must be left in the part of the house which the defendant inhabits and frequents; or it is not duly served upon him, as being left at his last and usual place of abode. The statute intends, in such a case, a personal service, or what is equivalent thereto. 

Great injustice may be done to parties, when sued by wrong names, if a different construction should be given to the statute, and judgments be recovered against them without the slightest notice." (I)
