Comm. v. Gale, 11 Gray 320 (Government may prove defendant was called by:) e. Non-Joinder

Non-joinder is the omission of a person who is a necessary party, plaintiff or defendant. 

White v. E. T. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28, at 31 

Feigenspan v. McDonnell, 201 Mass. 341, at 345 

Townsend v. Wheatland, 186 Mass. 343 (I) Plaintiffs 

(A) Contracts 

Joint contractors, such as partners, joint owners, joint tenants, tenants in common, executors and assignees, should all be named as plaintiffs in order to maintain actions or suits. on joint obligations and debts.

Holton v. Amer. Pastry Products, 1931 A. S. 371, at 374 

Shapira v. Budish, 1931 A. S. 809, at 813 

Phillips v. Cummings, 11 Cush. 469, at 470

In Halliday v. Doggett, 6 Pick. 359, a suit to recover the price of goods sold by a partnership in Scotland through a commission merchant in Boston, the Court, under the general issue, ordered a nonsuit on account of the non-joinder of the other owners of the goods, observing that the action should have been in the names of all the owners, or that of the agent who made the contract. 38

ABATEMENT 

In Cushing v. Marston, 12 Cush. 431, the court said at page 432: "The contract of the defendant for board was made with the partners, who kept the lodging house jointly; the payment for it was therefore a debt owed to both jointly. The action, therefore, could not, by law, be brought and maintained by one only." 

In Fish v. Gates, 133 Mass. 441, the court said at page 442: "The defendant made a special contract with the plaintiffs as co-partners to do work for him. In any suit to enforce this contract or any liability growing out of it, both partners must be joined as plaintiffs. The defendant contracted with them jointly, not with either of them separately. The dissolution of the partnership before the work was completed had no effect upon the rights or liability of the defendant. It did not authorize the plaintiffs to sever the contract and sue the defendant separately. They must still sue jointly." 

Page v. Wolcott, 15 Gray, 536

Non-joinder of plaintiffs may be set up under the general issue, by plea in bar, as well as in abatement. 

Raymond v. Phipps, 215 Mass. 559, at 569 

Cushing v. Marston, 12 Cush. 431 

Gage v. Rollins, 10 Met. 348 

Hughes v. Bayley, 20 Pick. 96 

Halliday v. Doggett, 6 Pick. 359 

As was said in Thomas v. Benson, 264 Mass. 555, at 556: "The general denial put in issue the allegations that, in the first count, the plaintiff was employed by the defendants and, in the second count, the defendants owed him the commission. These were essential parts of the contract. The contention that they were not maintained went to the cause of action, not to the form of the writ. "In an action of contract all joint contracting parties must join in an action for its breach. If the partnership existed, the defendants' contract was with them jointly and not with either separately." 

In Baker v. Jewell, 6 Mass. 460, Chief Justice Parsons said at page 462: 66 .... the want of the proper plaintiffs in actions on contract, is an exception to the merits, and is to be taken advantage of, either on demurrer, in bar, or on the general issue, but not by plea in abatement." 39

ABATEMENT 

Furthermore if a defendant settles with or takes judgment against one of two contracting parties he severs the contract so that he may be liable in an action by the other alone. 

Thomas v. Benson, 264 Mass. 555, at 557 

B. & M. R.R., v. Portland etc. R.R., 119 Mass. 498, at 499 

Baker v. Jewell, 6 Mass. 460, at 462 

(B) Replevin 

Joint ownership of the plaintiff and another in replevin may be pleaded in bar, and need not necessarily be set up in abatement. 

Bray v. Raymond, 166 Mass. 146, at 150 

Corcoran v. White, 146 Mass. 329 

Fay v. Duggan, 135 Mass. 242, at 243 

Hackett v. Potter, 131 Mass. 50 

Hart v. Fitzgerald, 2 Mass. 509 (C) Torts In actions of tort the defendant must plead in abatement the non-joinder of those whom he contends should have been joined as plaintiffs, and cannot rely on this defence in bar of the action. 

Thomson v. Pentecost, 210 Mass. 223, at 226 

Russell v. Cole, 167 Mass. 6 

May v. Western Union Co., 112 Mass. 90 

Bullock v. Hayward, 10 Allen 460, at 462

Sherman v. F. R. Iron Works Co., 2 Allen 524; S. C. 5 

Allen 213 

Putney v. Lapham, 10 Cush. 232 

Call v. Buttrick, 4 Cush. 345, at 350 

Thompson v. Hoskins, 11 Mass. 419

In an action of tort, one of two persons jointly injured may alone maintain an action for the injury, unless the non-joinder of the other is pleaded in abatement; and it was said that, "under the general issue, evidence of such non-joinder will not defeat the action, but will merely restrict the plaintiff to a recovery of a moiety of the damage.' 

Putney v. Lapham, 10 Cush. 232, at 234 

See: Meaney v. Kehoe, 181 Mass. 424 

Webster v. Vandeventer, 6 Gray 428, at 431 

In Phillips v. Cummings, 11 Cush. 469, the court said: "The rule is fully and clearly established that in actions of tort, such as quare clausum, or trover for taking 40

ABATEMENT 

goods, case for malfeasance, misfeasance, or nonfeasance, and the like, if one only of two or more joint tenants, tenants in common, executors, assignees, and others who ought regularly to join, bring any such actions, the defendant must plead the non-joinder in abatement, and cannot rely upon it to defeat the action under the general issue or avail himself of it by that purpose by plea in bar, arrest of judgment or otherwise." 

But even though the defendant does not set up the fact of non-joinder, a plaintiff who should have others join with him, cannot collect the full damage for the tort. His recovery can be his for his proportionate share alone and such limitation of damage may be shown under the general issue.

Sherman v. F. R. Iron Works Co., 5 Allen 213 

Putney v. Lapham, 10 Cush. 232 

Call v. Buttrick, 4 Cush. 345, at 350 

Thompson v. Hoskins, 11 Mass. 419

Under Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 51, an amendment may be allowed at any time before judgment, permitting the plaintiff to add a necessary co-plaintiff in order to cure the defect caused by the non-joinder. 

Richardson v. Bartlett, 223 Mass. 454 

Fay v. Duggan, 135 Mass. 242 

(II) Defendants (A) Contracts 

Non-joinder of a defendant in an action of contract can be raised only by answer or plea in abatement. 

Thomas v. Benson, 264 Mass. 555, at 556 

Leonard v. Speidel, 104 Mass. 356, at 359

It is not a matter which can be shown under the general issue or pleaded in bar. 

Feigenspan v. McDonnell, 201 Mass. 341, at 345 

Kendall v. Weaver, 1 Allen 277 

Elder v. Thompson, 13 Gray 91 

Shelton v. Banks, 10 Gray 401 

Scott v. Shears, 9 Cush. 504 

Bliss v. Bliss, 12 Met. 266 

Wilson v. Nevers, 20 Pick. 20 

Holmes v. Marden, 12 Pick. 169

In Wilson v. Nevers, 20 Pick. 20, it is said at page 22: "In the earlier reported cases the want of proper parties as defendants was held a good defense under the general 41

ABATEMENT 

issue, upon the ground of variance between the promise described in the declaration, and the proof offered in the case. But as such defense was bound on matters more particularly within the knowledge of the defendant, and as in all joint contracts each one is liable to the plaintiff for the whole amount, whether the action be against him alone, or jointly with his co-promisors, with a view to avoid the evils that would result from repeated non-suits on the same cause of action the rule was established, that the omission to include all the promisors was a defect in form merely, and could be taken advantage of only by plea in abatement."

The reasons stated for establishing this rule as to defendants are not applicable in case of non-joinder of plaintiffs in actions of contract, and no such change as to plaintiffs seems to have been made. 

Thomas v. Benson, 264 Mass. 555, at 556 and 557

So in an action of contract against two defendants jointly, if the declaration is amended by striking out the name of one of the defendants and the trial proceeds against the other, and there is evidence of a joint promise made to the plaintiff by the two original defendants, a verdict for the plaintiff will be sustained, as the remaining defendant could take advantage of the non-joinder of the other only by plea in abatement. 

Townsend v. Wheatland, 186 Mass. 343 and cases cited

For example, if one joint contractor is sued alone, and does not plead in abatement the non-joinder of the other, and judgment is rendered against the one sued, it merges the cause of action against him and (unless otherwise provided by statute, as the two are no longer jointly liable,) prevents a subsequent recovery against the other joint contractor. 

Cowley v. Patch, 120 Mass. 137, at 138 

See: Lee v. Blodget, 214 Mass. 374, at 377 (B) Torts

Non-joinder of defendants cannot arise in actions of tort. 

This result follows from the liability of joint tortfeasors being individual and collective, joint and several. 

Wheeler v. Worcester, 10 Allen 601 

Milford v. Holbrook, 9 Allen 17, at 23 

Buddington v. Shearer, 22 Pick. 427

In Proctor v. Dillon, 235 Mass. 538, the court said at page 549: 42

ABATEMENT 

"It is a general and familiar principle of the common law that in cases of tort, where two or more are liable for the same cause of action, they are liable severally as well as jointly, and if one is sued alone the entire damages may be recovered against him." 3. 

Old Dom. v. Bigelow, 203 Mass. 159, at 216 and 217 

Corey v. Havener, 182 Mass. 250 

Boston & Albany R.R. v. Shanly, 107 Mass. 568 at 579

Pendency of Another Action 

A plaintiff will not commonly be allowed to prosecute another action when there is: a. another action pending; b. in the same jurisdiction; c. for the same cause; and d. between the same parties. 

Alpert v. Mercury Pub. Co., 1930 A. S. 1497, at 1499 

Corey v. Tuttle, 249 Mass. 135, at 138 

Comm. v. Churchill, 5 Mass. 174

The pendency of a prior action between the same parties for the same cause of action is a good ground of abatement. 

White v. E. T. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28, at 31 

Worcester v. Lakeside Mfg. Co., 174 Mass. 299, at 302 

Moore v. Spiegel, 143 Mass. 413 

Comm. v. Churchill, 5 Mass. 174 

Chief Justice Parsons said in Comm. v. Churchill, 5 Mass. 

174, at page 176: "It is very well known that a man cannot bring a second action for the same cause, for which he has a prior action pending. 

At page 177: "I believe that it has been sometimes supposed that in pleading in abatement to a second writ the pendency of a former one, the former must be pending at the time of the plea..... but . . . . . it is sufficient if the first action was pending when the second writ was [issued]. 

At page 180: "A subsequent writ is not abatable unless the plaintiff enter his action on his prior writ. The reason of the law applies to these cases, which is to prevent a man from being twice vexed for the same cause.

The principle .... 43

ABATEMENT 

is, when the prior action is pending the subsequent writ is bad ab initio; it is wrongly sued out, while another action is pending for the same cause.' 

The reason assigned in the elementary books for allowing such plea in abatement upon this ground was "that if it were allowed that a man should be twice arrested, or twice attached by his goods, for the same thing, by the same reason he might suffer in infinitum." 

Colt v. Partridge, 7 Met. 570, at 575

The plea must be in abatement and not in bar. 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262, at 266 

Mattel v. Conant, 156 Mass. 418, at 424 

Moore v. Spiegel, 143 Mass. 413

It is a defence which arises from matters which do not appear upon the face of the record as it cannot be the subject of a motion to dismiss. It must be alleged by plea or answer in abatement so it may be traversed, put in issue and tried, if it is not admitted by demurrer. 

Morton v. Sweetser, 12 Allen 134, at 135 a.

Another Action Pending (I) When Prior Action Deemed Pending 

The first case must have been alive and pending at the time of bringing the second case. 

Alpert v. Mercury Pub. Co., 1930 A. S. 1497, at 1498 

Donovan v. Danielson, 263 Mass. 419, at 424 

Comm. v. Daskalakis, 246 Mass. 12, at 19 

See: Meredith v. Wall, 14 Allen 155

So, it is necessary that the writ in the prior action shall have been served, returned to court and entered on the court's record. 66 

Comm. v. Churchill, 5 Mass. 174, at 180 

As was said in Mattel v. Conant, 156 Mass. 418, at 424: as the logic of the defence is that the matter in controversy is already the subject of a litigation, in which the rights of the parties may be adjudicated by a competent tribunal, it is essential that the plea shall show that the parties are before that tribunal, and that their rights. may be there determined."

Once entered in court the prior action at law remains alive until judgment is entered. 

Alpert v. Mercury Pub. Co., 1930 A. S. 1497, at 1498 44

ABATEMENT 

So, a discontinuance of the prior action does not operate to put an end to that action. It does not then go to judgment. 

Up to the time of judgment the plaintiff may be allowed by permission of the court upon good cause shown to withdraw his discontinuance and otherwise to amend his pleading or process. The case is alive and pending up to the time of judgment. 

Alpert v. Mercury Pub. Co., 1930 A. S. 1497, at 1498 

But See: Meredith v. Wall, 14 Allen 155 

(II) When Second Action Deemed Pending 

The second action is begun on the date of the writ. 

Alpert v. Mercury Pub. Co., 1930 A. S. 1497, at 1499 

Rosenblatt v. Foley, 252 Mass. 188 

Richardson v. Greenhood, 225 Mass. 608, at 609 b. In the Same Jurisdiction (I) Courts of this Commonwealth

There is strong reason for the application of the principle that a plaintiff will not commonly be allowed to prosecute an action when there is pending another action for the same cause between the same parties, when the two cases are pending in the same court. 

Alpert v. Mercury Pub. Co., 1930 A. S. 1497, at 1499

When two courts have concurrent jurisdiction over a particular subject matter, such as the appointment of a trustee, the court which first receives the petition or application and proceeds to act thereon, acquires jurisdiction to the exclusion of the other court, so that the pendency in the former court is a bar to like proceedings in the latter court as to the same subject matter. 

Dorsey v. Corkery, 227 Mass. 498, at 500 

Old Dom. Cop. Min. and Smelt. Co. v. Bigelow, 203 

Mass. 159, at 221 

Brockton v. Cross, 138 Mass. 297 

Miller v. County Commissioners, 119 Mass. 485 

Stearns v. Stearns, 16 Mass. 167 

(II) Foreign Courts 

The pendency of an action in a court of one jurisdiction is not an absolute bar to the maintenance of another action for the same cause in another jurisdiction. 

Consol. Ordnance Co. v. Marsh, 227 Mass. 15, at 20 

H. C. Miner Co. v. Wagner, 177 Mass. 404 

Moore v. Spiegel, 143 Mass. 413 

Merrill v. N. E. Ins. Co., 103 Mass. 245, at 249 45

ABATEMENT 

In the last cited case it was said at page 

"It was unduly vexatious for the plaintiff to undertake to maintain contemporaneously the two proceedings under these circumstances. The pendency of the action in the 

Federal courts was not a bar to the maintenance of the present suit, but both ought not to be prosecuted simultaneously. The single justice rightly put the plaintiff to an election. When that was refused, the order for final decree followed correctly." 

C. For the Same Cause 

(I) Equity Suits 

The pendency of a bill in equity is not usually a sufficient ground for sustaining a plea in abatement to an action at law, Colt v. Partridge, 7 Met. 570, at 576 and if the defendant is entitled to any advantage from the pendency of the bill in equity, it is only by injunction from the equity court to stay proceedings at law. 

Mattel v. Conant, 156 Mass. 418, at 424 

(A) Election 

In Powers v. Heggie, 268 Mass.

233, the court said at page 239: "The institution of simultaneous proceedings at law and in equity, based upon the same facts as matter of law does not require the court to dismiss both suits or either of them. In such a situation the court may be called upon to determine whether the two proceedings result from doubt or mistake as to the proper form of action, or whether the action or suit is vexatious and intended to harass and hector the defendant in his defence, or that such is the natural result of two or more proceedings for the same cause of action. Finding that the prosecution of two or more proceedings may impede the defendant, the court may require the plaintiff to elect between them.

C. For the Same Cause 

(I) Law Actions 

If two suits are actions at law, and if the pendency of the former action has been pleaded in abatement in the second suit, that suit necessarily must abate, when the suits are both pending in the same jurisdiction.

A court of law will not permit a defendant to be vexed at the same time, in the same jurisdiction, by the prosecution of two suits for the same cause of action by the same plaintiff. 

Sanford v. Wright, 164 Mass. 85, at 87 

(II) Equity Suits 

A court of equity will not permit the abatement of the second suit pending in the same jurisdiction; but, instead of dismissing the second suit, it usually permits the plaintiff to elect with which suit he will proceed and when the plaintiff has brought an action at law and afterwards a suit in equity, if the plaintiff elects to discontinue the action at law, he is usually permitted to prosecute the suit in equity. 

Sanford v. Wright, 164 Mass. 85, at 87 

Connihan v. Thompson, 111 Mass. 270 

Sears v. Carrier, 4 Allen 339 

Insurance Co. v. Brune, 96 U. S. 588

ABATEMENT 

"Nor does a suit in equity abate by reason of the pendency of an action at law for the same cause of action." 

Corey v. Tuttle, 249 Mass. 135 

As was said in Colt v. Partridge, 7 Met. 570, at 576: "The pendency of a bill in equity has not usually been considered as a sufficient ground for sustaining a plea in abatement to an action at law. When both suits are com- 

menced by the same party, it may furnish a proper occasion for a motion to require the party to elect which action he will proceed in; and this is the proper course.

Where an action at law is pending for the same cause, relief is open to the defendant by plea setting up the facts. As the pendency of the action at law is averred in the instant bill, the court takes notice of it on demurrer.

(II) Set-Off in Prior Action 

The pendency of an action by a defendant, in the form of a declaration in set-off, is as good a reason for a plea or 49

ABATEMENT 

answer in abatement to a subsequent action upon the same claim, as is the pendency of an original and independent suit for the same cause of action. 

Mfrs. Bottle Co. v. Taylor Co., 208 Mass. 593, at 594

A declaration in set-off, filed under the provisions of General Laws, c. 232, is a statement of an action in favor of the defendant to the amount claimed in the declaration, and in substance and effect does, in most particulars, act like the · bringing of an independent suit to recover the sum alleged to be due. 

Mfrs. Bottle Co. v. Taylor Co., 208 Mass. 593, at 594

III. 

Cross Actions 

The bringing of a cross action is not ground of abatement. 

Colt v. Partridge, 7 Metcalf 570, at 574 and 575 d. Between the Same Parties

The pendency of another action as a good ground for abatement is restricted to the same parties, except in a penal action, where an action for the same cause has been instituted by a third person.

When the parties stand in different relations, (such as where the defendant in the first action becomes the plaintiff in the second) the second action should be abated only when the first affords a full, plain and adequate remedy to the defendant in such action, and opens all the grounds set up as the foundation of the second action. 

Aldrich v. Hodges, 164 Mass. 570 (Consignor's action against officer for conversion of goods is not ground in abatement for consignee's suit against same officer for same goods even though title remained in consignor.) 

Merrill v. New England Co., 103 Mass. 245 (Abatement allowed where difference in parties merely nominal-such as different administrators of same estate.) 

State Bank v. Wells, 3 Pickering 15 (Different defendant in other action.) 

Tracy v. Preble, 117 Mass 4 

Moore v. Loring, 106 Mass. 455 

Murray v. Shearer, 7 Cushing 333 50

Comm. v. Churchill, 5 Mass. 174 (Prior indictment by Commonwealth will abate action for statutory penalty by individuals.) 

Comm. v. Cheney, 6 Mass. 374 

Isley v. Stubbs, 5 Mass. 280 (No abatement where pending action for replevin by same plaintiff against third person.) 

e. Modern Doctrine 

It was said in Mfrs. Bottle Co. v. Taylor Co., 208 Mass. 

593, at 595 and 596: "At common law and in early practice of the courts in this country, the doctrine that one should not be vexed by the pendency of two actions for the same cause, at the same time, was enforced with great strictness. "The subject was fully and ably considered by Chief 

Justice Parsons in Comm. v. Churchill, 5 Mass. 174, and it was held to be sufficient to abate a writ, that a former action for the same cause was pending when the second suit was begun, even if it was discontinued or otherwise disposed of before the plea in abatement was filed. It was implied, if not distinctly decided, that if the second writ was for the same cause of action, the suit must be deemed vexatious if it was begun while the former was pending, without reference to the reasons for bringing it. "But later adjudications are more liberal in favor of plaintiffs who have brought a second suit during the pendency of the first, for the same cause of action, for the purpose of curing a defect in the former proceedings, or who have discontinued the first action before the decision of the court upon the plea in abatement in the second action. "A plea in abatement, founded on the pendency of a former action for the same cause, may be avoided by the discontinuance or other termination of the former action after the plea is filed. "However, it is more equitable, where a second action is brought for a cause that was made the foundation of a former suit which is defective in some essential particular, to allow the plaintiff to discontinue the former suit upon proper terms, and proceed with the later one, rather than to order an abatement of the last action, and to compel him to begin anew after the termination of the first suit. 51

ABATEMENT 

"It would have been better to have compelled the plaintiff to elect between the two actions when the answer in abatement first came up for a hearing in the Superior court, by an order for an abatement, unless the declaration in set-off was abandoned."

Also, Chief Justice Rugg said, in Consolidated Ordnance 

Co. v. Marsh, 227 Mass. 15, at 20 and 21: "It is elementary that courts of the same jurisdiction will not permit a party to be vexed at the same time by two proceedings arising from the same cause of action unless there is some sound reason having its foundation in justice for an exception to the general rule. The stringency of the common law rule against the concurrent pendency of two or more proceedings for the same cause has been relaxed somewhat in order to prevent a plaintiff from failing in the prosecution of a just claim because of doubt or mistake as to the right form of relief and perhaps for other reasons. Manifest justice requires that a defendant be not hectored by useless and unnecessary litigating. 

Spear v. Coggan, 223 Mass. 156 

Mfrs. Bottle Co. v. Taylor Co., 208 Mass. 593 "That is a sound and salutary doctrine. It is the correlative of the principle that a plaintiff ought to find a certain remedy by having recourse to the courts for all wrongs suffered by him in his person, property and character. It is a part of the liberty of a citizen of a free government that he be protected against wrongful harassment by others. Therefore, where two actions are pending between the same parties for the same cause within the same governmental unit, one in the Federal and the other in the State court, we do not conceive it to be the law that the plaintiff has an absolute right to maintain both up to the point of obtaining a final judgment. The establishment of such an inflexible rule might work great hardship in some cases. "Justice requires the court in which the point is raised to determine, after an examination of the merits in this respect, whether the defendant is in truth being doubly vexed by the contemporaneous prosecution of both actions, and make appropriate order in the light of what is revealed by such an inquiry. That proposition has been declared broadly in well considered judgments, even with reference to an action pending in a foreign country. 52

ABATEMENT 

There is an intimation in the same direction in Merrill v.

New England Mutual Life Ins. Co., 103 Mass. 245, at 

248 and 249. "But without deciding more than is raised by the present record, it is the duty of this court to ascertain from all the circumstances whether the maintenance of these two cases ought to go forward simultaneously and, if not, what ought to be done, having regard to the fundamental ethical rules of the right and wrong."

But modern relaxation of this strictness has been confined to instances where the second action has been justified by reason of defects or peculiar conditions in the former one, or to the broader relief available in the second action. 

Alpert v. Mercury Pub. Co., 1930 A. S. 1497, at 1499

So, where there are no defects, peculiar conditions or narrowness of relief attendant upon the earlier action the bringing of the second action is unjustified and will be abated. 

Alpert v. Mercury Pub. Co., 1930 A. S. 1497, at 1499 (Plaintiff failed to claim jury in first action, his motion for jury was denied and he discontinued first action and brought second action before first action went to final judgment. Second action abated.)

Process a. Defects and Irregularities in Writ or Summons 

An action may be abated whenever the writ or summons contains a defect, informality or irregularity in its form, structure or terms, or the manner in which either was issued. 

Lincoln v. Taunton, 11 Cush. 440, at 442 ("If the defendants relied on the fact that [an affidavit necessary to the issuance of process] was made too late, they should have averred it by answer [in abatement] to the jurisdiction") 

Brewer v. Sibley, 13 Met. 175, at 176: "The omission to affix a proper seal to a writ issuing from this court, is such error as will abate the writ if properly taken. ་་ ཟེ ར་སྐ ་ ་ 54

ABATEMENT 

"But such objection must be taken at the first term of the appearance of the defendant. Although a seal is one of the requisites of a proper writ, yet the want of it will furnish no cause for a motion in arrest of judgment. "It is a mere defect in form, which if relied upon, must be taken in due season; and if not thus taken, the exception is waived." 

Foot v. Knowles, 4 Met. 386, at 391 and 392 "A motion was afterwards made in arrest of judgment, on the ground that the writ was not under seal of this court, in which the action was commenced, but under the seal of the court of common pleas. "By the Court. The motion, if otherwise well founded, comes too late. The objection is merely formal, and affects the regularity of the process only. If a defect in form is relied on, the objection must be taken in due season, before expense is incurred. The defendant shall not take his chance upon the merits, and upon failure there resort back to an early defect in the process, by which he was brought into court. This does not depend on the rule of positive law, that a plea in abatement must be made at the first term; but upon the broad ground, that when a party pleads to the merits he waives the exception and tacitly consents to abide the decision of the court upon that issue.” 

Stevens v. Ewer, 2 Met. 74, at 75: 

it is immaterial whether a blank writ be signed by the clerk, or his signature be annexed thereto by his order. That the clerk's name was annexed by his order before service is to be presumed, and cannot be contested except by plea denying the fact, which the plaintiffs might traverse, and thus it might be put in issue and tried". 

Carlisle v. Weston, 21 Pick. 535, at 536: "The service of process by a coroner, being a special authority, and not coming within the general duties of that officer, all the facts necessary to give him the power should be made to appear in the writ itself; and a general direction to him is not sufficient." 

Hall v. Jones, 9 Pick. 446 (Writ of one court made returnable in another, plea in abatement sustained, amendment to affix seal of latter court denied) 55

b. Impropriety of Service or Officer's Return 

Abatement is well grounded when there is a fatal defect or irregularity in the service or return of the process by which a defendant is brought into court. 

Although the general rule in this Commonwealth without exception is, that as between the parties, or their privies, the return of the officer is conclusive as to all matters which are properly the subject of a return by him; 

United Drug Co. v. Cordley, 239 Mass. 334, at 339 

Simmons v. Richards, 171 Mass. 281, at 283 

Lowery v. Caldwell, 139 Mass. 88, at 89 

Stewart v. Griswold, 134 Mass. 391 

Baker v. Baker, 125 Mass. 7, at 9 

Taylor v. Clarke, 121 Mass. 319 

Hannum v. Tourtellott, 10 Allen 494 

Smith v. Randall, 1 Allen 456 

Campbell v. Webster, 15 Gray 28

Chappell v. Hunt, 8 Gray 427 Davis v. Putnam, 5 Gray 321 

Collins v. Douglass, 1 Gray 167 

Eastman v. Perkins, 10 Cush. 249 

Tilden v. Johnson, 6 Cush. 345 

Niles v. Hancock, 3 Met. 568 

Bean v. Parker, 17 Mass. 591 

Bott v. Burnell, 11 Mass. 163 

Slayton v. Chester, 4 Mass. 478 yet, the service or return of the officer can be controverted where it is: (I) contradictory, (II) inconsistent with other matters that appear of record in the case, (III) concerns matters which cannot be supposed to be within the officer's own knowledge, (IV) relates to collateral matters, or (V) conclu- 56

ABATEMENT 

sion of fact or law.

Also, (VI) it may be shown that the person by whom the service was made was not in fact an officer or had not the authority which he assumed. 

In Tilden v. Johnson, 6 Cush. 354, the return by the officer stated that "The within T. not having any residence, last and usual place of abode, or agent, or attorney within my precinct, I have been unable to summon him." The court said at page 359: "In our view, this return can only properly be understood as a return, that no such last and usual abode of the party, within the State, was known to the officer. To this extent he may properly certify the fact in his return, beyond this, we think his return is not conclusive; and it is open to the party to show, under proper pleading and proofs, that he was such resident, having a last and usual place of abode here, and thus abate the writ for want of proper service."

Irrespective of the contents of an officer's return, a nonresident may always show even after judgment against him, unless his non-residence was previously litigated, that he was such non-resident at the time the original action was brought and neither was personally served with process nor appeared therein. 

United Drug Co. v. Cordley, 239 Mass. 334, at 339. 

Needham v. Thayer, 147 Mass. 537

So, a foreign corporation can show by plea in abatement that it had no place of business in this Commonwealth or that if it had a place of business the person named in the officer's return was not in charge thereof as its agent. 

United Drug Co. v. Cordley, 239 Mass. 334, at 338. 

Porter v. Prince, 188 Mass. 80 

Tilden v. Johnson, 6 Cushing 354, at 359 

Stevens v. Ewer, 2 Metcalf 74

Hearing and Determination 

Upon the filing of a plea or answer in abatement, (1) the plaintiff may demur; (if the plea or answer is insufficient as matter of law) or 

Thurman v. Chicago R. R., 254 Mass. 569 

Oliver Ditson Co. v. Testa, 216 Mass. 123 (Motion to disallow plea not equivalent to demurrer) 

Nashua Co. v. Hammermill, Co., 223 Mass 8, at 19 (Demurrer to answer in abatement and also demurrer to part of answer in bar) 

Whiton v. Balch, 203 Mass. 576, at 579 (Demurrer sustained to answer that defendant was not executor or administrator, as alleged in writ and declaration, because such defence goes to the cause of action not to answer in abatement) (2) set the plea or answer down for hearing or trial. 

Wright v. Graustein, 229 Mass. 68, at 70 ("The plaintiff filed a motion to overrule 'defendant's answer in abatement', this was irregular. All that was necessary was to set case down for hearing on the answer and abatement.") 60

ABATEMENT 

1. Demurrer a. Matter of Law

Upon demurrer, the facts well pleaded in the plea or answer in abatement must be accepted as true. 

Thurman v. Chicago etc. R.R., 254 Mass. 569, at 570 

It was said in Clifford v. Cony, 1 Mass. 495, at 502: "The greatest exactness is required in pleas of abatement; because no plea which goes to prevent discussion of the merits of the case ought to be offered." 

2. Trial a. 

Matters of Fact 

(I) Burden of Proof

The burden of proving the facts alleged in a plea or answer in abatement is upon the defendant.

The plaintiff has a right to have the witnesses called and to cross-examine them if he desires. 

Wright v. Graustein, 229 Mass. 68, at 70 

(II) Jury 

Either party is entitled to a jury trial on the issues of fact raised by the plea or answer in abatement. 

Young v. Duncan, 218 Mass. 346, at 348 

Oliver Ditson Co. v. Testa, 216 Mass 123 

Boyden v. Lamb, 152 Mass. 416, at 419 

O'Laughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass 600 

(A) Waiver of Jury Trial 

Either party or both may waive respective rights to a jury trial. This waiver may result from an express relinquishment or from conduct inconsistent with the exercise of the right to a jury trial.

So. if a party has a right to claim a trial by jury upon the facts raised by a plea or answer in abatement, and proceeds to a hearing upon the plea or answer in abatement before a judge, without objection, and without insisting upon a trial by jury as to the facts raised by it, that right, [to a trial by jury] if preserved up to that time, is waived as to that point. 

Young v. Duncan, 218 Mass. 346, at 348 

Oliver Ditson Co. v. Testa, 216 Mass 123 

Wood v. Farmer, 200 Mass. 209 

Mittenthal v. Mascagni, 183 Mass. 19 

Willard v. Boston, 149 Mass. 176 

O'Laughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass 600 61

Overruling the Plea or Answer in Abatement 

(I) 

Matters of Law 

When the plea or answer is overruled as matter of law the defendant must answer. 

Young v. Giles, 113 Mass. 34 62

ABATEMENT 

Superior Court Rule 25 (1931) provides in part: "Whenever by reason of amendment, action upon some pleading, or other cause, occasion arises for further pleading by any party, he shall file the same within ten days after such occasion arises, or within such other time, greater or less as may be prescribed by special order of the court."

Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 53, provides in part that: "The court may allow the defendant to amend an answer in abatement." 

Matters of Fact 

When the plea or answer in abatement is overruled on an issue or issues of fact, judgment should be entered for the plaintiff, unless the court by special order and "for good cause shown" allows the defendant to answer to the merits. 

Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 50 provides that: "If an issue of fact is found against the defendant upon a plea or answer in abatement, final judgment, subject to section fifty-three, [Gen. Laws, c. 231] shall be rendered against him." 

It was said in Boyden v. Lamb, 152 Mass. 416, at 419: "In a suit at common law, where there is a plea in abatement which raises a question of fact not determinable by the record, as that the plaintiff is under a disability to sue, or is dead, or that the suit was commenced without authority, this question, although, if it is decided against him, the defendant may be unable to place any other issue of fact, [Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 50] is to be passed upon by a jury. Where a fact relating to a process is drawn in question, which, according to the forms of proceeding, cannot appear on inspection of the record, it is to be determined by the jury." 

Parks v. Hall, 2 Pick. 206 

Also in Parks v. Smith, 155 Mass. 26, at 30: "Upon the question whether judgment should have been entered for the plaintiff upon the overruling of the answer in abatement, the case is governed by Fisher v. Fraprie, 125 Mass. 472. In that case, as in this, the answer filed contained both an answer in abatement and an answer to the merits; and, as was there held, 'If the answer in abatement was overruled as matter of law, the defendant 63

ABATEMENT 

had the right to answer over; if as matter of fact, he might do so at the discretion of the judge'." 

O'Laughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass 600 

Machinists' Nat. Bank v. Dean, 124 Mass. 81 

Comm. v. Carr, 114 Mass. 280 

Young v. Gilles, 113 Mass. 34 

Austin v. Lamar Ins. Co., 108 Mass. 338 

Good v. Lehan, 8 Cush. 301 

Ocean Ins. Co. v. Portsmouth etc. Ry., 3 Met. 420

Boston Glass Mfg. v. Langdon, 24 Pick. 49 (HI) Defendant's Remedies 

(A) 

Amendment 

But Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 3, provides in part that: "The court may allow the defendant to amend an answer in abatement or to answer over by special order of the court for good cause shown, and not otherwise.” (B) Answer to Merits 

Gen. Laws, c. 231, s. 21 provides that: "If an answer in abatement is overruled on demurrer, or if, in consequence of such answer in abatement, the plaintiff amends, the defendant, within such time as the court orders, shall in a personal action answer, and in a real or mixed action plead, to the merits." 64

NDREYCHOA

ACCORD AND SATISFACTION A. NATURE AND EFFECT 

1. Definitions a. Accord

In the case of contracts, an "accord" is an agreement, where the creditor agrees to accept some other thing in lieu of that which is contracted or promised to be done. 

In the case of torts, an "accord" is an agreement, consent or concurrence of the minds and intentions of two or more individuals. It is an agreement between a party injuring and a party injured to make satisfaction for the injury which, when terminated, is a bar for the recovery of the original claim. The principle is that the party who has a legal right against another may accept some other thing in discharge of his claim or demand. 

When the accord is fully performed or executed it is called satisfaction. b. Satisfaction

A "satisfaction" is the performance of the terms of an accord. 

The acceptance by the creditor or injured party of the consideration of an accord is a satisfaction and extinguishes the obligation created by the accord. 

C. Accord and Satisfaction

An "accord and satisfaction" is the substitution of another agreement between the parties in satisfaction of the former one and an execution of the latter agreement, and forms a complete bar to any further action on the original claim. 

An "accord and satisfaction" is defined to be an agreement between two persons, one of whom has a right of action against the other, that the latter should do or give and the former accept something, in satisfaction of the right of action, different from, and usually less than, what might be legally enforced. 

An "accord and satisfaction" is a substitution by agreement of the parties, of something else in place of the original claim, and when executed its effect is to extinguish the antecedent liability.

An "accord and satisfaction" has been defined to be an agreement in the case of a contract where a creditor agrees to accept some other thing in lieu of that which is contracted or promised to be done. 

2. Terminates Original Claim 

Performance by the defendant of the new agreement operates as an accord and satisfaction for any breach, and discharges the old contract.

Atty. General v. Supreme Council, 196 Mass. 151 

Alden v. Thurber, 149 Mass. 271, at 275 

Curley v. Harris, 11 Allen 112. 

3. General Statement 

An accord without a satisfaction will not constitute a defence to an action upon the original claim unless the parties have agreed that the new obligation shall take the place of the old one. 

Alden v. Thurber, 149 Mass. 271

D. PARTIES TO EXECUTION 7. Persons Acting in Representative Capacities a. Agents 

Usually an agent has no implied, ostensible authority to effect an accord and satisfaction. So, the action of an agent in accepting less than the amount due of itself is not conclusive upon the principal, without either the authority of the agent or ratification by the principal. 

Saunders v. Whitcomb, 177 Mass. 457

The action of a collection agent in receiving less than the full amount of debt in satisfaction of the whole does not bar a suit to recover the balance, unless made either by the original authority of the principal or subsequently ratified by him. 

Saunders v. Whitcomb, 177 Mass. 457, at 462

When the agent is merely a collection agent, without authority to compromise and the principal receives the money from the agent without knowledge that it was accepted in full satisfaction or paid by anyone other than the debtor, in the absence of such knowledge the retention of the money is not authorization or ratification by the principal of the agent's acts. 

Saunders v. Whitcomb, 177 Mass. 457, at 466

A power of attorney to collect moneys and give discharges therefor, authorizes the attorney to give a receipt in full. 

Chouteau v. U. S., 95 U. S. 61 

b. Attorneys at Law 

It was said in Hahn v. Loker, 229 Mass. 363, at page 365: "It is a general rule that 'An attorney at law has authority, by virtue of his employment as such, to do in behalf of his client all acts, in or out of court, necessary or incidental to the prosecution and management of the suit, and which affect the remedy only, and not the cause of action.' 

Moulton v. Bowker, 115 Mass. 36, at 40 "He has power to release an attachment before judgment, D. 7. 1

and do many other things incidental to the proceedings and necessary or advisable for the interest of his client. 

Shattuck v. Bill, 142 Mass. 56, at 63 and 64 

Moulton v. Bowker, 115 Mass. 36, at 40 "Notwithstanding the broad discretionary power vested generally in an attorney, in behalf of his client, to do whatever is reasonably necessary to obtain judgment and to collect it afterwards, he cannot, by virtue of his employment, acknowledge satisfaction of a judgment except by payment in full. 

Shattuck v. Bill, 142 Mass. 56, at 63 

Brown v. Kendall, 8 Allen, 209 

Shores v. Caswell, 13 Met. 413 

Lewis v. Gamage, 1 Pick. 347 "Nor has an attorney authority to bind his client by the discharge of a debtor from arrest except on payment in full of the judgment. 

Brown v. Kendall, 8 Allen, 209 "In Anglo-American Land, Mortgage & Agency Co. v. 

Dyer, 181 Mass. 593, at page 598, this court stated, 'it is said that the weight of authority in this country seems to be against' the authority of an attorney at law by virtue of his employment to agree to a compromise of a suit out of court without his client's sanction." 

Gilman v. Cary, 198 Mass. 318 

Brewer v. Casey, 196 Mass. 384 

N. Y., N. H., & H. R. R. v. Martin, 158 Mass. 313 

Lewis v. Gamage, 1 Pick. 347

An attorney has no implied power to effect an accord and satisfaction or settle or receive payment for the case of his client. 

Precious v. O'Rourke, 270 Mass. 305

It is not within the general powers of the attorney employed to represent the plaintiff in the litigation to settle the plaintiff's cause of action by entering into the compromise agreement for judgment and judgment satisfied filed in the case. 

Precious v. O'Rourke, 270 Mass. 305

D. 7. 2

Dorchester Trust Co. v. Casey, 268 Mass. 494 

See v. Norris, 234 Mass. 345, at 349 

Hahn v. Loker, 229 Mass. 363 

Smith v. Abbott, 221 Mass. 326 

Anglo-American Land, Mortgage & Agency Co. v. Dyer, 181 Mass. 593, at 598 

N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R. v. Martin, 158 Mass. 313

U. S. v. Beebe, 180 U. S. 343, at 352 

Moulton v. Bowker, 115 Mass. 36

The general relation of an attorney and client does not authorize the attorney, without the knowledge and consent of the client, to settle or compromise the client's case. 

Precious v. O'Rourke, 270 Mass. 305

An attorney under his general employment has broad powers to do the things necessary or incidental to the prosecution and management of the case which affect the remedy and not the cause of action. 

Precious v. O'Rourke, 270 Mass. 305, at 307 

Steffe v. Old Colony, 156 Mass. 262, at 263 

Shattuck v. Bill, 142 Mass. 56, at 60 and 63 

Moulton v. Bowker, 115 Mass. 36, at 40 

Lewis v. Sumner, 14 Met. 269 

Lewis v. Gamage, 1 Pick. 346

When the attorney undertakes to bind his client to an agreement to compromise his client's substantial rights, the opposing party must ascertain at his peril whether the attorney has authority to make the settlement. 

Precious v. O'Rourke, 270 Mass. 305

Such an agreement is not binding on the client either when made or when approved by the court and filed in the case as the basis for judgment. If the approval of the court must be given and notice is given to the client and an opportunity for him to be heard and if at a hearing before the court a party has been given full opportunity to be heard, he cannot afterwards contend either that his counsel was without authority or that the settlement was not binding upon him. The judgment entered upon an 

D. 7.3

unauthorized compromise agreement made by an attorney in settlement of his client's claim may be set aside on the ground of lack of authority in the attorney to make the compromise on which it rests. 

Precious v. O'Rourke, 270 Mass. 305, at 308

Dalton v. West End St. Ry., 159 Mass. 221 U. S. v. Beebe, 180 U. S. 343, at 352 

In making this payment he must be held to have known that the agreement did not come within the implied authority of the attorney, and the defendant must be held to have taken the chance that it might later appear that the plaintiff was not bound by the settlement.

However, it is otherwise if the plaintiff's attorney has been held out to the defendant as having any other or greater power than an attorney authorized to take charge of litigation for a client, commonly has. 

Precious v. O'Rourke, 270 Mass. 305, at 308

Where a party has settled a case with an attorney and paid the attorney who was unauthorized to make such settlement, and the party has paid the amount of the same, the party, in making this payment, is held to have known that the agreement of settlement does not come within the implied authority of the attorney, and such party is held to take the chance that it might later appear that the client is not bound by the settlement. 

Precious v. O'Rourke, 270 Mass. 305, at 308

If a duly authorized attorney gives a receipt acknowledging a certain sum paid to him in settlement which is made with full knowledge of all the facts by both parties, including his client, and no mistake is shown, and no fraud or deceit is proved, it is a good accord and satisfaction and the client who is the creditor cannot go behind it and recover any balance. 

Small v. Sumner, 6 Gray 239 

c. Corporate Officers (I) Directors 

Corporate directors, acting as a board and not individually, D. 7. 4

have power to effect an accord and satisfaction of a claim due the corporation. 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262

So, the directors may delegate this authority to one of their number, or some other officer or agent of the corporation. 

Carver C. v. Manufacturers' Ins. Co., 6 Gray, 214 

Dedham Savings Institution v. Slack, 6 Cush. 408 

(II) Others 

Officers, stockholders, agents and representatives of a corporation, unless specifically authorized by the board of directors, have no authority or power to effect an accord and satisfaction of any claims of the corporation, whether liquidated or unliquidated. 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262 (Treasurer had no authority) 

Carver C. v. Manufacturers' Ins. Co., 6 Gray, 214 (Treasurer had no authority) 

Dedham Savings Institution v. Slack, 6 Cush. 408 (Treasurer had no authority) 

Ind. Rolling Mill Co. v. St. Louis Co., 120 U. S. 256

But such power may be expressly authorized or implied by special circumstances and facts. 

d. Exeutors and Administrators 

There is a valid accord and satisfaction when an executor, who is not obliged to do so, pays out of his own funds, and the creditor accepts, a sum less than the creditor claims against the testator's estate. 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 551

If at the time of the payment the creditor could not maintain an action on the executor's bond then the executor's personally paying the creditor the lesser sum in settlement of the creditor's claim and the executor's abandoning of his right to contest the amount claimed by the creditor together are, and separately each is, valid' consideration for the agreement of the creditor to accept in full settlement the amount which he received. 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 551 

D. 7.5

But there may be no valid accord and satisfaction by the acceptance from the executor or administrator of a sum less than is due from the estate, if at the time of payment the executor or administrator is personally liable on his bond and hence the part payment affords no consideration for the full settlement of the liquidated claim against the estate. 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 550

There was sufficient accord and satisfaction in Chamberlain v. 

Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, where the action was: 

First: For a balance due on two judgments against the defendant in her capacity as executrix; and 

Second: For the penal sum of the bond filed by the defendant as executrix.

The estate was in insolvency, commissioners were appointed and claims filed but no decree of distribution was ever entered. 

The commissioners allowed the plaintiff creditor's claim for an amount substantially less than he claimed; from this allowance he appealed. In reliance upon, and in consideration of, the plaintiff's promise to discharge his entire claim against the estate the defendant refrained from pressing to a conclusion the insolvency proceedings in the Probate Court, with the reasonable expectation that an adjudication of insolvency and an order of distribution would be made in due course, which would bar the collection of the full amount of the plaintiff's claim. If that course had been pursued and if the plaintiff had pressed for the immediate payment of his entire claim, the defendant would have been entitled to have the case continued until an adjudication had been rendered on the insolvency proceedings then pending.

As a result of previous negotiations between the parties the defendant paid and the plaintiff accepted the sum of $1,000 in full satisfaction of all claims and demands of the plaintiff against the estate of the testator. At that time it was apparent, and the plaintiff believed, the estate was hopelessly insolvent, and that it was in fact insolvent. At the time of the payment, the amount which the plaintiff would be entitled to collect on his judgment had not been determined, and the defendant was under no present obligation to pay the judgment in full either as executrix, or by 

D. 7. 6

reason of any personal obligation on the bond given by her as such executrix.

The larger part of said payment, as the plaintiff well knew, represented personal funds of the executrix, advanced by her pursuant to a collateral agreement with her in her personal capacity and not as the agent of, or in the form of a loan to, herself as executrix. The agreement of the plaintiff to remit the amount of his claim in excess of $1,000 was not a mere gratuitous act but was supported by a good and valid consideration. 

The ultimate finding in favor of the defendant was upon the ground that the defendant had shown that the payment of $1,000 to the plaintiff was an accord and satisfaction of his claim. The plaintiff had agreed that upon such payment he would sign a release of all demands, and that a letter was sent by the defendant's attorney to the plaintiff enclosing a check for $1,000 and a release of all demands, with a request that the release be signed and returned. The plaintiff kept the check but failed to sign and return the release. e.

D. 7.7

E. MODES 1. Part Payment a. Liquidated Debts (I) General Statement 

(A) Exceptions 

(II) Necessity of New Consideration 

Where, by a mode or time of payment, variant from that provided for in the contract, a new benefit is or may be conferred upon the creditor, or a burden imposed upon the debtor, a new consideration arises out of the transaction and gives validity to the agreement of the creditor. 

Saunders v. Whitcomb, 177 Mass. 457, at 463 

(III) Sufficiency of New Consideration 

It is not necessary that an agreement to accept less than a sum now due must be under seal, so as to conclusively import consideration. There are other ways by which an agreement to accept a smaller sum than the amount due, can be shown to be based upon a consideration valid in law. "It is . now well settled, that ordinarily a written contract, before breach, may be varied by a subsequent oral agreement, made on a sufficient consideration, as to the terms of it which are to be observed in the future. Such a subsequent oral agreement may enlarge the time of performance, or may vary any other terms of the contract, or may waive and discharge it altogether." 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 549 and 550 

Moskow v. Burke, 255 Mass. 563, at 566 and 567 

Conroy v. Toomay, 234 Mass. 384, at 386 

Hastings v. Lovejoy, 140 Mass. 261, at 264 

(E) Payment by Third Person 

The part payment of a liquidated indebtedness, by a third person under no obligation to pay, is a sufficient consideration for its acceptance by the creditor in discharge of the entire debt. 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 549 

Guild v. Butler, 127 Mass. 386 

Brooks v. White, 2 Met. 283

So, the payment, by an executor or administrator, who is under no obligation to pay the claim out of his personal funds, of a sum less than the original obligation owed by the estate of the testator which is received by the creditor in discharge of the whole amount is a new and valuable consideration and constitutes a valid discharge of the whole. 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 550 

Vaughn v. Robbins, 254 Mass. 35, at 36 

Barnett v. Rosen, 235 Mass. 244, at 247 and 248 

Harriman v. Harriman, 12 Gray, 341, at 344 

b. Unliquidated or Disputed Claims (I) General Statement 

"If a creditor, having an unliquidated or disputed claim against his debtor, accepts a sum smaller than the amount claimed in satisfaction of the claim, he cannot afterwards maintain an action for the unpaid balance of his original claim." 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 550

A claim is unliquidated and disputed while the debtor's appeal is pending from a commissioners' finding that a certain sum is due the creditor estate from the debtor, for the amount of the debt due the creditor estate has not been finally adjudicated. 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 550

ALIMONY A. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS 5. Defenses and Objections a. 

Purely Statutory 

Before Statute 1855, c. 137, s. 6, was passed, the court had no power to grant alimony for the period before the decree for divorce is entered. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62 at 64 

Shannon v. Shannon, 2 Gray, 285, at 287

Before that statute was passed, however, the court had author. ity to grant alimony in the final decree. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62, at 64 

Burrows. Purple, 107 Mass. 428, at 432 

Chase v. Chase, 105 Mass. 385 

Orrok v Orrok, 1 Mass. 341

The power of the courts of this Commonwealth to grant alimony and attorney's fees is purely statutory. It does not fall under any branch of jurisdiction in equity. Relief of such nature can be afforded only as an incident to proceedings for divorce. 

It cannot be allowed by independent suit in equity. b. 

Weidman v. Weidman, 274 Mass. 118, at 121 

Parker v. Parker, 211 Mass. 139, and cases cited

Counsel Fees 

The only ground upon which an allowance for counsel fees and expenses can be awarded is under G. L. c. 208, s. 17, and such award must be made upon a petition filed prior to the entry of a decree absolute in the divorce proceedings. Such an allowance cannot be made for legal services and expenses incurred upon a petition for modification of that decree relating to care, custody and maintainence of minor children of the parties. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62

The right of the court to grant counsel fees under its general equity powers is not material in matters involving divorce proceedings. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62 

Drew v. Drew, 250 Mass. 41 

Friedrich v. Friedrich, 230 Mass. 59, at 61 

Waterhouse v. Waterhouse, 225 Mass. 228, at 230 

Adams v. Holt, 214 Mass. 77, at 79

ALIMONY Greenia v. Greenia, 206 Mass. 449, at 450 

Robbins v. Robbins, 140 Mass. 528, at 530 

See G. L. c. 208, s. 33

The power of the court to make orders for payments to the libellee for counsel fees and expenses in proceedings for modification of the decree in respect to custody of a child incurred after the decree for the divorce has become absolute does not exist unless it is found in the statutory provisions. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62 at 63 

G. L. c. 208, s. 17, provides: "The court may require the husband to pay into court for the use of the wife during the pendency of the libel an amount to enable her to maintain or defend the libel, and to pay to the wife alimony during the pendency of the libel." 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62

This section by its express terms assumes that the relationship of husband and wife has not been legally terminated. The payment is to be made by the husband to the wife. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62

Before such a statute was enacted the court had no authority to order counsel fees pendente lite. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62 at 63 

Baldwin v. Baldwin, 6 Gray 341, at 342 

Coffin v. Dunham, 8 Cush. 404, at 405

The only purpose for such payments can be made under this statute is to enable the wife to "Maintain or defend the libel."

The natural meaning of these words is to refer to a period before the marriage tie is severed by a decree absolute. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62, at 64

So, the Court has no power to allow counsel fees after the decree absolute has been entered. 

Wallace v. Wallace, 273 Mass. 62 at 65

E. MODES 1. Part Payment a. Liquidated Debts 

(I) General Statement 

Payment by a debtor and receipt by a creditor of a sum less than the liquidated and undisputed debt is not a satisfaction, even though the debtor gives the same as full payment and the creditor agrees to so accept it, unless there is a release or satisfaction under seal, or a new consideration is given. 

Puritan v. Winstead, 263 Mass. 463 

Moss v. Goldstein, 254 Mass. 334, at 337 

Barnett v. Rosen, 235 Mass. 244 

Whittaker etc. Co., v. Standard etc. Co., 216 Mass. 204 

Parrott v. Mexican, 207 Mass. 184, at 194 

Gilman v. Carey, 198 Mass. 318 

Attorney General v. Supreme Council, 196 Mass. 151 

Specialty Glass v. Daley, 172 Mass. 460, at 461 

Lathrop v. Page, 129 Mass. 19 

Guild v. Butler, 127 Mass. 386 

Curran v. Rummell, 118 Mass. 482 

Perkins v. Lockwood, 100 Mass. 249 

Twitchell v. Shaw, 10 Cush. 46 

Jackman v. Bowker, 4 Met. 283 

Brooks v. White, 2 Met. 283 

Smith v. Bartholomew, 1 Met. 276

The creditor may apply the amount paid on his account and sue the debtor for the balance. 

Smith v. Johnson, 224 Mass. 50 

Curran v. Rummell, 118 Mass. 482 

Smith v. Metcalf, 1 Met. 276

Correspondence between the parties together with their subsequent conduct constitutes an accord and satisfaction. 

Mardes v. Damon, 271 Mass. 401

The question whether there was an accord and satisfaction is one of fact. 

Marden v. Damon, 271 Mass. 401 

Worcester Color Co. v. Wond's Sons Co., 209 Mass. 105, at 110 

Alden v. Thurber, 149 Mass. 271 (A) Exceptions 

(II) Effect of Sending and Accepting Check in Full 

When a check is sent to be accepted on condition, as by the writing on its face, one who accepts and uses it is bound by

the condition where the check is sent in full discharge of a claim no part of which is admitted to be due. 

Dedham Lumber Co. v. Hartung, 1932 A. S. 527, at 529

Whittaker Chain Tread Co. v. Standard Auto Supply Co., 

216 Mass. 204, at 208

But it is not so where a debtor undertakes to make part of what he admits to be fue conditioned on its being accepted in discharge of what is in dispute. Such a condition is void and the creditor can take the payment admittedly due free of the void condition which the debtor has sought to impose. 

Dedham Lumber Co. v. Hartung, 1932 A. S. 527, at 529

Whittaker Chain Tread Co. v. Standard Auto Supply Co., 

216 Mass. 204, at 208

If the creditor receives a check from his debtor for an amount less than the debtor's admitted liability or the agreed sum between them, the creditor may strike out the words written on the check and the creditor is not precluded by an accord and atisfaction on cashing it. 

Dedham Lumber Co. v. Hartung, 1932 A. S. 527, at 529 (Plaintiff and defendant agreed upon a settlement of $727; defendant sent plaintiff a check for $712.00 on which was written "to balance account, per agreement, covering Elliott houses"; plaintiff struck out these words and cashed the check.)

So, the jury should be precluded from basing a verdict upon an accord and satisfaction through [the creditor's] cashing the che-k after striking out the condition written upon it. 

Dedham Lumber Co. v. Hartung, 1932 A. S. 527, at 529 

Moss v. Goldstein, 254 Mass. 334

Acceptance of a check given in full payment of a liquidated debt does not constitute an accord and satisfaction and this is true whether or not the acceptance of the check may be construed as an acceptance of the condition on which it was given. 

Specialty Glass Co. v. Daley, 172 Mass. 460

(4) What is Not Unliquidated Debt or 

Claim

An unliquidated claim may become liquidated by an agreement between the parties that a definite consideration shall be paid for its extinguishment. So, when the creditor's claim is liquidated at a certain time, though not liquidated before, a subsequent payment of all or part of the liquidated sum is a payment of an amount admittedly due, and the creditor, whether or not he understands the condition that the sum paid shall be accepted by him in discharge of all his claims against the debtor, can accept the payment and repudiate the condition. 

Rosenthal v. Holstein Rubber Co., 1933 A. S. 1, at 5 

Shumaker v. Lucerne-in-Maine Com. Ass., 275 Mass. 201 and cases cited 

Compare: Williston on Contracts, sec. 129 

So, in Rosenblatt v. Holstein Rubber Company, 1933 A. S. 1, where in May, 1928, the debtor orally agreed to pay the plaintiff for his services in connection with the establishment by the defendant of a business, $75 a week, of which $40 was to be paid each week until the factory was located, $50 each week until production was begun and thereafter $75 a week, that the remainder of the plaintiff's weekly salary of $75 and an additional sum of $5,000.00 were to be paid to him upon the completion of the factory, that the contemplated services were performed, payments made on the basis of $40 and $50 a week, and the factory was completed and production was commenced on October 15, 1928. 

In June, 1928, a written agreement was entered into, subject to termination on thirty days' notice, whereby the plaintiff was to receive $75 a week for services at the factory after production began, that he worked under this contract from October 18, 1928, until about July 23rd, 1929, being paid thereunder up to July 20, 1929, and thereafter worked for the defendant as a salesman on a commission basis, but that on July 12, or 13, 1929, the plaintiff was given notice that his employment under the contract would terminate in thirty days.

E-2

The indebtedness owed to the plaintiff was: (1) Part of the plaintiff's weekly salary for the period before October 15, 1928, under the oral agreement; (2) An additional sum of $5,000 under the oral agreement and (3) Services performed, ready to be performed for thirty days, from July 12th, 1929, under the written contract agreed upon to be $150.00.

There were negotiations between the parties directed solely to the settlement of the plaintiff's claim under his written contract of employment. Both parties understood that this claim only was being settled

On July 23, 1929, the plaintiff received from the defendant debtor, by check or in cash, $100 and signed a receipt therefor prepared by the defendant in the following terms: "... Received from Holstein Rubber Co., Inc. One hundred dollars, week ending in full to apply on settlement for $150 in full for services and demands to date," that on the following day the debtor sent to the plaintiff his check for $50, which bore on its back the following typewritten statement: "Received in full settlement of all balances, dues and demands for services and for other obligations to date."

The plaintiff received the check, read the statement quoted, signed his name thereunder and collected it. 

The action was to recover (1) and (2) above, the sums due under the oral agreement. 

The court said, at pages 3-4: "The oral evidence did not require (the) finding.. (that the payments in cash and by check were offered upon the condition that they be accepted in discharge of all claims of the plaintiff against the defendant including the claims in question and that the plaintiff accepted the payments on this condition).

E-3

"It did not require either a finding that the debtor offered be accepted in discharge of the claims nov in question, or a finding that the creditor understood, or ought to have understood, that any such condition was imposed. 

the writings signed by the plaintiff as matter of law (did not) require the conclusion that the payments were offered and accepted in discharge of all the plaintiff's claims against the defendant or those now in question. "Neither of the writings was a release under seal. The indorsement on the back of the check was in form a release 'in full settlement of all balances, dues and demands for service and for other obligations to date,' but it contained no words of release or discharge, 

(Compare Boston Supply Co. v. Rubin, 214 Mass. 217 

Dunham v. Branch, 5 Cush. 558, at 561) and did not purport to embody an agreement. (Compare Squires v. Amherst, 145 Mass. 192, at 194 

See Wigmore on Evidence (2d Ed.), p. 2432) "It is purported to recite facts and, as against the plaintiff, was evidence of the facts recited, but it was not conclusive and could be explained or contradicted by other evidence." 

Foster v. Commer. Na. Bk., 248 Mass. 279, at 282 and 283 

Grinnell v. Spink, 128 Mass. 25 

Bard v. Wood, 3 Met. 74

3. Admissibility a.

General Statement b. Documentary Evidence (I) Parol Evidence 

The submission of a receipt on account by the debtor to the creditor for his signature and the subsequent sending by the debtor to the creditor of a check with a form of receipt in full indorsed thereon are evidence that the debtor offered the payments to the plaintiff on the condition that they be accepted in discharg of all claims of the debtor. And the creditor's signing of the receipt on account and his acceptance and indorsement of the check are evidence of his acceptance of the payments on that condition. But this evidence can be controlled by other evidence. 

Rosenthal v. Holstein Rubber Co., 1933 A. S. 1, at 4

Such documents purport to recite facts and, as against the creditor are evidence of the facts recited, but are not conclusive and can be explained or contradicted by other evidence. 

Foster v. Com'l Nat. Bk., 243 Mass. 279, at 282 and 283 

Grinnll v. Spink, 128 Mass. 25 

Bard v. Wood, 3 Met. 74 

Brooks v. White, 2 Met. 283

So, a receipt on account at most stands no better as a defence than the receipt in full. 

Rosenthal v. Holstein Rubber Co., 1933 A. S. 1, at 4

ADJOINING LANDOWNERS

ADJOINING LANDOWNERS B. ENCROACHMENTS 2. Rights of Adjoining Owner C. To Maintain Legal Proceedings 

(I) Equitable Relief 

(A) Trespass (1) Removal of Wall 

In Tyler v. City of Haverhill, 272 Mass. 313, the plaintiff and defendant owned adjoining lands. Neither was able to show by any recorded plan or deed the exact location of the boundary line between them. The defendant constructed a heavy masonry wall upon what it contended was its own land near the true boundary. 

This wall in large part encroached upon the land of the plaintiff. 

A decree was entered directing the defendant to remove the encroachment. 

The court said at pages 315 and 316: "The master has found that the defendant entered upon the land of the plaintiff and built its wall as aforesaid in good faith and under the belief that it was not trespassing upon the land of the plaintiff, but that notice was given by the plaintiff, within a few days after excavations for the wall were begun, that she owned the land on which it was proposed to build the wall and protested against its use. The bill was filed on September 6, 1927; and there is nothing to show any unreasonable delay in asserting plaintiff's rights.

The report discloses that doubt might well exist whether the title asserted by the plaintiff arose from anything other than long continued adverse possession in her predecessors; but evidence of such adverse possession was abundant and within the defendant's control. The master found that no financial loss to the plaintiff had been caused. One who knows of claims to land which he proposes to use as his own, proceeds at his peril if he goes forward in the face of protests from the claimant and places structures upon the land. It is familiar law that buildings placed upon real estate by a trespasser become the property of the true owner of the real estate. The ruling was right and the order proper."

An adjoining owner may invoke the aid of a court of equity to enjoin the maintenance of the encroachment or compel its re-

ADJOINING LANDOWNERS 

moval or the restoration of plaintiff's premises to their original condition as near as may be. 

Kershishian v. Johnson, 210 Mass. 135 

Harrington v. McCarthy, 169 Mass. 492 

Tucker v. Howard, 128 Mass. 361

Where the wall of a bay window built outside of the main wall of a building and forming no part of it is built partly on adjoining land, its maintenance may be enjoined and its removal compelled by a mandatory injunction at the suit of the adjoining owner.

Ordinance denouncing an encroachment is no ground for equitable relief. An ordinance imposing penalties for encroachments on public streets will furnish an adjoining owner no ground for equitable relief unless the encroachment amounts to a public nuisance, Jenks v. Williams, 115 Mass. 217 although no actual damage is sustained. 

Harrington v. McCarthy, 169 Mass. 492

Relief by injunction will not be refused on the ground that plaintiff has been guilty of laches. 

Hodgkins v. Farrington, 150 Mass. 19

2. Distinguished from Confessions

In Comm. v. Haywood, 247 Mass. 16, the court said at page 18: "Where the accused claims that a confession made by him was induced by promises or threats of the arresting officer, he has a right to have a preliminary decision by the judge as to its competency before it is admitted in evidence for the consideration of the jury. 

Comm. v. Culver, 126 Mass. 464 "This right, however, exists only with reference to a confession, as that word is accurately used in the criminal law; that is, to an acknowledgment by the accused in express words of the truth of the guilty fact charged. "It does not exist in case of mere incriminating admissions or declarations of subordinate or independent facts, which may tend in connection with other facts and circumstances to prove the defendant's guilt, but do not constitute an acknowledgment that he is guilty of the precise crime with which he is charged. "The distinction between a confession and an admission, as applied in criminal law, is not a technical refinement, but is based upon the substantive differences of the character of the evidence educed from each. A confession is a direct ac- 1

ADMISSIONS 

knowledgment of guilt on the part of the accused, and by the very force of the definition, excludes an admission, which, of itself, as applied in criminal law, is a statement by the accused, direct or implied, of facts pertinent to the issue, and tending, in connection with proof of other facts, to prove his guilt, but of itself is insufficient to authorize a conviction.' 

Comm. v. Dascalakis, 243 Mass. 519 

Underhill's Crim. Ev. (3d ed.), s. 215 

Wharton Crim. Ev. (10th ed.), s. 67a

2. Implied a.

General Statement 

The rule is that dishonest and criminal conduct of a party in the preparation or trial of a case is in the nature of an admission, implied from his conduct, that his claim or defence is false and unjust. 

Comm. v. Min Sing, 202 Mass. 121, at 125 

Boyle v. Columbian Fire Pr'fing Co., 182 Mass. 93, at 103 

Simes v. Rockwell, 156 Mass. 372, at 374

Hastings v. Stetson, 130 Mass. 76 

Egan v. Bowker, 5 Allen 449

Such conduct of a party implies a consciousness that his case cannot rest upon its merits, and is in the nature of an admission that he is in the wrong in his contention before the court. 

Comm. v. Min Sing, 202 Mass. 121, at 125

The principle and the rule founded upon it are applicable to conduct of a defendant in a criminal case, as well as to that of a party in a civil suit. 

Comm. v. Min Sing, 202 Mass. 121, at 125 

Comm. v. Sullivan, 156 Mass. 487 

Comm. v. Wallace, 123 Mass. 400 

Comm. v. Webster, 5 Cush. 295, at 316

It is however a familiar rule that if any party to a cause suborns a witness to testify falsely, this may be shown as an admission on his part that he has not a just claim. 

Bennett v. Susser, 191 Mass. 329, at 331 

Egan v. Bowker, 5 Allen 449

The rule is the same if a person whose liability is in question immediately after the act upon which it is sought to charge him assigns or conveys all his property. 

Bennett v. Susser, 191 Mass. 329, at 331 

Banfield v. Whipple, 10 Allen 27

ADMISSIONS 

It may a juror at a previous trial of a case. also be shown that a party to a cause attempted to bribe 

Bennett v. Susser, 191 Mass. 329, at 331

Hastings v. Stetson, 130 Mass. 76 

So the suppression of important evidence is a fact to be weighed against the party suppressing it. 

Bennett v. Susser, 191 Mass. 329, at 331 

Simes v. Rockwell, 156 Mass. 372 

In Boyle v. Columbian Fire Proofing Co., 182 Mass. 93, at 103, it was said by Mr. Justice Loring: "The presiding judge instructed the jury that if they found that one party or the other had put in testimony knowing it to be false they had a right to take that into consideration when they came to weigh the testimony." 

In Egan v. Bowker, 5 Allen 449, at 451 and 452, it was said: "The evidence offered for the purpose of showing that the plaintiff had suborned a witness to testify in support of his claim against the defendants, and, in connection therewith that in procuring such false testimony he had acted under an assumed name, was clearly competent and ought to have been admitted. "These facts were in the nature of admissions implied from the conduct of the party that his claim against the defendant was false and unjust. "The inference is a reasonable and proper one, that a person having an honest and fair debt which he claims to be due will not endeavor to support it by falsehood and fraud; and the fact that he resorts to such means of proof has a tendency to show that he knows he cannot maintain his suit by evidence derived from pure and incorrupt sources. "Truth does not ally itself with falsehoods, but falsehood will often endeavor to make it appear that truth is on its side. When therefore it is shown that a party to a suit has sought to suborn witnesses to swear falsely in his behalf, and has been guilty in his own person of fraud and deceit in the maintenance of his action, such evidence is competent, as an admission of the falsity or fraudulent nature of the claim. "On the same ground it is held that the suppression of documents in a party's possession or control is an admission that their contents are unfavorable to the party suppressing them, and will not sustain his case."

ADMISSIONS 

The admission of a defendant is evidence of negligence which required the submission of the case to the jury. 

Tully v. Mandell, 269 Mass. 307, at 309 

Barnett v. Roberts, 243 Mass. 233, at 236 

Zandan v. Radner, 242 Mass. 503, at 505

But the jury are not bound to find a defendant negligent even if he made a statement that the accident was attributable to his fault. 

Tully v. Mandell, 269 Mass. 307, at 309 

Leary v. Keith, 256 Mass. 157, at 158 

Hawkes v. Lackey, 207 Mass. 424, at 433 

Conant v. Evans, 202 Mass. 34 

Bowditch v. Buffum, 2 Gray 550, at 552

An admission is only a part of the evidence to be weighed with the rest, and the party making it is not concluded by it. 

Tully v. Mandell, 269 Mass. 303, at 309

The jury may find if they consider all the evidence on that issue that a plaintiff has not maintained the burden of proving the defendant negligent even though he may have made an admission that he was at fault. 

Tully v. Mandell, 269 Mass. 307, at 309

Declaration of a wife of the owner of an automobile that if the plaintiff had to go to the hospital she would pay expenses, is not an admission of liability or any legal obligation of wife. 

Kindell v. Ayles, 263 Mass. 244 

Bernasconi v. Bassi, 261 Mass. 26

In Comm. v. Madeiros, 255 Mass. 304, the court said at page 313: "When a defendant while under arrest is charged with a crime by an accusation made in his presence, and makes an equivocal reply or one susceptible of being interpreted as an admission or one not likely to be made by an innocent man, the question or statement and the answer or comment are admissible." 

b. By Conduct 

If a party against whom liability or indebtedness is claimed conveyed or incumbered all or part of his property with intent to prevent the collection of any judgment against him, which might be founded on that liability or indebtedness, the circumstances and facts may be shown and if proved, his conduct in conveying or encumbering his property may be found to be an admission of the existence of the liability or debt.

Zandan v. Radner, 242 Mass. 503 

Comm. v. Min Sing, 202 Mass. 121

Hastings v. Stetson, 130 Mass. 76 

Banfield v. Whipple, 10 Allen 31

If a defendant testifies falsely on material points, such as denying that he was present at the crime, the jury may take into account such denial and consider such false testimony as evidence of guilt. 

Comm. v. MacCarthy, 272 Mass. 207 

Comm. v. Sokorelis, 254 Mass. 454, at 457 

Comm. v. Devaney, 182 Mass. 33, at 35

The jury may have found that the defendant's denials were knowingly false and tended to show a consciousness of guilt. If so, the evidence was admissible. 

Comm. v. Anderson, 220 Mass. 142, at 146
