(I) Consciousness of Liability (A) Defendant's Voluntary Conveyance of All His Attachable Property 

The voluntary conveyance of all of one attachable property after notice of the plaintiff's claim, to avoid an attachment by the plaintiff may be admitted as evidence of consciousness of liability on the part of the defendant as to amount to admission of the plaintiff's claims. 

Wilson v. 

Grace, 273 Mass. 146

Hastings v. Stetson, 130 Mass. 76

The mere fact that, having notice of the plaintiff's claim, the next year after the accident though continuing to own the automobile, the defendant had it registered in the name of his daughter who was not licensed to operate motor vehicles, does not warrant a finding that the automobile "constituted all of the defendant's attachable property, and was voluntarily conveyed to avoid an attachment by the plaintiff" thereby showing such consciousness of liability on the part of the defendant for the results of the accident as to amount to an admission thereof. 

Wilson v. Grace, 273 Mass. 146

ADMISSIONS 

In Carroll v. Carroll, 262 Mass. 10 where the judge permitted the plaintiff in cross-examination of the defendant to show that after he had been notified by the plaintiff's attorney of her claim and before action was brought, he conveyed all his property to the woman who later became his wife, after this conveyance, when the plaintiff told the defendant that he would hear from her claim soon, he said, "you are too late," the court said at page 12: "Upon the evidence introduced, the jury could infer that the house constituted all of the defendant's property, and that it was voluntarily conveyed to avoid an attachment by the plaintiff. "The testimony objected to was competent. It had some tendency to show that the defendant was 'conscious of liability and endeavored to escape from it'. "The fact that a promise to marry is a good consideration for a conveyance is immaterial, because there was no evidence to prove that such a promise was the consideration for the conveyance." 

In Portland Gas Light Co. v. Ruud, 242 Mass. 272 the court said at page 275: "The jury could infer and find, in the absence of any positive evidence to the contrary that the house constituted all of his [the defendant's] property which could be come at to be attached, and that it was voluntarily conveyed, to avoid an attachment to secure the payment of damages if the plaintiff prevailed in the impending actions of which he [the defendant] had been fully informed," [and that this conveyance showed an admission by the defendant of liability to the plaintiff.]

In Bennett v. Susser, 191 Mass. 329, the court said at page 331: "If a person whose liability is in question immediately after the act upon which it is sought to charge him assigns or conveys all his property" [this may be shown as an admission on his part that he has not a just defence.] 

In Banfield v. Whipple, 10 Allen 27, the court said at page 31: ". . . the assignments made by both defendants of all their property on the day after the accident . . . made. . . simultaneously... without any proof of consideration except the recitals in the assignments, were some evidence that the defendants were conscious of liability and endeavored to escape from it, the weight of which was to be determined by the jury.”

ADMISSIONS c. By Silence 

If a defendant while under arrest is charged with the crime by an accusation made in his presence and hearing, and he remains mute or unequivocally denies it, his silence or denial is not admissible in evidence against him. But if he makes an equivocal reply, the question or statement by which it was elicited and the answer or comment are admissible. 

Comm. v. Fesso, 251 Mass. 275, at 280 

Comm. v. Anderson, 245 Mass. 177, at 188 

Comm. v. Gangi, 243 Mass. 341 

Comm. v. Spiropoulos, 208 Mass. 71, at 74 

Comm. v. Herbert, 264 Mass. 571 

Comm. v. Hamel, 264 Mass. 564, at 569

Comm. v. Madeiros, 255 Mass. 304 

The distinction is, that before arrest if he remains silent when statements are made to him or questions asked which naturally call for a reply if he is innocent, proof of his conduct is admissible. 

But when under arrest he is not called upon to speak, and what he may have said or done while only under suspicion cannot be used as a reason from which to infer that proof of his silence raises a presumption of his guilt. 

Comm. v. Spiropoulos, 208 Mass. 71, at 74 

Comm. v. Coughlin, 182 Mass. 558, at 565 

Comm. v. Trefethen, 157 Mass. 180 

Comm. v. McDermott, 123 Mass. 440 

Comm. v. Brown, 121 Mass. 69, at 80 

Comm. v. Walker, 13 Allen 570 

Comm. v. Galavan, 9 Allen 235 

Comm. v. Kenney, 12 Met. 235

If one receives bills for services rendered by the adverse party, he is not required to make any reply to them. 

Holton v. Denaro, 1932 A. S. 257, at 258 

Kumin v. Fine, 229 Mass. 75, at 76 

Callahan v. Goldman, 216 Mass. 234, at 237 and 238

2. Implied c. By Silence (I) When Person Is Under Arrest 

When a statement accusatory of a crime is made in the presence of the defendant who is under arrest and he does not deny the accusation the evidence of the accusation and his failure to deny is inadmissible. 

Comm. v. Graham, 1932 A. S. 1077 

Comm. v. Herbert, 264 Mass. 571, at 578 

Comm. v. Hamel, 264 Mass. 564, at 569 

Comm. v. Merrick, 255 Mass. 510, at 512 

Comm. v. Sherman, 234 Mass. 7, at 12 

Comm. v. Spiripoulos, 208 Mass. 71, at 74 

Comm. v. Trefethen, 157 Mass. 180, at 197 and 198 

Comm. v. Brown, 121 Mass. 69, at 80

So, also if the defendant clearly and unequivocally denies the accusation. 

See cases just cited above.

However, it is also the established law of the Commonwealth that not only may such a defendant make a direct verbal admission of the truth of a statement made in his presence, but also by reason of an equivocal, evasive or irresponsive reply or comment may be found by a jury under proper instructions from the judge to have made an admission of evidential value on the issue of his guilt. 

See cases just cited above.

In Comm. v. Graham, 1932 A. S. 1077, where a police officer was permitted to testify that he brought the defendant to the bedside of A at the hospital and that there A said she knew the defendant; that the officer asked A, "Did he [the defendant] cut you?" and A replied "He must have, there was no other man there"; that the officer then said to the defendant, "What do you say about that?" and that the defendant replied, "I must have been crazy if I did it." Mr. Justice Donohue said, at pages 1078 and 1079: "The evidence. was properly admitted... It was for the jury to say whether or not the testimony of the police officer was true and if so whether or not the reply of the defendant to the statement of [A] . . . was indicative of the defendant's guilt of the crime charged. 

Comm. v. Madeiros, 255 Mass. 304, at 313 "... the conversation could be considered on the question whether or not it tended to show consciousness of guilt." 

Comm. v. Sherman, 234 Mass. 7, at 12 9a

 OF AGENTS Section 1 A. DEFINITIONS 1. Agency 

Agency is a term signifying the legal relations established when one man is authorized to represent and act for another and does so represent and act for another. 

The relation of agency is the status existing between two persons, based upon their voluntary action, by virtue of which one of them is to act for and in behalf of the other and subject to his control.

Agency is the legal relation which exists where one person, called the agent, is authorized, either by act of the parties or operation of law, to represent and act for another, called the principal, in the contractual dealings of the latter with third persons. 

Agency is created by contract, express or implied. It is a legal relation by virtue of which one party (the agent) is employed and authorized to represent and act for the other (the principal) in business dealings with third persons. The distinguishing features of the agent are his representative character and his derivative authority.

Agency is the relation created either by express or implied contract or by law whereby one party sui juris, called the principal, constituent or employer, delegates the transaction of some lawful

§1 

business with more or less discretionary power to another party called the agent, attorney, proxy or delegate, who undertakes to manage that affair and render to him an account thereof. 

Agency indicates the relation which exists when one person is hired to act for another. It has three chief forms, in the following relations: a. Principal and Agent b. Master and Servant, commonly called Employer and Employee; and c. Employer or Proprietor and Independent Contractor. 

All of these have some points of similarity but, at the same time, many aspects of real distinction. 

2. Agency of Necessity 

Agency of necessity is that relation which arises when one is under a legal obligation to perform certain acts because of the proximity of relationship (either through blood or marriage) and because of neglect or refusal to so perform these legal obligations the person to whom the performance is owed is forced to perform the duties on the credit of the obligor. In such a case the law conclusively presumes an agency.

Groce v. First Nat. Stores, 268 Mass. 210 

Benjamin v. Dockham, 134 Mass. 418 

Conant v. Burnham, 133 Mass. 503 

3. Agent

An agent is a person who acts to represent another in contractual negotiations, bargainings or transactions involving business dealing with third persons, or appears for or represents the other in hearings or proceedings in which the other may be interested. 

An agent is a person having express or implied authority to represent or act on behalf of another person, who is called his principal.

§3 

AGENCY 

4. Attorney in Fact

An attorney in fact is any person appointed to do some act of agency not connected with law. 

5. Auctioneer

An auctioneer is an agent whose ordinary course of business is to sell by public auction goods or other property of which he may or may not be entrusted with the possession or control. 

An auctioneer is the agent of the person who employs him to sell. From the nature of his business he is the agent of the buyer for the single purpose of binding him by a memorandum in writing to satisfy the statute of frauds, but in all other respects he is an agent of the auctioneer. 

Curtis v. Aspinwall, 114 Mass. 187, at 195 

6. Broker

A broker is an agent whose ordinary course of business is to negotiate and make contracts for the sale and purchase of goods and other property, of which he is not entrusted with the possession or control.

A broker is an agent employed to make bargains and contracts between other persons in matters of trade and commerce or navigation for a compensation commonly called "brokerage."

A broker is, strictly, a middleman or intermediate negotiator between the parties. He is primarily deemed merely the agent of the parties by whom he is employed, and he becomes the agent of the other party only when the contract or bargain is definitely settled as to its terms between the principal. As a general proposition, the same individual cannot be agent for both parties, but persons having undertaken certain duties of a particular character, are treated as agents of both parties; such are brokers. 

7. Del Credere Agent

A del credere agent is a mercantile agent who, in consideration of an extra remuneration, which is called a del credere commission, guarantees to his principal that third persons with whom he enters into contracts on behalf of the principal shall duly pay any şums coming due under those contracts.

§1 

DEFINITIONS, DISTINCTIONS, And Classes 

In effect, a del credere agent is a surety for the persons with whom he deals. But it has been held that an agreement by an agent to sell on a del credere commissions is not a promise to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another person, within the meaning of the 4th section of the Statute of Frauds, and it is not necessary that such an agreement be in writing. A del credere agency may be inferred from a course of conduct between the parties.

The principal is not entitled to litigate with a del credere agent any disputes arising out of contracts made by him. The obligation of the agent is confined to answering for the failure by the other contracting parties, owing to insolvency or the like, to pay any ascertained sums which may become due from them as debts. 

8. Factor

A factor is a mercantile agent whose ordinary course of business is to sell or dispose of goods, of which he is entrusted with the possession or control by his principal.

A factor is an agent who, in the pursuit of an independent calling, is employed by another to sell property for him, and is vested by the latter with the possession or control of the property, or authorized to receive payment therefor from the purchaser. 

A factor is an agent for the sale of merchandise and ordinarily has the possession, management and control of the property and subject of the agency; but the actual possession is not essential to constitute an agency which would pass under that name as it is ordinarily applied to distinguish it from agencies of other descriptions.

A factor is a commercial agent employed by the principal to sell merchandise consigned to him for that purpose on behalf of the principal. He may hold them either in his own name or the name of the principal and he is remunerated by a fixed commission, either expressed or implied. He is authorized to sell and receive payment therefor from the purchaser. 

In Re Rabenau, 118 Fed. 471, at 474 

9. Foreign Principal

The expression "foreign principal" means a principal who does not reside or carry on business in the United States of America.

§5 

AGENCY 

10. General Agent

A general agent is an agent who has authority: a. to act for his principal in all matters, or in all matters concerning a particular trade or business, or of a particular nature; or b. to do some act in the ordinary course of his trade, profession or business as an agent on behalf of his principal. 

11. Home Agent 

The expression "home agent" means an agent residing and carrying on business as such in the United States of America. 

12. Independent Contractor 

An independent contractor is a person who undertakes to execute certain work or to accomplish a stipulated result for another, under such circumstances that the right of control of the doing of the work, and the forces and agencies employed in doing it, is in the contractor.

An independent contractor is one who renders service in the course of an occupation, representing the will of his employer only as to the result of his work, and not as to the means by which it is accomplished.

An independent contractor is one who, exercising an independent employment, contracts to do a piece of work according to his own methods and without being subject to the control of his employer except as to the result of the work. 

An independent contractor is one who contracts, to perform the work at his own risk and cost, the workmen being his servants, and he, and not the person with whom he contracts, being liable for their misconduct. 

13. Mercantile Agent

A mercantile agent is an agent having in the customary course of his business as such agent, authority either to sell goods, or to consign goods for the purpose of sale, or to buy goods, or to raise money on the security of goods.

§1 DEFINITIONS, Distinctions, and Classes act. 

14. Principal

The principal is the person for whom the agent is to, or does, 15. Public Agent 

The expression "public agent" means an agent of the domestic government. 

16. Servant

A servant, or employee, is a person who performs labor, or renders personal service, for or under the direction of another, called the master or employer.

A servant is one who is employed to render personal service to his employer, otherwise than in the pursuit of an independent calling, and who in such service remains entirely under the control and direction of the latter, who is called his master. 

A servant is one who does work under the direction of another, who not only prescribes to the workman the nature of his work, but directs, or at any moment may direct, the means also, or, as it has been put, retains the power of controlling the work. 17.

Powers v. Mass. Homeopathic Hospital, 109 Fed. 294 Special Agent 

A special agent is an agent who has only authority to do some particular act, or represent his principal in some particular transaction, such act or transaction not being in the ordinary course of his trade, profession, or business as agent. 

A special agent is one authorized to do one or more specific acts, in pursuance of particular instructions, or within restrictions necessarily implied from the act to be done. 

A person employed by another for a particular purpose and acting under limited and circumscribed powers is a special agent. 

18. Sub-Agent 

A person is a sub-agent when he is appointed by an agent to assist him in the performance of duties delegated to him in his capacity as agent.

$7 

AGENCY 

19. Third Person

The expression "third person" means any person other than the principal or agent. 

20. Undisclosed Principal

The expression "undisclosed principal" means a principal who is not known to be such by the person dealing with the agent. 

21. Universal Agent

A universal agent is one who is given the power to do all the acts that the principal might lawfully do or might lawfully delegate to another person.

B. DISTINCTIONS Section 2 

1. Agency Distinguished from Sale

An agency to sell is sometimes confused with a sale of the goods delivered to the receiver; that is, whether the receiver of the goods is an agent of the deliverer or a purchaser, is sometimes a matter of doubt.

The distinction is whether the delivery of the goods is to a person who is to sell them, not as his own property, but as the property of the principal, who remains the owner of the goods and therefore has the right to control the sale, fix the price and terms, to recall the goods, and to demand and receive their proceeds when sold, less the agent's commission, but who has not right to a price for them before sale or unless sold by the agent; and a transfer to the title to the goods for a price paid or to be paid, which transfer puts the transferee in the position of one who is selling his own goods, and makes him liable to the person from whom he received them as a debtor for the price to be paid and not liable as an agent for the proceeds of the resale. 

Walker v. Butterick, 105 Mass. 237 

Eldridge v. Benson, 7 Cush., 483 

Sturm v. Bowker, 150 U. S. 312 

Herryford v. Davis, 102 U. S. 235

Hervey v. Locomotive Works, 93 U. S. 664

§

2. Agent and Independent Contractor 

The difference between an agent and an independent contractor is, that an agent is bound to act in the matter of the agency subject to the directions and control of the principal, whereas an independent contractor merely undertakes to perform certain specified work or to produce a certain specified result, the manner and means of performance being left to his discretion, except so far as they are specified by the contractor. 

Baker v. Texas Co., 262 Mass. 425 

Rockport Gr. Co. v. Plum Isl. Beach Co., 248 Mass. at 290 

Gallagher's Case, 240 Mass. 455, and cases coll. 

Nugent v. Boston Cons. Gas, 238 Mass. 221, at 232 

Whalen v. Sheehan, 237 Mass. 112, at 114

N. Eng. Co. v. Jas. Russell Works, 231 Mass. 274 

Morrissey v. Boston & Maine R. R., 230 Mass. 171, at 174 

Harding v. Boston, 163 Mass. 14, at 18

The characteristics of the independent contractor are that he is a person who for a stipulated compensation (usually a lump sum) undertakes to do a piece of work by his own forces and instrumentalities being responsible to his employer for the stipulated results, but being left in control of the operation of the forces and instrumentalities by which the stipulated result is to be accomplished.

The status of independent contractor is not destroyed because the work is done under a contract which requires it to be performed in accordance with plans and specifications prescribed by the employer or permits the employer before or during the progress of the work to give directions as to the results to be achieved. 

If the independent contractor is deprived of the control of the operation of the forces and agencies by which the stipulated result is to be accomplished, then his relation as an independent contractor is destroyed.

It is by reason of this freedom from control of the employer, that he is an independent contractor and is not the agent or servant of the employer, consequently the agents or servants employed by the independent contractor are not the agents or servants of the employer.

§

9 

AGENCY 

An independent contractor, not the employer, is responsible for his own acts and contracts. 

Pearl v. West End St. Ry., 176 Mass. 177

Casement v. Brown, 148 U. S. 615 

New Orleans R. Co. v. Hanning, 15 Wall., (U.S.) 649 

Robbins v. Chicago, 14 Wall., (U.S.) 657

The fact that the employer retains the right to make and does make, daily supervision and approval of the work does not necessarily render the employee and agent or servant, but he may continue to be an independent contractor. 

Casement v. Brown, 148 U. S. 615 

The owner or occupant of a building who uses due care in selecting and agreeing with an independent contractor to do lawful work, is not responsible to third persons for the negligence of such contractor or his servants in the performance of the contract, unless the nature of the work is such that a nuisance will be created or wrongful consequences be brought to pass unless guarded against. 

Pickett v. Waldorf Co., 241 Mass. 569, at 570 (Water frozen on sidewalk from window cleaning, employer not liable) 

Regan v. Superb Theatre, 220 Mass. 259

Davis v. Whiting, 201 Mass. 91 

Boomer v. Wilber, 176 Mass. 482

Pye v. Faxon, 156 Mass. 471 

Hilliard v. Richardson, 3 Gray, 349

In determining whether the person hired is an agent or an independent contractor the test is whether the employer or the person hired has the power of directing or controlling the actions of that person, or way and manner in which the work shall be done. 

Forsyth v. Hooper, 11 Allen, 419, at 421

That is, it is a question of the right of interference, the right of control. 

Linneban v. Rollins, 137 Mass. 123, at 125

The terms and mode of payment are not a decisive test. 

Morgan v. Smith, 159 Mass. 570, at 574

$2 

But a specific price for the job usually makes the workman an independent contractor. 

Brackett v. Luske, 4 Allen, 138 

Hilliard v. Richardson, 3 Gray, 349

Also, the right to do the work in his own way makes the workman an independent contractor. 

Comerford's Case, 224 Mass. 571 

Randall v. Peerless Motor Car Co., 212 Mass. 352, at 353 

3. Between Principal and Agent and Landlord and Tenant 

In Fiske v. Framingham Man. Co., 14 Pick. 491, where the defendants, being the owners of a factory and pond, made a written contract with one B, by which B was to run the defendant's mill for one year, and to manufacture for the defendant, at a specified price, cotton furnished by the defendant and to keep the mill in good running order at his own expense, except the main gearing which was to be repaired by the defendant if necessary; and no rent was to be charged by the defendant, and he was not to be called upon for any expense unless the main gearing should fail or some injury should arise to the dam; and several acres of land where the factory stood with the factory houses, and blacksmith shops were to be used by B. The plaintiff sustained injury in consequence of B's letting off the water from the pond so rapidly as to overflow the plaintiff's land. The court, in deciding that B was the lessee and not the servant of the defendant, and consequently that the defendant was not responsible for the injury complained of, said at pages 493 and 494: "... whatever words are sufficient to explain the intent of the parties, that one shall divest himself of the possession, and the other come into it for such a determinate time, such words whether they run in the form of a license, covenant, or agreement, are of themselves sufficient and will in construction of the law amount to a lease for years. "[B] was to keep the factory in repair, except that the defendant [was] to repair the main gearing if it should be necessary; [B] was to have the possession, for the purpose of doing what he had stipulated to perform; he had the control of the factory, and he could employ what servants he would,

§11 

AGENCY 

and regulate their wages; he might determine how much water could be turned upon the mill; he was entitled to the use of the land about the factory, and to the buildings thereon; and whether these buildings were let to laborers employed by him, or to others, rent would probably be paid to him, either in a diminution of wages or otherwise. These provisions are appropriate in the case of a lease. "The words 'that no rent is to be charged by the company' also tend to prove that the letting was contemplated. ... '. . . the defendant received rent in the price at which [his] goods were manufactured. [B] was not the servant sion of the premises mentioned in their agreement, and conof the defendant, but his lessee, having the control and possessequently. . . the defendant [is] not liable to the plaintiff in this action."

The fact that a person is termed the agent of the landlord is not enough to do away with the legal results of stipulations in an agreement of letting which create the relation of landlord and tenant. 

Stewart v. Putnam, 127 Mass. 403, at 407

So, where the defendant entered into an agreement with one providing that he should have the right to lease all the vacant parts of the premises and to receive the rents thereof as well as the rents of the parts already let; and then this lease was terminated and a new lease was executed where the right to collect all the rents and lease the premises as before remained the only distinction between the original and subsequent leases being that the original lessee was relieved from paying taxes and from making outside repairs and that he should pay such rent for the property as the defendants should have received for the whole year as though the lease had not been terminated, it was held that this agreement amounted practically to a lease to G for three months of that part of the property not let to tenants and the reversion of the part which was let, and the fact that G was termed the agent of the defendants was not enough to do away with the legal results of the stipulations of the agreement. 

Stewart v. Putnam, 127 Mass. 403

§2 

 4. Between Principal and Agent and Master and Servant 

The agent is clothed with a greater discretion as to the means to be adopted, while the servant is bound to perform his service in the manner commanded by the master. 

Singer Man. Co. v. Rahn, 132 U. S. 518 

An agent is a representative vested with authority, real or ostensible, to create voluntary primary obligations for his principal, by making contracts with third person, or by making promises or representations to third persons calculated to induce them to change their legal position. 

A servant is a representative vested with authority to perform operative acts for his master not creating new primary obligations, or bringing third persons into contractual relations with the master, or otherwise causing them to change their legal position. 

The principal appoints the agent while the master employs the servant.

The relation of principal and agent contemplates relations with third persons, while the relation of master and servant does not necessarily contemplate such relations, though it may do so. The servant may incidentally or accidentally come in contact with third persons in performing the service, while the agent necessarily must come into such contact.

Agency, in its legal sense, always imports commercial dealings between parties through the medium of another. An agent negotiates with third parties in commercial matters for another, while the word servant relates more to matters of manual or mechanical execution.

The words "agent" and "servant" in a general sense both apply to persons on the service of another; but in the legal sense an agent is one who stands in the place of his principal-his representative—while a servant is one in the master's employment but not clothed with any representative character. 

As used in the Massachusetts statutes the term "agents" is much wider in its significations than servants or clerks. The latter are restricted to the performance of specific acts in a specific way; the former may or may not be restricted, and may in fact, be clothed

§13 

AGENCY 

with full power to represent their principal with the same discretion he might exercise himself. 

5. Partnership

Mutual agency is the result of partnership, not partnership the result of mutual agency.

In Meehan v. Valentine, 145 U. S. 611, the court said, at page 622: "As has been pointed out in later English cases, the reference to agency as a test of partnership was unfortunate and inconclusive inasmuch as agency results from partnership rather than partnership from agency. . . . Such a test seems to give a synonym, rather than a definition; another name for the conclusion rather than a statement of the premises from which the conclusion is to be drawn. To say that a person is liable as a partner who stands in the relation of a principal to those by whom the business is actually carried on adds nothing by way of precision for the very idea of partnership includes the relation of principal and agent." 

A contract of partnership is a contract of agency, and it differs from a pure agency only in this; that in a pure agency the agent binds his principal only; in a partnership all of the principals or partners are bound, which, of course, includes the actor. 

A partner virtually embraces the character of both principal and agent.

So far as he acts for himself and his own interests in the common concern of the partnership he may properly be deemed a principal, and so far as he acts for his partners he may as properly be deemed an agent. 

6. Trusteeship

A trustee is not an agent. An agent represents and acts for his principal, who may be either a natural or artificial person. A trustee may be defined generally as a person in whom some estate, interest, or power in or affecting property is vested for the benefit of another. 

Taylor v. Davis, 110 U. S. 330, at 334

§3 

In Shepard v. Abbott, 179 Mass. 300, where a mortgagee placed the money for which the mortgage was given in the hands of the broker through whom the loan was negotiated, to be paid out for building material on the order of the mortgagor, the broker was not an agent of the mortgagee os as to bind him by accepting a bill of exchange drawn by the mortgagor on the broker as trustee of the fund.

A trustee who makes a contract binds himself and not the cestui que trust. 

Shepard v. Abbot, 179 Mass. 300 

Everett v. Drew, 129 Mass. 150

When an agent contracts in the name of his principal, the principal contracts and is bound but the agent is not. When a trustee contracts as such, unless he is bound, no one is bound for he has no principal; and the contract is therefore the personal undertaking of the trustee. He is personally bound by the contracts he makes as trustee even when designating himself as such. 

See cases just cited above.

Section 3 C. CLASSES OF AGENTS 

Agents and agencies are divided into several classes. 

The most important classification of agents is universal, general and special agent, being based upon the nature and extent of the authority conferred upon them. 

When an agent is authorized to do all acts for his principal which can lawfully be delegated to an agent, he is deemed to be a universal agent. The agent has universal authority so far as it is possible for a principal to grant the same.

When the agent is authorized to do all acts pertaining to a business of a certain kind at a particular place, or all the acts of a particular class or service, he is deemed to be a general agent. 

A general agency exists where there is a delegation to do all acts connected with a particular trade, business or employment. 

A general agent is one authorized to transact all his principal's business, or all his business of a particular kind,

§15 

AGENCY 

A general agent is usually a person to whom the principal has entrusted the management of a particular business, such as an estate agent, or the manager of a business. 

An agent authorized to do some particular act or to act on some particular occasion is a special agent. Such an agent acts usually in accordance with specific instructions of the principal or under limitations, which the nature of the act to be done necessarily implies.

A special agency properly exists, when there is a delegation of authority to do a single act.

A special agent is one authorized to do one or two special things. 

A special agent is authorized to act only in a single transaction. 

A special agent is one given authority to deliver a particular message or buy or sell a particular thing on one occasion or do some special thing, and has no implied authority arising from his position or the nature of his business. 

There is a distinction between the general and special agents, as was said in Butler v. Maples, 9 Wall. (U. S.) 766, at 770: "The distinction between a general and a special agency is in most cases a plain one. The purpose of the latter is a single transaction, or a transaction with designated persons.

It does not leave to the agent any discretion as to the persons with whom he may contract for the principal, if he be empowered to make more than one contract. Authority to buy for a principal a single article of merchandise by one contract, or to buy several articles from a person named, is a special agency; but authority to make purchases from any persons with whom the agent may chose to deal, or to make an indefinite number of purchases, is a general agency. And it is not the less a general agency because it does not extend over the whole business of the principal. "A man may have many general agents-one to buy cotton, another to buy wheat and another to buy horses. So he may have a general agent to buy cotton in one neighborhood, and another general agent to buy cotton in another neighborhood.

§3  

The distinction between the two kinds of agencies is, that the one is created by power given to do acts of a class, and the other by power given to do individual acts only. Whether, therefore, an agency is general or special is wholly independent of the question whether the power to act within the scope of the authority given is unrestricted, or whether it is restrained by instructions or conditions imposed by the principal relative to the mode of its exercise."

AGENCY J. DUTIES AND LIABILITIES OF AGENT TO PRINCIPAL 2. Gratuitous Undertakings b. Agent Given Possession of Property 

A gratuitous agent is liable to his principal if he negligently or disobediently deals with property of which he has received possession.

In Jenkins v. Bacon, 111 Mass. 373, the principal, on the point of starting upon a long voyage requested the defendant agent to buy a government bond and keep it for him. The agent was to receive nothing for his services. The agent bought the bond, and after keeping it a year, sent it by mail to the principal's wife, and it was lost on the way. Neither the principal nor his wife requested the agent to send the bond to her. The agent was held liable for the bond, without regard to the question of diligence on his part. The court said at pages 376, 377, 378 and 379: "In that class of bailments described in the text books under the title of 'deposits', the obligation of the bailee [agent] is that he will keep the thing deposited with reasonable care, and that he will upon request restore it to the depositor [principal], or otherwise deliver it according to the original trust. "According to the well settled rule, the bailee [agent] who acts without compensation can only be held responsible for bad faith, or gross negligence, if the deposit should be lost or injured while in his custody. 

Whitney v. Lee, 8 Met. 91 

Foster v. Essex Bank, 17 Mass. 479 "Except as to the degree of diligence and care required to him, his general obligation is the same as if he assumed the trust upon the promise or with the expectation of reward. "If he should deliver the property to person not authorized to receive it, he would make himself responsible for its value, without regard to the question of due care or the degree of negligence. 

Cass v. Boston & Lowell R. R., 14 Allen 448, at 453 

Hall v. Boston & Worcester R. R., 14 Allen 439 

Lichtenbein v. Boston & Providence R. R., 11 Cush. 70 "In this instance, the transaction was more than a simple deposit for safe keeping. The plaintiff claimed, and there was evidence to the effect that the defendant was to collect the coupons as they became due for the benefit of the plaintiff's wife. The bond was delivered to the defendant in trust; 

Duties and Liabilities, 2.b.

AGENCY 

he accepted the trust and entered upon its performance. “The owner's trusting him with the goods is a sufficient consideration to oblige him to a careful management.' "Notwithstanding the gratuitous character of the bailment, 'it is held that the bailor has a remedy, in an action ex contractu, if the bailee does not perform his undertaking, and that there is a sufficient consideration to support a contract.' "A mere agreement to undertake a trust in futuro without compensation is not obligatory; but when once undertaken and the trust actually entered upon, the bailee is bound to perform it according to the terms of his agreement. "The substance of the defendant's contract and duty was to keep the deposit with reasonable care, and to restore it when properly called upon. We do not interpret this contract as restricting him to one place or uniform mode of keeping. All that could reasonably be expected of him was that he should keep it with his own papers, and in the same manner and with the same degree of care, as a man of ordinary prudence would exercise in the custody of papers of his own of like character. "Circumstances might occur which would render it reasonable and proper that he should change the place of deposit. If his own place of business should be destroyed by fire, or if, from change of residence or temporary absence from the country, or for other sufficient reason, it should become inconvenient or unsafe that he should retain the manual possession of the bond, he would undoubtedly be at liberty to deposit it in any other place or mode, in which he with reasonable prudence might deposit his own property of the like description. "But, as between the original depositor and himself, he would continue to be the lawful and responsible custodian, and bound to practise that degree of care which the law requires of gratuitous bailees. The complaint against him is, not that he kept it negligently, or lost it by gross carelessness, but he intentionally disposed of it in a manner not authorized by the terms of the trust. For the purposes of this case, it is wholly immaterial whether the post-office furnishes a reasonably safe mode of transmission, in the case of valuable papers of such a description, or not. if the defendant had delivered the bond by mistake to a person not entitled to receive it, he would make himself responsible, without regard to the question of due care, or degree of negligence. His duty was to keep the deposit; he

It will not be contended that the case shows any express authority for sending it by mail to the plaintiff's wife, and certainly none can be implied from the circumstances. In so doing, he subjected the plaintiff to a risk which he had not contemplated, and did an act not authorized by the terms of his trust. It was left to the jury to say whether, in the words of the presiding judge, it was 'a disposition of the bond contrary to the original understanding,' whereby the defendant lost it."

Extent of Duty and Liability (III) Doubtful Matters of Fact 

When the principal specifies, or is in control of, the precautions to be taken to determine the existence of certain facts or conditions, the principal bears the risk of error in the ascertainment of those facts or conditions. 

In these circumstances the principal, and not the agent, takes the risk of reasonable mistakes of facts. The agent is not liable in the absence of negligence. 

Richardson v. Taylor, 136 Mass. 143 (Bookkeeper acting carefully was not liable for mistake in ascertaining amounts due upon dissolution of partnership.)

But in the delivery of property entrusted to the agent the risk of proper delivery falls on the agent and the exercise of ordinary care by the agent is immaterial. 

Baer v. Slater, 261 Mass. 153, at 155 (Salesman in executing principal's instructions to return samples by express gave same in good faith to an impostor.)

AGENCY (IV) Doubtful Matters of Law 

Although an agent is liable to his principal for damage caused by want of reasonable skill and ordinary diligence in the exercise of his agency, the agent is not liable for damage caused by his mistakes in doubtful matters of law. 

Mechanics' Bank v. Merchants' Bank, 6 Met. 13

So, where an agent acts improperly in the performance of his authorization as shown by later events because of an error of law which he might reasonably make, the agent is not thereby liable to the principal. 

Mechanics' Bank v. Merchants' Bank, 6 Met. 13

In the last cited case the court said, at pages 26, 27, 28 and 29: "But it does not by any means follow, because the plaintiffs have lost their remedy over against the indorsers, for want of due presentment and demand being made by the defendants on the promisors, and due notice thereof given to the indorsers, that such proof alone is sufficient to enable the plaintiffs to sustain this action. "This fact must undoubtedly be proved; but it is necessary further to prove, that this result was attributable directly to such neglect and want of due skill of the defendants, as in law is sufficient to render them responsible. et 'Although, says Mr. Chief Justice Marshall, in the case of 

Bank of Washington v. Triplett, 1 Pet. 36, the liability of the bank, charged with negligence, will depend on the question, whether the liability of the drawer or indorser has been discharged by want of demand and notice; the bank was the agent of the holder, and not of the drawers, and might consequently so act as to discharge the drawer, without becoming liable to its principal. "The rule of law, we think is stated with sufficient accuracy in a recent case, and it is this: where a bank receives a note for collection, it is bound to use reasonable skill in making the collection, and for that purpose is bound to make a seasonable demand on the promissor, and in case of dishonor to give due notice to the indorsers, so that the security of the holder shall not be lost or essentially impaired, by the discharge of the indorsers. 

Fabens v. Mercantile Bank, 23 Pick. 330 "As an agent, such bank is bound to the use of reasonable skill and ordinary diligence. By reasonable skill is understood such as is ordinarily possessed and exercised by persons 

Duties and Liabilities, 3.a.(IV)

AGENCY 

of common capacity, engaged in the same business or employment; and by ordinary diligence is to be understood that degree of diligence, which persons of common prudence are accustomed to use about their own affairs. "This is applicable to a great variety of employments, requiring a considerable degree of care and skill; as attorneys, insurance brokers, factors, surgeons and so of all similar employments. "In general, the rules of law in regard to the presentment of bills of exchange and promissory.notes for payment, and for giving notice to indorsers, in case of dishonor, are too plain and simple, so well known by notaries public, cashiers of banks, attorneys and brokers, that any failure to comply with them, by an agent, acting in behalf of another, would carry with it such proof of either want of skill or want of ordinary diligence, as to render him liable to his principal. "It is therefore often laid down in general terms, that when the holder of a bill or note has lost his remedy, by these means, against a responsible party, and thereby sustained damage, he has his remedy against his agent. "But the specific question to be considered is, whether in all cases an agent is bound to know the rules of law, and conform to them at his peril, in the transaction of his employer's business, although the course of proceeding may depend upon statute provisions so recently passed as not to be generally known, or decisions of those courts whose judgments are usually regarded as precedents and rules of practice, either not promulgated at the time, or so recently given, as not to be generally known among business men. "It is undoubtedly a salutary maxim, that every man is bound to know the law, and that ignorance of the law excuses no one; yet these maxims must be confined to the cases for which they were adopted. 

'... But the maxim has no application to the duty of an agent, of whom ordinary skill only is required. Reasonable skill and knowledge only is demanded in every other branch of science; why should absolute knowledge and consummate skill be required in a department, where it is often impossible to know the law in its application to a particular state of facts, until it has been authoritatively declared?"

AGENCY 7. Duty to Act Only as Authorized and to Obey Instructions a. General Statement 

It is the first duty of an agent, whose authority is limited to adhere faithfully to his instructions, in all cases to which they can be properly applied. If he exceeds or violates or neglects them, he is responsible for all losses which are the natural consequence of his act. 

Whitney v. Merchants' etc. Co., 104 Mass. 152, at 154

An agent is liable for any damage to the principal caused by the agent's knowingly performing any unauthorized acts whether or not those acts are contrary to specific instructions of the principal. 

It is immaterial that the agent intends to act for the best interests of the principal and is of the opinion that his acts are the most proper or expedient. 

Coker v. Roper, 125 Mass. 577

Also it is unimportant that the agent reasonably could have believed his acts to be the best suited for his principal's interests, if the limitations on his authority had not been made. 

In the performance of such unauthorized acts the agent assumes all risk of loss to the principal. The agent's position is that of an insurer of the success of his unauthorized acts. Therefore he is responsible to indemnify the principal for any loss caused thereby, irrespective of the manner or method of their performance. 

Jenkins v. Bacon, 111 Mass. 373 (Agent liable for loss of bond mailed without authority to principal's wife.) 

Gilbert v. Williams, 8 Mass. 51 (Attorney failed to make attachment as principal instructed.) 

In Whitney v. Merchant's Union Express Co., 104 Mass. 152, an express company, having received from the drawer, for collection, with instructions to return it at once if not paid, a draft for a sum overdue from the drawee to the drawer, with interest, presented it for payment, when the drawee declined to pay more than the principal sum. Thereupon the company, without collecting anything on the draft, agreed with him that they would hold it till he could inquire of the drawer as to the additional amount; and he wrote, the same day, making such inquiry, and adding, "The parties will hold the draft until I hear from you." Upon receiving a reply, in due course of mail, from the drawer, that the 

Duties and Liabilities, 7.a.

AGENCY 

additional sum was for interest, the drawee was, and for two days continued to be, ready to pay the draft, which the express company continued to hold but neglected again to present. The third day was Sunday; and on the fourth day he became insolvent. 

In holding the express company liable for the drawer's loss on the draft by the drawee's insolvency, the court said at page 156: "They trusted to others, instead of corresponding themselves with the plaintiffs, who in this matter are in no respect chargeable with neglect. The loss is wholly due to the neglect of the defendants, and must be borne by them."

AGENT'S LIABILITY 1. To Third Persons a. General Statement 

An agent does not become subject to liability for the nonperformance of a contract which he makes on behalf of a competent disclosed or partially disclosed principal when the agent has power to make a contract and bind the principal, but it does not follow as matter of law in every instance that there is no contractual relationship between the agent and the third person, if the agent is in fact active in behalf of an alleged principal.

Groce v. First Nat. Stores, Inc., 268 Mass. 210, at 213 

(Husband and wife.)

Such contractual relationship arises when (I) the agent has pledged his own responsibility; or (II) acted in his own name for an undisclosed principal.

Groce v. First Nat. Stores, Inc., 268 Mass. 210, at 213 

Brigham v. Herrick, 173 Mass. 460 

Welch v. Goodwin, 123 Mass. 71

In either case the agent makes himself personally liable and may enforce the contract, even though the principal has renounced it.

Groce v. First Nat. Stores, Inc., 268 Mass. 210, at 213 

Brigham v. Herrick, 173 Mass. 460 

Welch v. Goodwin, 123 Mass. 71

As between the agent and the third person, the agent of the undisclosed principal has the same rights and is subject to the same obligations as if he had not been acting for the undisclosed principal. 

Groce v. First Nat. Stores, Inc., 268 Mass. 210, at 213 

Buffington v. McNally, 192 Mass. 198 

Colburn v. Phillips, 13 Gray 64 

Kelly v. Barber, 211 New York 68, at 72

So, a contract may impose reciprocal rights and obligations upon the agent and the third person, which are not unaffected by the agency of that agent. 

Groce v. First Nat. Stores, Inc., 268 Mass. 210, at 214

However, in the case of a disclosed principal, the agent does not become liable for the nonperformance of the principal. 

Nor is the agent liable because the principal's nonperformance is due to the principal's incapacity to contract or perform. 

The rule may be otherwise when the agent knows or should know of the principal's lack of capacity and that the third party is ignorant thereof or deceived. 51

AGENCY 

Unless the agent indicates that he does not warrant his authority or that the third person knows that the agent has not the authority, an agent impliedly warrants that he has the authority, which he purports to exercise in making a contract, conveyance or representation on behalf of the principal, even though in fact he had no power to bind the principal thereby. 

Also, the agent is subject to liability in an action of tort for deceit to a third person who sustains loss by relying upon the agent's misrepresentation that he has authority to make the contract, conveyance or representation on behalf of the principal, when in fact he has no power to bind that principal thereby.

But if the agent sufficiently indicates or manifests that he does not warrant his authority and makes no tortious misrepresentation concerning his authority he does not become subject to liability to the third person, even though he, the agent, makes a contract, conveyance or representation on behalf of the principal, whom he has no power to bind thereby. b. Lack of Authority (I) 

Deceit, Misrepresentation, Warranty of Au thority.

The agent is liable in damages to a third person who is misled to his injury because the agent has not in fact the authority which he purports to exercise and these damages may include any loss that the third person suffered by reason of not having a valid contract. 

Mendelsohn v. Holton, 253 Mass. 362, at 365

Where a person, either expressly or by his conduct, invites another to engage with him upon the assertion that he is filling a certain character, and a contract is entered into upon that footing, he is liable to an action if he does not fill that character; but the liability arises not from the misrepresentation only, but from the invitation to act and from the acting in consequences of that invitation. 

Oliver v. Bank of England (1902), 21 Chancery 610

A person who induces another to contract with him as agent of a third party by an unqualified assertion of his being authorized to act as such agent, is answerable to the person who so contracts for any damages which he may sustain by reason of the assertion of the authority being untrue. This is not the case of a bare misstatement by a person not bound by any duty to give information. The fact that the professed 52

AGENCY 

agent honestly thinks that he has authority affects the moral character of his act, but moral innocence, so far as the person he has induced to contract, in no way aids such person or alleviates the inconvenience and damages which he sustains. 

The obligation arising in such a case is that a person professing to contract as agent for another, impliedly, if not expressly, undertakes to and promises the person who enters into such contract, upon the faith of the professed agent being duly authorized, that the authority which he professes to have does in point of fact exist. The fact of entering into the transaction with the professed agent, as such, is good consideration for the promise.

Colen v. Wright, 8 El. & Bl. (Eng.), 647 cited in 

Conant v. Alvord, 166 Mass. 311, at 315 where English cases are collected

But the third person cannot sue the agent on the contract which the agent makes in the name of an alleged principal, even though the agent made that contract without authority. 

Mendelsohn v. Holton, 253 Mass. 362, at 365

An action of tort is proper remedy against the agent, who without authority purports to contract in the name of an alleged principal. 

Mendelsohn v. Holton, 253 Mass. 362, at 365

To recover against an agent in tort on the ground that he purported to have authority to make a contract to bind an alleged principal, when in fact he had no such authority, it is incumbent upon a third person to prove: (A) That the agent made a contract in such form that the alleged principal would have been bound if the agent had the authority to act in the matter; (B)) That the third person believed the representation implied in the transaction that the agent had authority to act for the alleged principal in making the contract; and (C) That the third person acted upon that belief to his damage. 

Horowitz v. Slater & Sons, Inc., 265 Mass. 143, at 152 

In Magaw v. Beals, 242 Mass. 321 an action of tort in which the plaintiff recovered damages for being evicted from premises which she had occupied under a lease made to her by the defendant purporting to act as attorney for one Little. 

The court said, at page 323: "The defendant by assuming to act as the agent of Mr. Little, impliedly held himself out as having authority 53

AGENCY 

to lease in Little's name to the plaintiff. 

By so doing he made himself personally liable. And this is so, even if he knew of his lack of authority and assumed to act as if he were authorized, or whether he honestly was of opinion that he possessed authority when as matter of fact he had none. "And the defendant who acted with full knowledge of the title at the time of the demise, is estopped as between himself and the plaintiff from denying the validity of the execution of the lease."

In Peoples National Bank of Boston v. Dixwell, 217 Mass. 

436, at 437 an action in the nature of deceit against the defendant for signing the name of a corporation to a note without authority, the court said: "Whatever may be the rule elsewhere, it is settled in this Commonwealth that 'if the instrument purports to express the contract of the principal, the agent is not personally liable on it, but that the remedy in such a case against him is by an action upon the case for falsely representing himself to be authorized to bind his principal... 

In Conant v. Alvord, 166 Mass. 311, orders were drawn on a bank to the order of the plaintiff. The defendants accepted the orders as agent for the bank signing their name and describing themselves as "agents for the negotiation of the within mentioned loan." At the time the plaintiff called on the defendants and asked them if the orders were genuine and had some conversation with them with regard to their authority to act as agents for the Savings Bank. The defendants said that those were their signatures and that they were agents for the loan. 

The judge found: (1) That the defendants, knowing all the facts material thereto, represented themselves as the duly authorized agents of the Savings Bank to accept the drafts; (2) That the representation was untrue; and (3) That the plaintiff, relied on such representation and believing it, gave up his prior security and made further advances of materials and monies. 

At Page 315: 

The act of writing the words, "Accepted ... Cape Ann 

Savings Bank, by [the defendant agents]," was a representation that they had authority from the bank to accept the order. 54

AGENCY 

1 and the words added after their names cannot be said to set forth that they had no such authority.

They are to be construed as a descriptio personarum; and, reading the entire acceptance together, it is plain, that the defendants, describing themselves as "agents for the negotiation of the within mentioned loan," represented that they had authority to accept the orders for the Cape Ann Savings Bank. 

This representation has been found to be untrue. 

As the plaintiff relied upon the representation, and has suffered injury from the breach of the representation, he has a right of action for such breach, irrespective of the question of fraud on the part of the defendants. This rule of law is well settled.

In Nash v. Minnesota Title Ins. & Trust Co., 163 Mass. 

574 [Dissent of Holmes, J.] at 587: "Neither, in my opinion, are there any peculiar safeguards set up about the action for deceit. That action was given by the common law for any false statement of present facts of which the defendant took the risk, and which was followed by damage. He might take the risk at different points in different cases. A false warranty used to be laid as a deceit in tort for a false and fraudulent representation. So even an implied warranty yet it was not necessary to lay the scienter, or if you laid it, to prove it, for the plain reason, as Shaw, C. J. puts it, in substance, that the plaintiff is answerable for the facts, however honest he may have been." 

In Boston & Albany Railroad v. Richardson, 135 Mass. 473, the plaintiff sought to recover damages against the defendant who presented a forged transfer or power of attorney upon the faith of which the plaintiff issued to the defendant a new certificate of stock. The court said at pages 475 and 476: "So it has been held that, if one, honestly believing himself to be authorized, acts as agent for another, and procures money or goods upon the credit of his supposed principal, and it turns out that he is not authorized, he is liable for the value of the money or goods. .... "We do not understand [Chief Justice Shaw] as intending to say that the only remedy is the technical action of deceit, and that a guilty knowledge must be proved. 

He used the word 'deceit' in the sense of tort..... "We can see no good reason why an action of contract upon the implied warranty should not be maintained, in 55

the same manner as it may be upon in the sale of chattels. 

the implied warranty 

But it is not necessary to discuss this, because in the case at bar there is both a count in contract and a count in tort in the nature of case, for falsely assuming to act as an agent." 

In May v. Western Union Telegraph Company, 112 Mass. 

90 where defendant delivered a message without authority re questing the plaintiffs to send certain goods to their partners, the court said at pages 94 and 95: "A statement by a person that he is authorized to do a certain act cannot be said to be a promise, and does not constitute a contract; and it does not change the character of the act to call it a promise. "It is merely a representation; there may be an action for false representation, but not for a breach of the representation, as for a breach of a contract. "In an action against a telegraph company for delivering a message never sent, and alleging that the defendant falsely represented that it was authorized to deliver such a message, and thereby causing the plaintiffs to send goods and suffer damage, it is not necessary to allege that it was done with intent to deceive or that it was false within the knowledge of the defendant. It is not an action for deceit. It is an action in the nature of a false warranty against one acting as agent, who represents that he has authority when he has not. "Whether such representation is made in terms, or tacitly and impliedly, he supposing but not knowing the fact to be true, he is liable to the person misled. "Nor in such an action for false representations is it necessary for the plaintiffs to allege and prove that they used due care and diligence to ascertain if the representations were true.” 

In Bartlett v. Tucker, 104 Mass. 336, the plaintiff sought to hold the defendant in contract on notes which he signed in the name of another without authority. The court in an opinion by Gray, J., said:

At Page 339: 

"If a person signs the name of another, as maker of a promissory note, who has not authorized him to do so, and who therefore is not bound by the signature, the signer is not personally liable in an action of contract upon the note itself, even if he signs his own name also as 56

that of the agent affixing the other signature, and the party whose name he assumes to put to the note is incapable of making such a contract; but only in an action of tort for falsely representing himself to be authorized to sign the name of the other person. This rule has been asserted and steadfastly maintained by this court for half a century.

At Page 342: 

"In such a case, it is clear that by the law of this Commonwealth, as shown by the cases already cited, the defendant could not be sued in contract upon the note, but only in tort." 

In Draper v. Massachusetts Steam Heating Co., 5 Allen 

338, the court in an opinion by Hoar, J., said: 66 ....in this Commonwealth it is settled that if the instrument purports to express the contract of the principal, the agent is not personally liable upon it; but that the remedy in such a case against him is by an action on the case for falsely representing himself to be authorized to bind his principal." 

In Trowbridge v. Scudder, 11 Cush. 83, at 86 and 87 the notes, on their face, though signed by the treasurer of the company, are not his notes, but legally purport to be the notes of the company. But, admitting that the company is not liable on these notes, as a corporation, yet it does not follow that its members are liable in a suit thereon. They may or may not be liable to the plaintiff, in some form of action, according to circumstances. The members of a corporation may doubtless so manage its concerns as to render themselves personally responsible to those with whom they deal. If they, in the name of the corporation, give notes which the corporation is not bound to pay, and which it refuses to pay, they may, in many supposable cases, be held to indemnify the holders of such notes. The remedy against them however, should not be by an action on the notes, but by an action of tort, as is the remedy against one who signs a note as agent for another, without authority.

In Jefts v. York, 10 Cush. 392, where one who purported to be an agent gave a promissory note in the body of which the alleged principal promised to pay a certain sum and was signed in the name of the principal by the purported agent, the court said at 394 and 395: "......by the law of Massachusetts, contrary to the rule in some other states, a person, professing to act as 57

AGENCY 

agent for another party, but either in law or in fact having no authority to bind such party, he does not necessarily bind himself. ..... "....where a person acting as agent borrows money for his principals, and gives their obligation for it, and it turns out that the principals were not of legal capacity to make such contract, and of course could confer no such power on another, the agent is not personally liable on the contract, as his contract. "But if in fact he was not so authorized, but under a belief that he was, and acted on such belief, and the party advancing the money did not know that he was not authorized, the agent would be liable in an action of the case, to an amount in damages equal to the sum advanced. "If one falsely represents that he has an authority, by which another, relying on the representation, is misled, he is liable; and by acting as agent for another, when he is not, though he thinks he is, he tacitly and impliedly represents himself authorized without knowing the fact to be true, it is in the nature of a false warranty, and he is liable. "But in both cases his liability is founded on the ground of deceit, and the remedy is by action of tort. "But if the defect of authority arises from a want of legal capacity, and if the parties act under a mutual mistake of the law, and are both equally well informed in regard to the facts so that the lender is not misled by any word or act of the agent, he would have no legal remedy against the agent; not in assumpsit, for it is not his contract; not in tort, for he is chargeable with no deceit."

In Abbey v. Case, 6 Cush. 54 where an agent executed, as such, a sealed instrument, purporting to be a deed of his property, the court said at 56 and 57: "When one who has no authority to act as another's agent, assumes so to act, and makes either a deed or a simple contract, in the name of the other, he is not personally liable on the covenants in the deed, or on the promise in the simple contract, unless it contains apt words to bind him personally....... The only remedy against him, in this Commonwealth, is an action on the case for falsely assuming authority to act as agent."

58

AGENCY 

In Jefts v. York, 4 Cush. 371, the agent signed a promissory note for a church without authority. The court said at 

"The only legal remedy was an action for falsely representing himself as an agent authorized to execute the contract for the principal in whose name he professed to act. 

This action cannot therefore be maintained, as upon a promise by the [agent].

In Inhabitants of Webster v. Larned, 6 Met. 522, the court said at 527, 528 and 529: "The declaration alleges that the defendant falsely and deceitfully represented himself as an agent of the Town of D and authorized by said town to enter into a contract with the plaintiffs for the erection of a certain bridge.. whereby the plaintiffs were induced to expend a large sum of money, which the town of Dudley not being liable to refund, refused so to do. .... "To maintain this action, the plaintiffs must prove that the defendant made the false affirmation or representation,, as alleged in the declaration and that the plaintiffs, giving credit thereto, having incurred a liability whereby they have been subjected to a loss or damage. 66 .does not appear that the defendant represented himself as agent of the Town of D, authorized by them to make the contract, as alleged. He assumed to act as one of the selectmen of the Town of D; and if he mistook his authority, we would not support the charge against him of fraud or deceit, although it might perhaps make him liable on an implied promise. "Another objection to the action remains, which is well founded......the Town of D was not authorized to build any part of the bridge in question." 

In Ballou v. Talbot, 16 Mass. 461 where an agent without authority gave a note, the court said at 463: "The legal inference from this fact [that the defendant had no authority to sign the note for the alleged principal] is, not that it became his promise directly, but that he is answerable in damages for acting without authority. "....in such a case, a special action upon the case would be the proper action. .... ..If [the agent] was sued for falsely assuming an authority, he might defend himself by showing that the person, for whom he assumed to act, had afterwards rati- 59

AGENCY 

fied his act, or that he otherwise satisfied the debt for which the note was given, or, perhaps he might show that no debt was due for which the note was given, or that he had authority to make it. It is, in short, a proper subject for a special action, in which damages would be recovered according to the injuries sustained." 

In Long v. Colburn, 11 Mass. 97, the court said at 98: 2. "It appears upon the face of the note itself, that the present defendant was not to be considered as the promisor. He signed his own name, Pro W. G.; and the plaintiff's remedy is against G, if the defendant had authority to make the promise for him and if he had not, a special action of the case might make the defendant answerable." (II) As to Negotiable Instruments

In the law of negotiable instruments (Gen. Laws, C. 107, Sec. 42) when the agent merely describes himself as such, the negotiable instrument becomes his personal obligation, for the reference to the fact that he is an agent is merely descriptio personarum. 

Dunham v. Blood, 207 Mass. 512 (Trustee as such gave note to borrow money in bchalf of trust.)

Tuttle v. First Nat. Bank of Greenfield, 187 Mass. 533 

Plimpton v. Goodell, 126 Mass: 120 (The word administrator followed the name of the payee.)

Ballou v. Talbot, 16 Mass. 461

AIRCRAFT E. CAUSING INJURIES AND DEATH FROM OPERATION 1. Reciprocal Rights and Duties a. General Statement 

The rules of law relating to the operation of aircraft, in the absence of statute, in general are rules relating to negligence and nuisance, and are not distinguishable from those which relate to the operation of vehicles, perhaps more closely to motor vehicles on land.

In this Commonwealth at present there is no statute specifically applicable to the issue of negligence in the operation of aircraft, and the ordinary rules of negligence and due care obtain. 

Wilson v. Colonial Tr. Inc., 1932 A. S. 443, at 447 

See: St. 1922, c. 534, as amended by St. 1928, c. 388

There is at present no common knowledge of which courts can take cognizance concerning the customs or usual practice of air transport companies as to operation, inspection and repair of their airplanes. There must be evidence.

Wilson v. Colonial Tr. Inc., 1932 A. S. 443, at 448 

We are not as yet, in respect to the operation, care and characteristics of aircraft, in a position where the doctrine of cases like 

Ware v. Gay, 11 Pick. 106, as to a stage-coach, O'Neil v. Toomey, 218 Mass. 242, as to the qualities of ice, or Gilchrist v. Boston El. 

Ry., 272 Mass. 346, as to trolley cars or steam railroad trains, can be applied. The decision of cases of that nature rests upon facts constituting a part of a widespread fund of information. 

Wilson v. Colonial Tr. Inc., 1932 A. S., 443, at 448

AIRCRAFT H. CARE AS TO PERSONS 

15. Persons in or on Aircraft b. Passengers for Hire 

(I) Common Carriers 

The degree of care of a common carrier for hire is measurably greater than the law imposes on a private carrier for hire, and proof of the facts and surrounding circumstances need only be slight in order to set up the presumptive rule of negligence and call upon the defendant for an explanation; and in either case negligence will not be presumed from the mere happening of an accident.

Wilson v. Colonial Tr. Inc., 1932 A.S. 443, at 446 and 447 

DiLeo v. Eastern Mass. St. Ry., 255 Mass. 140

ALIMONY A. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS 7. Effect of Order by Courts of Sister State 

The defendant and the plaintiff are husband and wife accord ing to the averments of the bill. The obligation disclosed by the allegations of the bill on which the suit is founded is the judg ment of the court of a sister state. The scope and purpose of that judgment is solely the payment of money. It was settled by 

Purdon v. Blinn, 192 Mass. 387, at 389 after an exhaustive review of our authorities, that a decree for alimony for a gross sum established an obligation that "is plainly in the nature of a debt, and for most purposes it can fairly be called a debt." Commonly, action by a court ordering the payment of alimony is termed a decree. It is alleged in this bill to be a judgment. While a decree for alimony is not always accurately describable as a debt, Williamson v. Williamson, 246 Mass. 270, at 273 it seems clear that the allegations of the present bill set forth an obligation constituting a debt of record. 

Dorey v. Dorey, 248 Mass. 359, at 361 

Wells v. Wells, 209 Mass. 282, at 288 

Mclllroy v. Mclllroy, 208 Mass. 458 

Shepherd v. Shepherd, 196 Mass. 179

B. TEMPORARY 

6. 

Commencement and Continuance of Allowance 

The allowance of alimony pendente lite is described by the terminology. This allowance continues during the pendency of the libel in the court of original jurisdiction unless modified or revoked. 

Eldridge v. Eldridge, 1932 A. S. 285, at 289 

10. Modification of Allowance a. General Statement 

The power of the courts over alimony and the support and care of children in connection with divorce is broad. Extensive revision and alteration of previous decrees is authorized and exercised. 

Perkins v. Perkins, 225 Mass. 392, at 397 

Brown v. Brown, 222 Mass. 415

ALIMONY Parker v. Parker, 211 Mass. 139 Graves v. Graves, 108 Mass. 314 

Burrows v. Purple, 107 Mass. 428 

G. L. c. 208, s. 37, I. O.

Appropriate orders as to the support and care of children are an important part of the proceedings for divorce. They may be modified from time to time to meet changing conditions. 

b. Nunc Pro Tunc Order 

The order of the Superior Court that its modification of the earlier decree should be entered nunc pro tunc was within its power. Both parties were before the court. So far as their rights as to one another are concerned, they are concluded by the order. 

Perkins v. Perkins, 225 Mass. 392, at 397 and 398

In divorce proceedings it would be beyond the power of a court to establish, by the jury of a nunc pro tunc order authorizing the libellant to employ any physician she chose, a legal liability for such employment of a physician by her at a time when she had no such authority and could not pledge the credit of the libellee therefor. 

A liability to a third person for a debt for which there is no liability whatever cannot be wronght by the entry of such nunc pro tunc order. 

Perkins v. Perkins, 225 Mass. 392, at 398

C. PERMANENT 

8. Mode of Allowance b. Money Allowances (III) Allowances in Gross Sum A decree for alimony for a gross sum establishes an obligation that is in the nature of a debt and for most purposes it can be called a debt.

Weidman v. Weidman, 1931 A. S. 143, at 144 

Dorey v. Dorey, 248 Mass. 359 

Williamson v. Williamson, 246 Mass. 270, at 273 (Where a decree for alimony was not accurately described as a debt.)

Shepherd v. Shepherd, 196 Mass. 179, at 182 

Purdon v. Blinn, 192 Mass. 387, at 389

(I) Generally

The general rule is well established in this Commonwealth that a husband's duty to pay alimony for the support of his wife ceases with his death. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Tr. Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1377

C. 1

ALIMONY 

Stone v. Duffy, 219 Mass. 178, and cases cited at page 182 

Mcllroy v. Mcllroy, 208 Mass. 458 

Knapp v. Knapp, 134 Mass. 353 

(II) Effect of Decree (A) Assent of Parties 

The fact that both the husband and wife assent to the terms of the decree for alimony is of no importance for the effect of such assent would be to create an agreement between the husband and the wife as to alimony at the time of the entry of the decree, whether nisi or final, which would not be enforceable under Gen. Laws, c. 209, s. 2, as contracts between them would be a nullity. To enforce a decree because assented to would be on the theory that the court would decree specific performance of their contract, but this the court cannot do. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Tr. Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1378 

Oakes v. Oakes, 266 Mass. 150

For this reason it is immaterial what the parties themselves have in mind when they assent to a decree. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Trust Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1378

It is only the language of the court embodied in the decree that is to be interpreted. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Tr. Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1378 (B) Language of Decree 

(1) Extending Beyond Libellee's Life 

The court has the power to decree that the payment of alimony shall extend beyond the life of the libellee and that it shall be collected out of the assets of his estate. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Trust Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1378 

In Southard v. Southard, 262 Mass. 278, at 280 and 281, the decree for alimony provided that: "In the event of the death of the libellee during the life of the libellant before February 1, 1926, the amounts as above set forth shall be paid to the libellant out of his estate as a charge thereon. In the event of the death of the libellee during the life of the libellant after February 1, 1926, the sum of $583.33 shall be paid to the libellant out of the libellee's estate on the first day of each month as a charge thereon 2

ALIMONY 

10 77 until further order of this court," and the court said, at pages 

280 and 281: "[the parties] agreed upon the amount and extent of alimony. The court could in these circumstances decree that the alimony should extend beyond the life-time of the libellee."

When the decree expressly or impliedly makes this provision it is binding on the libellee's estate. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Trust Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1380 

(a) Express Provisions 

Where the language of the decree expressly states that the payment of alimony is to continue after the death of the libellee, the authorities hold that it will so continue. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Trust Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1379 

(b) By Implication 

The decree need not expressly provide that the alimony payments shall be made "out of the libellee's estate as a charge threon" but such requirement may arise from a reasonable inference. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Trust Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1379

So, where the decree provides that the libellee should pay to the libellant a certain sum each month "during the term of her life" there is a reasonable implication provided that the payments should continue to be made during the term of the life of the libellant, notwithstanding the death of the libellee before the death of the libellant. The libellant's rights under the decree do not end with the death of the libellee. 

Farrington v. Boston Safe Deposit & Trust Co., 1932 A. S. 

1375, at 1379
