DECLARATION 6. Subject Matter of Amendment k. Introducing New or Different Cause of Action (II) What Constitutes (H) Instances Held to be (1) Count Under Federal Employer's Liability Act After Statute of 

Limitations Has Run

A cause of action arising under the Federal Employer's Liability Act is a different cause from one based upon our Massachusetts statute, and an amendment adding to allegations confined to the latter, allegations under the former, introduce a new cause of action, and cannot properly be allowed after the Federal statute of limitations, which limits actions to two years after the death. 

Hughes v. Gaston, 1932 A. S. 2215, at 2217

Renaldi v. New York Central R. R., 256 Mass. 337 

This rule applies only where the declaration before amendment is complete and asserts a cause of action under the Massachusetts statute, without disclosing facts which make out a case under the 

Federal statute. 

Hughes v. Gaston, 1932 A. S. 2215, at 2217

But such an amendtment properly may be allowed when it is merely amplification of allegations in the earlier declaration which discloses a cause of action under the Federal Act. 

Hughes v. Gaston, 1932 A. S. 2215, at 2217 

Baltimore & Ohio R. R. v. Carroll, 280 U. S. 491 

N. Y. Central & Hudson R. R., v. Kinney, 260 U. S. 340 

Seaboard Air Line v. Renn, 241 U. S. 290, at 293

ASSAULT AND BATTERY A. DEFINITIONS 

1. Assault 

An assault is an unlawful physical force partly or fully put in motion, which creates a reasonable apprehension of immediate physical injury. 

Comm. v. White, 110 Mass. 407, at 408 (Pointing unloaded shotgun was)

An assault is an intentional attempt by force to injure the person of another. 

Cluff v. Ins. Co., 13 Allen, 308, at 317 

Comm. v. Ordway, 12 Cush. 270

The definition of assault is an attempt or offer with force and violence to do injury to a person either from malice or wantonness. 

Comm. v. Ruggles, 6 Allen, 588, at 591 

2. Battery

A battery is committed whenever the menaced violence of an assault is done in the least degree to the person. 

Cluff v. Ins. Co., 13 Allen, 308, at 317

Battery is where an injury is actually inflicted with force and violence to a person either from malice or wantonness. 

Comm. v. Ruggles, 6 Allen, at 591

Every touching of another's person, wilfully or in anger, without his consent, is technically a battery, unless justifiable. 

Commonwealth v. Clark, 2 Met. 23, 24 

3. Assault and Battery

Assault and battery is the intentional and unjustified use of force upon the person of another however slight, or the intentional doing of a wanton or grossly negligent act causing personal injury to another. 

Comm. v. McCan, 277 Mass. 199, at 203 

Comm. v. Arone, 265 Mass. 128, at 131 

Comm. v. Hawkins, 157 Mass. 551, at 553 

Comm. v. McKie, 1 Gray, 61, at 63

A-1

ASSAULT AND BATTERY 

An assault and battery consists in the unlawful and unjusti fiable use of force and violence upon the person of another, however slight. If justifiable, it is not an assault and battery. 

Comm. v. McKi?, 1 Gray, 61, at 63 "Where there is physical injury to another person, it is sufficient that the cause is set in motion by the defendant, it cannot be material whether it acts upon the person injured externally, by mechanical or chemical force." 

Commonwealth v. Stratton, 114 Mass. 303.

Under Contract Not in Existence General Statement 

(B) Wages

An assignment is void which purports to assign money, to be earned in futuro under the terms of a contract, that at the time the assignment is executed and delivered, is not in existence. 

Commercial Co. v. Murphy, 1933 A. S. 339, at 343 

Raulins v. Levi, 232 Mass. 42 

Citizens' Loan Assoc. v. Boston Co., 196 Mass. 528 

Egan v. Luby, 133 Mass. 543 

Herbert v. Bronson, 125 Mass. 475 

Lightbody v. Smith, 125 Mass. 51 

Twiss v. Cheever, 2 Allen, 40 

Mulball v. Quinn, 1 Gray, 105

But when the contract and the assignment of its payments are executed and delivered concurrently and are essential parts of one transaction, the assignment is valid. 

Commercial Co. v. Murphy, 1933 A. S. 339, at 343

So, where the undertakings are so interrelated as to constitute one transaction and the assignment does not become effective as a binding obligation upon the debtor until the contract is executed, the assignment and contract are so interrelated as to constitute a single transaction. 

Commercial Co. v. Murphy, 1933 A. S. 339, at 343

Wages to be earned under an engagement existing at the time of giving the order are assignable; but not money to be thereafter earned under a new engagement. 

Raulins v. Levi, 232 Mass. 42 

Hartley v. Tapley, 2 Gray, 565, at 566

E-1

ASSIGNMENTS 

The reason for this rule is future wages or earnings constitute a mere possibility not coupled with an interest. 

As was said in Low v. Pew, 108 Mass. 347, at 350: "It is equally well settled that it is sufficient if the seller has a potential interest in the thing sold. But a mere possibility or expectancy of acquiring property, not coupled with any interest does not constitute a potential interest in it, within the meaning of this rule. The seller must have a present interest in the property, of which the thing sold is the product, growth, or increase. Having such interest, the right to the thing sold, when it shall come into existence, is a present vested right, and the sale of it is valid. Thus a man may sell the wool to grow upon his own sheep, but not upon the sheep of another; or the crops to grow upon his own land, but not upon land in which he has no interest. 

Jones v. Richardson, 10 Met. 481

The same principles have been applied by this court to the assignment of future wages or earnings.

In Mulhall v. Quinn, 1 Gray, 105, it was held that an assignment of future wages, there being no contract of service, was held invalid. 

In Hartley v. Tapley, 2 Gray, 565, it was held that, if a person is under a contract of service, he may assign his future earnings growing out of such contract. The distinction between the cases is that in the former the future earnings are a mere possibility, coupled with no interest, while in the latter the possibility of future earnings is coupled with an interest, and the right to them, though contingent and liable to be defeated, is a vested right. "In the case at bar, the sellers, at the time of the sale, had no interest in the thing sold. There was a possibility that they might catch halibut; but it was a mere possibility and expectancy, coupled with no interest. We are of opinion that they had no actual or potential possession of, or interest in, the fish; and that the sale to the plaintiffs was void." E-2

ATTACHMENTS Q. DISSOLUTION 

1. 

General Statement 

Gen. Laws, c. 223, s. 114, is designed to provide a speedy and summary hearing for relief against excessive or unreasonable attachments. But it is a proceeding incidental to the action in which the attachments has been made. 

Richardson v. Greenhood, 225 Mass. 608, at 609

Such an action begins on the date of the writ. 

Richardson v. Greenhood, 225 Mass. 608, at 609

When the writ has not been entered in court, either before or after the return day, a petition may be filed to reduce or discharge the attachment for the action is deemed to be pending and the petition is incidental to it. 

Richardson v. Greenhood, 225 Mass. 608, at 609

So, any order made on the petition relating to the attachment is an interlocutory order in the action. 

Richardson v. Greenhood, 225 Mass. 608, at 609

Q-la 

Additional Material, Page Q-2 7. Effect of Dissolution 8. Effect of Refusal to Dissolve Attachment 9. Review of Disposition of Petition or Motion 

No appeal from an interlocutory order relating to the discharge or the reduction of the attachment can be entered in the Supreme Judicial Court for there is no jurisdiction to consider. 

Richardson v. Greenhood, 225 Mass. 608, at 610 

Weil v. Boston El. Rlwy., 216 Mass. 545, at 546

If any question of law can be opened upon such a petition, the procedure (in the absence of a report by the presiding judge, John Hetherington & Sons, Ltd. v. Willis Firth Co., 212 Mass. 

257) would be to file a bill of exceptions, which, if allowed, would await the stage of the final disposition of the case, when it might be brought to the Supreme Judicial Court. 

Richardson v. Greenhood, 225 Mass. 608, at 610 

Brooks v. Shaw, 197 Mass. 376

Operation of Law (New) 

Appointment of Receiver 

(I) By Courts of This Commonwealth (A) Statutory Provisions 

G. L. c. 223, s. 130, provides that, "An attachment of property by mesne process shall be dissolved by the appointment by any court competent jurisdiction in the commonwealth of a receiver to take possession of such property, if the bill or petition praying for the appointment of such receiver is filed in said court within four months after such attachment was made, unless the court at any time in its discretion, continues such attachment for the benefit of the estate of the defendant. In such case, the court may authorize the receiver to prosecute the action upon which the attachment was made for the benefit of the estate of the defendant and may make further orders to enable the receiver to recover for its benefit the amount due to the plaintiff in the original action." 

G. L. c. 223, s. 131, provides that, "If the attachment has been dissolved in the manner provided in the preceding section, the proceedings for the appointment of a receiver shall not thereafter be dismissed and the receiver discharged until all the assets which have come into his hands as receiver have been fully distributed or the claim upon which the attachment was made has been fully paid and discharged, unless the debtor, before such dismissal, deposits with the officer who made the attachment such amount as the court before which such receivership proceedings are pending, after notice to the attaching creditor and a hearing, finds reasonable for the protection of his claim in the action in which the attachment was made. Such money shall be held by the officer in place of the property held under the attachment before its dissolution and shall be disposed of as such property would have been disposed of had the attachment not been dissolved.” Q-la

ATTACHMENTS (B) General Statement In Second National Bank v. J. C. Lappe Tanning Co., 198 

Mass. 159, an attachment which was less than four months old upon certain property of the defendant corporation was dissolved upon the appointment of an ancilliary receiver for the corporation in the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts. The court said at pages 160 and 161, "Under the law before the enactment of the St. 1898, c. 

420, the appointment of a receiver did not affect a previous attachment for a debt, but the attaching creditor retained his security.

Kittredge v. Osgood, 161 Mass. 384 

This statute (which now appears as G. L. Ter. Ed. c. 

223, ss. 130 and 131) was passed to compel such attaching creditors to share in the distribution with others, under the receivership which works a dissolution of the attachment. 

The second section, above referred to (which is now sec. 

131), secures to the attaching creditor either payment of his claim or a certainty of distribution in the proceedings before the court, whereby he will receive his share with the others." 

It was in Borden v. Enterprise Trans. Co., 198 Mass. 593, in consequence of this latter section that the court held that an attachment of property on mesne process is not dissolved by the appointment of a receiver to take possession of such property by the Circuit Court of the United States. The words of the statute 

Mass. G. L. c. 223, s. 130, "by any court of competent jurisdiction in this Commonwealth" were held to mean any court which is subject to the legislation of this Commonwealth, and the Massachusetts legislature has no power to control a federal court, or to interfere with its proceedings authorized by laws outside of this statute. 

Boyle v. Zacharie, 6 Pet. 648, at 658

A federal court might disregard sec. 131 as an attempt at unlawful interference with its rights and powers. Q-1b

ATTACHMENTS (II) By Federal Courts (A) Statutory Provisions U. S. Rev. St. s. 95, U. S. C. A. Title 28, s. 726, entitled "At tachments as provided by State law," provides that, "In common-law causes in the district courts the plaintiff shall be entitled to similar remedies, by attachment or other process, against the property of the defendant, which are now (were on June 1, 1872) provided by the laws of the State in which such court is held for the courts thereof; and such district courts may, from time to time, by general rule, adopt such State laws as may be in force in the States where they are held in relation to attachments and other process. 

Similar preliminary affidavits or proofs, and similar security, as required by such State laws, shall be first furnished by the party seeking such attachment or other remedy." 

Under this section, the method of making and prosecuting attachments in the federal court is governed by state laws. 

Russia Cement Co. v. Le Page Co., 174 Mass. 351 

U. S. Rev. St. s. 933, U. S. C. A. Title 28,, s. 746, entitled, "An act to make attachments which are made under process issuing from the courts of the United States conform to the laws regulating such attachments in the courts of the states," provides that, "An attachment of property, upon process instituted in any court of the United States, to satisfy such judgment as may be recovered by the plaintiff therein, except in the cases mentioned in the preceding nine sections (U. S. Rev. St. ss. 

924 to 933), shall be dissolved when any contingency occurs by which, according to the laws of the State where said court is held, such attachment would be dissolved upon like process instituted in the courts of said State. Nothing herein contained shall interfere with any priority of the United 

States in the payment of debts." 

(B) General Statement 

Attachments made on mesne process returnable to the courts of the United States sitting in Massachusetts are dissolved when- Q-1d

ATTACHMENTS 

ever, by the laws of the State, they would be dissolved had they been returnable before a court of the State. 

U. S. Rev. St. s. 915 standing alone would give rise to a strong argument that the federal courts would be bound to place attachments sued out of them upon the same footing with regard to all incidents thereto as like cases in the courts of the State. To make the matter clear, however, that such effect is to be given, U. S. 

Rev. St. s. 933 was enacted. From the latter section it seems to be clear that, wherever attachments in the state courts are affected after issuance by matters arising under other laws of the state, the federal courts would be bound to give the same effect to such matters as would be given them in the courts of the state in similar cases, and therefore that, where an attachment would be dissolved by some contingency under the state law, the same effect would naturally follow in the federal courts. 

A contingency arises in a Massachusetts statute which is provided for in U. S. Rev. St. s. 933, and was so constructed in 

M'Dermott v. Hayes, 197 Fed. 129

The plaintiff made an attachment on writs issued from the United States Circuit Court of Massachusetts on certain property of defendant. The defendant filed a motion for discharge of the attachment stating that, although the record title was in his name, he held the property under an oral trust for X. The plaintiff had no notice of the trust. A statute, Mass R. L. c. 147, s. 3 (Mass. G. L. Ter. Ed. c. 203, s. 3), provides that "no trust implied by law or declared by the parties shall prevent a creditor, having no notice of the trust, from attaching the property as if no trust existed," and he may attach the real estate of his debtor held by him under an oral trust of which plaintiff has no notice. The court held that U. S. Rev. St. ss. 915, 933, applied and the attachment was valid.

By U. S. Rev. St. s. 915 the federal court was granted authority to adopt the remedy by attachment provided by state laws. In 

Mather v. Nesbitt, 13 Fed. 872, an attachment issued from the Q-1c

ATTACHMENTS 

federal court and the defendant's property was seized by the 

United States marshal. By the insolvency statute of Minnesota, if the defendant subsequent to the attachment, made an assignment for the distribution of his property under said law, the attachment is dissolved. The court dissolved the attachment and ordered the United States marshal to turn over the property to the assignee, holding on page 873 that, "a state insolvent law which dissolves attachments under certain contingencies, dissolves attachments in the federal courts under similar contingencies. If the attachment had issued from the State court it would be dissolved; and it is clear that a contingency has arisen which is provided for in 

U. S. Rev. St. s. 933." 

Schwartz v. H. B. Claflin Co., 60 Fed. 676 

Newfeld v. Newfeld, 37 Fed. 560

It is seen that attachments sued out in the State courts of Massachusetts are not dissolved by the appointment of a receiver to take possession of the property, by a federal court sitting in the same State. It would seem that the purpose of U. S. Rev. St. ss. 915, 933 is to give to the non-resident creditor, who may obtain jurisdiction of the federal courts, no unfair advantage over the resident creditor who would be bound to attach the property of the defendant in the state courts, and also to provide for the non-resident creditor all such rights in respect to attachment as are enjoyed by the resident creditors. Therefore, drawing the proper conclusions from the cases cited where attachments sued out in federal courts were placed upon the same footing with regard to all incidents of state laws affecting them as like cases in the courts of the state, and giving due weight to the acknowledged purpose of U. S. Rev. St. ss. 915, 933, it follows that the contingency in Mass. G. L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 223, s. 130, affecting attachments upon mesne process sued out in courts of the State, will have like effect when the attachment is sued out in the federal courts.

ATTORNEY AND CLIENT OFFICE OF ATTORNEY 

Disbarment B. .-4. a.

General Statement 

Disbarment is an administrative proceeding. "A proceeding for disbarment is at common law and not in equity." 

Matter of Sleeper, 251 Mass. 6

This ruling is criticized by Mr. Frank W. Grinnell, editor in the August, 1932 number of the Massachusetts Law Quarterly.

The supreme judicial court limited its power and responsibility by holding in this proceeding that "the only matter for us to decide, even upon a full review of the evidence," is whether "the general or special findings made can be sustained on any reasonable view of the case as presented to the trial court." 

Mr. Grinnell refers to "the direct responsibility of the supreme judicial court for the character of the bar" and adds that "such a proceeding does not seem to be accurately described as one either at law or in equity. Like an admission proceeding it is an 'administrative' proceeding which does not fall within any class of litigation. It is a proceeding in which there is only one party brought before the court for a judicial inquiry in which the court seems bound by no technical rules, except those dictated by the fair judicial performance of its own duties and responsibilities to the public."

ATTORNEY AND CLIENT SYLLABUS E. ATTORNEY'S FEES AND EXPENSES 2. Liability of Client d. Express Agreements (I) Contingent Compensation (A) Validity (1) Champertous Arrangements

ATTORNEY AND CLIENT 

E.

ATTORNEY AND CLIENT ATTORNEY'S FEES AND EXPENSES 2. Liability of Client d. Express Agreements (I) Contingent Compensation 

(A) Validity 

(1) Champerious Arrangements 

An agreement that an attorney undertaking to prosecute a suit shall have a share of the thing recovered may not be champertous. 

In order to make it so, the bargain must contain the further element that the attorney's services shall not create a debt due to him from his client and that his prospective share shall be his only compensation.

There may be circumstances under which an attorney may agree to give his services to prosecute a suit without charge if unsuccessful and that in case of success and not otherwise his fees shall constitute a debt due to him from his client for which the amount recovered in the suit or a part of it shall be security. 

Hadlock v. Brooks, 178 Mass. 425

In the last cited case, there was a question whether the plaintiff, an attorney, was employed under a champertous agreement. 

The following instruction was upheld, at pages 430 and 431: "He [the defendant] says that the contract which took place was champertous, and therefore illegal, and therefore a void contract, and no contract at all. What is the meaning of a champertous contract? It is this: If in the assumed case of you going to a lawyer to hire him to take a certain case, you said to him, 'I haven't any money, and unless I win this case, I sha'n't have any money to pay you. Will you take this case, charge me either a certain percentage or such amount as you think best, if you win the case; and if you lose the case, charge me nothing'; that is a champertous contract; that is an illegal contract and is a void contract. There are contracts that look a great deal like it upon the face of it that are not void; that is, are not champertous. It is competent for the parties to say, I have no money and I can't pay you until I get the verdict. If they stop there, if they simply make it a question of the time of payment, it is perfectly competent. It is perfectly competent for the client to say, and the lawyer to agree to it, 'I will pay you, if you are successful, a quarter of what you recover'; if they don't add the further condition,

THE

ATTORNEY AND CLIENT 

'Nothing if you don't recover.' Or, in other words, to put it in brief, if they make the payment of any fee at all contingent on the success, that is a champertous contract; but any other kind of a contract they may make; and there are infinite varieties of it, and there are infinite ways in which they may make the size of the fee depend upon the result, and they may make the time of payment dependent upon the result.” 

As between an attorney at law and his client it is of the essence of champerty that the attorney, having no previous interest to justify him pon recovery is to have as his own some part of the thing recoed, or some profit out of it. 

Hadlock v. Brooks, 178 Mass. 425, at 432

Lancy v. Havender, 146 Mass. 615 Thurston v. Percival, 1 Pick. 415 

Lathrop v. Amherst Bank, 9 Met. 489

But an agreement that one not previously interested and who agrees to prosecute a suit, upon recovery shall have a share of the thing recovered is not for that reason alone champertous. 

Hadlock v. Brooks, 178 Mass. 425, at 432

The bargain to be illegal must have the further element that the attorney's services shall not constitute a debt due him from the client, and that his prospective share is to be the only compensation which the attorney shall receive. If in effect he "agreed to look for his compensation to that alone which might be recovered, and thus to make his pay depend upon his success" the bargain is champertous and void. 

Hadlock v. Brooks, 178 Mass. 425, at 432 

Ackert v. Backer, 131 Mass. 436, at 438 "Where the right to compensation is not confined to an interest in the thing recovered, but gives a right of action against the party," the agreement is not champertous. 

Hadlock v. Brooks, 178 Mass. 425, at 432 

Blaisdell v. Ahern, 144 Mass. 393, at 395 

See: Scott v. Harmon, 109 Mass. 237

But the contract may be illegal without stipulating in terms that compensation is to be solely by way of an interest in the thing to be recovered. That element of illegality may be inferred from an agreement to prosecute at one's own expense and risk unless successful. 

Hadlock v. Brooks, 178 Mass. 425, at 432 

Belding v. Smythe, 138 Mass. 530 

See: Williams v. Fowle, 132 Mass. 385, at 388

s to ​།་ ་ 300 Tea ent com mpen greed!

As was held in Blaisdell v. Ahern, 144 Mass. 393, there may be circumstances in which the attorney may lawfully agree to give his services without charge, if the suit should not be successful, and if in case of success, and not otherwise, the attorney's fees are to constitute a debt due from the client and give a right of action against him to recover them, so that the attorney's right is not confined to an interest in the thing recovered, it is immaterial that the avails of the suit or a part of them are pledged as security, or that such avails are the means and the security on which the attorney relies for payment. 

And as was also said in Blaisdell v. Ahern, 144 Mass. 393, there may be circumstances in which an agreement by an attorney to give his services in the prosecution of a suit with the understanding that they are to be free unless the suit is successful may partake of the worst evils of maintenance. 

Hadlock v. Erooks, 178 Mass. 425, at 432

Whereas both of those things might concur and yet if there was a personal obligation upon his employer to pay his compensation his employment would be legal. 

Hadlock v. Brooks, 178 Mass. 425, at 433

Whereas under many circumstances such a stipulation alone does not constitute champerty. 

Hadlock v. Brooks, 178 Mass. 425, at 433

AWNINGS A. DEFINITIONS AWNINGS 

In Webster's International Dictionary, the word "awning" is defined as follows: 

"A roof-like cover, usually of canvas, extended over or before any place as a shelter from the sun, rain, or wind." 

In the Century Dictionary, as follows: 

"A movable, roof-like covering of canvas or other cloth spread over in any place, or in front of a window, door, etc., as a protection from the sun's rays."

As thus defined, "awning" means the covering which shelters. or protects, as distinct from its frame or support, and this covering may extend over or hang in front of the protected place. It is in the sense of the covering, as distinct from its frame, that the word "awning" is used in a city ordinance prohibiting the erection or use of any awning, except the same be upon a suitable frame and attached entirely to the building. AWNINGS A. DEFINITIONS AWNINGS 

In Webster's International Dictionary, the word "awning" is defined as follows: 

"A roof-like cover, usually of canvas, extended over or before any place as a shelter from the sun, rain, or wind." 

In the Century Dictionary, as follows: 

"A movable, roof-like covering of canvas or other cloth spread over in any place, or in front of a window, door, etc., as a protection from the sun's rays."

As thus defined, "awning" means the covering which shelters or protects, as distinct from its frame or support, and this covering may extend over or hang in front of the protected place. It is in the sense of the covering, as distinct from its frame, that the word "awning" is used in a city ordinance prohibiting the erection or use of any awning, except the same be upon a suitable frame and attached entirely to the building. over the sidewalk of a street by the owner of a building, if the awning be dangerous to travellers for the space of twenty-four hours before the injury happens. 

Drake v. Lowell, 13 Met. 292

Gen. Laws, c. 84, s. 15. 

3. Independent Contractor 4. Landlord 

A landlord is not liable for renting or leasing to a tenant the whole or a portion of a building with an awning which is appurtenant to the premises rented or leased, when the tenant maintains and cares for the awning, re-covering it and renewing the tackle and pulleys when necessary and the landlord exercising at no time during the tenancy any supervision or direction over the maintenance of the awning or its repair and use, even though the tenant fails to obtain permit for the maintenance of the awning required by a city ordinance. 

Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S. 767, at 772

The fact that the manner of the tenant's maintenance of awning causes the awning to become a nuisance does not create any liability on the landlord. 

Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S. 767, at 772

It is a general rule that a landlord is not liable to strangers for the consequences to the plaintiff of a nuisance in connection with the building in the possession and control of his tenant, unless the nuisance occasioning the injury existed at the time the premises were demised or the structure was in such condition that it would be likely to become a nuisance in the ordinary and reasonable use of the same. 

Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S. 767, at 772 

As was said in Coman v. Alles, 198 Mass. 99, at page 103: ". . . if the premises can be used by the tenant in the manner intended by the landlord without becoming a nuisance, then the landlord is not liable for any nuisance created by an act of omission or commission, done by the tenant . . . after he has entered into possession."

The owner of a building, who has leased the lower story for shops, and portions of the upper story for various purposes, including one or two rooms to the town in which the building is situated, and has himself remained in possession of the residue thereof, is, in the absence of an express agreement with tenants to the contrary, responsible for the safety of an awning erected along the whole front of the building, for the benefit of the shops. 

Milford v. Holbrook, 9 Allen 17 2

AWNINGS 

If in such case the owner has had due notice, he may be held liable to the town for damages which they have been compelled to pay to one who has suffered an injury by reason of the falling of the awning, through a defect; and the occupants of the shops need not be joined as defendants. 

Milford v. Holbrook, 9 Allen 17

A notice by the town to such owner of an action brought against them to recover damages for an injury sustained "on the sidewalk in front of or near Union Block, so called, in Milford," (that being the name of his building), requesting him to defend the same, and stating that, if the town was liable, he was responsible to them, because the injury, if it occurred, must have occurred through his negligence, sufficiently connects the defendant and his property with the alleged injury. 

Milford v. Holbrook, 9 Allen 17

In such action by the town against such owner, after such notice, the verdict and judgment against the town are conclusive evidence of the existence of a defect in the highway, the injury to the individual while he was in the exercise of due care, and the amount of the injury. 

Milford v. Holbrook, 9 Allen 17 

5. Tenant

An awning and supporting frame and mechanism may be appurtenant to and a part of the premises rented by the landlord. 

Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S. 767, at 771

The renting or leasing of a part of a building prima facie passes the control of the outer walls adjacent thereto to the tenant with the incidental right to use the outside of the outer walls for the support of awnings and signs in a manner which is consistent with the presumed intention of the landlord.

Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S. 767, at 771 and 772 

Lowell v. Strahan, 145 Mass. 1, at 11

An awning, maintained over a public way in the city of Boston by a tenant of a building adjoining the way in a manner and at a time which are not in compliance with regulations of the board of street commissioners, is a nuisance; and, if the violations of the terms of the regulations are the proximate cause of personal injuries received by a traveller on the highway who came in contact with the awning, the traveller may maintain an action of tort for such personal injuries against the tenant of the building, although there was no negilgence or wrongful act on the part of the tenant other than the violation of the terms of the regulation, and although some natural cause or negligent act of a third per-

AWNINGS 

son, intervening between the violation of the terms of the regulation and the injury, contributed to cause the injury. 

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pacific Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400 F. LICENSING

LEGISLATIVE AND MUNICIPAL REGULATIONS 1. Constitutionality of 

Statutes, ordinances and by-laws relating to awnings are to be construed as intended as to regulate their construction and maintenance as not to interfere with the safety of persons rightfully using the public ways, except as will be necessarily involved by compliance with their provisions. 

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pacific Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400 2. Statutes 3. City Ordinances and Town By-Laws a. Violation 

(I) As Evidence of Negligence 

The question of proximate cause arises if the awning itself is a lawful structure and the evidence of negligence consists of the violation of an ordinance relating to its maintenance. 

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pac. Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400, at 403 

Hartnett v. Tripp, 231 Mass. 382 

Simpson v. Phillipsdale, 227 Mass. 430 

Newcomb v. Boston Pro. Dept., 146 Mass. 596 

(A) Proximate Cause (1) Whether Cause or Condition 

When there is no evidence of negligence or any other wrong on the part of the defendant except by the maintenance of an awning in violation of the terms of a city ordinance or town by law or of the common law, the question arises whether the unauthorized act was an effective and contributing cause of the plaintiff's injury and not merely a condition or an attendant circumstance.

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pac. Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400, at 403 Berdos v. Tremont & Suffolk Mills, 209 Mass. 489 

In Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S.

767, the court said, at page 771: "The absence of a permit is a mere condition, an attending circumstance, and not a cause of the injury to a traveller." 

(2) Intervening Act of Third Per sons When an awning is illegally maintained over a public sidewalk and an accident would not have happened except for the wrongful or negligent act of a third person, the defendant's original wrong-

AWNINGS 

14 ful act can be found to cause the accident, if, the third person's act reasonably ought to have been anticipated or foreseen, although the precise manner in which it may occur can not be foreseen. 

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pac. T Co., 241 Mass. 400, at 403 and 404 and cases collected

The fact that a natural cause may have contributed with the unlawful or negligent act of the defendant does not relieve it from liability. 

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pac. Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400, at 404 

Salisbury v. Herchenroder, 106 Mass. 458 

As was said in Dalton v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Tea Company, 241 Mass. 400, at 404: "The ordinance is to be construed as intended so to regulate the construction and maintenance of awnings as not to interfere with the safety of persons rightfully using the way, except as was necessarily involved by compliance with its provisions. 'Although other acts or omissions to act may have contributed to the injury, the illegal maintenance of the awning could have been found to be the proximate cause. It was the first step in the chain of causation. Whatever thereafter contributed to the accident was not an independent act but one connected with the unlawful act. The defendant, when it wrongfully maintained an obstruction in the street, was forewarned that it might turn out to be an object of peril to travellers. ""The particular manifestation of the result of careless conditions is not infrequently quite out of the usual experience, but if the conditions possess elements of negligence, the person responsible for them may also be held responsible for the result.' 

Dulligan v. Barber Asph. Pav'g Co., 201 Mass. 227, at 231 

Where the plaintifi was injured by coming in contact with an awning owned by the defendant illegally hanging over the sidewalk the intervening act of third person should have been foreseen in unlawfully maintaining awning over public highway. 

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pacific Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400 

(3) Question for Court or Jury

In Dalton v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400, the court said, at page 404: "While in ordinary cases the question of causation is for the jury, yet when upon all the evidence the court is able to

AWNINGS 

say that the result of the injury was not proximate but remote, it is for the court. 

Farrell v. Sturtevant Co., 194 Mss. 431 

Butler v. N. E. Structural Co., 191 Mass. 397

Glassey v. Worcester Con. Rlwy., 18 Mass. 315 

Stone v. Boston & Albany R. R., 171 Mass. 536

Lane v. Atlantic Works, 107 Mass." H. NUISANCE CREATED BY 1. General Statement 

An awning constructed over a public sidewalk not maintained at the height required by the city ordinance is a nuisance. 

Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S. 767, at 771

Such an awning is a nuisance irrespective of the absence of a permit, because its presence is an interference with a right common to all travellers to use the sidewalk. 

Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S. 767, at 771

The absence of a permit is a mere condition, an attendant circumstance, and not a cause of the injury to a traveller. 

Anderson v. Kopelman, 1932 A. S. 767, at 771

A person maintaining an awning as a nuisance within a public way is liable for damages of which it is the proximate cause, wholly apart from evidence aliunde (from another source). 

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pac. Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400, at 403 

Leahan v. Cochran, 178 Mass. 566 

Stone v. Boston & Albany R. R., 171 Mass. 536, at 544 

Shipley v. Fifty Associates, 106 Mass. 194 

2. License as Affecting Legality

A license to maintain an awning and its frame and connections over a public sidewalk legalizes the obstruction which otherwise would constitute what is in legal effect a nuisance. 

Dalton v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400, at 402 and 403 

Union Inst. for Savings v. Boston, 224 Mass. 286, at 287 

Atty. Gen. v. Williams, 174 Mass. 476, at 483

But such license affords no protection unless its terms are observed. 

Dalton v. Great Atl. & Pac. Tea Co., 241 Mass. 400, at 403

Duties, Powers and Liabilities a. Actions by or Against Trustees (VI) Jurisdiction (B) Federal Courts (2) Consent of Defendant (b) Avoiding Illegal Transfer 

Section 23b, 11 USCA, ss. 96 (b), 107 (e), 110 (e), which permits certain suits to be brought in a District Court of the United States only by consent of the defendant, has no application to suits by a trustee to recover a preference, or property conveyed in fraud of creditors.

Jurisdiction in such cases is expressly vested under the sections above referred to concurrently in "courts of bankruptcy" and in any state court which would have had jurisdiction in case bankruptcy had not intervened. 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 830 

Courts of bankruptcy, under section 1 (8) of the act, 11 USCA, s. 1 (8), include the District Courts of the United States, but not referees in bankruptcy. 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 830

It obviously does not in this connection, include a referee. 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 830

BANKRUPTCY H. TRUSTEES 2. Duties, Powers and Liabilities a. Actions by or Against Trustees (II) Nature and Form (B) Summary Proceedings

(5) Mortgage of Property

Transfer of the bankrupt's property can be made by mortgage. 

Hertzmark v. Lynch, 54 Fed. (2d) 38

So, an unlawful preference can be created by the giving of a mortgage. 

Hertzmark v. Lynch, 54 Fed. (2d) 38

A mortgage securing a loan made to an insolvent mercantile corporation by a former owner of the business within four months of the corporation's bankruptcy, to enable the corporation to pay certain creditors may be found to be preferential and void under the Bankruptcy Act, Section 67e. 

Hertzman v. Lynch, 54 Fed. (2d) 38, at 40

Where the mortgage is tainted with the intent of the mortgagee that the bankrupt should give such unlawful preference, or, in other words, the new loan is made to enable the bankrupt to do so, the mortgage is invalid. 

Hertzmark v. Lynch, 54 Fed. (2d) 38, at 40 

As was said in Dean v. Davis, 242 U. S. 438, at 444: "A transfer, the intent (or obviously necessary effect) of which is to deprive creditors of the benefit sought to be secured by the Bankruptcy Act, 'hinders, delays or defrauds creditors' within the meaning of Section 67e; and this court will not disturb the District Court's decision affirming the order of the referee if the mortgages appear to be invalid on any ground." 

Hertzmark v. Lynch, 54 Fed. (2d) 38, at 40 

Dean v. Davis (C.C.A.) 212 Fed. 88 

In Hertzmark v. Lynch, 54 Fed. (2d) 38, the corporation was indebted to the mortgagee for money loaned without security, also owed a son of the mortgagee for merchandise and in addition owed other creditors. The bank was unwilling to renew its note. 

The mortgagee was a former owner of the business and had served as treasurer of the corporation, thereafter he withdrew and left 1

BANKRUPTCY I 3 d (III) continued (5) Mortgage of Property (continued) 

the management of the business to his son and son-in-law, his withdrawal was because he did not like the way things were going. He sold his shares of stock to the remaining stockholders but had not received payment therefor and refused to endorse the corporation's note and knew that the corporation had not paid one of his sons for merchandise sold to the corporation as a cash transaction. The mortgagee advanced the corporation $4,500.00 and took a mortgage on all its stock and fixtures to secure a note in the principal sum of $6,250.00, which included the amount due to the mortgagee on his prior unsecured loan. The referee found as a fact that the mortgagee must have known of the insolvency of the corporation at the time the mortgages were given and held that the mortgages not only constituted a preference to the mortgagee but that the loan was also knowingly given to enable the bankrupt corporation to prefer the bank, the son-in-law, and the son.

The court said at pages 40 and 41: "The officers of the corporation must be held to have intended the obvious consequences of their act; and, knowing its insolvent condition, to pay the bank, thus relieving the sonin-law of his liability as an indorser, Chapman v. Hunt, (D. C.) 248 Fed. 160 

Smith v. Coury (D. C.) 247 Fed. 168, at 172 and to pay the other brother the sum due him for merchandise, and to secure to the father his previous loan, clearly constituted preferences; and a mortgage or mortgages of all its assets within four months of a petition being filed in bankruptcy, to secure the money to pay these obligations, would obviously hinder and delay its other creditors by depriving them of the benefit of the Bankruptcy Act. "Under Section 67e, the burden is on the mortgagee to show that in such a transaction he acted in good faith.

Walbrun v. Babbitt, 16 Wall. (U.S.) 577 

In re Sutherland Co. (D. C.) 245 Fed. 663, at 665 "Reasonable investigation on the part of the appellant would then have disclosed that the shoe company was insolvent and the extent of its liabilities, if he did not already know it, that the mortgages would not only constitute a preference as to him, at least to the extent of his previous indebtedness, but the proposed disposition of the loan would also result in preferences as to the bank, his son-in-law, and his son Joseph, and the mortgages of all the assets would of necessity hinder and delay the other creditors of the corporation, and would undoubtedly, sooner or later, result in the corporation being adjudged a bankrupt. "It is common knowledge that a retail shopkeeper usually mortgages his stock in trade and fixtures only as a last resort, and that the immediate effect of doing so is to destroy all further credit, and eventually under the conditions disclosed here would result in bankruptcy. It was futile for this appellant, as a man of wide business experience, to deny any knowledge that such was the usual effect of such a mortgage. "If, as the referee found, the appellant was cognizant of the insolvent condition of the corporation at the time he made the loan and took the mortgages, or knew of facts sufficient to put a reasonable man on inquiry, in which case he was bound by what an inquiry would have disclosed and knowing the purpose to which the bankrupt proposed to put the new loan he was advancing, he became a party to the intent, actual or presumptive, to give the preferences and delay and defraud the other creditors of the corporation. 'In cases where the direct issue of fraud is involved, knowledge may be imputed where one wilfully closes his eyes to information within his reach.'

Weeker v. National Enameling & Stamping Co., 204 U. S. 

176, at 185

BANKRUPTCY I 3d (III) continued (5) Mortgage of Property (continued) 

"Under the circumstances disclosed by the record, the mortgages under Section 67e of the act were clearly fraudulent as to the other creditors of the bankrupt, who were thereby deprived of the benefits of the act. 

Dean v. Davis, 242 U. S. 438 

Marsh v. Walters (C. C. A.) 220 Fed. 805

BANKRUPTCY J. REFEREES 

3.

Jurisdiction b. Under General Order 

A referee in bankruptcy has no jurisdiction under a general order of reference to him to hear and determine matters properly determinable only in a plenary suit. 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 829

Nor can a referee acquire jurisdiction by consent of the parties in a summary proceeding to decide matters which are beyond the jurisdiction conferred upon him by the general order of reference. 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 829 

As was said in the last cited case at page 829: "A referee in bankruptcy under a general order of reference has no jurisdiction, either in a summary proceeding or a plenary suit, to recover property in the possession of a third party prior to bankruptcy, if held under a substantial claim of right." 

Weidhorn v. Levy, 253 U. S. 268, at 273 

Louisville Trust Co. v. Comingor, 184 U. S. 18, at 26 

In Weidhorn v. Levy, 253 U. S. 268, the court said, at page 273: "We find nothing in the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act that makes it necessary or reasonable to extend the authority and jurisdiction of the referee beyond the ordinary administrative proceedings in bankruptcy and such controversial matters as arise therein and are in effect a part thereof, or to extend the authority of the referee under the general reference so as to include jurisdiction over an independent and plenary suit such as the one under consideration. The provisions of the act, as well as the title of his office, indicate that the referee is to exercise powers not equal to or co-ordinate with those of the court or judge, but subordinate thereto, and he becomes 'the court' only by virtue of the order of reference. 

In the General Orders the word 'proceedings' occurs frequently, but never in a sense to include a plenary suit. On the other hand, 'proceedings in equity' and 'proceedings at law' are specially dealt with in General Order XXXVII [11 

USCA, s. 53] . . .' 

"Reviewing the entire matter, we conclude that under the language of the Bankruptcy Act and of the general orders in bankruptcy a referee, by virtue of a general reference under

BANKRUPTCY order XII (1) [11 USCA, s. 53], has not jurisdiction over a plenary suit in equity brought by the trustee in bankruptcy against a third party to set aside a fraudulent transfer or conveyance under section 70e [11 USCA, s. 110] (e), and affecting property not in custody of the court of bankruptcy." 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 829

When a referee under a general order of reference has no jurisdiction over the subject matter, he cannot acquire jurisdiction by consent of the parties. 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 830

Mfrs.' Products v. Butterworth-Judson Co., 258 U. S. 365 

Chicago, B. & Q. Ry. Co. v. Willard, 220 U. S. 413, at 420 

Nixon v. Michaels (C. C. A.), 38 F. (2d) 420, at 423 

Chicago, B. & Q. Ry. Co. v. Quincy Co., 220 U. S. 413

The objection to the jurisdiction of the referee before the District Court after the appellant has consented to the referee hearing the matter may be "unsportsmanlike"; but lack of jurisdiction may be raised on review, and at any stage of the proceedings. 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 830 

Chicago, B. & Q. Ry. Co. v. Wilard, 220 U. S. 419

Louisville Trust Co. v. Comingor, 184 U. S. 26 

Mansfield, C. & L. M. Ry. Co. v. Swan, 111 U. S. 379, at 382 A litigant is not bound by the findings of any tribunal having no jurisdiction over the subject-matter, even if found with his The proceedings before the referee were coram non consent. judice. 

Ply. C'ty Tr. Co. v. MacDonald, 53 Fed. (2d) 827, at 830

BANKRUPTCY Q. ACTIONS AND SUITS AGAINST BANKRUPT 1. General Statement 

An action or suit may be commenced against a person even though he has filed a petition in bankruptcy. 

As was said in Hackett v. Supreme Council, 206 Mass. 139 at 142: "When a debtor becomes bankrupt the creditor is put to an election, to proceed against the debtor or take his share of the debtor's assets in bankruptcy. The object of proceeding against the debtor is in the hope that he (the debtor) may not get a discharge or may not plead it or may not take the necessary steps to be in a position to plead it. In either of these cases the creditor will get a judgment against the debtor which he can satisfy out of the property of the debtor (if any) acquired after the date of the bankruptcy proceedings. 

On the other hand if the creditor wishes to entitle himself to his share of the bankrupt's estate he must make his proof against that estate in the court which has the collection and distribution of it. A judgment procured in a common law court after the date of bankruptcy proceedings does not entitle the creditor to share in the assets administered in and by the bankrupt court." 

Attorney General v. American Legion of Honor, 196 

Mass. 151 

However, such action or suit may be stayed. 

2. Stay of Proceedings a. Actions or Suits Pending When Petition Filed (I) General Statement 

The Bankruptcy Act, provides that:

SECTION 11 [a]. "A suit which is founded upon a claim from which a discharge would be a release, and which is pending against a person at the time of the filing of a petition against him, shall be stayed until after an adjudication or the dismissal of the petition; if such person is adjudged a bankrupt, such action may be further stayed until twelve months after the date of such adjudication, or if within that time such person applies for a discharge, then until the question of such discharge is determined." 

This section provides in substance for a mandatory stay of the suit until after adjudication, or dismissal of the petition. 

Thereafter it is for the court to determine, in the exercise of sound discretion, whether the suit shall be further stayed or whether it shall be allowed to go to judgment. 151

BANKRUPTCY 

In this Commonwealth, the plaintiff is entitled to a judgment with a perpetual stay of execution. 

Berry Clothing Company v. Shopnick, 249 Mass. 459 

Barry v. New York Holding, etc. Co., 229 Mass. 308 

Smith v. Miller, 226 Mass. 187 

Parker v. Murphy, 215 Mass. 72 

Rogers v. Abbot, 206 Mass. 270

Feigenspan v. McDonnell, 201 Mass. 341 

American Wood etc. Co. v. Furbush, 193 Mass. 455 

Rosenthal v. Nove, 175 Mass. 559

A plaintiff is entitled to judgment even though the bankruptcy proceedings were instituted within four months from the date of the attachment. 

See cases just cited above.

The action or suit may also be stayed at any time after adjudication, even before judgment for a period not exceeding a year following the adjudication. But whether such further stay shall be granted is to be determined by the trial judge in the exercise of his discretion. 

Smith v. Miller, 226 Mass. 187, at 188

In Berry Clothing Company v. Shopnick, 249 Mass. 459, the court said at page 463: "The words of this Section [11a] do not require a peremptory stay of a pending action after adjudication in bankruptcy. "The state court has jurisdiction of such action and may proceed to judgment. As was pointed out in Boynton v. 

Ball, 121 U. S. 457, at 467, substantial reasons may make it desirable to proceed to trial and to judgment in such a case. "It was decided in Rosenthal v. Nove, 175 Mass. 559, with reference to Section 11[a], that the court in which is pending a suit against a bankrupt is not after the adjudication bound to stay proceedings further therein until the termination of the bankruptcy proceeding, although it may do so and to such extent as justice may require. The action is not barred and the court has power to proceed to judgment. "The provisions of General Laws, c. 223, s. 124, requiring peremptory stay, are confined in terms to proceedings in insolvency under the laws of this Commonwealth. Those laws are superseded by the Federal Bankruptcy Law. 

Parmenter Mfg. Co. v. Hamilton, 172 Mass. 178 

Comm. v. Nickerson, 236 Mass. 281, at 292 "They are not pertinent to proceedings in bankruptcy or to the effect of bankruptcy on bonds given to dissolve attachments." 152

BANKRUPTCY 

In Barry v. New York Holding etc. Co., 229 Mass. 308, which was an action of contract, where the plaintiff would have been entitled to a judgment but for the discharge in bankruptcy of the defendant which was pleaded as a defence to the action, the plaintiff upon motion became entitled to an order to have the judgment entered for him in the sum ascertained, such judgment not to be enforced against the bankrupt personally or to be operative beyond such value as the Bankruptcy Act attributes to it as evidence of the amount due as a provable claim in bankruptcy, and the execution on said judgment was stayed perpetually. (Good form for court order at page 312.) 

In Smith v. Miller, 226 Mass. 187, the court said at pages 188 and 189: "The Bankruptcy Act requires a stay of action pending upon a claim to which a discharge would be a bar, until after an adjudication or the dismissal of the petition; but whether such an action is to be further stayed after an adjudication of bankruptcy, is to be determined by the trial judge in the exercise of his discretion. "In construing Section 11[a] of the Bankruptcy Act, which deals with this question, this court said in the case of Rosenthal v. Nove, 175 Mass. 559, at page 563: 'we hold that the court in which a suit against a bankrupt is pending is not, after the adjudication of bankruptcy, bound to stay proceedings further therein, while it may do so if, and to such an extent as, justice may require. The action is not absolutely barred, and the court has power to proceed to judgment.' "The discretion vested in the trial court by Section 11[a] of the Bankruptcy Act does not depend upon the question whether an attachment was made in the pending action within, or more than four months before the filing of the petition in bankruptcy, or whether any attachment has been made. It follows that the defendant was not entitled as a right to a continuance of the action after he was adjudicated a bankrupt." 

In Parker v. Murphy, 215 Mass. 72, the court said at pages 73 and 74: "It is true that the present Federal Bankruptcy Act makes compulsory a stay of an action, pending upon a claim to which a discharge in bankruptcy would be a bar, only until after an adjudication upon or dismissal of the petition in bankruptcy. Further stay for a period of twelve months, or until the question of the discharge is determined, if application therefor is made within such time, is discretionary with the court. 153

BANKRUPTCY 

"Nevertheless, in the simple action at law upon a claim to which a discharge in bankruptcy would be a bar, where no rights of or against third persons are involved, such as existed in Rosenthal v. Nove, 175 Mass. 559, and no ulterior interests are affected, the usual procedure is for the bankrupt to plead the pendency of bankruptcy proceedings and ask for a continuance until he can obtain and plead his discharge. 

This is pointed out in Rogers v. Abbot, 206 Mass. 270, at 

274. See also Faxon v. Baxter, 11 Cush. 35." 

In Rogers v. Abbot, 206 Mass. 270, the court said at page 274: "The defendants went to trial before obtaining a discharge in bankruptcy. Until a discharge is granted and is pleaded as a defense no question arises as to the debt sued on being or not being provable. If the defendants had wished to plead their discharge in bankruptcy as a bar, they should have moved for a continuance to see whether they procured a discharge, and if they did obtain one they should have pleaded it. The bankrupt is not entitled as of right to a stay of proceedings after he is adjudicated a bankrupt. "In the case at bar, the defendants by an amendment to their answer in the present action on the bond filed and allowed on February 5, 1908, pleaded that they were adjudicated bankrupts on May 11, 1903, five years before. If the debt was provable in bankruptcy and so would have been barred by a discharge, the defendants did not take the proper steps to plead that defense. See in this connection Hackett v. American Legion, 206 Mass. 139.” 

In Feigenspan v. McDonnell, 201 Mass. 341, the court said at page 346: "Nor is the defendant's bankruptcy a defense. While a court in which an action in contract is pending against a bankrupt may after adjudication stay further proceedings pending the obtaining of a discharge, it is not required to do so, but can proceed to judgment. 

Rosenthal v. Nove, 175 Mass. 559"

In American Wood Working Machinery Company v. Furbush, 193 Mass. 455, the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act of 1898, c. 

541, Section 11[a], in regard to the staying of pending suits against a bankrupt founded on claims to which a discharge would be a release, require the court to grant a continuance in cases within the terms of the act. The court said at page 457: "Unlike our statutes in regard to insolvency, this act does not leave the continuance of a case upon the application of 154

BANKRUPTCY 

the bankrupt defendant therefor to the discretion of the court, but it requires the court to grant the continuance. "In this respect the case differs from Dalton-Ingersoll Co. v. Fiske, 175 Mass. 15, relied on by the plaintiff. See Sullings v. Ginn, 131 Mass. 479.”

When the last entries in the record of an action are a suggestion by the defendant of his bankruptcy and a motion for a continuance founded thereon, under the Bankruptcy Act the case is not ripe for judgment until the motion is passed upon by the court. The court said further at page 457: "It may be difficult to give a definition of the term 'ripe for judgment,' applicable to all cases; but in general we may say that it is when, under the last entry, the case seems to have been brought to a final determination, and everything seems to have been done that ought to be done before the entry of a final adjudication upon the rights of the parties. "When the last entry is a suggestion by the defendant of his bankruptcy, and a motion for a continuance founded on this fact, it is evident, under the present Bankruptcy Act, that judgment should not be entered until the motion is passed upon by the court.”

The fact that a defendant has been defaulted does not deprive him of the right to file a motion for a continuance based on a suggestion of his bankruptcy and to have such motion heard. The court said, at pages 457 and 458: "The filing of the motion itself is, in substance, a motion to take off the default, so far as to enable the defendant to be heard on the question whether the case shall go to judgment or be continued to enable him to obtain and plead a discharge."

In Rosenthal v. Nove, 175 Mass. 559, the court said at page 562: "Congress was legislating upon a subject as to which its power is unquestionable. Successive bankruptcy acts had been in turn enacted and repealed. Numerous state insolvency laws had been in force in the intervals when no bankruptcy had been in force. "Under the last previous bankruptcy act, no suit or proceeding upon a provable debt could be prosecuted against the bankrupt until the question of his discharge should have been determined, and any suit or proceeding must, upon his application, be stayed to await the determination of the bank- 155

BANKRUPTCY 

ruptcy court on the question of the discharge unless there was unreasonable delay on his part. 

Ray v. Wight, 119 Mass. 426 

Hill v. Harding, 107 U. S. 631 "This requirement of a stay, if asked for by the debtor, might well operate to inflict upon creditors such serious delay in enforcing their rights against other persons than the bankrupt as is shown in the last case cited, where for several years the creditor could not place himself in a position to resort to his admitted security. "Congress chose the language of the present statute in view of that of the former bankruptcy act, and of the decisions under it, and of its practical operation. If the power of the bankrupt to force a stay for twelve months, or until the question of his discharge should be settled, of all suits pending against him at the initiation of the bankruptcy proceedings, was a feature which Congress wished to place in the new act, it need choose no ambiguous language. "If it wished to make a different provision, and thought it more reasonable to provide for a peremptory stay, without any request therefor, in all cases until the question of an adjudication or the dismissal of the petition was determined, and to leave the question of any further stay to the determination of the court in which the action was pending, no more apt words could have been used than those which Congress has adopted. We see no good reason to give them in the enactment now in question any other than their usual meaning, and we hold that the court in which a suit against a bankrupt is pending is not, after the adjudication of bankruptcy, bound to stay proceedings further therein, while it may do so if, and to such an extent as, justice may require. 

The action is not absolutely barred, and the court has power to proceed to judgment. 

Holland v. Martin, 123 Mass. 278"

BANKS AND BANKING P. ACTIONS AND SUITS AGAINST BANKS 1. By Depositor g. 

Defences (I) Estoppel (A) Forgery 

When the bank seeks to invoke the doctrine of estoppel against the depositor because of his delay in advising the bank of any forgery concerned in the relations between them, it is necessary that the bank shall have sustained injury by reason of that delay. 

DiLorenzo v. Atlantic Nat. Bank, 1932 A. S. 347, at 350 

Boston & Albany R. R. v. Reardon, 226 Mass. 286, at 291 

Murphy v. Metropolitan Nat. Bank, 191 Mass. 159, at 165 

(II) Ratification (A) Forgery 

When the depositor for many years was constantly active in efforts to secure restitution from the forger for the wrong done by him and through all this time the depositor maintained silence and inaction toward the bank, it may be found that, so far as the depositor's conduct affected his relation with the bank, the depositor impliedly ratified the forgery.

DiLorenzo v. Atl. Nat. Bk. of Boston, 1932 A. S. 347, at 351 and 352

BURDEN OF PROOF 

See: 

EVIDENCE TRIAL 

A. 

GENERAL STATEMENT 

The fundamental rule as to the burden of proof is, that, whenever the existence of any fact is necessary in order that a party may make out his case or establish a defence, the burden is on such party to show the existence of such fact. 

Willett v. Rich, 142 Mass. 356, at 357

In Stephen's Digest of Law of Evidence, the rule is stated. to be that "whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability dependent on the existence or nonexistence of facts which he asserts or denies to exist, must prove that those facts do or do not exist." 

Stephen Evidence (Am. ed.) 175 

The general rule is that the plaintiff, by asserting in his declaration facts which if proved establish liability to him on the part of the defendant, has the burden of proving those facts. 

Smith v. Hill, 232 Mass. 188, at 190 

Barker v. Comins, 110 Mass. 477

It was said by Chief Justice Shaw in Powers v. Russell, 13 

Pick. 69, at pages 76 and 77 that: "Where the party having the burden of proof establishes a prima facie case, and no proof to the contrary is offered, he will prevail. Therefore the other party, if he would avoid the effect of such prima facie case, must produce evidence, of equal or greater weight, to balance and. control it, or he will fail. "Still the proof upon both sides applies to the affirmative or negative of one and the same issue, or proposition of fact; and the party whose case requires the proof of that fact, has all along the burden of proof. "[The burden of proof] does not shift, though the weight in either scale may at times preponderate. "But where the party having the burden of proof gives competent and prima facie evidence of a fact, and the adverse party, instead of producing proof which would go to negative the same proposition of fact, proposes to show another and a distinct proposition which avoids the effect 1

of it, there the burden shifts, and rests upon the party proposing to show the latter fact." 

Hughes v. Williams, 229 Mass. 467 and cases collected 

Comm. v. Thurlow, 24 Pick. 374, at 380 and 381

When the defendant does not attack the plaintiff's prima facie case but seeks to avoid its force by proof of another independent, distinct and subsequent fact, this raises a new issue which is an affirmative defence. The burden of proving it rests on the defendant as the party alleging it. 

Smith v. Hill, 232 Mass. 188, at 190 and 191 (Defendent's discharge in bankruptcy-plaintiff not scheduled as creditor and had no knowledge of bankruptcy proceedings.)

A prima facie case or prima facie evidence does not change the burden of proof. It only stands until its weight is met by evidence to the contrary. 

Smith v. Hill, 232 Mass. 188, at 191 

Carroll v. Boston El. Ry., 200 Mass. 527, at 536

The burden of proof continues to rest upon the party who either as plaintiff or as defendant asserts the fact necessary to enable him to prevail. He must ultimately establish that fact before he can become entitled to a finding or verdict in his favor, and the burden rests on him to do that, whatever may be the intervening effect of different kinds of evidence or evidence possessing under the law varying degrees of probative value. 

Smith v. Hill, 232 Mass. 188, at 191 

Friedman v. County of Hampden, 204 Mass. 494 

Funcheon v. Harvey, 119 Mass. 469 

Blake v. Damon, 103 Mass. 199 

Pratt v. Lamson, 6 Allen 457, at 464 

Cunningham v. Hall, 4 Allen 268, at 270 

Crowninshield v. Crowninshield, 2 Gray 524, at 527 

O'Brien v. Cheney, 5 Cush. 148 

Sawyer v. Spofford, 4 Cush. 598 

Beals v. Merriam, 11 Met. 470 

Comm. v. Bradford, 9 Met. 268 

Ashby v. Eastern R. R. Co., 5 Met. 368 

Cockayne v. Summer, 22 Pick. 117 

Whitaker v. Salisbury, 15 Pick. 534 

Phillips v. Ford, 9 Pick. 39

s. 1  

It was said in Hughes v. Williams, 229 Mass. 467, at 470: "The party who makes and is required to make an assertion of a fact in or to set forth a case as matter of law entitling him to prevail, and whose case requires the proof of that fact, has at all times the burden of proving such fact. But where the party upon whom the burden of proof is cast offers competent proof of that fact, and his adversary instead of producing proof to negative that same fact proposes to show another and a distinct fact which avoids the effect of the first fact, then the burden of proof rests upon the party proposing to show the latter fact. This is an affirmative defence, the burden of proving which rests upon the party asserting it." 

Parker v. Murphy, 215 Mass. 72, at 75 

Stocker v. Foster, 178 Mass. 591, at 600 and 601 

Wylie v. Marinofsky, 201 Mass. 583, at 584 

Powers v. Russell, 13 Pick. 69, at 76 and 77 

And in Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503, at 511: "The burden of proof rests upon the party who has the affirmative of the issue."

The burden of proof remains throughout the trial on the plaintiff to establish his case on all the evidence where liability is denied, or the amount to be recovered is in issue. 

Ginley's Case, 244 Mass. 346, at 347 

Bigelow Carpet Co. v. Wiggin, 209 Mass 542

That a certain fact or finding is .... prima facie evidence does not change the burden of proof. It determines the verdict or finding if no other evidence is introduced. But the moment that opposing evidence is received, the case is to be determined upon all the evidence .... the prima facie evidence and all the other evidence and the question is whether the weight preponderates in favor of the party having the burden of proof.

B. 1. 

West v. State St. Ex., 250 Mass. 537, at 539 

King's Case, 220 Mass. 290, at 293 

Cohasset v. Moors, 204 Mass. 173, at 179

DISTINCTIONS Distinguished from WEIGHT OF THE EVIDENCE 

In Central Bridge Corp. v. Butler, 2 Gray 130, at 132: "The burden of proof and the weight of the evidence are two very different things. The former remains on the

party affirming a fact in support of his case, and does not change in any aspect of the cause; the latter shifts from side to side in the progress of a trial, according to the nature and strength of the proofs offered in support or denial of the main fact to be established." 

C. CIVIL CASES 

Generally the rule of evidence requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt in criminal proceedings does not apply to civil actions even when they arise from an act which is penal in its nature. 

Grella v. Lewis Wharf Co., 211 Mass. 54, at 59

In civil proceedings the burden of proof is sustained by a fair preponderance of the evidence, and proof beyond reasonable doubt is not essential. 

Callahan v. Fleischman Co., 262 Mass. 437

Grella v. Lewis Wharf Co., 211 Mass. 54 

Preponderance of evidence in civil cases must be preponderance of credible testimony, not balance of probabilities. 

Callahan v. Fleischman Co., 262 Mass. 437

But cause may be found to be established by a preponderance of the evidence even if the evidence does not exclude all other possible causes. 

Crisafi v. Sells, 262 Mass. 120

When the evidence tends equally to sustain either of two inconsistent propositions, neither of them can be said to have been established by legitimate proof. A verdict in favor of the party bound to maintain one of those propositions against the other is necessarily wrong. 

Smith v. First Nat. Bank, 99 Mass. 605, at 612

Mere disbelief of the testimony offered by the defendants, when that is the only evidence, is not affirmative proof and does not establish the fraud nor sustain the burden of proof resting on the plaintiffs. The cases then would stand as if there were no evidence. Nevertheless the testimony, although not worthy of credence, might be of such character as to lead to the conclusion that if the transaction were honest such testimony would not have been presented, and thus might tend to support the affirmative burden resting on the plaintiffs. 

Rioux v. Cronin, 222 Mass. 131

The rule of evidence requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt is generally applicable only in strictly criminal pro-

19 00 ceedings. It is founded upon the reason that a greater degree of probability should be required as a ground of judgment in criminal cases, which affect life or liberty, than may safely be adopted in cases where civil rights only are ascertained. 

Roberge v. Burnham, 124 Mass. 277, at 278

An instruction to jurors in civil cases that all reasonable doubt must be removed before they properly can reach a verdict is erroneous. Yet it may be proper to instruct them with regard to doubt. The preponderance which determines the verdict must be a preponderance of credible testimony not a "balance of probabilities." Evidence which is open to serious doubt may not be credible. 

Callahan v. Fleischman Co., 262 Mass. 437 

1. Plaintiff

The burden upon the plaintiff is co-extensive only with the legal proposition upon which his case rests. It applies to every fact which is essential, or necessarily involved in that proposition. It does not apply to facts relied upon in defence to establish an independent proposition, however inconsistent it may be with that upon which the plaintiff's case depends. 

It is for the defendant to furnish the proof of such facts; and when he has done so, the burden is upon the plaintiff, not to disprove those particular facts, nor the proposition which they tend to establish, but to maintain the proposition upon which his own case rests, notwithstanding such controlling testimony, and upon the whole evidence in that case. The distinction may be narrow, but it is real, and may often be decisive. 

The plaintiff is required to prove by the preponderance of the evidence-not beyond a reasonable doubt that his injuries or damage were caused by the defendant's negligence, that is, that this was the reasonably probable explanation of the cause of his injuries or damage. 

Young v. N.Y.N.H. & H. R.R., 1931 A. S. 213, at 215 

Highland Foundry Co. v. N.Y. N. H. & H. R.R., 199 

Mass. 403, at 405 and 406 (Fire communicated by a railroad locomotive engine.) 

But the plaintiff is not required to exclude all other possibilities as to the cause of his injury or damage. 

Young v. N.Y.N.H. & H. R.R., 1931 A. S. 213, at 215 

Navien v. Cohen, 268 Mass. 427, at 431 and cases cited

Commonly it cannot be ruled as matter of law that one upon whom rests the burden of proof as to fact has sustained that burden. 

Rosenberg v. Rome, 1931 A. S. 743, at 746 

Thomas v. Meyer Store, Inc., 268 Mass. 587, at 590 

Lennon v. Cohen, 264 Mass. 414, at 426 

Warner v. Fuller, 245 Mass. 520, at 529 and 530 

Int. Textbook Co. v. Martin, 221 Mass. 1, at 8

Coleman v. N.Y., N.H. & H. R.R., 215 Mass. 45, at 47 

Marcy v. Shelburne Falls Ry., 210 Mass. 197, at 199 

Shea v. American Hide Co., 221 Mass. 282, at 283

The judge and jury are not bound to believe the witnesses of the party having the burden of proof. 

Rosenberg v. Rome, 1931 A. S. 743, at 746

The only instance where the judge can properly direct a verdict for the plaintiff has clearly made out his case and there is no controverted material issue of fact for the consideration of the jury; 

Leonard v. Wheeler, 261 Mass. 130, at 133 

Spevack v. Budish, 238 Mass. 215

or the defendant relies solely on an affirmative defense and the evidence introduced would not warrant a finding in the defendant's favor; 

Doyle v. Boston Elevated Ry., 248 Mass. 89, at 91

Spevack v. Budish, 238 Mass. 215

ཏུ The plaintiff is bound to show a greater likelihood that the injury came from an act of negligence for which the defendant is responsible than from some other cause. 

Crisafi v. Sells, 262 Mass. 120 

Gates v. B. & M. R. R., 225 Mass. 297, at 301 and 302

Where the facts proved are as consistent with one view of the case as with another, the plaintiff has not sustained the burden of proving the second. 

Crowell v. Moley, 188 Mass. 116, at 119

Although in criminal cases the juror must be left with no reasonable doubt that his finding is correct, yet in a civil case he should be satisfied if, after fairly weighing the conflicting evidence, he feels sure that his finding is supported by a greater weight of trustworthy evidence than is opposed to it. 2.
