CRIMINAL LAW 

E. 1. 

PARTIES TO OFFENCES 

8. 

General Considerations

Who Are Parties 

A person is a party to a crime if he does some act in its inducement or perpetration. So, everyone is a party to a crime who actually commits the ultimate criminal act, or does some act that forms a part thereof, or aids, assists, or encourages the actual commission of the crime by being personally present, or directly or indirectly counsels, hires or procures any person to commit the offence or do any act which forms a part of the offence. 

b. Classification of Parties (I) General Statement 

Crimes, being divided into three degrees, treason, felonies and misdemeanors, have created classifications of the parties thereto. In treasons, all parties are principals, likewise in misdemeanors, but in felonies, the parties are divided into four distinct classifications: (A) Principal in the first degree; one who is the actual perpetrator of the crime. (B) Principal in the second degree; one who is actually or constructively present by arrangement with the principal in the first degree, and who aids, assists or encourages the perpetration of the crime. (C) Accessory before the fact; one who counsels, hires or otherwise procures the principal in the first degree to commit the crime. (D) Accessory after the fact; one who knowing the felony to have been committed, assists, comforts, receives or relieves the felon. 

(II) Treason and Misdemeanors (A) All Are Principals 

Because the crime of treason is of such a heinous character, the law will not classify the parties but will consider all participants as principals.

On the other hand, because misdemeanors are crimes of the lowest degree, the law will not trouble to distinguish between the E-1

CRIMINAL LAW 

participants and separate them into different classes; therefore, all are principals. 

Trial of Aaron Burr, 4 Cranch, (U. S.) 470

In misdemeanors, the distinction between principals of the first and second degree is unknown. Neither is there any difference between accessories and principals; all participants being principals, the same as in treason. 

At common law, in misdemeanors, there are no accessories. All concerned, whether instigators or perpetrators, being principals, are subject to be indicted as such. 

Com. v. Brown, 154 Mass. 55, at 56 

Com. v. Dale, 144 Mass. 363 

Com. v. Nichols, 10 Met. 259 

Com. v. Macomber, 3 Mass. 254

In misdemeanors, all who are concerned in aiding and abetting, as well as those who perpetrate the act, are principals. 

Com. v. Brown, 154 Mass. 55, at 56

In misdemeanors, as in treason, it is a general rule that all who take part in the offence may be charged simply as principals. 

Com. v. Ahearn, 160 Mass. 300, at 301 

Com. v. Wallace, 108 Mass. 12 

Com. v. Gannett, 1 Allen, 7 

Com. v. Ray, 3 Gray, 441, at 448

In misdemeanors it has always been the rule that one charged with a misdemeanor may be convicted either on proof of his being a principal or on proof of his being an accessory. 

Com. v. Gannett, 1 Allen, 7 

As was said in Com. v. Brown, 154 Mass. 55, at 56: "It is well settled that one who aids another in committing a misdemeanor is equally guilty with one who actually commits it."

The distinction between principals and accessories applies only in the case of felonies, and all who participate in treason and in E-2

CRIMINAL LAW 

misdemeanors, if guilty and punishable at all, being principals are indictable as such. 

Com. v. Sherman, 191 Mass. 439 

Com. v. Ahearn, 160 Mass. 300 

Com. v. Dale, 144 Mass. 363 

Com. v. Maroney, 105 Mass. 467 

Com. v. Kimball, 105 Mass. 465 

Com. v. Gannett, 1 Allen, 7 

Com. v. Ray, 5 Gray, 441 

Com. v. Mann, 4 Gray, 213 

Com. v. Park, 1 Gray, 553 

Com. v. Drew, 3 Cush., 279 

Com. v. Nichols, 10 Met. 259 

Com. v. Willard, 22 Pick. 476 

Com. v. Harrington, 3 Pick. 26 

Com. v. Barlow, 4 Mass. 439 

Com. v. Macomber, 3 Mass. 254

The effect of Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 274, s. 1, which is the present statutory definition of felony, is to eliminate all common law felonies and establish only those offences which are "punishable by death or imprisonment in the State prison." 

Com. v. Carey, 12 Cush. 246

This section gives a new and technical definition of felony, differing from that of the common law. 

Beard v. Boston, 151 Mass. 96 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243, at 257 

(III) 

Felonies 

(A) Classified as Principals and Accessories 

Criminals guilty of a felony are classified according to the nearness or remoteness of their connection with the crime committed, as principals or accessories.

Principals are of the first and second degrees. The accessories are divided into two classes, before and after the fact. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211 

Com. v. Lucas, 2 Allen, 170 

E-3

CRIMINAL LAW C. Who May Be Principals in Second Degree or Accessories (I) General Statement 

One may be guilty as principal in second degree, or as an accessory before the fact, by aiding in, or procuring or instigating a crime, although he or she is incompetent to commit the crime in person. 

(II) Principals in Second Degree 

There are many offences which can only be committed by particular classes of persons, such as bigamy (by married persons); rape, seduction, and bastardy (by males); larceny after trust (by bailees), or embezzlement (by officers). But because one is of a class that cannot be principals in such offences it by no means follows that he cannot be punished as an aider and abettor. Thus an unmarried man may be convicted of bigamy as a principal in the second degree; a woman may be punished for aiding one attempting rape; a husband, although he cannot individually commit rape upon his wife, may be liable as principal for aiding and abetting another in the commission of the crime. 

Com. v. Fogerty, 8 Gray, 489

In this way one may be guilty as principal in the second degree of a crime which he could not personally commit; for instance, a woman present aiding and abetting may be guilty of rape, and the same principle applies to a boy under fourteen years of age; and persons not named may be convicted as accessories in the statutory offence of "mother concealing death of illegitimate child" or "postmaster making false returns." Where a principal and his agent participate as such in the commission of a misdemeanor, they are joint principals since the criminal law does not recognize this civil relation. 

(III) Accessories Before the Fact 

A person may be convicted as an accessory before the fact although he is incapable of committing the offence as principal in the first degree, by reason of not being of a particular age, sex, condition, or class. For example, a person not connected with a corporation as officer or otherwise, may be an accessory to the em bezzlement of funds by one of its officers; and a woman, not E-4

CRIMINAL LAW 

present, who encourages and assists a man in the crime of rape is liable to be punished as an accessory before the fact. 

Upon similar grounds a husband may be an accessory to the crime of rape upon his own wife, and it has been said that a man may be accessory in stealing his own goods, if he procures another to do so with felonious intent, although, it seems that a person is not an accessory to the crime of arson merely because he procures his dwelling house to be burned by another if he would not have been guilty of arson had he burned the house himself. 

A corporation, being able to act only through its agents, cannot be an accessory to a criminal act of the agent done in the course of the business of the corporation, as the act of the agent is the act of the corporation, and therefore to call the corporation an accessory would make it an accessory to its own act, a legal absurdity. 

Com. v. Knapp, 10 Pick., 477

A wife may be an accessory before the fact in the husband's crime. d. In Offenses Which May Be Committed by One Only

There are crimes of such nature that they can be committed only by one person. In these crimes, although there may be several participants yet only the actual participator is a guilty party. e. 

U. S. v. Farrar, 281 (U. S.) 624; S. C. 38 F. (2d) 515

Criminal Responsibility of One Person for Act of Another (I) General Statement 

One person is not responsible for the criminal acts of another if he does not participate in them either directly or indirectly.

So, a principal or master is not liable criminally for the unauthorized conduct of his agent or servant.

Also, a partner or joint adventurer is not criminally liable for the acts of his associates performed without his knowledge or consent.

But a corporate officer cannot escape the consequences of his own criminal act on the ground that it was an official act of the corporation and not for himself personally.

E-5

CRIMINAL LAW 

The civil doctrine that a principal is bound by the acts of his agent within the scope of the agent's authority has no application to criminal law. 

Com. v. Stevens, 155 Mass. 291

Therefore, the mere relation of principal and agent or of master and servant does not render the principal or master criminally liable for the acts of his agent or servant, although done in the course of his employment; it must be further shown that they were directed or authorized by him. 

Com. v. Stevens, 155 Mass. 291 

Com. v. Holmes, 119 Mass. 195 

Com. v. Park, 1 Gray, 553 

Com. v. Nichols, 10 Met. 259

A shopkeeper is liable criminally for an unlawful sale in his shop, made with his assent, by a servant or agent employed in his business. But an unlawful sale by the servant or agent is only prima facie evidence of the assent thereto by the storekeeper, and of his liability to punishment therefor. 

Com. v. Nichols, 10 Met. 259 

See also: Com. v. Park, 1 Gray, 553

In fine, the legal relations created by agency, partnership or joint adventureship do not by themselves create responsibility in regard to the commission of criminal offenses, so that where the accused in no way personally participated in the commission of the criminal act, he is not made responsible for it by construction. 

(II) Relation of Principal and Agent or Master and 

Servant (A) General Rule

A principal is criminally liable for his agent's acts when he par- ticipates therein, or gives such assent or concurrence thereto as involves him morally in the guilt of the performance of the act. 

Com. v. Nichols, 10 Met. 259

But a principal is not responsible for acts of agents unless the principal approves, countenances or authorizes the agent's acts in such a way as to assume initial responsibility. 

Com. v. Riley, 210 Mass. 387, at 396 

Com. v. Riley, 196 Mass. 60

E-6

CRIMINAL LAW 

Com. v. Joslin, 158 Mass. 482, at 495 

Com. v. Stevens, 153 Mass. 421, at 438 

Com. v. Houle, 147 Mass. 380, at 383 

Com. v. Hayes, 145 Mass. 289, at 294 and 295 

Com. v. Stevenson, 142 Mass. 466, at 468 

Com. v. Briant, 142 Mass. 463, at 464 

Com. v. Wachendorf, 141 Mass. 270, at 271 

Com. v. Park, 1 Gray, 553 

Com. v. Hadley, 11 Met. 66 

Com. v. Nichols, 10 Met. 259 

Clark and Marshall, Criminal Law, 260 et seq. 

16 C. J. 123, Sec. 106

Also, a principal is not responsible criminally for an act of his agent done in opposition to his will and against his orders, provided such orders are given in good faith and are not merely colorable. 

Com. v. Stevens, 153 Mass. 421

But where from the nature of the crime the defendant acts at his peril he may be responsible for the agent's acts without express authority. 

Com. v. Sacks, 214 Mass. 72 

Com. v. N. Y. Cent. & H. R. R., 202 Mass. 394 

Com. v. Warren, 160 Mass. 553 

Com. v. Gray, 150 Mass. 327

A principal is not criminally responsible by reason of his ratification of his agent's acts, since there can be no ratification of a crime. 

16 C. J. 123, Sec. 106 

8 R. C. L. 65, Sec. 17 (B) 

Exception to the Rule

A class of cases forms an exception to the general rule that a principal is not responsible for criminal acts of his agent unless specifically authorized by him, and makes the principal liable for the act of his agent, even though committed in violation of his instructions.

E-7

CRIMINAL LAW 

These cases involve the following crimes:

Libel 

Maintenance of Public Nuisance Violation of Intoxicating Liquor Statutes 

The owner of a saloon is criminally liable for all violations of the liquor laws committed by his servants, although committed without his knowledge, or even against his express prohibition. 

Com. v. Nichols, 10 Met. 259

Violation of Revenue or Police Regulations 

As to the foregoing, the principal may be convicted even in the absence of proof that he authorized the commission of the crime and even if he forbade it. 

Com. v. Sacks, 214 Mass. 72 

2. Principal in First Degree a. Definition

The principal in the first degree is the actual perpetrator of the crime, that is, the one who actually commits the act which constitutes the offense. 

b. General Statement 

Although only the actual and immediate perpetrator of the crime is considered to be the principal in the first degree, yet, more than one person may be actual perpetrators of that crime, so that each is a principal in the first degree. 

Com. v. Ahearn, 160 Mass. 300 of Therefore, when each does an act which constitutes a part the crime itself, that is, constitutes a part of the preparation, each is guilty as a principal in the first degree. 

Com. v. Ahearn, 160 Mass. 300

There may be more than one principal in the first degree but each must be personally present and actually commit some act constituting the offense.

E-8

CRIMINAL LAW 

C. 

Commission of Crime by Agent (I) Innocent Agent 

If a person causes a crime to be committed through the instrumentality of an innocent agent, he is the principal in the crime, and punishable accordingly, although he was not present at the time and place of the offence, as is ordinarily required to render one guilty as a principal. 

Com. v. White, 123 Mass. 430 

Com. v. Hill, 11 Mass. 136 (Passing counterfeit bill) 

(II) Guilty Agent 

A guilty agent is a principal in the first degree, his employer may be a co-principal in the first degree, or a principal in the second degree if his presence is actual or constructive, or an accessory before the fact, if he is absent at the time of the commission of the offense. The agent in this case is likewise responsible. 

(III) Test of Innocence of Agent 

The innocence of the agent depends on whether he has knowledge of the fact that the particular crime is being committed and whether he does any act tending towards its commission while having that knowledge. 

(IV) 

Feigned Accomplice

Upon the same theory that one who procures an innocent person to do an act is himself the principal in the first degree, one who procures a feigned accomplice to procure the act is likewise guilty. 

3. Principals in Second Degree or Aider and Abettor a.

Definitions 

A principal in the second degree, or an aider and abettor as he is frequently called, is one who is present, actually or constructively, aiding, abetting or assisting in, or encouraging the commission of the felony. 

Com. v. Lucas, 2 Allen, 170 at 171 

, at 516

E-9

CRIMINAL LAW 

A principal in the second degree is one who is present when a felony is committed by another, and who aids or abets in its commission.

A principal in the second degree is one, who in the meaning of the law, is present and abetting, assisting, and encouraging the performance, or, the perpetration of the crime. 

A principal in the second degree is one who is present lending his countenance, encouragement, or other mental aid while another does the act.

Principals in the second degree are those who are present, aiding and abetting the commission of the offence. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211 

Com. v. Lowrey, 158 Mass. 18

A principal in the second degree is one, who so far participates in the commission of a crime as to be present for the purpose of assisting therein if necessary; one who gives aid and comfort, or who, while present, either commands, advises, instigates, or encourages another to commit a crime; one who does some act to help or to render aid in the actual perpetration of a crime; a person who, by being present, by words or conduct, assists or incites another to commit the criminal act. 

, at 516

Principals in the second degree are those present, actively aiding and encouraging. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211 

Com. v. Lowrey, 158 Mass. 18

Principals in the second degree are persons who are present at the time a crime is committed, lending their countenance, aid, encouragement or other mental aid while another person does the actual criminal act. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211

Principals in the second degree are those who, without actually participating in the act itself, are present, aiding and encouraging the party who commits the act. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496, at 517

E-10

CRIMINAL LAW 

b. 

Distinctions (I) Distinguished from Principal in First Degree 

Whether the crime is treason or a felony or a misdemeanor, the principal in the first degree is he, that is the actor or actual and immediate perpetrator of the crime, while the principal in the second degree is not the immediate perpetrator, but is present, actually or constructively, at the time of the perpetration by the principal in the first degree and is abetting, assisting or encouraging him in performance of the act. 

(II) Distinguished from Accessories 

(A) Generally

The distinction between an aider or abettor, or principal in the second degree, and an accessory, is that the former must be present at the commission of the offence, while the latter must not be present.

Assuming one's will to contribute to the commission or beneficial consummation of the criminal act, the test to determine whether he is a principal rather than an accessory is, whether he is so near or otherwise so situated as to make his personal assistance, if required to any degree, available. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496, at 510 to 519

Presence, actual or constructive, determines whether a person is a principal in the second degree or an accessory. If he is present, he is a principal; if not present, he is an accessory. (B) Before the Fact

The accessory before the fact counsels, hires or otherwise procures, or commands another to commit the act. 

The distinction between a principal in the second degree and an accessory before the fact is, as follows: (1) A principal is one who is present, aiding and abetting, assisting, and encouraging the performance, or,the perpetration of the crime, while an accessory before the fact is one who, not being present to aid, abet, assist, and encourage, has beforehand procured or taken other steps to have the crime committed.

E-110

CRIMINAL LAW 

(2) The abettor, the principal in the second degree, must be in a situation in which he might render his assistance in some manner to the commission of the offence, while the accessory before the fact must not be in such a situation. (3) The principal in the second degree must be in such a situation by agreement with the perpetrator of the crime, or with his previous knowledge, consenting to the crime, and for the purpose of rendering aid and encouragement in the commission of it, while the accessory before the fact need not have made such agreement. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211 (C) After the Fact A principal in the second degree aids, abets, assists, or encourages in the commission of the crime and is present at its perpetration, while an accessory after the fact does nothing toward the commission of the crime, and is not present at its perpetration, his offence being distinctly his own, committed after the commission of the crime and he, being liable to a different punishment, cannot be indicted jointly with the principal. 

Com. v. Woods, 11 Gray, 85 (III) Distinguished from Accomplice

An "accomplice" is a person who knowingly, voluntarily, and in common intent with the principal offender (the principal in the first degree), unites in the commission of the crime. The term "accomplice" in its fullness includes all persons who are concerned in the commission of the crime; all particepes criminis, whether they are considered in strict legal propriety as principals in the first or second degrees or as accessories before the fact. 

The distinction between the word "accomplice" and the term "principal in the second degree" is that the former is broad enough to include the latter while the latter is limited and does not mean the same as the former but designates only one class under its meaning.

So, an "accomplice" when created from the status of being an accessory before the fact, is, necessarily, one who is not present E-12

CRIMINAL LAW 

π at the perpetration of the crime while the "principal in the second degree” must always be present, either actually or constructively. 

(IV) Distinguished from Conspirator or Confederate 

To create the status of principal in the second degree, there must be the perpetration of a crime in which an overt act is committed by the principal in the first degree, at which the principal in the second degree must be present, either actually or constructivly, and in which the principal in the second degree must aid, abet, assist or lend his encouragement. The actual commission of a crime by an overt act and presence at such commission are necessary to constitute one a principal in the second degree. 

To constitute one a conspirator, there need not be an overt act, as the agreement of conspiracy is itself the complete crime; there need not be a principal in the first degree because all conspirators are equally principals in the first degree; there need not be any actual or constructive presence because the crime of conspiracy is complete when there is a meeting of the minds, no matter where the parties may be located; and there need not be any overt act committed by anyone in furtherance of the agreement of the con spiracy. 

Com. v. Dyer, 243 Mass. 472 

Attorney General v. Pelletier, 240 Mass. 264 

Attorney General v. Tufts, 239 Mass. 458 

Com. v. Hunt, 4 Met. 111

The essential distinctions between a principal in the second degree and a conspirator are:

The principal in the second degree must, while the conspirator need not (A) Have a principal in the first degree. (B) Have a crime actually perpetrated by commission of an overt act. (C) Be present at the commission of the crime whereof the principal in the first degree performs the overt act. (D) Aid, abet, assist or encourage the commission of the overt act.

CRIMINAL LAW 

C. 

Statutory Provision 

Gen. Laws, (Ter. Ed.), c. 274, s. 2, provides that: "Whoever AIDS in the commission of a felony... shall be punished in the manner provided for the punishment of the principal felon." 

d. General Statement 

The law as to principals in the second degree was settled in the reign of Henry IV. 

The most ancient authorities of the law considered a person an accessory at the fact; but to avoid the technicalities of the law regarding accessories, aiders and abettors were early held to be principals in the second degree. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496

All persons who are actually or constructively present at the time and place of a felony and who either actually aid, abet, assist, or advise its commission, or are there with that purpose in mind, to the knowledge of the party actually committing the crime, are guilty as principals in the second degree, although they did not themselves accomplish the purpose. 

Com. v. Stevens, 10 Mass. 181

At common law, persons who were present at the commission of a crime only for the purpose of aiding, countenancing or encouraging its perpetration were described as accesories at the fact. They could not, therefore, be brought to trial until the principal offenders had been convicted or outlawed. This circumstance, together with the fact that the distinction be ween an aider and abettor and a principal was found to be a distin tion without a difference, long since led to the classifying of aides and abettors as principals in the second degree.

esent whet may be mod c. He must aid or abet the commission of the offense. Some participation is necessary, though it need not necessarily be active. d. Mere knowledge of the offense and mental approval is not enough.

To constitute one a principal in the second degree, he must not only be present when the crime was committed, but must aid and abet the actual perpetrator in the commission of the crime. One who is present when a crime is committed, but neither assists in its commission nor shares in the criminal intent of its perpetrator is not guilty as principal in the second degree. Mere presence is not sufficient to render one an aider or abettor. 

When the defendant did not personally perform the act constituting the crime with his own hand, and it is contended that he was present, aiding and abetting the perpetrator at the time when the crime was committed, it is necessary to consider what facts are necessary to be proved to constitute him, who is aiding and abetting, a principal in the crime; or, in other words, what, in the sense of the law, is meant by being present, aiding and abetting 

When the law requires the presence of the accomplice at the perpetration of the fact, in order to render him a principal, it does not require a strict, actual, immediate presence, that is, such a presence as would make him an eye or ear witness of what is done. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick., 494, at 516

In the last cited case the court said, at page 516: "Several persons set out together, or in small parties, upon one common design, be it murder or other felony, or for any other purpose unlawful in itself, and each takes the part assigned him; some to commit the act, others to watch at proper distances and stations to prevent a surprise, or to favor, if need be, the escape of those who are more immediately engaged. They are all, provided the act be committed, in the of the law present at it; for it was made a common cause eye E-15

CRIMINAL LAW 

with them, each man operated in his station at one and the same instant towards the same common end; and the part each man took tended to give countenance, encouragement and protection to the whole gang, and to insure the success of their common enterprise." 

Com. v. Devereux, 256 Mass. 387, at 396 

In order to render a person an accomplice and a principal in felony, he must be aiding and abetting at the fact, or ready to afford assistance, if necessary. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 494, at 517

Being present in judgment of the law, is equivalent to being actually present, for, the hope of their immediate assistance encourages and emboldens the perpetrator to commit the fact, which otherwise perhaps he would not have dared to do, and makes them guilty in the same degree (as principals) as if they had actually stood by, with their swords drawn, ready to second the villainy. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 494, at 517

These principles have been fully recognized by the very learned and distinguished Chief Justice Marshall of the Supreme Court of the United States, in 

Matter of Aaron Burr, 4 Cranch (U. S.) 492

The person charged as a principal in the second degree must be present; and he must be aiding and abetting the crime. But if the abettor, at the time of the commission of the crime, was assenting to the crime, and in a situation where he might render some aid to the perpetrator, ready to give it if necessary, according to an appointment or agreement with him for that purpose, he would, in the judgment of the law, be present and aiding in the commission of the crime. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick., 494, at 516

IT MUST BE PROVED THAT: 

(1) The abettor was in a situation in which he might render his assistance, in some manner, towards the commission of the offence.

E-16

CRIMINAL LAW 

(II) He was in such a situation, by agreement with the perpetrator of the crime, or with his previous knowledge, consenting to the crime, and for the purpose of rendering aid and encouragement in the commission of it, and (III) He was actually aiding and abetting the perpetrator at the time of the crime. 

But if the abettor were consenting to the crime, and in a situation in which he might render any aid, by arrangement with the perpetrator, for the purpose of aiding and assisting him in the crime, then it would follow as a necessary inference, that he was actually aiding and abetting at the commission of the crime. 

The presence of the abettor under such circumstances, must encourage and embolden the perpetrator to do the deed, by giving him hopes of immediate assistance; and this would in law be considered as actually aiding and abetting him, although no further assistance should be given. For it is clear, that if a person is present, aiding and consenting to a murder or other felony, that alone is sufficient to charge him as a principal in the crime. And the presence by construction or judgment of the law, is in this respect equivalent to actual presence. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 494, at 516

A person is principal in the second degree only to the act which was committed when his aid or encouragement was actually rendered, or he was willing and able to so do. e. 

Com. v. Campbell, 7 Allen, 541, at 544

Essentials to Create Status (I) Guilty Principal in First Degree (A) General Statement 

To make a person a principal in the second degree, there must be a principal in the first degree; that is to say, there must be one who does the thing or act without which there is no crime, and with respect to the doing of which, the other, or principal in the second degree, was present, aiding and abetting. E-17

CRIMINAL LAW 

If there be no principal in the first degree (no one who does the act or thing constituting the crime), there can of course be no principal in the second degree.

One cannot be guilty of aiding and abetting the perpetrator of a crime without its first being shown that the crime was actually committed.

In order that one may be guilty as a principal in the second degree, there must be a crime committed and a principal in the first degree. 

There cannot be a principal in the second degree unless there is a "guilty" principal in the first degree. But, one who procures the commission of a crime by an innocent agent is himself guilty as the principal in the first degree. 

Com. v. Askerowski, 196 Mass. 342

On the trial of a person indicted as a principal in the second degree, it is necessary to show the guilt of the principal in the first degree. 

(B) Trial of Principal in First Degree Need Not 

Precede A principal in the second degree may be indicted, tried and convicted before, at the same time as, or after the principal in the first degree. The former rule as to trial of the principal in the first degree before accessories, which brought about the enactment of Gen. Laws, 274, s. 3, does not apply to principals in the second degree. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick., 496 

(C) Effect of Conviction or Acquittal of Principal in First Degree 

(1) Conviction The guilt, but not the conviction, of the principal in the first degree must necessarily be proved and is a condition precedent to the conviction of the principal in the second degree. 

The guilt of the principal in the first degree may be shown either by parol evidence concerning his perpetration of the crimi- E-18

CRIMINAL LAW 

nal act or by the court record of his conviction. When the court record is introduced, it is merely prima facie evidence and the principal in the second degree may prove the innocence of the principal in the first degree. 

(2) Acquittal 

The acquittal of the principal in the first degree prevents a conviction of the principal in the second degree, as such. 

However, when the actual perpetrator of the crime is not known with certainty, the fact that one mistakenly supposed to have committed the crime and was acquitted thereof, does not affect the principal in the second degree where it is claimed that he aided and abetted the perpetrator of the crime who is a person other than the one acquitted, whether the identity of that person is known or unknown.

Where the person charged as principal in the first degree has been acquitted, then the person accused as principal in the second degree, because of his aiding and abetting that alleged principal in the first degree, must be acquitted. 

But when the government contends that the accused was a principal in the second degree, and aided and abetted some person other than the one acquitted, the accused may be convicted as a principal in the second degree, and the acquittal of that person does not affect the status of the principal in the second degree. 

(II) Presence (A) General Statement 

In order to render one a principal in the second degree, as an aider and abettor, it is essential that he was present, either actually or constructively, at the time and place of the commission of the felony. 

The person charged as a principal in the second degree must be present, aiding and abetting the crime or in such contiguity as to enable him actually to render aid. 

In order to render a person an accomplice and a principal in felony, he must be aiding and abetting at the fact, or ready to af- E-19

CRIMINAL LAW 

ford assistance if necessary. That is, at the particular fact which is charged, he must be ready to render assistance to those who are committing that particular fact; he must be ready to give immediate and direct assistance.

Where there is a perpetrator of a crime no one will be a principal in the second degree as abetting him, unless he is in a position to render, if necessary, some personal assistance. 

He need not be in the actual presence of the other principal; it is enough if he is constructively there. 

, at 510 to 519

The principal of the second degree need not be actually on the spot where the crime was committed. Thus, where one, in pursuance of a plan, enticed the owner of a shop to a place at some distance, and kept him there while his confederates broke into the shop, he was held guilty of burglary as principal in the second degree.

Presence, actual or constructive, at the time the offence is committed, is necessary to render one a principal in the second degree. 

If a person procures or counsels the commission of a crime by another, and is absent when it is committed, he is merely an accessory, and at common law he cannot be convicted under an indictment charging him as a principal.

Thus, where a servant let a person into his master's house on an afternoon, and concealed him there all night, in order that he might commit a larceny in the house, but left the house early the next morning, and was absent when the larceny was committed, it was held that he was not a principal in the second degree, but an accessory before the fact.

It is not necessary, however, in order to charge one as a principal in the second degree, as distinguished from an accessory before the fact, that there shall be a strict, actual, and immediate presence at the time and place of the commission of the offense. 

Nor is it necessary that he shall be an eye or ear witness of the criminal act.

A person is constructively present, and therefore guilty as a principal, if he is acting with the person who actually commits E-20

CRIMINAL LAW 

the deed in pursuance of a common design, and is aiding his associate, either by keeping watch or otherwise, or is so situated as to be able to aid him, with a view, known to the other, to insure success in the accomplishment of the common enterprise. 

Com. v. Lowrey, 158 Mass. 18 

Com. v. Wallace, 108 Mass. 14 

, at 516

To constitute a person a principal in a crime, he must be present aiding by acts, words or gestures, and consenting to the commission of the crime.

It is not necessary, however, that he should do some act at the time, in order to constitute him a principal, but he must encourage its commission by acts or gestures, either before or at the time of the commission of the offense, with full knowledge of the intent of the persons who commit the offense. 

However, mere presence without the knowledge and approval of the principal in the first degree, or other assistance or encouragement, evidenced by some act, does not make one a principal in the second degree.

If the accused was not present but counselled, hired or procured the felony to be committed, he can be convicted only of having been an accessory before the fact, which offence must be separately and specifically alleged in some count of the indictment. 

To warrant a conviction as a principal in the second degree, it must, therefore, be proved that the abettor was in a situation in which he might render his assistance in some manner to the commission of the offence.

It must be proved that he was in such a situation by agreement with the perpetrator of the crime, or, with previous knowledge, consenting to the crime, and for the purpose of rendering aid and encouragement in the commission of it. 

So, when the government proves that the defendant and the actual committer of the criminal act had some transaction and later met, the following considerations are important to determine whether the defendant was a principal in the second degree: E-21

CRIMINAL LAW 

What were their relations to each other? 

What was the understanding between them?

Where was the defendant with reference to the committer of the crime? case any

Was the defendant nearby for the purpose of giving encouragement and consent, so as to assist the committer in sudden matter should arise, or did he simply, if at all, procure the commission of the crime and leave the actual overt acts to the principal in the first degree, with direction to commit the crime, the defendant himself being absent or so far off as not to be present within the sense and fair meaning of this rule of law? 

It does not depend necessarily upon any given number of feet, or upon any number of rods. It depends somewhat upon the nature of the crime.

So, consideration must be given to the evidence as to what took place between the defendant and the committer of the crime, what their understanding was, where they went, and how they conducted themselves, where the defendant was, and with what purpose. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211 and 214

In the last cited case, the court said, at page 210: "If the order was a false, forged, or counterfeit order, and

Clune, knowing it, handed the same to M and told M to get a messenger boy and get the money on the same, and M, knowing or having reasonable cause to know that the order was forged or counterfeit, gave the same to the messenger boy to obtain at the bank the money on the same, and he gave the money to M, who in turn found Clune and the gave same to him, and Clune was not present aiding or encouraging M at the uttering of the order, then Clune cannot be convicted on this indictment. . . ." (B) Constructive Presence 

While the law requires the presence of the aider or abettor, in order to render him a principal, it does not require a strict, actual, E-22

CRIMINAL LAW 

immediate presence, that is, such a presence as would make him an eye or ear witness of what occurs, for if the abettor, at the time of the commission of the crime, was assenting to it, and in a situation where he might render some aid to the perpetrator, ready to give it if necessary, according to an appointment or agreement with him for that purpose, he would, in the judgment of the law, be present and aiding in the commission of the crime. 

The presence at the place and time of the crime required to make one a principal in the second degree, or an aider and abettor, may be constructive, as where one, acting with another in the pursuance of a criminal design, is so situated when the crime is committed as to be able to assist in its commission. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 208 

Com. v. Lucas, 2 Allen, 170, at 171

One is deemed constructively present if, at the time, he is performing any act in furtherance of the felony or is in a position to give information to the principal which would be helpful to the end in view, or would prevent others from doing any act by way of warning or which would put an obstacle in the way of the consummation of the crime or render its consummation more difficult. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496, at 508

But where several persons are acting together with a common intent to commit a crime, and each performs some part of the crime, they are all guilty as principals, although all are not actually present when the offense is finally consummated. 

Com. v. Devereaux, 256 Mass. 387, at 396

In Com. v. Ahearn, 160 Mass. 300, the court said, at page 301: "Where several persons are engaged in a common criminal design, with a distribution of the parts, and each takes the part assigned to him, all may be held guilty [as principals]." 

So, where the keeping of intoxicating liquor in the defendant's dwelling house one mile away is the joint act of the defendant E-23

CRIMINAL LAW 

and another, and there is a joint intent on their part that the liquor shall be sold by the other person alone in violation of law, and that the keeping is for the purpose of facilitating such unlawful sale, the defendant and the other person, upon a complaint against them jointly, may both be convicted. The defendant is aiding and abetting the other person in the latter's act of keeping the liquor with intent to sell the same unlawfully. 

Com. v. Ahearn, 160 Mass. 300, at 301 and 302

It must therefore be proved that the abettor was in a situation in which he might render his assistance, in some manner, to the commission of the offense.

It must be proved that he was in such a situation, by agreement with the perpetrator of the crime, or with his previous knowledge consenting to the crime, and for the purpose of rendering aid and encouragement in the commission of it. 

It must also be proved that he was actually aiding and abetting the perpetrator at the time of the crime. But if the abettor was consenting to the crime, and in a situation in which he might render any aid by arrangement with the perpetrator, for the purpose of aiding and assisting him in the crime, then it would follow as a necessary legal inference that he was actually aiding and abetting at the commission of the crime. For the presence of the abettor under such circumstances must encourage and embolden the perpetrator to do the deed, by giving him hopes of immediate assistance; and this would in law be considered as actually aiding and abetting him, although no further assistance should be given. For if a person is present aiding and consenting to a felony, that alone is sufficient to charge him as a principal in the crime. And the presence by construction or judgment of the law is in this respect equivalent to actual presence. 

The question to be determined in ascertaining whether a person is in a position to aid and abet in the commission of an offense, is not so much where he may happen to be, as whether he is in a position to render aid and encouragement to the actual perpetrator, with a view of insuring the success of the common purpose. E-24

CRIMINAL LAW 

N 

As was said in Com. v. Lucas, 2 Allen, 170, at 171: "To charge a person as principal, a strict, actual, immediate presence at the time and place of the commission of the crime is not necessary. Nor is it requisite that he should be so situated as to be an eye or ear witness of the criminal act. It is the expectation of aid, in case it is necessary to the completion of the crime, and the belief that his associate is near and ready to render it, which encourage and embolden the chief perpetrator, and inetic him to accomplish the act. By the countenance and assistance which the accomplice thus renders, he participates in the commission of the offence. It is therefore sufficient to hold a party as principal, if it is made to appear that he acted with another in pursuance of a common design; that he operated at one and the same time for the fulfilment of the same preconcerted end, and was so situated as to be able to furnish aid to his associate, with a view to insure success in the accomplishment of the common enterprise. Thus, if two persons agree to commit a burglary, and in order to effect their purpose one of them breaks and enters a house and commits a larceny therein, while the other remains outside, even at a distance, in order to guard against surprise and detection, and to receive the goods, or a portion of them, after the larceny has been committed, there can be no doubt that the latter would be liable as principal, although he did not see his accomplice do any act towards the commission of the offence. He would be, it is true, an accessory before the fact, by advising and procuring the commission of the felony; and after the fact, by receiving the property after it was stolen; but he would also be a principal, because, at the time when the felony was committed, he co-operated with the chief perpetrator, and aided and abetted him in doing the acts which constituted the crime." (2) Limit of Rule 

(a) General Statement 

To be present, aiding and abetting the commission of a felony, the abettor must be in a situation where he may actually aid the perpetrator; it is not enough that he is at an appointed place, E-25

CRIMINAL LAW 

where the perpetrator erroneously supposes that he might render aid,  and it is immaterial at what distance he may be from the scene of the felony.

A fortiori he is deemed constructively present if he is near enough to render assistance, if need be, and to encourage the actual perpetration of the felony. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 209 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496, at 513 (b) Must be Near Enough to be Able to Assist

Although a person may be constructively present, even though actually at a considerable distance, yet, to be constructively present within this principle, he must at least be in such a situation that he might render assistance in some manner, not necessarily physical, in the commission of the offence. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496 (3) Co-Conspirators 

(a) General Statement 

The mere fact that one is a party to a conspiracy to commit a felony does not show constructive presence. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496, at 516 

But see: Com. v. Devereux, 256 Mass. 387, at 396

If it should be proved that the defendant conspired with others to procure the crime to be committed, it follows as a legal presumption that the defendant aided in the actual perpetration of the crime unless he can show the contrary to the jury. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 494, at 518

The fact of the conspiracy being proved against the defendant, is to be weighed as evidence in the case, having a tendency to prove that the defendant aided, but it is not in itself to be taken as a legal presumption of his having aided and may be disproved by him. It is a question of evidence for the consideration of the jury. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick., 494, at 518

CRIMINAL LAW 

If, however, the jury should be of opinion, that the defendant was one of the conspirators, and in a situation in which he might have given some aid to the perpetrator at the time of the crime, then it would follow, as a legal presumption, that he was there to carry into effect the concerted crime, and it would be for the defendant to rebut that presumption, by showing to the jury that he was there for another purpose unconnected with the conspiracy. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick 494, at 518 

(b) Conspiracy for Wrongful Purpose Charges All with Incidental Felony

I. General Statement 

Any participation in a general felonious plan, provided such participation be concerted, and there be constructive presence, is enough to make one a principal in the second degree, as to any crime committed in execution of the plan. 

Where persons combine to stand by one another in a breach of the peace, with a general resolution to resist to the death all opposers, and a murder is committed in the execution of their design, all of the company are equally principals in the murder, though at the time of the fact some of them were at such a distance as to be out of view. 

Com. v. Devereux, 256 Mass. 387, at 396 

As was said in Com. v. Campbell, 7 Allen, 541, at 543 and 544: "There can be no doubt of the general rule of law, that a person engaged in the commission of an unlawful act is legally responsible for all the consequences which may naturally or necessarily flow from it, and that, if he combines and confederates with others to accomplish an illegal purpose, he is liable criminaliter for the acts of each and all who participate with him in the execution of the unlawful design. 

As they all act in concert for a common object, each is the agent of all the others, and the acts done are therefore the acts of each and all. "This doctrine, as applied to cases of homicide, is fully stated in 1 Hale P. C. 441, in a quotation from Dalton in these words: 'If divers persons come in one company to do E-27

CRIMINAL LAW 

any unlawful thing, as to kill, rob or beat a man, or to commit a riot, or to do any other trespass, and one of them in doing thereof kill a man, this shall be adjudged murder in them all that are present of that party abetting him and consenting to the act or ready to aid him, although they did but look on.' "So in 1 East P. C. 257, it is laid down that 'where divers persons resolve generally to resist all opposers in the commission of any breach of the peace, and to execute it with violence, or in such a manner as naturally tends to raise tumults and affrays; as by committing a violent disseisin with great numbers, or going to beat a man, or rob a park, or standing in opposition to the sheriff's posse, they must at their peril abide the event of their actions;' and if doing any of these or similar acts any person interfering with them is killed, all who took part in the fact or abetted thereto are guilty of murder. "These citations, to which many others of a similar tenor might be added, show that the rule of criminal responsibility for the acts of others is subject to the reasonable limitation that the particular act of one of a party for which his associates and confederates are to be held liable must be shown to have been done for the furtherance or in prosecution of the common object and design for which they combined together. 

Without such limitation, a person might be held responsible for acts which were not the natural or necessary consequences of the enterprise or undertaking in which he was engaged, and which he could not either in fact or in law be deemed to have contemplated or intended."

So, a rioter is not responsible, on an indictment for murder, for a death accidentally caused by officers engaged in suppressing the riot. 

Com. v. Campbell, 7 Allen, 541, at 543 and 544

The court said, in the last cited case, at pages 544, 545, and 546: "No person can be held guilty of homicide unless the act is either actually or constructively his, and it cannot be his act E-28
