"So in 1 East P. C. 257, it is laid down that 'where divers persons resolve generally to resist all opposers in the commission of any breach of the peace, and to execute it with violence, or in such a manner as naturally tends to raise tumults and affrays; as by committing a violent disseisin with great numbers, or going to beat a man, or rob a park, or standing in opposition to the sheriff's posse, they must at their peril abide the event of their actions;' and if doing any of these or similar acts any person interfering with them is killed, all who took part in the fact or abetted thereto are guilty of murder. "These citations, to which many others of a similar tenor might be added, show that the rule of criminal responsibility for the acts of others is subject to the reasonable limitation that the particular act of one of a party for which his associ ates and confederates are to be held liable must be shown to have been done for the furtherance or in prosecution of the common object and design for which they combined together. 

Without such limitation, a person might be held responsible for acts which were not the natural or necessary consequences of the enterprise or undertaking in which he was engaged, and which he could not either in fact or in law be deemed to have contemplated or intended.”

So, a rioter is not responsible, on an indictment for murder, for a death accidentally caused by officers engaged in suppressing the riot. 

Com. v. Campbell, 7 Allen, 541, at 543 and 544

The court said, in the last cited case, at pages 544, 545, and 546: "No person can be held guilty of homicide unless the act is either actually or constructively his, and it cannot be his act E-28

CRIMINAL LAW 

in either sense unless committed by his own hand or by some one acting in concert with him or in furtherance of a common object or purpose. Certainly that cannot be said to be an act of a party in any just sense, or on any sound legal principle, which is not only not done by him, or by any one with whom he is associated or connected in a common enterprise, or in attempting to accomplish the same end, but is committed by a person who is his direct and immediate adversary, and who is, at the moment when the alleged criminal act is done, actually engaged in opposing and resisting him and his confederates and abettors in the accomplishment of the unlawful object for which they are united. Suppose, for example, a burglar attempts to break into a dwelling-house, and the owner or occupant, while striving to resist and prevent the unlawful entrance, by misadventure kills his own servant. Can the burglar in such case be deemed guilty of criminal homicide? Certainly not. The act was not done by him, or with his knowledge or consent nor was it a necessary or natural consequence of the commission of the offence in which he was engaged. He could not therefore have contemplated or intended it. Another illustration will perhaps be more apposite to the case before us. Suppose, during the progress of the riot in which it is alleged the prisoner was engaged, and while the soldiers and others in possession of the armory were in the act of repelling the attack of the mob in the street, by firing upon it with the cannon which was used on the occasion, that it had burst by reason of some secret defect, and killed several of those who were in its immediate vicinity; or that a soldier while handling his musket had by accident inflicted a mortal wound on himself; it would hardly be contended that in either of these cases the whole body of rioters could be held legally responsible for criminal homicide, by reason of the lives that were thus destroyed. And yet there is no real distinction between the cases supposed and that of the prisoner at the bar, if the rule insisted on by the attorney general is a sound one. "The taking of human life, under the circumstances supposed, in a certain sense was the result of the unlawful acts of the mob that is, it would not have occurred but for the E-29

CRIMINAL LAW 

riot which furnished the cause and occasion of the use of the musket or cannon. "Indeed, it seems to us that in every aspect the doctrine contended for, if followed to its legitimate and logical conclusion, would lead to extraordinary consequences. It would render everybody who participated in a transaction, whether acting in concert or in opposition, whether united in a common design or arrayed on opposite sides in a contest or affray in which each contending party was striving to defeat the purposes of the other, if all acted without legal justification, responsible for every criminal act which was done by any person during the progress of the affair in which they were all engaged. Nor, in applying the principle in question to a case like the one before us, can we see any good reason why the soldiers who defended the armory and resisted the mob, if it should turn out that they acted without sufficient legal authority to justify their acts, might not be held guilty of manslaughter for homicides committed by the rioters, if the latter are to be held responsible for deaths caused by the acts of the soldiers. But the rules of law do not give any countenance to such a doctrine." 

Abandonment of the conspiracy relieves the defendant from responsibility for all acts perpetrated thereafter. 

But see: Com. v. Devereux, 256 Mass. 387, at 396

Thus, if several act in concert to steal a man's goods, and he is induced by fraud to trust one of them in the presence of others with the possession of the goods, and then another of the party entice the owner away so that he who has the goods may carry them off, all are guilty as principals. 

Com. v. Campbell, 7 Allen, 541

The mere concurrence of the minds of persons in a previously formed design to commit a crime does not alone constitute them principals. or To constitute a principal in crime there must be presence participancy, or the doing of some act at the time of the commission of the crime, in furtherance of the common design. E-30

CRIMINAL LAW II. Act Must Result from, and Have Causal 

Connection with the Conspiracy

The killing of one who interferes, by one of two conspirators in robbery, as they seek to escape, is murder as to the other who is away from the premises. 

Com. v. Devereux, 256 Mass. 387, at 396 

But see: Com. v. Campbell, 7 Allen, 541, at 544 (c) Mere Sympathy not Participation in Conspiracy Mere sympathy, also, even by a bystander, does not by itself constitute confederacy. 

Com. v. Cooley, 6 Gray, 350 (C) Presence as Spectator Only

Mere presence at the commission of a felony does not render the person liable as a participator therein. If he is innocent of any unlawful intent, and does not encourage or approve the conduct of the principal in the first degree and is only a spectator, he is not criminally responsible merely because he happens to be an observer and does not use active endeavors to prevent the commission of the crime.

To make a spectator a principal in the second degree, he must do something showing his consent to the felonious purpose and contribute in some way to its execution.

However, proof that a person was present at the commission of the felony without disapproving or opposing is evidence from which, in connection with other circumstances, it may be inferred that he was assenting thereto, lending his countenance and approval and was aiding and abetting the same. 

(III) Criminal Intent and Community of Unlawful Pur pose 

(A) General Statement 

To be guilty as a principal in the second degree, a criminal intent is necessary.

Thus, a person who enters into communication with one who is suspected of criminal acts, and apparently aids or abets him in the commission of an act, is not a principal in the second degree, if he did so, not with a criminal intent, but for the purpose of E-31

CRIMINAL LAW 

detecting the other party, and disclosing his guilt for the benefit of the public. And it can make no difference in such a case whether he was a public officer or merely a private person. 

 (B) Specific Intent

Where a particular intent is an element of a felony, it is essential that one aiding and abetting the commission of such offense should have been aware of the existence of such intent in the mind of the actual perpetrator. 

Com. v. Ryan, 154 Mass. 422

When a specific intent is necessary to constitute a particular crime, one cannot be a principal in the second degree to that particular offense unless he entertains such an intent, or knows that the party actually doing the act entertains such intent. 

Where an essential element of a crime is a specific intent, the person charged as the principal in the second degree must be shown to have known of the existence of the required intent on the part of the principal in the first degree. The common purpose between them must be proved in order to warrant a conviction of the principal in the second degree for aiding and abetting. 

Also, it is required that the principal in the second degree shall have performed his part of the crime with the felonious intent. 

The guilt of the principal in the second degree is determined by the intent of the principal in the first degree, if both have the same intent and purpose.

Although one assists with a criminal intent, in the doing of an act which he believes to be a crime, yet if the person whom he so assists has no such criminal intent, the aider and abettor is not guilty of the crime unless in his participation he performs some criminal act and then he is punishable for that act personally. 

Com. v. Brown, 154 Mass. 55 

(C) Necessity for Preconcert 

There is no necessity for preconcert between the principal in the second degree and the principal in the first degree, if the former actually aids, abets, encourages or commits any act which enables E-32

CRIMINAL LAW 

the principal in the first degree to perpetrate the crime. But where the aiding and abetting consists solely of the presence of the principal in the second degree, in a position where he might render assistance, it is essential that his presence must be known to the principal in the first degree and have been in consequence of preconcert between them. This is so even though the principal in the second degree, without the knowledge on the part of the principal in the first degree, intended to render assistance if necessary. 

If the alleged principal in the second degree is merely present and does nothing, it is necessary to warrant his conviction that there shall have been some previous conspiracy or arrangement between him and the principal in the first degree. 

Hicks v. U. S., 150 U. S. 442, at 450

So, if the Commonwealth contends that the principal in the second degree was present for the purpose of aiding, abetting, advising or encouraging the principal in the first degree in the perpetration of the crime, but the principal in the second degree did not do anything because it was not necessary and the crime was committed without his assistance, it is essential to the conviction of the principal in the second degree for the government to prove that there was some preconcert or previous conspiracy between the principal in the second degree and the principal in the first degree, whereby the principal in the second degree was to assist if it was found necessary to do so. 

Hicks v. U. S., 150 U. S. 442, at 450

It is insufficient to warrant the conviction of the principal in the second degree if he was merely present at the time and place of the commission of the crime, if he contributed neither by word or action to the crime and there is no substantial evidence of any prior arrangement or conspiracy between him and the principal in the first degree. 

Hicks v. U. S., 150 U. S. 442, at 450 

(IV) Aiding and Abetting or Other Participation in 

Crime 

(A) General Statement 

The words "aid" and "abet" are not necessarily restricted in their application to principals in the second degree, but the latter also apply to an accessory after the fact. may

E-33

CRIMINAL LAW 

The words "aid and consent" in the commission of an offense, used in a statute wherein the offence is not called a felony, includes aiding and consenting, whether the accused was present or absent, and do not necessarily extend to accessories before the fact. 

Com. v. Macomber, 3 Mass. 254

They are usually applied, however, to principals in the second degree, and as a general rule they comprehend all assistance rendered by acts or words of encouragement, incitement, or support, or presence, actual or constructive, with preconcert, with the intention of rendering assistance if necessary. 

Com. v. Lowrey, 158 Mass. 18 

Com. v. Stevens, 10 Mass. 181

It is not sufficient, however, to charge one with crime, that the crime was in pursuance of his advice, counsel, or encouragement, unless it was induced thereby. 

(B) What Constitutes Aiding and Abetting  

It is not necessary that actual physical aid shall be given. It is enough to make one a principal in the second degree, if he is present in concert with the actual perpetrator of the offense, for the purpose of assisting, if necessary, or of watching and preventing interference or detection, or for the purpose of encouragement. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496

The aiding, abetting, advise or encouragement by which one becomes a principal in the second degree in a felony may be created by acts, signs or words. 

Com. v. Knapp, 9 Pick. 496 (2) Approbation and Consent 

(a) General Statement 

If one is outside of an enclosure, watching to prevent surprise, or for the purpose of keeping guard, while his confederates are inside committing the felony, such constructive presence is sufficient to make him a principal in the second degree. 

Com. v. Devereux, 256 Mass. 387, at 396 

Com. v. Wallace, 108 Mass. 14

E-34

CRIMINAL LAW 

Com. v. Lucas, 2 Allen, 170 

So, if the defendant's acts or words were done or used for a different purpose, and yet have had the actual effect of inciting the principal in the first degree to commit the crime, the alleged principal in the second degree is not guilty as such, even though the effect of his acts or words may have had the effect of encouraging the principal in the first degree, because, it is essential that the conduct of the alleged principal in the second degree must have been with the deliberate intention of aiding, abetting or assisting the principal in the first degree, in the commission of the offense. 

Hicks v. U. S., 150 U. S. 442, at 449 (b) Mere Mental Approval

Mere mental approval is not enough to render one an aider and abettor. (3) Intention to Assist

To warrant a conviction as principal in the second degree, the conduct of the defendant, his acts or words of encouragement and abetting, must have been done for, or used by the accused with the intention of encouraging or abetting the principal in the first degree, in the perpetration of the exact crime charged against the principal. 

Hicks v. U. S., 150 U. S. 442, at 449

It is not necessary that the alleged principal in the second degree should know at every moment and every step what the principal in the first degree and every one else did, or are doing, who were engaged in aiding, or abetting, or committing the crime. All that is necessary is that he knowingly aided in the commission of the crime charged. 

Com. v. Brown, 154 Mass. 55, at 60

If he is a link in the chain and knowingly occupies that position, that is sufficient to create his status as principal in the second degree. 

Com. v. Brown, 154 Mass. 55, at 60

E-35

CRIMINAL LAW 

(4) Keeping Watch

A person who watches nearby to prevent surprise or interference, while a confederate breaks and enters a house with felonious intent, or robs a man, or sets fire to a building, or commits a larcency, is guilty as a principal in the second degree, though he may not be near enough to see the other commit the offense. 

Keeping watch while a crime is being perpetrated, so as to facilitate the escape of the actual perpetrator or to prevent his being interrupted, is an aiding and abetting and renders one guilty as a principal in the second degree. 

(5) Mere Presence 

But if his presence is by preconcert, he may be guilty as an aider and abettor, although neither by word nor by act does he encourage or discourage the commission of the felony. 

Com. v. Ryan, 154 Mass. 422

To render one guilty as principal in the second degree, he must in some way participate in the commission of the offense, by aiding or abetting the actual perpetrator of the deed. Mere presence at the time the offense is committed, and acquiescence or failure to make any effort to prevent its commission, or to apprehend the offender, is not enough.

If he is present, and not aiding or abetting the felony, he is neither principal nor accessory. (6) Words

Aiding, abetting, or encouraging, may consist of mere words. 

However, it is not necessary that any words be spoken. Signs, motions, acts and other indications are sufficient to constitute aiding or abetting. 

(V) Withdrawal or Abandonment of Aid or Encourage ment

A person who encourages the commission of an unlawful act cannot escape responsibility by quietly withdrawing from the The influence and effect of encouragement continue until he renounces the common purpose and makes it plain to the scene. others that he has done so and that he does not intend to participate further. He cannot, by the coward's expedient of running E-36

CRIMINAL LAW 

away after he has incited his associates to crime, escape punishment. 

Miller v. U. S., 277 Fed. 721 

f. Crimes Admitting of Principal in Second Degree (I) General Statement 

As a general proposition of law there may be principals in the second degree in all felonies, whether common law or statutory, even though the particular crime is of such a kind that it can be committed only by persons of a certain class. 

U. S. v. Gooding, 12 Wheat. (U. S.) 462 (II) 

Statutory Crime Confined to Principals in First Degree

The rule that all felonies, admit of principals in the second degree is subject to the exception that where a statute applies only to the person actually doing the thing which constitutes the offense, and not to all who are guilty, e. g. persons selling liquor without a license, persons aiding and abetting such offenses are not principals. 

U. S. v. Farrar, 281 U. S. 624; s. c. 38 Fed. (2nd) 515 (Buyer of liquor not aider and abettor to seller) 

In Commonwealth v. Willard, 22 Pick., 476, the purchaser of the liquor, sold without license, was held not guilty of participation in the crime and consequently was not excusable from testifying against the seller, on the ground that he would incriminate himself. In the opinion, Shaw, C. J., after saying that "no precedent and no authority has been shown for such a prosecution, and no such prosecution has been attempted within the knowledge of the court, although a similar law has been in force almost from the foundation of the government, and thousands of prosecutions and convictions of sellers have been had under it, most of which have been sustained by the testimony of the buyers," proceeded: "It is difficult to draw any precise line of distinction between the cases in which the law holds it a misdemeanor to counsel, entice, or induce another to commit a crime, and where it does not. In general, it has been considered as applying to cases of felony, though it has been held that it does E-37

CRIMINAL LAW 

not depend upon the mere legal and technical distinction between felony and misdemeanor. One consideration, however, is manifest in all the cases, and that is that the offence proposed to be committed by the counsel, advice or enticement of another is of a high and aggravated nature and character, tending to breaches of the peace or other great disorder and violence, being what are usually considered mala in se, or criminal in themselves, in contradistinction to mala prohibita, or acts otherwise indifferent than as they are restrained by positive law." 

Com. v. Macomber, 3 Mass. 254 

(III) Particular Crimes (A) Felonious Assault 

One may be convicted as principal in a felonious assault where he advised, procured, or incited the assault. For example, when one of two persons resisting arrest aids, abets, advises, or encourages the other by signs or motions to assault the arresting officer, he is guilty of such assault the same as if made by him personally. 

Com. v. Morgan, 1932 A. S. 1807, at 1808 

Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 265 

(B) Forgery (1) 

General Statement 

If persons make distinct parts of a forged instrument, each is a principal as to the whole, even though he does not know by whom the other parts are executed, and one finishes it alone while the rest are absent. Were the law not so, no one could be punished; for a person whose hand does the criminal act, either wholly or in part, is not an accessory. (2) Uttering In forgery, if several persons plan the uttering of a forged or der, and one of them utters it in the absence of the rest, he only is a principal, while the others are accessories. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206

It was held not to be sufficient to convict one as a principal in the uttering of a forged note (assumed to be a felony) that he came with the utterer to town, put up at the same inn with him, walked out with him, two hours later the other alone passed the E-38

CRIMINAL LAW 

note, in twenty minutes more the two came together, and when he saw that the utterer was arrested he ran from the officer and each affected ignorance of the other. 

(C) Keeping and Exposing Intoxicating Liquor for 

Sale Under the statutes making it penal for unlicensed persons to sell intoxicating liquor, it is generally held that one who by purchasing it lends the concurrence of his will thereto, and tempts the seller with his money, and is present encouraging him, is still not liable to punishment.

U. S. v. Farrar, 281 U. S. 624 

(D) Manslaughter 

While the characteristic element of the crime of manslaughter is, that although a homicide, it is committed in sudden heat and passion and without malice aforethought, and will not therefore admit of accessories before the fact, yet this does not necessarily limit the offense to the persons who actually did the deed when several were present and engaged in a common quarrel. The provocation given may extend to others as well as to the principal actor. Although the crime is said to be "sudden and unpremeditated," it need not be on the instant the provocation is received. 

In its regard for the weakness of human nature the law allows a certain time-reasonable time-for the transport of passion to continue before "cooling," and during that time it is possible for others present, affected by the same provocation and passion, to stimulate and incite the principal actor to the perpetration of the deed, thereby becoming aiders and abettors. (E) Murder 

Those who advise, encourage, aid or abet the killing of another are as guilty as though they took his life with their own hands. 

A principal in the crime of murder need not be specifically a party to the killing, if he is present and consenting to the assemblage by which it is perpetrated in pursuance of the common design. This rule applies even in the absence of special malice against the person slain, or of deliberate intention to hurt him, if the killing was committed in the prosecution of an original unlawful purpose. 

But it is not sufficient to charge one with murder, that the killing E-39

CRIMINAL LAW 

was in pursuance of his advice, counsel and encouragement, unless it was induced thereby. It is of course competent, under an indictment charging several persons as principals in murder, to convict one of such principals of one degree of felonious homicide, and another of some other degree of felonious homicide, according to the intent with which such principals may have performed the particular act attributed to and proved against them. 

(2) Murder of Child 

If, before the birth of a child, a person advises the mother to murder it when born, and she does so, the advisor not being present at the murder, is an accessory. (F) Rape The crime of rape admits of aiders and abettors or principals in the second degree, even though they would not be capable of actually committing the offense. 

At common law, suicide was considered a crime against the laws of God and man, and one who persuaded another to kill himself, and was present when he did so, was guilty of murder as a principal in the second degree. And this would appear still to be the rule. 

Com. v. Bowen, 13 Mass. 356

Likewise, if two persons mutually agree to kill themselves and the means employed to produce death take effect upon one only, the survivor is guilty of the murder of the one who dies; and if one compels another by threats to take his own life, he may be punished as a principal for the crime of murder. Where, however, to escape anticipated violence a person does an act resulting in his death, to render the person producing the fear liable as a principal, the reason to apprehend violence must have been such that the step leading to death was one which a reasonable man might take, though the circumstances need not be such as to satisfy the jury that there was no other escape. But, though one knows of the intention of another to commit suicide, and assents to it, it must be shown beyond a reasonable doubt, in order to E-40

CRIMINAL LAW 

render him guilty of murder, that he did or said something which aided, encouraged or induced the deceased to kill himself. When two persons enter into a suicide pact, there is always a place of repentence, a locus poentitentiae, and if one of the parties abandons his purpose of committing suicide, and endeavors to persuade the other also to abandon it, he has done all the law requires him to do, under the general principal of criminal law permitting conspirators to withdraw from the conspiracy, and if the latter nevertheless commits suicide, the former incurs no criminal liability. 

At common law, since an accessory before the fact in felony could not be punished until the principal had been convicted, one who counseled another to commit suicide, but who was not present at the time of suicide, escaped prosecution entirely. But this escape was largely cut off by regarding him as a principal whenever he was present at the time of the fatal act, or whenever it was his act through an innocent agent, and as an abettor only when there was another guilty as a principal. This rule of the common law has sometimes been departed from; authority is not lacking that a person otherwise guilty as an accessory in such a case cannot escape punishment because there is no one in being to be connected as principal. The same result has also been reached under modern statutes, providing for the punishment of accessories before the fact in felony, as principals; it therefore seems that it is possible that one who counsels or advises another to commit suicide may be punished for the offense. But where suicide is not a crime, it seems that one furnishing another with means to kill himself is innocent of violating the law. 

(2) Persons Abetting Suicide are Principals in Mur der Whether the influence of the defendant was the exclusive cause of the suicide is immaterial. 

Com, v. Bowen, 13 Mass. 356

In Massachusetts, two prisoners being within hearing of each other in adjoining cells, one counselled the other to take his own life, which he did; and it was ruled that if the advice caused the deed, the adviser was guilty of murder. 

Com. v. Bowen, 13 Mass. 356

To some extent, at present, this question is regulated by statute. E-41

CRIMINAL LAW (H) Trespass 

Any person who is present at the commission of a trespass, encouraging or inciting the same by words, gestures, looks, or signs, or who in any way or by any means countenances or approves the same, is in law deemed to be an aider or abettor, and liable as a principal; and proof that a person is present at the commission of a trespass, without disapproving or opposing it, is evidence from which, in connection with other circumstances, it is competent for the jury to infer that he assented thereto, lent to it his countenance and approval, and was thereby aiding and abetting the same. 

4. Accessory Before the Fact a. Definitions

An accessory before the fact is one who was not present, actually or constructively, at the time when a felony was committed, but who counseled, hired or otherwise procured, or commanded another to commit it. 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 43 

Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 274, s. 2

An accessory before the fact is one who, not being present to aid, abet, assist, and encourage, has beforehand procured or taken other steps to have the crime perpetrated. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211

An accessory before the fact is one who, being absent at the time the crime is committed, yet procures, counsels, or commands another to commit it. 

Trial of Aaron Burr, 4 Cranch (U. S.) 470, at 492

An accessory is one who participates in a felony too remotely to be a principal.

An accessory before the fact is a person whose will contributes to a felony committed by another as a principal while he is too far away to aid in the felonious act. 

A person incapable of committing the criminal act himself may be guilty as an accessory to the crime. 

An accessory before the fact is one who procures, commands, or counsels the commission of a felony by another, but who is not E-42

CRIMINAL LAW 

present, either actually or constructively, when the felony is committed.

An accessory before the fact is one who, without being present, aiding and abetting, procures, advises, or commands another to commit the crime.

No person can be a principal in felony unless he be present. 

An accessory before the fact is he, though being absent at the time of the felony committed, does yet procure, counsel, or command another to commit a felony. 

The language, "incite, move, and procure, aid, counsel, hire, and command the said person as aforesaid unknown, the said felony and abortion in manner and form aforesaid to do and commit," has been sustained in this Commonwealth as sufficiently describing the offense of an accessory before the fact. 

Com. v. Adams, 127 Mass. 15 b. Distinctions (I) Distinguished from Principals (A) Generally

In felonies, and not in treason or misdemeanors, accessories before the fact are distinguished from principals in the first degree and principals in the second degree. These distinctions are purely technical. As to punishment, there is no distinction between a principal and an accessory, the offense of each being a felony of which the penalty is the same. 

Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 274, s. 2

There are circumstances when more blame is attached to the accessory before the fact than to any principal. Generally, this is so, when the accessory before the fact is a domineering personality who overpowers the mind or will of the principal through fear, affection or confidence although the principal acts reluctantly.

In this Commonwealth, an accessory before the fact, though by statute (Gen. Laws, c. 274, s. 2) punishable as principal, must nevertheless be indicted, not as principal, but as accessory before the fact. 

E-43

CRIMINAL LAW 

The offence of the accessory before the fact continues distinct from that of the principal, so that acquittal as a principal does not bar a prosecution as accessory. 

Pettes v. Com., 126 Mass. 242 

(B) Principals in the First Degree 

The principal in the first degree is the actual doer or perpetrator of the act which constitutes the crime, while the accessory before the fact takes no part in the actual commission of the offense but completes his part in the crime before the vital act occurs and is absent at the time of its performance. 

(C) Principals in the Second Degree 

The principal in the second degree is present, assisting the prin cipal in the first degree, who personally commits the felony, while the accessory before the fact, who counseled the commission of the crime, is absent at the time of its commission. 

Com. v. Clune, 162 Mass. 208, at 211

If the participant is a principal, though of the second degree, he cannot be charged in an indictment as an accessory; if he is an accessory, he cannot be held as a principal. 

By separate acts, one may become both a principal and an accessory in the same felony; as, by commanding another to kill a third person, rendering him an accessory before the fact when the murder is done; and afterward joining with the person commanded in doing it, which makes him a principal. 

(II) Disingutished from Accessory after the Fact 

The principal distinction between an accessory before the fact and an accessory after the fact is the point of time at which he participates in the crime. Although both are absent at the actual commission of the crime, the former acts before its perpetration by procuring, counseling, hiring or commanding the principal in the first degree to commit it, while the latter acts after the crime has been committed, knowing of its perpetration, and relieves, receives, comforts or assists the principal in the first degree to ob tain the benefit of his crime, or escape detection or punishment. 

By Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 274, s. 4, certain relatives cannot be accessories after the fact, while they may be accessories before the fact. 

Com. v. Sokorelis, 254 Mass. 454, at 458 and 459

E-44

CRIMINAL LAW (III) Distinguished from Accomplice 

An accomplice includes all participes criminis (partners in crime). So, an accessory before the fact is necessarily an accomplice, while an accomplice need not necessarily be an accessory before the fact. 

(IV) Distinguished from Conspirator or Confederate 

(A) A conspirator is a party to an agreement to accomplish an illegal object or a lawful object by illegal means. The word "illegal" in this sense does not necessarily mean criminal, but may be immoral or creating civil wrong. 

Com. v. Hunt, 4 Met. 111, at 125

However, an accessory before the fact must be a party to an act that is a felony. (B) The conspirator may be an original party to the unlawful agreement of conspiracy or may join in it at any time after its original formation, while an accessory before the fact must participate in the crime before its commission and must counsel, hire, procure or command its commission. (C) The conspirator need not originate the thought of the conspiracy or induce others to join it, while the accessory must conduct himself so that his acts tend to procure, counsel, hire or command the principle in the first degree to perpetrate the crime. (D) To constitute one a conspirator, there need be no act committed, beyond the agreement of conspiracy, while to constitute one an accessory before the fact an actual perpetration of the crime by overt act must occur. C. 

Statutory Provisions 

Gen. Laws. (Ter. Ed.), c. 274, s. 2, provides in part that: "Whoever... in the commission of a felony, is accessory thereto before the fact by counselling, hiring or otherwise procuring such felony to be committed, shall be punished in the manner provided for the punishment of the principal felon." 

Com. v. Donoghue, 266 Mass. 391 

Com. v. Derry, 221 Mass. 45

An accessory to a felony before the fact may be indicted, tried and punished in the same county where the principal felon might be indicted and tried, although the counselling, hiring or procuring the commission of such felony was committed within or without this commonwealth or on the high seas."

(I) General Statement 

In Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243, it was, at pages 256, 257, 258 and 259: "Whoever procures a felony to be committed, though it be by the intervention of a third person, is an accessory before the fact, for it is not necessary that there should be any direct communication between the accessory and the principal. 

Rex. v. Cooper, 5 C. & P. 535 

Foster's Crown Law, 125 

2 Hawk. c. 29, ss. 1, 10 

Earl of Somerset's case, cited in 19 Howell's State Trials, 804 E-46

CRIMINAL LAW 

"And the accessory is a felon, though his felony is different in kind from that of the principal.

Foster's Crown Law, 343 

"So it is said to be a principle in law which can never be controverted that he who procures a felony to be done is a felon. 

1 Russ. on Crimes, 32 "We cannot see that the application of these principles is changed, when the crime of the accessory before the fact is made by statute a substantive felony. The object of making it a substantive felony may be either to provide a distinct or milder punishment upon conviction, or to authorize the indictment and conviction of the accessory where the principal has not been convicted. But whether the crime is made the subject of separate prosecution and punishment or is to be included in an indictment with the principal offence will not, in the opinion of the court, change the definition of it, or alter the facts or circumstances in which the commission of it consists. The same facts, to be averred and proved in the same way, will substantiate the crime in one case as in the other. Thus, without any special provision of statute, any one inciting or counselling a murder afterward committed would be an accessory before the fact, whether he incited or counselled the actual perpetrator directly or through the intervention of another accessory. So he that procured the commission of perjury was guilty of subornation of perjury, whether his procurement was immediate or by the instrumentality of another suborner. In either case a change in the mode of indictment would not change the proof of what constitutes the crime. The crime of inciting or counselling the murder could be committed by the same person and by the same acts, although the guilt of the accessory were made a substantive felony, to be punished without reference to the prosecution of the principal. The crime of subornation of perjury would consist in procuring perjury to be committed, directly or indirectly, as much after subornation was made a felony as before.

E-47

CRIMINAL LAW 

"In construing the provisions of Gen. Stats., c. 168, we must have reference not only to their apparent design and meaning, but to other provisions of the body of laws, of which that chapter forms a part. The first section gives a new and technical definition of felony, differing from that of the common law. The common law incidents of felony would generally be held to attach to the felonies thus defined; but they would not be so held, where such a result would conflict with other statute provisions. Thus, s. 4 provides that 'whoever counsels, hires or otherwise procures a felony to be committed may be indicted and convicted as an accessory before the fact, either with the principal felon, or after his conviction; or may be indicted and convicted of a substantive felony, whether the principal felon has or has not been convicted, or is or is not amenable to justice; and in the last mentioned case may be punished in the same manner as if convicted of being an accessory before the fact.' This section materially alters the common law in relation to the indictment and trial of accessories. But it was held in State v. 

Ricker, 29 Maine 84, in construing a similar statute of the State of Maine, that the defendant must still be charged in the indictment as an accessory and not as a principal. And on the other hand, we cannot suppose that the provision as to punishment would apply to a case where the accessory is expressly made subject to a penalty less than that allotted to the principal, as in c. 160, ss. 15 and 16. The section makes a general provision for the case of accessories before the fact to felonies, which is made to some extent in other parts of the statutes in regard to particular felonies, and for which there is a different provision elsewhere in regard to others. It is undoubtedy specially designed for the case of accessories to felonies before the fact for which no other provision is specifically made; but we see no reason why it is not applicable to all cases within the scope of its terms, when not inconsistent with any other statute. "A similar rule of construction may be applied to s. 5, which declares that 'a person charged with the offence mentioned in the preceding section'-that is, with the offence of E-48

CRIMINAL LAW 

counselling, hiring or otherwise procuring a felony to be committed-'may be indicted, tried and punished in the same court and county where the principal felon might be indicted and tried, although the offence of counselling, hiring or procuring the commission of such felony is committed on the high seas or on land within or without the limits of this state.' 

(II) Place of Offence 

One may be an accessory by counselling, hiring, inciting, or otherwise procuring the principal in the first degree, to commit the felony within this commonwealth, even though, he, the accessory, performed all acts of "counselling, hiring, inciting or procuring" out of the state. e. 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243, at 259 (Letter written out of state, contents of which, communicated to principal within state by agent who participated in guilty purpose.)

Essentials to Create Status 

To constitute one an accessory before the fact— (I) There must be a guilty principal in the first degree. (II) The accessory must be neither actually nor constructively present when the offense is committed. (III) There must be some participation by way of procurement, command, or counsel. Mere knowledge that the offense is to be committed, or even mental approval, is not enough. 

(I) Guilty Principal in First Degree (A) General Statement 

In order to convict one as an accessory before the fact it is necessary that some person shall have committed the principal felony (even though his identity is unknown). 

Com. v. Asherowski, 196 Mass. 342, at 345 even though the principal is convicted of committing the crime in another Commonwealth or State. 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243

E-49

CRIMINAL LAW 

Without a guilty principal there can be no accessory. Nor can the accessory be convicted of an offence in a degree higher than that of the principal.

To constitute such accessory there must be a principal; and while the crime is being committed, the accessory must not be so near him that he could render personal assistance since then he would be himself a principal. Also, the thing counselled must be done else the counselling only will be an indictable attempt. 

Where the principal crime requires a specific intent for its commission it is necessary to prove that the principal in the first degree had that specific intent. 

Com. v. Asherowski, 196 Mass. 342, at 345 

Com. v. Goldstein, 114 Mass. 272 

Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 266, s. 10 

So, as was said in Com. v. Asherowski, 196 Mass. 342, at 345 and 346: "The intent to injure the insurer is a necessary ingredient of the crime described in R. L., c. 208, s. 10; and unless the person who did the burning is shown to have acted with that intent, the crime is not proved to have been committed. And these defendants, who are charged in the court before us only as accessories before the fact, could not be convicted unless it was proved that the principal offense was in fact committed in violation of the statute. 

Com. v. Adams, 127 Mass. 15, at 17 and 19 

Com. v. Glover, 111 Mass. 395 

Com. v. Phillips, 16 Mass. 423 "Even though the defendants may have procured this fire to be set, yet if the person who set it, though acting by their procurement, was in fact wholly ignorant of the insurance, and had no actual intent to injure the insurer, he acted innocently so far as this charge is concerned, and could not be found to have committed the offence charged in the indictment. These defendants, in that event, very likely may committed a substantive crime; it may well be that they could have E-50

CRIMINAL LAW 

N themselves be held to be guilty of the offence which they would thus have committed by an innocent hand. 

Com. v. Hill, 11 Mass. 136 "But they could not be convicted as accessories before the fact to a felony which had not been actually committed." 

The person actually committing the deed must be a guilty party, and not an innocent agent, for, one who procures the commission of a felony through the instrumentality of an innocent agent is himself the principal in the first degree.

So, a person who counsels, hires or procures another to commit a felony cannot be an accessory, if the other does not actually commit the felony.

The legal guilt of the accessory depends upon the guilt of the principal. 

Trial of Aaron Burr, 4 Cranch (U. S.) 470, at 504

The legal guilt of the person who counseled, hired or procured the commission of the crime depends not simply on the criminality of any previous conspiracy or previous counseling, hiring or procuring but upon the criminality of the acts done by the principal in the first degree as the proximate result of such counseling, hiring or procuring. If the one who perpetrates the fact is not a felon, he who advises the fact cannot be an accessory. His guilt, then, depends on the guilt of the principal in the first degree. 

Trial of Aaron Burr, 4 Cranch (U. S.) 470, at 504 

(B) Act Through Innocent Agent 

Since there must always be a principal, one is such who does the criminal thing through an innocent agent while personally absent. For example, when a dose of poison or any inanimate object, or a human being with or without general accountability, but not criminal in the particular instance, inflicts death or other injuries in the absence of him whose will set the force in motion, and there is no one whom the law can punish, it of necessity fixes upon him as the doer. But if the agent employed incurs guilt, then the employer is simply an accessory before the fact. E-51

CRIMINAL LAW (C) Trial of Principal in First Degree Need Not 

Precede

At common law, the conviction of the principal in the first degree was a prerequisite to the trial of one charged as accessory. 

Com. v. Briggs, 5 Pick. 429 

Com. v. Phillips, 16 Mass. 423 

Com. v. Andrews, 3 Mass. 126

But even at common law, where there are two principals, and only one convicted, the other being dead, the accessory must answer notwithstanding the nonconviction of the deceased. 

Com. v. Knapp, 10 Pick. 477

Now, because of Gen. Laws, c. 274, s. 3, the trial of the accessory before the fact may precede, be simultaneous with, or occur after the trial of the principal in the first degree. 

However, this statute does not eliminate the necessity of proving the guilt of the principal in the first degree; for one cannot be an accessory before the fact by procuring what is never done. 

The principal in the first degree may be averred to be unknown. 

Com. v. Adams, 127 Mass. 15

An accessory cannot take advantage of an error in the record against the principal. 

Com. v. Knapp, 10 Pick. 477

An accessory before the fact may be tried in the county of the consummated act, though the act of accessoryship was committed elsewhere. 

Com. v. Pettes, 114 Mass. 307 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243 

(D) Effect of Conviction or Acquittal of Principal in First Degree (1) Conviction 

When principal and accessory are tried separately, conviction of the principal is prima facie evidence of his guilt, on the trial of the accessory, but may be collaterally disputed when the issue is the guilt of the accessory. 

Com. v. Knapp, 10 Pick. 477 

Com. v. Stow, 1 Mass. 54

E-52

CRIMINAL LAW 

Where the accessory is tried after the principal, it is prima facie sufficient in proof of the latter's guilt to produce the record of his conviction,—a rule which does not exclude other evidence. 

However, a mere conviction is not sufficient, and it must have been followed by a sentence to be admissible. 

Com. v. Knapp, 10 Pick. 477

Though the record of the principal's conviction is prima facie evidence of the guilt of such principal, as against an accessory tried separately, it is not conclusive as against such accessory, because the record was in a proceeding between other parties, and such accessory may show the principal's innocence.

An accessory in Massachusetts to a crime committed outside of the Commonwealth may be convicted here. 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243 · (2) Acquittal

The rule creating prima facie evidence in the trial of the accessory arising from the record of the trial of the principal makes the principal's acquittal a complete bar to the indictment against the accessory. In this connection the accessory is attached completely to his principal and if the principal is acquitted the accessory must be also acquitted. 

Com. v. Phillips, 16 Mass. 423 

Ex Parte Garland, 4 Wall. (U. S.) 333, at 387 

(II) The Felony (A) General Statement 

To constitute one an accessory before the fact, it is essential that the felony, which the accused counselled, hired and procured shall have been in fact committed. 

Com. v. Asherowski, 196 Mass. 342 (B) Nature of Felony

Not every felony permits the existence of an accessory before the fact. So, in order to render one an accessory before the fact, the nature of the felony must not be such as to render it impossible that there should be an accessory before the fact. 

Such is the case in manslaughter, for manslaughter can exist only when the killing is without premeditation or previous malice. If E-53

CRIMINAL LAW 

the killing was with either premeditation or previous malice, it is murder. However, there may be principals in the second degree to manslaughter. (C) Impossible Crime

A person cannot be an accessory before the fact to an impossible crime, as, for example, an accessory to the crime of burglary by inciting one to break and enter a place not the subject of burglary. 

Com. v. Makely, 131 Mass. 421 

(III) 

Absence

To be an accessory before the fact, the accused must have been absent at the time the offence was committed, that is, the instant when the deed was done. Actual or constructive presence makes one a principal in the second degree, as distinguished from the accessory before the fact. 

The charge of the trial judge, which was approved in Com. v. 

Clune, 162 Mass. 206, at 211, was: "An accessory before the fact is one who, not being present to aid, abet, assist, and encourage, has beforehand procured or taken other steps to have the crime perpetrated. . . ." 

(IV) Causal Connection Between Incitement and Com mission of Crime To be an accessory before the fact the person inciting, procuring or commanding must become a principal in the commission of the contemplated crime as the result of the defendant's acts. 

Com. v. Derry, 221 Mass. 45, at 47 

Com. v. Campbell, 7 Allen, 541, at 544 

(V) Criminal Intent and Community of Unlawful Pur pose

To render one guilty as an accessory to a crime he must have a criminal intent. Thus, one who joins a conspiracy to commit a robbery merely for the purpose of exposing it, and honestly carries out the plan, is not an accessory before the fact to the robbery when committed by the others. 

Also, the aid of a person who enters into a previously formed plan of criminals for the purpose of detecting them does not make him an accessory.

CRIMINAL LAW 

The criminal intent required is the same for an accessory before the fact as for a principal. Often the former is one who originated the idea of the crime, whereupon he excited the latter thereto. But the case is the same in law whether the evil purpose was born in one or the other.

Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 274, s. 2 

Where a particular intent is requisite to constitute a crime, an accessory before the fact must have participated in that particular intent. 

Com. v. Asherowski, 196 Mass. 342

For one to be guilty, his intent must concur sufficiently with his act.

To warrant a conviction of a person as accessory before the fact it is necessary that there be evidence showing directly or inferentially that, between the accused and the principal in the first degree there existed or had existed some business connection or interest other than such as naturally appertains to acquaintance, friendship, or relationship, of employer or employee, or the presence of some unusual bond of sympathy as sometimes marks near relationship of blood or kinship. 

Com. v. Derry, 221 Mass. 45, at 47

So, if the accused, at the request of the principal in the first degree, does some act which might be inferred to be procurement of the crime there must be evidence that the accused knew the purpose for which he did the act or in some way participated in the commission of the crime. 

Com. v. Derry, 221 Mass. 45, at 48 and 49 (Defendant purchased corks which were used to plug sprinkler heads, in indictment for burning building to defraud insurance company.) 

(VI) Counseling, Hiring, Inciting or Otherwise Procuring 

Felony to be Committed 

(A) General Statement 

To render one an accessory before the fact he must have counseled, hired or otherwise procured the commission of the felony by the principal in the first degree. 

Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 274, ss. 2 and 3

E-55

CRIMINAL LAW 

Words that sound in, or acts which indicate bare permission, do not make one an accessory before the fact. Likewise, mere nondisclosure or concealment of a fact, or the intention of a third person to commit a felony, is not enough. 

So, if one says to the accused, "I will kill W" and the accused says, "I would be pleased if you did so," this does not make the accused an accessory before the fact. 

However, approbation and consent are something more than words and acts of bare permission. They are conduct constituting "counseling, hiring, inciting or otherwise procuring." 

The counseling, hiring, or procuring which will render one an accessory before the fact may be by acts or words but, to create guilt, the acts must be done or the words spoken with the intent to produce the felony. The number of acts done or words spoken is immaterial, the important consideration is their effect in inducing the perpetration of the crime. 

The time of counseling, hiring or procuring is not an important element. It may determine the causal connection between the conduct of the alleged accessory before the fact and the principal in the first degree.

The procurement, however, need not be direct. It is sufficient if it be through the agency of another; and it may be by approba tion or consent to an expressed felonious design. 

QUERY, Can there be an accessory to an accessory? 

So, where one hires a second person to procure a third person commit a felony, the first two are accessories to the third principal in the first degree. 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243 to person as One does not become an accessory before the fact by merely concealing knowledge that a felony is to be committed. 

It is not essential that the crime shall have been originally conceived, contrived or invented by the accessory. He may have the status of an accessory before the fact to the crime even though it was originated by thoughts or acts of another. E-56

CRIMINAL LAW (B) Concealment or Failure to Prevent Intended Crime 

One does not become an accessory before the fact merely because he has knowledge of, or fails to prevent a crime intended to be committed by another. 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243 (C) Acquiescence, Approval, Consent or Knowledge One is not liable as an accessory before the fact from his mere acquiescence, approval, consent or knowledge in the commission or omission of any act which creates a felony. 

Com. v. Smith, 11 Allen, 243

To warrant a conviction, the accused must participate in the commission of the crime by furthering its commission in the counseling, hiring, inciting or otherwise procuring the perpetration of the criminal act by the principal in the first degree. 

(VII) Repentance, Abandonment and Withdrawal 

One who would otherwise be an accessory before the fact if the felonious crime were committed by the principal in the first degree, may relieve himself from all connection with the crime if he repents, abandons and withdraws therefrom before the crime is committed and brings the fact of his repentance, abandonment or withdrawal to the knowledge and attention of the principal in the first degree. So, he is liable as accessory before the fact if he fails to withdraw before the crime is committed or does not inform the principal in the first degree.

When the accessory before the fact withdraws his counsel and advice before the felony is committed and actively does what he can to prevent its consummation, he is not liable criminally. 

Nor is he responsible if, after his making known to the principal in the first degree the fact that he has repented and withdrawn, the crime results from some new and intervening cause. 

However, mere change of mind without conveying that fact to the principal in the first degree will not of itself exonerate the accessory before the fact. f. Crimes Admitting of Accessories before the Fact 

(I) General Statement 

Practically all felonies admit of accessories before the fact.

(II) 

It is not necessary that a statutory felony should require or permit the existence of the status of accessory before the fact. So, it is not infrequent from the very nature of the object of the statute that a crime is created which is confined in some instances to principals and in other instances to the principal in the first degree, without permitting the existence of accessories thereto. 

Statutory Crime Confined to Principals

An illustration of the above is found in the instance of sales of intoxicating liquor. Technically, the buyer may be deemed to have aided, abetted, encouraged, been present at, and otherwise constituted himself a principal in the second degree but the cases hold that he is not such, the crime being confined to the principal in the first degree. 

U. S. v. Farrar, 281 U. S. 624, at 634 

S. C. 38 Fed. (2nd) 515, at 517

The same reasoning would lead to the conclusion that statutory crimes may be created with the exclusion of accessories before the fact.

The offense of manslaughter, however, from its legal character, when the result of a misadventure, or when committed in the heat of passion, excludes the possibility of an accessory before the fact as an element of its composition. PROCEEDING PRELIMINARY TO TRIAL 5. Ordering Separate or Joint Trials 

The question of separate or joint trials rests in sound judicial discretion: 

Comm. v. Snyder, 1933 A. S. 809, at 813 

Comm. v. Gallo, 275 Mass. 320, at 326 

Comm. v. Sacco, 255 Mass. 369, at 413 

Comm. v. Borasky, 214 Mass. 313

The allowance of a motion by the Commonwealth that the trial proceed against certain defendants and not against others is an exercise of judicial discretion and does not require a hearing upon facts presented to the judge in support of the request of the district attorney. 

Comm. v. Snyder, 1933 A. S. 809, at 813 10. a.

Specifications or Bill of Particulars General Statement 

The office of specifications is merely to inform the defendant of certain facts to enable him to present his defence. 

Comm. v. Snyder, 1933 A. S. 809, at 815

The reason for allowing a defendant to obtain a bill of particulars is to inform him fully of the nature of the offence "where the indictment alone does not sufficiently inform the defendants, and this as matter of right.” 

Comm. v. Snyder, 1933 A. S. 809, at 815 

Comm. v. Belenski, 276 Mass. 35, at 40 

Comm. v. Farmer, 218 Mass. 507, at 509

The specifications affect the proof, mode of trial and the indictment, and are a part of the record. 

Comm. v. Snyder, 1933 A. S. 809, at 815 

Comm. v. Gedzium, 259 Mass. 453, at 457 and 458 b. Right to Demand or Require

It is held that where the charges of a valid indictment are so general in their nature that they do not fully advise accused of the specific acts with which he is charged, so that he may

CRIMINAL LAW 

properly prepare his defense, the court has power to order a bill of particulars to be furnished him. 

Comm. v. Min Sing, 202 Mass. 121 

Comm. v. Sinclair, 195 Mass. 100 

Comm. v. Hartford, 193 Mass. 464 

Comm. v. Wood, 4 Gray 11 

Comm. v. Giles, 1 Gray 466 

Comm. v. Snelling, 15 Pick. 321 

Comm. v. Davis, 11 Pick. 432 

Bartell v. U. S., 227 U. S. 427

Kirby v. U. S. 174 U. S. 47 Rosen v. U. S. 161 U. S. 29 

Where a writing is too obscene or indecent to be set forth in the indictment, defendant has the right to apply for a bill of particulars, and it is within the judicial discretion to grant an order therefor if necessary to protect the rights of defendant. 

Bartell v. U. S., 227 U. S. 427

And when the charge in the indictment is too general and indefinite to apprise the defendant of the cause and nature of his accusation without the aid of a bill of particulars, it is error for the trial court to refuse to require such bill. 

Comm. v. Massad, 242 Mass. 532

Held improperly refused. In a prosecution of an automobile driver for going away, after injuring a person without giving his name, residence, and automobile number, where the complaint failed to name the person injured, the defendant was entitled as of right to a statement of particulars, for the purpose of obtain ing such information. 

Comm. v. Massad, 242 Mass. 532

The motion should be allowed only where the charges of an indictment are so general that they do not advise the defendant of the specific acts of which he is accused, and the court feels that the bill should be furnished him so that he may properly prepare his defense.

CRIMINAL LAW 

Discretion of court. The granting or refusal of a bill of particulars rests within the discretion of the court to be exercised with reference to the circumstances of the peculiar case. 

Comm. v. Wakelin, 230 Mass. 567 

Comm. v. Jordan, 207 Mass. 259 

Comm. v. King, 202 Mass. 379

Rosen v. U. S. 161 U. S. 29. 

On an indictment for murder, the "specifications filed by the Commonwealth in addition to the allegations of the indictment, furnished to the defendant ample information as to the nature and groun of the crime with which he was charged. The crime particularly respecting the cause of death, and precise nicety as thus was 'fully and plainly, substantially and formally described' to him as required by the Constitution. Details of the assault, to the relation of the beating to the fatal result, are not required. 

The refusal of the requests for particulars, so far as denied, was within the discretion of the court." 

Comm. v. Wakelin, 230 Mass. 567

Nature and Effect. The sole office of the bill of particulars is to give the adverse party information which the pleadings by reason of their generality do not give; 

Comm. v. Jordan, 207 Mass. 259

The bill not being part of the record is not subject to demurrer, and will not be considered on the hearing of a demurrer. 

U. S. v. Comyns, 248 U. S. 349 Dunlop v. U. S., 165 U. S. 486 

Hence an indictment good upon its face is not thereby rendered demurrable or subject to a motion to quash. 

Dunlop v. U. S., 165 U. S. 486 

It is held that after the filing of the bill of particulars the state is confined in its proof, to the items therein set out. 

Comm v. Althouse, 207 Mass. 32 (Evidence admissible within bill of particulars.) 

Comm. v. Giles, 1 Gray 466 

Comm. v. Snelling, 15 Pick. 321

Dunlop v. U. S., 165 U. S. 486

7. Requests for Instructions a. Necessity for Requests 

(I) General Statement 

Superior Court Rule 71 (1932) provides in part that: "Requests for instructions or rulings in trials or hearings with or without jury shall be made in writing before the closing arguments unless special leave is given to present requests later." 

Com. v. Hassan, 235 Mass. 26, at 32

Requests upon obvious points of law are unnecessary. 

As was said in Com. v. Johnson, 250 Mass. 320, at 323 and 324: "At the close of the instructions, the defendant asked the judge to instruct the jury, that he came into court with a presumption of innocence in his favor. The request was denied, and the defendant excepted. But, even if no request in writing had been made before the arguments to the jury were begun, the defendant well might assume that this fundamental principle under our law would be stated. Very plainly justice to the defendant called for such instruction, and, the attention of the judge having been directed to the omission, it should have been given.' 

Mahoney v. Gooch, 246 Mass. 567, at 571 

Com. v. Anderson, 245 Mass. 177, at 190

The judge, even in the absence of written requests, should instruct the jury, fairly, clearly, adequately and correctly, concern- P-1

CRIMINAL LAW 

ing the principles of law that ought to guide and control their action. 

Mahoney v. Gooch, 246 Mass. 567, at 571

It is the judge's duty to state the principles of law to the jury. 

O'Brien v. Shea, 208 Mass. 528

Maxwell v. Mass. Title Ins. Co., 206 Mass. 197 

This duty is not affected by the absence of specific requests by counsel, and, where attention is properly directed to the omission and it is not remedied, an exception may be sustained if necessary to render substantial justice. 

Clark v. Mass. Title Ins. Co., 237 Mass. 155 

Sawyer v. Worcester Con. St. Ry., 231 Mass. 215 

Rocci v. Mass. Accident Co., 226 Mass. 545 

Williams v. Winthrop, 213 Mass. 581

In Brick v. Bosworth, 162 Mass. 334, where the request for instruction was made for the first time after the judge's charge, the court said, at pages 337 and 338: "It is contended that the request came too late, and that the plaintiff cannot now avail herself of it. It is true that, in order to be entitled as a matter of right to have instructions given upon a hypothetical state of facts which may be found from the evidence, a party must seasonably present a request in writing to the judge, and the ordinary rule of practice which has been approved by this court is that such a request must be made before the arguments. But a party may well assume that, without special requests therefor, the judge will properly instruct the jury on the leading points of the case, and if at the close of the charge he observes that the judge has omitted to refer to important matters which ought to be explained to the jury, or thinks he has instructed erroneously in regard to them, he may bring the omissions or errors to the attention of the court, and ask for proper instructions. This practice saves the judge from the necessity of dealing with elaborate, complicated prayers for rulings without an opportunity for reflection, and at the same time saves the parties their right to exceptions if the judge neglects and refuses to instruct upon the important questions in the case.

P-2

CRIMINAL LAW 

McMahon v. O'Connor, 137 Mass. 216

Ela v. Cockshott, 119 Mass. 416 

We think the plaintiff was entitled to have the jury told, on request, . . .' 

Particular Instructions (A) General Statement (B) Special Defenses (C) Rules of Evidence 

When the defendant wishes to have the jury instructed that particular evidence was admissible only for the certain limited purpose for which it was competent, and should be considered only for that purpose, he must seasonably request such an instruction, otherwise it is competent for the jury to consider this evidence for any purpose and no valid exception will lie. 

Com. v. Rivet, 205 Mass. 464, at 466 

Com. v. Wunsch, 129 Mass. 477 

Howe v. Ray, 113 Mass. 88 

(III) Additional or More Specific Instructions 

When the defendant claims that additional or more specific instructions should be given to the jury, he must call the judge's attention to the particular defect or insufficiency or inaccuracy in his instructions to the jury and it is not enough for him to wait until the close of the charge and then enumerate any different portions of the charge to which he excerpts unless he further specifies of what he complains or wherein he wishes for different rulings. 

It was said in Com. v. Meserve, 154 Mass. 64, at 75: "But under such circumstances it would hardly conduce to a due administration of justice to search out opportunities for making minute verbal criticisms of the language of the charge, or to look for omissions to say all that might properly have been said. It is incumbent on a defendant who takes his exceptions in this manner, without having made any specific requests for instructions, and without calling the attention of the court to the points relied on further than to allege a general exception to the specified portions of the charge, to make it plain that there has been some substantial error."

P-3

CRIMINAL LAW b. Making and Presentation of Requests (I) Form of Requests (A) General Statement 

The Superior Court Rules (1932) do not prescribe the form of requests for instructions or rulings. Common practice has created the custom that such requests should consist of separate sentences or paragraphs, numbered consecutively, each embodying a concise and accurate statement of the law as applicable to the entire case or the various phases or issues of fact involved. 

Requests for instructions or rulings are not part of the record of the case kept by the clerk and in order to preserve objections and exceptions based upon their denial, modification, or other disposition, the same must appear in the stenographic record by separate numbers and not by an exception involving them as a whole so far as they have not been granted in or disposed of by the charge. 

Com. v. Clancy, 191 Mass. 191, at 196

It is a convenient practice, to obviate the necessity of preserving the original requests, for the judge to direct the stenographer to copy into his notes the requests with respect to which exceptions have been taken. 

(B) Writing 

Superior Court Rule 71 (1932), requires that the request be in writing, but it would seem that an oral request made as to the important and obvious propositions of law material to the case, as distinguished from the minor, detailed or recondite ones, must be considered and given by the judge, Com. v. Enwright, 259 Mass. 152, at 158 and 159 

Com. v. Allen, 256 Mass. 452, at 455 

Rocci v. Mass. Co., 226 Mass. 545, at 553 and 554 

Whitney Co. v. Anderson, 172 Mass. 1, at 5 even though the request is not strictly accurate but is sufficient to direct the judge's attention to its general subject. 

Cork v. Blossom, 162 Mass. 330, at 334 

(II) Time for Presenting Requests 

Superior Court Rule 71 (1932) provides that requests for instructions or rulings shall be presented before the closing arguments unless special leave is given to present the requests later. P-4

CRIMINAL LAW 

This rule is applicable to criminal, as well as civil, cases. 

Com. v. Enwright, 259 Mass. 152, at 158 

Com. v. Sacco, 259 Mass. 128, at 139 

Com. v. Allen, 256 Mass. 452 

Com. v. Hassan, 235 Mass. 26

The presiding judge may receive and pass upon, if he so elects, requests for instructions presented for the first time after the closing arguments, or even after the charge, and allow an exception to the defendant by the giving or refusing of them. 

Com. v. Kelley, 165 Mass. 175, at 176 

Com. v. Costley, 118 Mass. 1, at 25

Leave need not be obtained before the closing arguments to present requests later, but requests presented later cannot be entertained without the leave of the judge. 

Chandler v. Prince, 221 Mass. 495, at 509 (late oral request) 

Robertson v. Boston & Northern St. Ry. Co., 190 Mass. 108, at 109 

c. Dispositions of Requests 

(I) Erroneous Requests (A) As to Facts (B) As to Law 

(II) On Collateral or Immaterial Issues (III) On Issues Already Covered 

When the defendant's requests for instructions or rulings are covered substantially by the judge's charge, he is not entitled to have any additional instructions given to the jury.

(IV) Modification by Court 

The judge in his charge to the jury may modify a request for instruction so as to conform to the true principle of law involved, or he may change the request, where disputed facts are at issue, so as to leave the jury to determine the truth of those facts without assuming their existence in the instruction given. 

Com. v. Uhrig, 167 Mass. 420, at 424 (V) Giving in Language of Request

Instructions and rulings requested, even if relevant and legally unobjectionable, need not be given in the form or language requested. If in the form of abstract propositions, they would often, indeed, be applied to the facts by a jury with difficulty. It is sufficient if the substance of them, so far as they are correct and appropriate to the case, is given. 

Com. v. Kronick, 196 Mass. 286 

Com. v. Tucker, 189 Mass. 457 

Com. v. Johnson, 188 Mass. 382 

Com. v. Clancy, 187 Mass. 191 

Com. v. Chance, 174 Mass. 245 

Com. v. Uhrig, 167 Mass. 420 

Com. v. Mullen, 150 Mass. 394 

McMahon v. O'Connor, 137 Mass. 216 

Randall v. Chase, 133 Mass. 210, at 215 

Com. v. Brown, 121 Mass. 69 

Com. v. Cobb, 120 Mass. 356 

Com. v. Costley, 118 Mass. 1

No exception lies to the refusal to give an instruction in the language requested, if it is given in substance. 

Com. v. Uhrig, 167 Mass. 420, at 423 

But See: Com. v. Madeiros, 255 Mass. 304 (where Chief

Justice Rugg said instruction in terms must be given on presumption of innocence)

When the instructions given to the jury are legal and appropriate, and cover the whole ground of the instruction request- P-6

CRIMINAL LAW 

ed, the omission or refusal of the court to rule in the very terms requested by counsel affords no ground of exception. 

Com. v. Crosley, 118 Mass. 1, at 25

When several forms of expression are equally accurate, it is within the discretion of the court at the trial to choose that form which it deems best adapted to make the rule of law intelligible to common minds. 

Com. v. Costley, 118 Mass. 1, at 25 

Blake v. Sawin, 10 Allen, 340 

Morris v. Bowman, 12 Gray, 467

Kelly v. Jackson, 6 Pet. (U. S.) 622 (VI) Proper Request Refused 

When the instructions given are meagre or do not cover the important issue embodied in the request for instruction, or request for additional instruction, and such request embodies a correct statement of the law, it is an error for the judge to refuse or fail to so instruct the jury. 

Com. v. Maddock, 207 Mass. 152, at 158 

(VII) Method of Giving Requested Instructions (VIII) Reasons for Refusal 8. Argument and Conduct of Counsel 9. Province of Judge and Jury 10. Objections and Exceptions to Instructions Given and Refusals to Instruct a. Necessity and Waiver b. Time of Objections 

Superior Court Rule No. 72, provides that: "No exception shall be allowed to any opinion, ruling, direction or judgment made in the presence of counsel, unless it be taken at the time such opinion, ruling, direction or judgment is given. Exceptions to a charge to the jury shall be taken before the jury are sent out. When further instructions, rulings or directions are given in the absence of counsel after the jury have been sent out, exceptions thereto shall be taken within twenty-four hours thereafter. Exceptions to any other opinion, ruling, direction or judgment made in the absence of counsel shall be taken by a writing filed with the clerk within three days after the receipt from the clerk of notice thereof." P-7

CRIMINAL LAW 

No set form of words is necessary to make an objection; it is sufficient if the judge should understand that the party intends to object. 

Com. v. Min Sing, 202 Mass. 121, at 125

An objection must be taken at the time of the remarks to the jury when they are originally instructed or when they come into court to receive further instructions, and the defendant is not entitled as of right to have his objections to the judge's remarks considered, if he did seasonably present the same. C. 

Com. v. Kelley, 165 Mass. 175, at 176 

Com. v. Costley, 118 Mass. 1, at 25

Form and Mode of Objections d. Sufficiency of Exceptions 

(I) To Instructions Given 

When at the close of the evidence the defendant's counsel presents a voluminous body of instructions, which he requests should be given to the jury, of which some are and some are not given, and then, at the close of the charge, the judge requests the defendant's counsel to call his attention to anything in the requests which was not covered by it, to which the defendant's counsel replies that he thinks everything has been covered and then he alleges exceptions to the charge in so far as it is inconsistent with the requests asked, and not otherwise, it is the duty of the defendant's counsel then and there to call attention to any respect in which the charge is inconsistent with the requests. However, if the judge does not insist upon this, upon review, the defendant must show clearly that the charge is inconsistent with the requests in some respect in which the requests were not objectionable, and that such requests ought to have been given in order to correct the disposition of the case. 

Com. v. Meserve, 154 Mass. 64 

Com. v. Mullen, 150 Mass. 394, at 399 and 400 

Com. v. Tolman, 149 Mass. 229 

McMahon v. O'Connor, 137 Mass. 216 

Randall v. Chase, 133 Mass. 210, at 215 

Com. v. Cobb, 120 Mass. 356 

Com. v. Costley, 118 Mass. 1

Particular Crimes (I) General Statement 

When sentences are indicated to be 212 years or less, they are to be served in the House of Correction or Jail, but in certain cases may be served at the State Farm, Massachusetts Re formatory or Reformatory for Women. 

Commitments of more than 22 years are to be served in State Prison, but in some instances may be served in the Massachusetts Reformatory, provided the person to be sentenced is under thirty years of age, and in the case of a woman, in the Reforma tory for Women. 

Where single period of imprisonment is given, it is the maximum, no minimum being set.

HABITUAL Criminal: 

Whoever has been twice convicted and sentenced to prison in this or any other state or once in this state and once in another state for terms of not less than 

3 years each, provided he was not pardoned for either crime, shall upon a conviction of a felony be considered an Habitual 

Criminal and be punished in the State Prison for the maximum term provided by Law as a Penalty for the felony for which he is then to be sentenced.

G. L. Chap. 279, Sec. 25.
