DECLARATIONS OF DECEASED PERSONS A. STATUTORY PROVISIONS 

B.

General Laws, Chapter 233 provides that: 

See: EVIDENCE Section 65: A declaration of a deceased person shall not be inadmissible in evidence as hearsay if the court finds that it was made in good faith before the commencement of the action and upon the personal knowledge of the declarant.

Section 66: If a cause of action brought against an executor or administrator is supported by oral testimony of a promise or statement made by the testator or intestate of the defendant, evidence of statements, written or oral, made by the decedent, memoranda and entries written by him, and evidence of his acts and habits of dealing tending to disprove or to show the improbability of the making of such promise or statement, shall be admissible. 

GENERAL STATEMENT 

Prior to the enactment of Gen. Laws, c. 233, ss. 65 and 66, declarations of deceased persons were inadmissible as hearsay, even though the declarant had died since the declarations were made. 

Comm. v. Felch, 132 Mass. 22 

Lund v. Tyngsborough, 9 Cush. 36 

Welch u. Barrett, 15 Mass. 380

But now by virtue of Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 a "declaration of a deceased person shall not be inadmissible in evidence as hearsay if the court finds that it was made in good faith before. the commencement of the action and upon the personal knowledge of the declarant." 

Kelley v. Jordan Marsh Co., 1932 A. S. 27 

Before declarations of a deceased person rightly can be admitted under. Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65, the trial judge must make a preliminary finding of the existence of the facts which alone render such declarations admissible. The burden of proving these precedent facts is upon the party who offers such declarations in evidence. Kelley 

Jordan Marsh Co., 1932 A. S. 27, at 30

First, the declaration must have been made before the commencement of the action. 1

Second, another of these essential facts is that the declarations must have been made in good faith. The judge must find this fact to exist or the declarations must be excluded. 

Kelley v. Jordan Marsh Co., 1932 4. S. 27, at 30 

Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475 

Horan v. Boston Elevated, 237 Mass. 245, at 247 

Corroll v. Boston Elevated, 210 Mass. 500

Third, declarations of a deceased person, to be admissible under the statute, must also relate to facts within the personal knowledge of the declarant. That is another fact to be proved to the reasonable satisfaction of the trial judge before such declaration can be admitted in evidence. This express requirement of the words of said section 65 has been emphasized in the decisions. 

Kelley v. Jordan Marsh Co., 1932 A. S. 27, at 30 

Warren v. Decoste, 269 Mass. 514, at 419 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183, at 187

Little v. Massachusetts etc. Rlwy, 223 Mass. 501 

The general rule has been established that the findings of the trial judge touching the existence of these essential preliminary facts will not be reversed unless they are unjusti fiable or involve some error of law. 

Kelley v. Jordan Marsh Co., 1932 4. S. 27, at 30 

Bodfish v. Cross, 235 Mass. 428 

Ames v. New York, etc. R. R., 221 Mass. 304

Slotofski v. Boston Elevated, 215 Mass. 318 

Such findings commonly rest upon the observation of witnesses and a determination by the trial judge of their capacity to comprehend that which was originally heard and to report it with reliable accuracy, and upon his conclusion as to the knowledge of the declarant and all the factors bearing upon his understanding, honesty of purpose, and faculty of correctly stating the facts. In short, the action of the trial judge rests upon circumstances which cannot be reflected with reasonable precision upon the printed page. A finding of that nature ordinarily will stand as conclusive in an action at law if there is any evidence to support it. 

Kelley v. Jordan Marsh Co., 1932 A. S. 27, at 31 

Moss v. Old Colony Trust Co., 246 Mass. 139, at 143

It can rarely be ruled as matter of law that the burden of proof has been sustained. 

Kelley v. Jordan Marsh Co., 1932 A. S. 27, at 31 

McDonough v. Met. L. Ins. Co., 228 Mass. 450, at 452 2

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 applies only to the admitting of hearsay evidence.

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 

If the evidence is inadmissible on any other ground, this statute does not render it admissible. 

Evers v. Gilfoil, 247 Mass. 219

The evidence must have a material bearing upon some issue in the case. 

Chandler v. Prince, 217 Mass. 451, at 459

Therefore, in the action for an accounting by a fiduciary testimony relative to a statement made by one, now dead, at the time of handling money to a third person for delivery to the defendant, to the effect that the money was to be paid to the plaintiff, is inadmissible as irrelevant, immaterial and res inter alios. 

Pappathanos v. Coakley, 263 Mass. 401 

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 "is remedial in its nature, and therefore should be liberally construed to extend rather than restrict the remedy."

Buckley v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 50 

(Statement to show state of mind admissible.) 

Randall v. Peerless M. Car Co., 212 Mass. 352, at 385 

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193, at 195 

Hall v. Reinherz, 192 Mass. 52, at 53 

Comm. v. Chance, 174 Mass. 245, at 250 (Criminal case.)

But "the statute should not be construed to go beyond cases plainly within the contemplation of the legislature." 

Knapp v. Bronson Co., 226 Mass. 416

White v. Boston El. Ry., 208 Mass. 193 

So, such a declaration is admissible although it was made before the passage of the statute. 

Hall v. Reinherz, 192 Mass. 52

It is no objection to the admission of a declaration otherwise admissible under this statute that it would have been inadmissible had the declarant been alive at the time of the trial. 

Stocker v. Foster, 178 Mass. 591 

But see: Taylor v. Whittier, 240 Mass. 513, at 516 "Interest of the declarant may affect the weight, but not the competency, of the testimony." 

Morrison v. Holder, 214 Mass. 366, at 370

The statute does not limit the declarations to be admitted to a single one; after one has been introduced in evidence other witnesses may testify to similar statements of the deceased, and also in modification or contradiction of those introduced. 

Weeks v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 190 Mass. 563 

Declarations are admissible under Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 although the deceased has survived the commencement of the action or suit and testified at a former trial. 

Randall v. Peerless Motor Car Co., 212 Mass. 352

But testimony of a witness, at a former trial of the action since deceased, should not be offered under this statute. It is admissible under the common law. 

McGivern v. Steele, 197 Mass. 164

Death before trial or prior to the commencement of the action or suit is not by itself sufficient to make the declaration admissible as evidence, the three essentials of the statute must be present. C. 

Freeman v. Freeman, 238 Mass. 150 

Boston etc. Co. v. Tyndale, 218 Mass. 428 (Proof and presumption of death.)

ESSENTIALS 1. Before Commencement of Action or Suit 

The declaration to be admissible under this statute must have been made before the commencement of the action or suit in which it is sought to be introduced. 

Quimby v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 248 Mass. 364 (Written statement signed by deceased 10 or 12 years before trial.)

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 

Carrol v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 500

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193 

The fact that the declaration was made before the action or suit began does not of itself make it competent evidence. 

So, although the declaration was made before the commencement of the action or suit it is inadmissible as evidence unless the trial judge makes an additional finding that the declaration was made in good faith and upon the personal knowledge of the deceased declarant. 

Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475

A cause of action is commenced on the date of the writ. 

Westcott v. Henshaw Motor Co., 1931 A. S. 765, at 766 

Bickford v. Furber, 271 Mass. 94

Westminister Nat. Bk. v. Graustein, 270 Mass. 565 

Krasnow v. Krasnow, 253 Mass. 528 

Rosenblatt v. Foley, 252 Mass. 188, at 190 

Cushing v. Brooklyn Trust Co., 235 Mass. 171 

Farrell v. German American Ins. Co., 175 Mass. 340

It was said in Westminister National Bank v. Graustein, 270 

Mass. 565, at page 581: .... "An action is commenced when a writ issues out and is delivered to an officer with a bona fide intent to have it served upon the defendant. 

The date of the writ is not conclusive evidence of the commencement of the action; it may be held to be commenced at any day after the issuance of the writ which may be most conducive to justice."

So, an action for injuries against a municipality caused by a defect in the highway is not commenced at the time of the service of the statutory notice of the injury upon the municipality. 

Dickinson v. Boston, 188 Mass. 595

The serving of the notice, required in Gen. Laws, c. 84, s. 

18, upon a city by one who has been injured by an alleged defect in a way is not the commencement of an action within the meaning of the statute; hence declarations by the plaintiff, who has since died, made subsequently to serving the notice and before the date of the writ, are admissible. 

Dickinson v. Boston, 188 Mass. 595

That a letter written in reply to one sent over seven months before an action was begun and being so dated, will warrant a finding that it was written before the commencement of the action.

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193 

A declaration made before the institution of proceedings under the Workmen's Compensation Act is made before the commencement of the action.

Pigeon's Case, 216 Mass. 51 

Declarations made before action brought "are not rendered inadmissible under this statute because the deceased has survived the beginning of the action and testified at one trial." 

Randall v. Peerless Co., 212 Mass. 352, at 384

а. Actions Against Administrator or Executor GEN. LAWS, C. 233, S. 66 

But Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 66 applies to any action begun in the lifetime of the deceased; and under this statute declarations are admissible even though made after the commencement of the action or suit. 

Brooks v. Holden, 175 Mass. 137, at 140

This statute does not affect the rule as to private conversations between husband and wife. 

Hyde v. Gannett, 175 Mass. 177

It has been held not to limit the effect of this statute, so as to exclude statements made by a deceased person, in an action against his personal representative, although not made until after the beginning of the action. 

Brooks v. Holden, 175 Mass. 137 

2. Good Faith

Before the declarations of a deceased person can be admitted in evidence it is necessary for the trial judge to make a preliminary finding that the deceased person made the declaration or statement in good faith. 

Ferris v. Ray Taxi Co., 259 Mass. 401 

McSweeney v. Edison Co., 228 Mass. 563 (The preliminary finding of good faith should be made by the judge and not submitted to the jury in the first instance, however, the jury later must find such good faith before it can give credence to the declaration.) 

Barney v. Magenis, 241 Mass. 268 

Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516 

Knapp v. Bronson Bldg. Co., 226 Mass. 416 (An admission against the interest made by a member to the deceased declarant is inadmissible.)

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168 

Johnson v. Foster, 221 Mass. 249 

Carroll v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 500 (The party producing the statement has the burden of proving the issue of declarant's good faith.) 

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193 

It was said in Glidden v. United States Fidelity etc. Co., 198 

Mass. 109: "The assertion made by the plaintiff in his statement that he had made such examination and audit, is not made

competent evidence under [Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65] by reason of the plaintiff's death before the trial of the case, because it does not appear to have been offered in evidence under that statute, and was not found by the judge to have been in good faith, which is made by the statute itself, one of the conditions precendent to its admissibility." 

When the preliminary finding of the trial judge is that the statement was not made in good faith its exclusion is rendered necessary. 

Comm. v. Wakelin, 230 Mass. 567, at 575 

McSweeney v. Edison E. I. Co., 228 Mass. 563

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 

Carroll v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 500

It then becomes unnecessary to consider the soundness of the judge's ruling upon other grounds. 

Comm. v. Wakelin, 230 Mass. 567, at 575 

Comm. v. Stuart, 207 Mass. 563, at 568

A statement may be found to have been made in good faith even though it is (a) self-serving; 

Barney v. Magenis, 241 Mass. 268 (b) a private conversation with a party's attorney. 3. 

Carroll v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 500

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193 Personal Knowledge of Declarant 

Declarations of deceased persons to be admissible under this section must be made not only in good faith, but "upon the personal knowledge of the declarant." 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 518 

Ames v. N.Y. N.H. & H. R.R., 221 Mass. 304 

Polvere v. Hugh Nawn Con. Co., 215 Mass. 199

They "must be derived from the exercise of the declarant's own senses as distinguished from opinions based upon data observed by him or furnished by others." 

Tenney v. Foss, 268 Mass. 69 

Ames v. N.Y. N.H. & H. R.R., 221 Mass. 304 

Enfield v. Wood, 212 Mass. 547, at 551

In Tenney v. Foss, 268 Mass. 69 where statements made by one deceased person of what another deceased person had said to him were admitted, the court said at page 71: "The statute is to be liberally construed. It is plain that if Tenney, during his lifetime, had been called as a

witness, he could have testified to what the declarant told him..... "It is obvious in the case at bar that Tenney was reciting facts to his wife which were within his personal knowledge, when he informed her of Mrs. Burley's conversation with him. "In the present case the declarant Tenney heard the statement of Mrs. Burley which constituted the parol contract declared upon. If living, he could have testified to the conversation he had with her during which she promised to pay him for his work. The testimony of the plaintiff, therefore, was admissible under the statute to prove the contract under which she seeks to recover." 

Hicks v. Church etc. Co., 259 Mass. 272, at 275

In an action for death and conscious suffering the declaration of the decedent cannot be admitted if there was not in fact any conscious suffering because he could not have made intelligent declarations. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183 

Jordan v. Adams Gas Co., 231 Mass. 186

Keough v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 229 Mass. 275 

Knapp v. Bronson Bldg. Co., 226 Mass. 416

Little v. Mass. etc. Railway, 223 Mass. 501 

Ames v. N.Y. N.H. & H. R.R., 221 Mass. 304

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 

Marston v. Reynolds, 211 Mass. 590 

Carroll v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 500

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193 

When the nature of the injury sustained by the declarant is such that he could not make intelligent declarations because he did not suffer consciously, the declaration is inadmissible. 

Jordan v. Adams Gas. Co., 231 Mass. 186, at 188

Statements made by the declarant based upon hearsay are not admissible. 

Dow v. Dow, 243 Mass. 587 (Declaration of one deceased person as to statement made to him by another cannot be upon the personal knowledge of declarant.) 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516 (Statement that declarant did not see accident but understood that plaintiff slipped on leaves is not admissible, since not on personal knowledge of declarant, who could not have testified to it if living.)

Knapp v. Bronson Bldg. Co., 226 Mass. 416 (Declaration of deceased that a party to the cause made an admission held inadmissible because not within personal knowledge of declarant.) 

Gettins v. Kelley, 212 Mass. 171 (Declarant's statement that others blamed him inadmissible.) 

Boyle v. Columbian Fire Proof. Co., 182 Mass. 93, at 98 (Question, "Did he say anything about his father?" is objectionable as calling for facts not within the personal knowledge of the declarant.) 

But see: Newton Centre Trust Co. v. Stuart, 208 Mass. 221 ("That scoundrel has persuaded her to put her name to over $1,000,000 worth of that paper, and I know it because she told me so," is admissible.) 

It has been held that while a declarant who has been in this country for eighteen months may have personal knowledge of the fact that his parents in Italy needed his money, he could not have such knowledge of the failure of their crops for the last two years. 

Polvere v. Hugh Nawn Co., 215 Mass. 199

A person cannot be said to have personal knowledge of a fact which he knows only through the admission of a party to the action. The declaration of such person, although he be deceased, that he heard such part admit a material fact, is therefore inadmissible. 

Knapp v. Bronson Co., 226 Mass. 146 a. Guess

A declaration or statement of a deceased person based upon guesswork or conjecture is inadmissible. 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 518

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168 

b. Inference

An inference of fact cannot properly form the basis of a declaration which is competent as evidence under Gen. Laws, c. 233, ss. 65 and 66. 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 518

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168 

A declaration as to the primary facts is proper but the inferential fact is not competent. 

See cases just cited above.

C. Opinions 

The opinion of a deceased physician as to the cause of an injury to a person whom he treated is not admissible. 

Little v. Mass. etc. Ry. Co., 223 Mass. 504

Nor can the physician's opinion of his patient's condition or his professional advice be shown. 

Keough v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 229 Mass. 275 

But where the statement involves more or less of opinion, if it is in substance an inference of fact from a set of collective facts observed by the person making the statement, which could not be described in detail as they appeared to him, the evidence will be admissible. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183, at 187 (Declarant said, "It is my fault; I am to blame.")

Ross v. John Hancock Mutual Life Ins. Co., 222 Mass. 

560, at 562 

Comm. v. Sturtivant, 117 Mass. 122, at 133 

It was said in Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183, at 187: "If the statement of the intestate was merely the assertion of an opinion (as distinguished from one of fact) it was not admissible under the statute. It is often difficult to trace the logical or legal distinction between fact and opinion, and, where the form of the statement leaves it doubtful, it is for the court to decide in which sense the declaration was made." 

Little v. Mass. etc. Ry. Co., 223 Mass. 501 

Johnson v. Foster, 221 Mass. 248

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 

Gray v. Kelley, 190 Mass. 184

Testamentary provisions of the deceased tending to show that he did not consider himself indebted to the plaintiff cannot be considered declarations of a deceased person under this statute. 

Whitcomb v. Whitcomb, 217 Mass. 558

The declaration must be a statement of fact within the personal knowledge of the declarant and not a statement of an opinion. 

McCabe v. Chelsea, 265 Mass. 494 

In Ames v. New York, New Haven, & Hartford R. R., 221 

Mass. 304, at pages 305 and 306 Mr. Justice Pierce said: "To establish the proposition that her buildings were destroyed by fire communicated by the locomotive engines of the defendant, the plaintiff offered in evidence the 10

deposition of Mrs. Eugenia M. Moore (who was deceased at the time of the trial) wherein she testified that shortly after the fire and before the commencement of this action her husband who afterwards had died made certain declarations relative to its origin. These declarations were made on the Sunday following the fire, to the plaintiff and her husband, at the house of the declarant. "The deponent testified: 'He said sparks from the engine, or locomotive, whatever you call it, had set the carriage house on fire, but he would not like to be called as a witness because he was in the employ of the railroad and he would not care to lose his job.' "Moore was then in the employ of the defendant as an assistant station agent, at the Spring Street station, which was located on the line of the railroad, was in plain view of the property destroyed, and distant four hundred and ninety feet therefrom. "There is no testimony in the deposition, or otherwise reported, which states how the subject matter of the origin of the fire was introduced, although it reasonably may be inferred that the owner came in search of information and that the declaration was made in answer to questions. "There is no evidence that at the time of the fire or immediately preceding it Moore was at the station or at any place from which he could see at the same moment both locomotives and buildings. "There was no evidence that he in fact saw sparks fly from a locomotive to the buildings and that following such flight he saw fire in, upon or near to the buildings. "The defendant seasonably excepted to the reading of the deposition, and especially to the declaration of Moore on the ground that it does not sufficiently appear that it was of his personal knowledge. "The plaintiff argues that as the judge has found that the declaration was made in good faith and of the man's own knowledge, this is the sole test of admissibility under 

R. L., c. 175, s. 66, and no exception lies to his ruling. "But we are of opinion that the admission or rejection. of evidence does not rest in the mere discretion of the judge who tries the case, but upon rules and principles of law, framed and adapted to promote justice between parties in differences; and that where a judge errs in the admission of testimony not admissible by the rules of law, or rejects testimony which ought to have been admitted, 11

such error is ground of exception, though he himself, and not the jury, may be called upon in the first instance to weigh the evidence. The judge is to consider the preliminary evidence, and he is of course to decide whether it is creditable or not; and his decision as to its credibility, like that of a jury, is conclusive. But in his decision as to its admission, he must be governed by the rules of law.' 

Foster v. Mackay, 7 Met. 531, at 537 "His decision is conclusive, unless he saves the question for revision by the full court, on a report of the evidence, or counsel bring up the question in a bill of exceptions which contains a statement of the evidence.' 

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318, at 320 

Comm. v. Robinson, 146 Mass. 571 

Gorton v. Hadsell, 9 Cush. 508, at 511 "All the evidence before the judge upon which he made his decision was contained in the deposition and is before us. It is clear that it does not establish that Moore made the declaration upon his personal knowledge. It is therefore inadmissible." 

Statement of price paid for property not opinion. 

Statement that one got splinter in finger while doing his work admissible. 

McCabe v. Chelsea, 265 Mass. 494 

Dorney's Case, 259 Mass. 350

Report of deceased president to corporation setting out matters held not opinion. 

N. Y. Cen. R. R. v. Cen. Vt. R. R., 243 Mass. 56, at 68 

Statement of damage to flour, by water. 

Gentile Flour Co. v. Moschella, 251 Mass. 512

Statement of deceased killed in automobile collision, "I don't see how he came to hit me", admitted. 

Hicks v. H. B. Church Truck Ser. Co., 259 Mass. 272

Statement that one saw conductor demand fare admitted. 

Dixon v. N. E. R.R., 179 Mass. 243

The statement of deceased police officer that in his opinion the bricks of a sidewalk, which was the place of the accident, were in very good condition is incompetent as being the expression of an opinion. 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 518 12

d. 

Statement of One Deceased Person Told to Him by Another Deceased Person 

Where the defendant offered in evidence, as bearing on damages, a statement signed by a physician since deceased and the judge remarked when objection was made that the requirement of the statute was that the deceased must have made a statement of facts of his own knowledge before the beginning of the action and in good faith, a ruling that whatever the plaintiff stated to the decedent might be read, imported a finding of the preliminary facts required by this section. 

Quimby v. Boston etc. Ry. Co., 248 Mass. 364

But a declaration by one deceased person to another, since deceased, who told the witness of the declaration, renders the testimony concerning the declaration inadmissible. 

Dow v. Dow, 243 Mass. 587

Some statements may be admitted on grounds, aside from the statute. 

Burke v. McLaughlin, 246 Mass. 544 (Boundary was determined by fence.) 

Daw v. Lally, 213 Mass. 578 e. (Admission against interest by agent of owner as to adverse use.)

Telephone Conversations 

Evidence is inadmissible that the deceased person told the witness that a third party telephoned in the presence of the deceased person to the plaintiff when the deceased person did not have personal knowledge of the identity of the plaintiff's voice on the telephone. 

Dorchester Trust Co. v. Casey, 268 Mass. 494

For the evidence does not rest on the personal knowledge of the declarant.

Especially when there is no evidence that the deceased knew who the third party telephoned to except that he called the plaintiff's place of business; and also when there is nothing to show that the deceased knew that the third party had secured the proper telephone connection, and further when there is nothing to show that the third party talked with any officer or employee of the plaintiff who was authorized to bind the plaintiff. 

Dorchester Trust Co. v. Casey, 268 Mass. 494

Telephone conversations that are part of the transaction or res gestae are admitted in evidence both in civil and criminal cases. 

71 A. L. R. 6 

13

Telephone conversations when otherwise relevant, have been held generally admissible in evidence under the same circumstances under which conversations face to face are admissible. 

71 A. L. R. 7 

Communications through the medium of the telephone may be shown in the same manner and with like effect, as conversations had between individuals face to face. But the identity of the party against whom the conversation is sought to be admitted must be established by some testimony, either direct or circumstantial; to hold parties responsible for answers made by unidentified persons opens the door for fraud and imposition. Slight circumstances will suffice for this purpose, however; and in case of conversations about business affairs, the rule seems to authorize the admission of the evidence without preliminary proof directed at identification of the voice. 

71 A. L. R. 7 1 R. C. L. 477 

It is necessary to the admission in evidence of a declaration of deceased person that he had a certain telephone conversation with a party, that it must appear that the voice of that party should have been identified by the decedent. D. 

Dorchester Trust Co. v. Casey, 268 Mass. 494

Stearns Lumber Co. v. Howlett, 260 Mass. 45 

Comm. v. Gettigan, 252 Mass. 450 

Larner v. Mass. Bond Ins. Co., 238 Mass. 80 

Comm. v. Harris, 232 Mass. 588 

Lord Electric Co. v. Morrill, 178 Mass. 304

FORM OR CHARACTER OF DECLARATION 

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 applies to written as well as oral declarations. 

Durham v. Holmes, 225 Mass. 68 

O'Driscoll v. Lynn & Boston Ry. Co., 180 Mass. 187

A witness may state the substance of the declaration. 

Hayes v. Pitts-Kimball Co., 183 Mass. 262

This section is to be liberally construed. 

Tenney v. Foss, 268 Mass. 69, at 71

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 does not permit the admission in evidence of a declaration of a deceased person that a party to a cause of action had made an admission against his interest. 

Knapp v. Bronson Bldg. Co., 226 Mass. 416

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 66: a ledger may be admissible to prove a negative declaration. 14

Whitcomb v. Whitcomb, 217 Mass. 558 

Tripp v. Macomber, 187 Mass. 109 

Cogswell v. Hall, 185 Mass. 455 

Heubener v. Childs, 180 Mass. 483 

It was said in Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168, at 170: "The statute prescribes no formula and we know of none as to the gram natical form in which the declarations are to be expressed by the witness. It is sufficient that, however phrased, the statements are not mere expressions of opinion or of inferences, but of relevant facts, and they are none the less ad nissible even if accompanied by irrelevant matter which is excluded, or where the witness can only recall the substance but not the exact words of the declarant."

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 renders evidence of declarations competent whenever the testimony of the decedent to the same effect would have been admissible. 

Sylvester v. N. Y. etc. R. R. Co., 217 Mass. 148

So, the declaration may be written, as well as oral. 

Carr. Dighton, 229 Mass. 304 

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193

The identical words of the declaration are not required to make it admissible, the substance of the declaration only is required. 

Hayes v. Pitts-Kimball Co., 183 Mass. 262 (In an action for death and conscious suffering, declarations of intestate's grandmother, made shortly after accident were admissible, although grandmother had since deceased. Also intestate's declarations were admitted as verbal acts, a part of the res gestae.) 

A statement of a person who was injured in an accident but who has since died, which was made in good faith before the bringing of the action as of his own knowledge in which he criticises the defendant's driving before the accident, is admissible. 

Dzura v. Phillips, 1931 A. S. 969, at 972 

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245, at 247 

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168

General evidence of a confession of the deceased that he was at fault is admissible provided the preliminary facts prerequisite to its admission are established. 

Ferris v. Ray Taxi Co., 259 Mass. 401 15

The statute does not permit the introduction of a declaration concerning facts which were merely hearsay to the declarant.

Nor is the opinion of the declarant upon an issue of fact admissible. 

Hasey v. Bolton, 228 Mass. 516, at 518

However, where the form of the statement leaves it doubtful whether it was an assertion of opinion or of fact, it is for the court to decide in which sense the declaration was made. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183

That is, whether a particular statement is admissible under the statute is a preliminary question for the court to decide. 

McSweeney v. Edison, 228 Mass. 563 1. 

Hasey v. Bolton, 228 Mass. 516, at 518

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 

Carroll v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 500 

Flynn v. Coolidge, 188 Mass. 214 Admissions

The statute does not authorize the admission in evidence of a declaration of a deceased person that a party to a cause had made an admission against his interest. 

Knapp v. Bronson Bldg. Co., 226 Mass. 416

An unauthorized admission of an agent is not admissible. 

Ames v. N.Y. N.H. & H. R.R., 221 Mass. 304

But an admission of liability, based upon fact, made by a deceased party is admissible. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183 ("It is my fault, I am to blame".)

However, if the statement is merely an opinion it must be excluded. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183 

Lee v. Prudential Ins. Co., 203 Mass. 299 

But see: Dixon v. N. E. R. R. Co., 179 Mass. 242

Also an admission may be a conclusion of fact and not a statement of fact and therefore inadmissible within the statute. 

Knapp v. Bronson Bldg. Co., 226 Mass. 416

However, if the deceased could testify to the admission, the declaration is competent. 2. 

Dixon v. New England R. R. Co., 179 Mass. 242

Intent Statements showing intent, when that fact is material, are also admissible.

Crosby v. Mutual B. Life Ins. Co., 221 Mass. 461 

16

3. Interrogatories

Acts of 1931, c. 386 provides that, if a party to an action. or suit who has filed answers to interrogatories under Sections 61 to 67 inclusive, of Chapter 231 dies, so much of such answers as the court finds have been made upon the personal knowledge of the deceased shall not be inadmissible as hearsay or selfserving if offered in evidence in said action or suit by a representative of the deceased party. 

4. Opinions 

But the statute cannot be extended to include a declaration of opinion of a deceased person, even if such person, if living would be allowed to testify to the opinion inquired about. 

Eldridge v. Boston, 232 Mass. 183

Keough v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 229 Mass. 275 

Little v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry., 223 Mass. 501, at 504 However, it is no error to admit the declarations of a deceased doctor, under the statute, where the statement was not an opinion, but made before commencement of the action, and on the personal knowledge of declarant. 

Carr v. Dighton, 229 Mass. 304

Regarding the form: "It is sufficient that, however phrased, the statements are not mere expressions of opinion or inferences," but contain relevant facts. 

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168, at 170 

Little v. Mass. Northeastern St. Ry., 223 Mass. 501, at 504 So a statement, "if anything does happen to me, I have had my life insured and Charlotte will have that anyway." 

Crosby v. Mutual Benefit Life Ins. Co., 221 Mass. 461 

a. Speed

A statement that an automobile which ran over the declarant "must have been going all of thirty or thirty-five miles an hour" was held to be an expression of fact derived from the exercise of the declarant's own senses, and not merely an opinion. 

Barney v. Magenis, 241 Mass. 268, at 272 

5. Oral Statements 

The declaration may be oral. 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518, at 523 

Gentile Flour Co. v. Moschella, 251 Mass. 512 17

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168 

(Landlord's oral declaration to keep premises in good repair made to deceased who told it to the witness.) 

Hayes v. Holmes, 225 Mass. 68

A declaration is not inadmissible because made in reply to a leading question, Nagle v. B. & N. St. Ry. Co., 188 Mass. 38 nor because made by the plaintiff and reduced to writing and signed by the deceased ten or twelve years before the trial. 

Quimby v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 248 Mass. 364 6. Self-Serving Statements 

Declarations, if otherwise admissible, are not rendered incompetent because they are self-serving statements. 

Hicks v. H. B. Church Co., 259 Mass. 272 (Where deceased was killed by auto, his statement was: "I don't see how he came to hit me.") 

Barney v. Magenis, 241 Mass. 268 (Deceased detailed the accident and estimates speed of defendant's automobile.) 

Lee v. Prudential Ins. Co., 203 Mass. 299 (In application for insurance assured said he was in good health.) 

7. Statements Against Public Policy 

When the declaration relates facts as to matters whose revelation is against public policy, the declaration is not admissible. 

Taylor v. Whittier, 240 Mass. 514 

(Revealing the illegitimacy of testator's children.

) 

8. Substance-Not Exact Words 

And it is sufficient if the witness can give the substance of what was said by the deceased without giving the exact words. 

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168 

Hayes v. Pitts-Kimball Co., 183 Mass. 262 

9. Written

Written statements of a deceased person are admissible as well as oral ones, and are not to be excluded because the writing also contains irrelevant matter. 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518, at 523

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168 

Dunham v. Holmes, 225 Mass. 68 

Phillips v. Chase, 201 Mass. 444 18

Randall v. Claflin, 194 Mass. 560 

Hall v. Reinherz, 192 Mass. 52 

O'Driscoll v. Lynn & Boston R.R. Co., 180 Mass. 187

A declaration is not inadmissible because made in reply to a leading question, Nagle v. B. & N. St. Ry. Co., 183 Mass. 38 nor because made by the plaintiff and reduced to writing and signed by the deceased ten or twelve years before the trial. 

Quimby v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 248 Mass. 364

Where a written statement of the circumstances of an accident was given by a witness to it, at the request of one of the parties to the suit, it alone warrants a finding that it was made in good faith and on the personal knowledge of the declarant. 

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193 

(Reply to letter of defendant asking questions about the accident-date showed before commencement of action good faith found.)

But witnessed instruments are governed by the common law. 

Giles v. Giles, 204 Mass. 383

Under this section, the fact that a statement was made by a party plaintiff and reduced to writing and signed by decedent ten or twelve years before the trial does not render it incompetent. 

Quimby v. Boston etc. Ry. Co., 248 Mass. 364 a. Copies

The contents of letters which a person, now deceased, has sent off in the ordinary course of business, may be shown by means of a letter press copy book kept by him. E. 

Green v. Crapo, 181 Mass. 55, at 63 ("The copying of letters into a business letter book, having reference to ordinary practice, imports a declaration that they are in the course of transmission, and when the copying was by a man now dead, it would not be a great strain to hold his implied declaration to be within the statute.") 

Holmes, C. J. (in the last cited case.)

PROCEEDINGS IN WHICH ADMISSIBLE 1. Civil Actions and Equity Suits 

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 66 is not limited in its operation by 

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65. 19

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 relates to civil procedure only, is remedial in its nature, and therefore should be liberally construed to extend rather than restrict the remedy. 

By civil procedure is included, actions at law and suits in equity. 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518, at 523

Declarations are admissible although their publication preceded the passage of the original statute (Statute 1898, c. 535). 

Also written statements made by declarant are admissible. 

Hall v. Reinherz, 192 Mass. 52 

а. Against Executor or Administrator 

By Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 66, "statements, written or oral, made by the decedent, memoranda and entries written by him and evidence of his acts and habits of dealing" are admissible. 

Loweth v. Bradford, 227 Mass. 584 

Tripp v. Macomber, 187 Mass. 109 

Cogswell v. Hall, 185 Mass. 455

But the cause of action must be supported by oral testimony of a promise or statement made by the deceased. 

National Granite Bank v. Tyndale, 179 Mass. 390

So, this statute does not apply where the cause of action is based upon a written contract. 

Whitcomb v. Whitcomb, 217 Mass. 558 

Coggswell v. Hall, 185 Mass. 455 (Mother's statement that she furnished part of the consideration to purchase real estate.) 

Huebener v. Childs, 180 Mass. 483 (Deceased's book containing all receipts showed that the claim was not entered and therefore did not receive.) 

Hyde v. Gannett, 175 Mass. 177 (Private conservations between husband and wife incompetent even after death.) 

Brooks v. Holden, 175 Mass. 137 b. (Statute makes competent statements made after, as well as before, commencement of action.)

Death and Conscious Suffering 

In an action for both death and conscious suffering, declarations admitted during the trial under Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65, became incompetent as soon as the jury find against the plaintiff on the count for conscious suffering, since, if there is no conscious suffering, the decedent could not have made intelligent declarations. 

Jordan v. Adams etc. Co., 231 Mass. 186 20

In an action for death the damages recovered are not assets of the estate in the hands of the administrator, but are in the nature of a fine which the State imposes upon one whose negligence caused the death of the intestate and which is given as a gratuity to the next of kin. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183, at 186 

Boott Mills v. B. & M. R.R., 218 Mass. 582

So, the next of kin are not in privity with, nor claiming under the intestate; and hence a declaration of the intestate in the nature of an admission made by him does not bind the next of kin, nor bind a plaintiff administrator so far as he is suing for the benefit of the next of kin, because of the death. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183, at 186 and 187 

Wall v. Mass. Northeastern Ry., 229 Mass. 506 

McCarthy v. Wood Lumber Co., 219 Mass. 566

Testimony of one injured by an automobile, and later dying, as to how far it dragged him, and how fast it was going, is admissible under this section. 

Barney v. Magenis, 241 Mass. 268

Where the plaintiff's intestate died from being struck from behind by an automobile truck driven by an employee of the defendant, the deceased's statements, "I don't see how he came to hit me." "Why didn't you see me?" are admissible, under this section upon the proper findings by the judge. 

McCabe v. City of Chelsea, 265 Mass. 494 

Comm. v. Morris, 264 Mass. 314 

Comm. v. McIntosh, 259 Mass. 388 

Hicks v. Church Truck Service Co., 259 Mass. 272.

And in an action against a landlord for death of his tenant from falling off a piazza, testimony of the tenant's daughter that just after they moved into the premises her mother told her she had spoken to defendant and hired the tenement for $12.00 a month, and that he had agreed to keep the place in repair, was admissible under this section. 

Crowe v. Bixby, 237 Mass. 249 

C. Equity Suits

The statute applies to equity suits. 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518, at 523 

d. Land Disputes 

The land court has power to admit such declarations. 

Murphy v. Hanright, 238 Mass. 201

In land dispute cases, evidence that the common grantor often spoke of a certain fence as the dividing line, admissible. 

Burke v. McLaughlin, 246 Mass. 533 21

e. Life Insurance 

Whether an application for insurance made by deceased would ever be competent to show that he was in good health has not been decided. 

Lee v. Prud. Life Ins. Co., 203 Mass. 299 at 303 

f. Oral Contracts 

In an action on an oral contract in which the defendant's decedent agreed that if the plaintiffs would stay with and care for him as long as he lived, he would see that they would be well taken care of and provided for during the remainder of their lives after his decease, the court correctly ruled that under this section the jury were permitted to hear evidence of the testator's statements, acts and habits of dealing, and that he said that $1000. or $1100. was sufficient to support a man in regard to the existence of the alleged contract and the defense of payment. 

Green v. Boston Safe Dep. Co., 255 Mass. 519 

g. Water Damage 

In an action for water damage, to flour stored in defendant's building, daughter of the deceased inspector was permitted to testify that her father told her of damage in stated particulars. 

Gentile Flour etc. Co. v. Moschella, 251 Mass. 512 

h. Written Instruments 

It does not deal directly with the proof of written instruments, and .... does not affect the rule at common law that a witnessed instrument must be proved by the testimony of the subscribing witnesses, if they are living and within the reach of process; and if not, that the execution can be proved only by the best evidence. 2. 

Giles v. Giles, 204 Mass. 383, at 388

Quoted with approval in 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518, at 524

Criminal Trials 

It was said in Comm. v. Gallo, 1931 A. S.

1013, at 1026 and 1027: "Evidence of the declaration of a person since deceased, made to some third person, offered by the defendant, was excluded. The trial judge made no preliminary finding as to the good faith of the statement and its having been made on the personal knowledge of the declarant, Comm. v. Chance, 174 Mass. 245, at 250 22

but excluded it as matter of law on the ground that Gen. 

Laws, c. 233, s. 65, was not applicable to criminal proceedings. "This section provides that 'A declaration of a deceased person shall not be inadmissible in evidence as hearsay if the court finds that it was made in good faith before the commencement of the action and upon the personal knowledge of the declarant.' "The provision was first enacted in substantially the same language in St. 1898, c. 535, except that the word 'suit' was used in place of the word 'action'. "By no possible stretch of meaning can 'suit' be held to include prosecutions for crime. 'Suit', while a word of comprehensive signification, is applied usually in our practice to proceedings in equity, while 'action' is the word descriptive of proceedings at law.' 

Gould's Case, 215 Mass. 480, at 482 "This distinction is not universally maintained. The statute in its original form was applied in the first case arising under it to an action at law in contract. 

Brooks v. Holden, 175 Mass. 137 "Action,' although a word of broad import, can hardly be interpreted in this connection as intended to include prosecutions for crime. Commonly it describes only civil proceedings. 

Boston v. Turner, 201 Mass. 190, at 196 "There is no indication of a legislative intention to enlarge or vary the meaning of the original enactment by the slight changes in subsequent reenactments. 

B. & M. R.R. v. Billerica, 262 Mass. 439, at 449 

Main v. County of Plymouth, 223 Mass. 66, at 69 "It was said respecting this statute in Hall v. Reinherz, 192 Mass. 52, at 53 that it 'relates to civil procedure only'; and in Commonwealth v. Stuart, 207 Mass. 563, at 568, 'It has been doubted among the profession whether the statute is applicable to criminal proceedings. Apparently it has been assumed not to be so in the trial of an indictment for unlawfully procuring a miscarriage' citing cases. "In Commonwealth v. Taylor, 265 Mass. 133, at 134, occurs this: 'the evidence offered was the statement of a deceased person, which the judge might well regard as inadmissible in the trial of a criminal case in view of the 23

language of this court in Hall v. Reinherz, 192 Mass. 52, at 53; Comm. v. Wakelin, 230 Mass. 567, at 575; and 

Comm. v. Stuart, 207 Mass. 563, at 568.' "No one, nor all, of these expressions constitute a decision; but, together covering a period of more than twenty years, they are an impressive indication of judicial im pression. "The ruling that the statute was not applicable to prosecutions for crime was right.' 

This statute, however, applies only to civil procedure. 

Hall v. Reinherz, 192 Mass. 52, at 53 

See Comm. v. Stuart, 207 Mass. 563, at 568

As to exclusion of such evidence in criminal case, where, however, it was not offered under the statute, See Comm. v. Sinclair, 195 Mass. 100, at 108 

3. Will Cases 

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 does not affect the rule as to proof of a will by the attesting witnesses. 

Giles v. Giles, 204 Mass. 383

Also, Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 66 is not applicable to the proof of wills. 

Giles v. Giles, 204 Mass. 383 

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 does not apply to proceedings concerning the probate of wills. This statute has reference only to an "action" and a hearing on the probate of a will is not an "action". 

Mahan v. Perkins, 1931 A. S. 231, at 235 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518 (Declaration of testator inadmissible on issue of invalidity of his will.) 

Giles v. Giles, 204 Mass. 383

However, such declarations may be admitted to show his testamentary capacity 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518 

Rowley v. Cole, 244 Mass. 375 or the existence of undue influence, but not his intent. 

Rowley v. Cole, 244 Mass. 375

Statements made by a testator both before and after the making of the will are frequently received in evidence as tending to show his mental condition and feelings. Where the state of mind of the testator is in issue such declarations, if not too remote, are admissible; they are received not as evidence of the fact of undue influence but merely to show the state of mind. : 24

Mahan v. Perkins, 1931 A. S. 231, at 233 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518, at 523 

Neill v. Brackett, 241 Mass. 534 

Lane v. Moore, 151 Mass. 87 

Pickens v. Davis, 134 Mass. 252 

May v. Bradlee, 127 Mass. 414 

Shailer v. Bumstead, 99 Mass. 112 

Bodfish v. Cross, 235 Mass. 428, at 431 

Giles v. Giles, 204 Mass. 383

Declarations of a decedent alleged to be the maker of a disputed document may be effective to show that the document was executed by him, and declarations by such a person of an intention or purpose to make such an instrument or an acknowledgement that the document is his may tend to show that it is genuine.

But a written will must be executed according to the statute with the formalities required by law; it must be proved if possible by the attesting witnesses and, if this is impossible, by the best evidence obtainable. 

Mahan v. Perkins, 1931 A. S. 231, at 234 

But declarations of a testator showing his intention, plan or purpose should not be received in support of the contention that the will was signed by him and attested by the witness or any witness. 

Mahan v. Perkins, 1931 A. S. 231, at 234 

Giles v. Giles, 204 Mass. 383 

Throckmorton v. Holt, 180 U. S. 552

Nor are the declarations of the testator even though statements of fact admissible at common law or under Gen. Laws c. 

233, s. 65, because this statute does not apply to proceedings concerning the probate of wills; it has reference to an "action" and is not applicable in a hearing on the probate of a will to prove a fact. 

Mahan v. Perkins, 1931 A. S. 231, at 235 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518 

Giles v. Giles, 204 Mass. 383 

And it does not apply to declarations of a testator offered to prove or disprove the validity of his will. 

Brady v. Doherty, 253 Mass. 518 

But see: Merrick v. Betts, 214 Mass. 223

The declaration of a testator that his alleged issue were illegitimate is inadmissible as being against public policy. 

Taylor v. Whittier, 240 Mass. 514

COURT'S DUTY Preliminary Determination 

The preliminary finding as to commencement of action or suit, good faith, personal knowledge and matters incident thereto, is to be made by the trial judge and should not be submitted to the jury. 

Mcweeney v. Edison, 228 Mass. 563 

Newton Centre Co. v. Stuart, 208 Mass. 221

Gen. Laws c. 233, s. 65 makes the declarations competent, but the questions as to their weight as evidence still remains with the jury.

Chaput v. Haverhill etc. Rlwy. 194 Mass. 218 

It is error for a trial judge to admit evidence as to such a declaration until he has made the preliminary finding. 

Iloran v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 

(Preliminary finding not made.)

But upon review an exception to the admission of evidence of a declaration, on the ground that the trial judge did not make a preliminary finding, will not be sustained, where the record does not show that the trial judge did not make such preliminary finding or that such a finding could not have been -made on the evidence. 

Murphy v. Hanright, 238 Mass. 200 

It was said in Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516, at 518: ".... The requirements of a preliminary decision upont the issues to be determined in the first instance by the presiding judge are not and cannot rationally be satisfied by the mere perfunctory determination of the preliminary issues of fact without knowledge of the substance at least of the proffered declaration."

The burden is on the proponent of the declaration sought to be admitted in evidence to show that it is competent. 1411 

McSweeney v. Edison E. I. Co., 228 Mass. 563 

Carrol u. Boston El. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 500 

But see: Jordon v. Adams Co., 231 Mass. 186 26

The decision of the trial judge is not conclusive and is reviewable when all the evidence material to the issue and the question raised is contained in the bill of exceptions. 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516, at 517

Ames v. New York etc. R. R., 221 Mass. 304 

It was further said in Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516, at 

518 that: "In requiring the preliminary decision of the presiding judge that the declaration of the deceased person was made in good faith before the commencement of the action and upon the personal knowledge of the declarant, the purpose of the statute [Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65] was plainly to safeguard against the natural weakness of hearsay testimony, as well as to make futile the temptation which would not be competent were the declarant living at the trial." 

Little v. Mass. etc. Rlwy., 223 Mass. 501, at 504 

Whitcomb v. Whitcomb, 217 Mass. 558, at 564

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 

Under this section, the declaration, whether oral or written, by a person since deceased, who, if living, would be a competent witness at the trial, cannot be admitted in evidence, unless the presiding judge finds that it was made in good faith before commencement of the action and on personal knowledge of declarant, judicial action which is to be inferred from the admission of the evidence itself, where the exceptions fail to state the inquiry was not made. 

Horan v. Boston etc. Rlwy. Co., 237 Mass. 245

And a written statement, if otherwise admissible, where there is neither evidence nor finding that it was made in good faith on personal knowledge, should be excluded. 

Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475

When a declaration of a deceased person has no tendency to prove anything except a contradiction of the fact that is conceded by the opposite party, it should not be admitted in evidence. 

Ellis v. Felt, 206 Mass. 472, at 476 and 477

So, when it is conceded that the deceased person did owe the debt, but the claim is that he was discharged therefrom, the declaration of that deceased person tending to prove that he never owed the debt, should be excluded. 

Ellis v. Felt, 206 Mass. 472, at 476 and 477 27

Whether a declaration under this statute was made in good faith before the beginning of the action and upon the personal knowledge of the deceased is a matter for the presiding judge to pass upon as a condition precedent to its admission in evidence, Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475 

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245, at 248 

Coghlan v. White, 236 Mass. 165 

McSweeney v. Edison E. I. Co., 228 Mass. 563 

Johnson v. Foster, 221 Mass. 248

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 Polvere v. Hugh Nawn Con. Co., 215 Mass. 199 

but his finding in favor of these facts is to be inferred from the admission of the declaration if the exceptions fail to show that the inquiry was not made.

Quimby v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 248 Mass. 364 

Murphy v. Hanright, 238 Mass. 200 

Crowe v. Bixby, 237 Mass. 249 

Marston v. Reynolds, 211 Mass. 590 

Supple v. Suffolk Sav. Bk., 198 Mass. 393, at 397 

Dickenson v. Boston, 188 Mass. 595 

Dixon v. New England R.R. Co., 179 Mass. 242

The judge is to consider the preliminary evidence, and his decision, as to its credibility, like that of a jury, is conclusive; 

Bodfish v. Cross, 235 Mass. 428 

McSweeney v. Edison E. I. Co., 228 Mass. 563, at 564 

Johnson v. Foster, 221 Mass. 248

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 

Such finding was set aside in Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass.

516. 

Polvere v. Hugh Nawn Con. Co., 215 Mass. 199

The burden is on the party offering the evidence to satisfy the judge that the conditions of the statute have been complied with. 

Carrol v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 210 Mass. 500

Where the form of statement made by the deceased leaves it doubtful whether it was a statement of fact, or of opinion, or prediction, it is for the court to decide in which sense it was made. 

Eldridge v. Barton, 232 Mass. 183 ("It is my fault, I am to blame.") 28

Gray v. Kelly, 190 Mass. 184 ("we will give and take" referring to straightening of the boundary admitted.) 

George v. George, 186 Mass. 75 (That value of estate was diminishing.) 

Stone v. Commonwealth, 181 Mass. 438 ("it would be safe to guarantee from eighteen to twenty feet of water" admitted.) 

See: Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry., 215 Mass. 318, at 321 а. 

Necessity 

Before the declaration of a deceased person can be admitted, it is necessary that the trial judge make a preliminary finding that the essentials of the statute existed which are, the declaration was made before the commencement of the action, in good faith, and upon personal knowledge of the declarant. 

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 

b. Basis of Decision

In his decision as to its admission, the judge must be governed by rules of law, and his decision on this is reviewable on a bill of exceptions or report. 

Little v. Mass. N. St. Ry. Co., 223 Mass. 501, at 504 

Ames v. N.Y. N. H. & H. R.R., 221 Mass. 304 .... "Where the judge cannot find the existence of the alleged declaration, it is difficult to conceive how he can find good faith and the other requisites plainly required by the statute," and such a preliminary decision is final and requires the exclusion of the declaration.

Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318 

The date of the statement may itself be sufficient to base the finding that it was made before commencement of the action. 

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193 

The preliminary determination of the essential facts required by the statute may be based upon the facts inferred from or set out in the declaration itself. 

As was said in Marston v. Reynolds, 211 Mass. 590, at 593: "This disposes of all the questions raised by the requests for rulings. The declarations of Otis were competent under R. L. c. 175, s. 66. From the preliminary inquiry made in the absence of the jury, it fairly may be inferred that the trial judge found that the declarations were made in good faith; and they bear internal evidence 29

that they were made upon the personal knowledge of the declarant."

White v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 208 Mass. 193 

Dickinson v. Boston, 188 Mass. 595 

(I) Burden of Proof 

The burden is on the proponent of the declaration sought to be admitted in evidence to show that it is competent. 

McSweeney v. Edison E. I. Co., 228 Mass. 563

Carrol v. Boston El. Ry. Co.. 210 Mass. 500 

But see: Jordan v. Adams Co., 231 Mass. 186 

(II) Retroactive Effects of Statute 

Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65, applies to declarations made before, as well as after, it took effect, provided the statutory requirements are present.

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168 Slotofski v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 215 Mass. 318

Hall v. Reinherz, 192 Mass. 52 

Dickinson v. Boston, 188 Mass. (III) When there was Opportunity to take Deposition Under this section and Rev. St. U. S., sec. 721 (U. S. Comp. 

St., sec. 1538), in an action for conscious suffering for the death of the plaintiff's intestate, the fact that the decedent's deposition might have been taken does not affect the admissibility of an attorney's testimony as to statements made to him by the deceased after injury. 

American Ry. Ex. Co. v. Rowe, 14 Fed. (2d) 269 

See dissenting opinion.

C. Presumption on Review 

The ruling of the trial judge as to the competency of evidence under Gen. Laws, c. 233, s. 65 will not be reviewed unless it is clearly wrong. 

Bodfish v. Cross, 235 Mass. 428

Where the record is silent as to the procedure and adjudication of fact at the preliminary hearing, no exception can be sustained. 

Murphy v. Hanright, 238 Mass. 201 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516, at 518 (Land Court properly admitted declaration.) 30

Also, where the excepting party has lost his right by failing to ask for appropriate rulings at the preliminary hearing. 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516, at 518

The preliminary decision of the trial judge admitting in evidence a statement of a deceased person offered under Gen. 

Laws, c. 233, s. 65, is not conclusive and, where all the evidence material to the question of the admission of the statement is contained in the bill of exceptions, the action of the judge may be reviewed by the S. J. C. and can be held to be wrong because unsupported by any evidence. 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516, at 517

Ames v. New York etc. R. R., 221 Mass. 304 

Where the trial judge admitted a declaration it will be presumed that he made the preliminary inquiry and the required finding, if the record does not show the fact. 

Newton Centre Trust Co. v. Stuart, 208 Mass. 221

Unless the record shows the contrary, the admission of the declaration in evidence requires the inference that the presiding judge was satisfied with the incidents of the facts which supported the preliminary issues (before commencement of action-good faith-declarant's personal knowledge). 

Heathcote v. Eldridge, 226 Mass. 168 

Dickinson v. Boston, 188 Mass. 595

While a preliminary finding of the good faith of the declarant by the court is required before such declarations can be received, this judicial action is to be inferred from the admission of the evidence itself where the exceptions fail to state that the inquiry was not made. 

Tenny v. Foss, 268 Mass. 69

The admission of evidence generally and without restriction imports a finding of the necessary preliminary facts which render it admissible under this statute. 

Ferris v. Ray Taxi Service Co., 259 Mass. 401

The findings of the trial judge will not be overruled unless plainly erroneous.

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 

Bodfish v. Cross, 235 Mass. 429 

McSweeney v. Edison E. I. Co., 228 Mass. 563 

Johnson v. Foster, 221 Mass. 248 

The proper mode of review is on exceptions or report.

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 

81 

Hasey v. Boston, 228 Mass. 516

If the record shows that no preliminary finding was made by the trial judge then the exceptions to the admission of the declaration will be sustained. 

Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 

But if the record does not negative the fact that the judge held a preliminary hearing and made a finding, the reviewing court must presume from the admission of the declaration that such hearing and finding existed. 

Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475 

Murphy v. Hanright, 238 Mass. 200 

Crowe v. Bixby, 237 Mass. 249, at 251

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 

Marston v. Reynolds, 211 Mass. 590

When the trial judge excludes the declaration upon the ground that as matter of law it does not come within the statute, is subject to review by an Appellate tribunal. 

Bodfish v. Cross, 235 Mass. 428 (Statement not made in good faith.) 

Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475

If the record shows that the judge did not make the necessary preliminary finding, but referred those facts to the jury, the evidence of the declaration is improperly admitted, and exception will be sustained.

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 

When the trial court excluded the evidence without any particular ruling or finding it will be presumed, unless the record shows the contrary, that the trial judge did not find the good faith or personal knowledge of the declarant or the statement was made in before the action or suit. 2. 

Crowley v. O'Donnell, 238 Mass. 475 (Memorandum in handwriting of deceased person properly excluded.) 

Bodfish v. Cross, 235 Mass. 428 (Good faith not found.) 

Instructions to Jury

Where there were two counts declared upon, one of conscious suffering and the other of death, and the preliminary facts as to the first were proved but not as to the second, but a confession affecting each was admitted without restriction, a charge that the declaration was admissible as to the first but 82

not as to the second was erroneous because it came too late since it deprived the defendant of the right to establish the preliminary fact to make the declaration admissible upon both counts. 

Ferris v. Ray Taxi Co., 259 Mass. 401

Although the judge determines the admissibility the declaration as evidence, yet he must finally leave to the jury the question of the existence and truth of the declaration and properly instruct them concerning the same. 

Horan v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 237 Mass. 245 Jordan v. Adams Gas Light Co., 231 Mass. 186 

McSweeney v. Edison E. I. Co., 228 Mass. 563 

Newton Centre Trust Co. v. Stuart, 208 Mass. 221

Chaput v. Haverhill etc. Ry., 194 Mass. 218 

The credibility and weight to be attached to the evidence of the witnesses at the trial relative to the existence of the declaration and then the question of the truth of the statements contained in the declaration are to be determined finally by the jury. 

See cases just cited above

So, the preliminary determination by the trial judge is not to be considered by the jury in determining the weight and credibility of the testimony at the trial or the truth of the statements contained in the declaration. 

See cases just cited above

So, if the jury is satisfied that the declaration was not made, as testified to by a witness or witnesses, the jury should reject it. The court is required to clearly and plainly instruct the jury upon this point.

G. 

Jordan v. Adams Gas Light Co., 231 Mass. 186

DISCRETION OF THE COURT DISCRETION OF THE COURT A. DEFINITIONS 

In Davis v. Boston Elevated Railway, 235 Mass. 482, Chief 

Justice Rugg said, at pages 496 and 497 "By such expression is implied absence of arbitrary determination, capricious disposition, or whimsical thinking. 

An exhibition of ungoverned will, or a manifestation of unbridled power is not the use of discretion. The word imports the exercise of discriminating judgment within the bounds of reason. Discretion in this connection means a sound judicial discretion, enlightened by intelligence and learning, controlled by sound principles of law, of firm courage combined with the calmness of a cool mind, free from partiality, not swayed by sympathy nor warped by prejudice nor moved by any kind of influence save alone the overwhelming passion to do that which is just. It may be assumed that conduct manifesting abuse of judicial discretion will be reviewed and some relief afforded." 

Berggren v. Mutual Life Ins. Co., of N. Y., 231 Mass.

DISCRETION OF THE COURT 

Keet v. Mason, 167 Mass. 154 

Freeman v. Boston, 178 Mass. 403 

Ellis v. Ginsberg, 163 Mass. 143 

In Russell v. Foley, 1932 A. S. 145, Mr. Justice Pierce said, at page 147: "Sound judicial discretion implies calmness, conscience, courage, impartiality, wisdom and discernment of the just result." 

Davis v. Boston El. Ry., 235 Mass. 482, at 496 and 497 

Langnes v. Green, 282 U. S. 531, at 541 

Osborn v. United States Bank, 9 Wheaton, 738, at 866 

In Osborne v. Banks of United States, 9 Wheaton 738, at page 866, it states: "Judicial power, as contradistinguished from the power of the laws, has no existence. Courts are the mere instruments of the law, and can will nothing. When they are said to exercise a discretion, it is a mere legal discretion, a discretion to be exercised in discerning the course prescribed by law; and, when that is discerned, it is the duty of the court to follow it. Judicial power is never exercised for the purpose of giving effect to the will of the judge; always for the purpose of giving effect to the will of the legislature; or, in other words, to the will of the law." 

In Langnes v. Green, 282 U. S. 531, at 541: "The term 'discretion' denotes the absence of a hard and fast rule, The Styria v. Morgan, 186 U. S. 1, at 9 "When invoked as a guide to judicial action it means a sound discretion, that is to say, a discretion exercised not arbitrarily or wilfully. But with regard to what is right and equitable under the circumstances and the law, and directed by the reason and conscience of the judge to a just result." 2

C.

Cruel and Abusive Treatment (I) Definitions 

Acts or words are sufficient to constitute cruel and abusive treatment within the purview of Gen. Laws, c. 208, s. 1, where the acts are committed, or the words are spoken with a malevolent motive, or an intention to injure or to cause suffering to the libellant, if that injury or the danger of injury to the libellant's life, limb or health, or a reasonable apprehension thereof, is thereby caused. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, at 53 

Freeman v. Freeman, 238 Mass. 150, at 160

The words "cruel and abusive treatment" import on their face conduct directed toward the other party, and with a malevolent motive. 

Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 593 W.v. 

W., 141 Mass. 495

Any acts or conduct which injures or endangers life, limb or health, or creates reasonable apprehension of such injury or danger from a continuance of the cohabitation, constitutes cruel and abusive treatment within the meaning of the statute. 

Lyster v. Lyster, 111 Mass. 327, at 328 and 329

Cruelty is such conduct as causes injury to life, limb, or health, or creates a danger of such injury, or a reasonable apprehension of such danger upon the parties continuing to live together. This is broad enough to include mere words, if they create a reasonable apprehension of personal violence, or tend to wound the feelings to such a degree as to affect the health of the party, or create a reasonable apprehension that it may be affected. 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373, at 381 

(II) Distinctions 

(A) Distinguished from Extreme Cruelty

The distinction between cruel and abusive treatment and extreme cruelty, also a ground for divorce under Gen. Sts., c. 107, F-1

DIVORCE 

s. 9, Pub. Sts., c. 146, s. 1, but omitted from R. L., c. 152, s. 1, is pointed out in 

Freeman v. Freeman, 238 Mass. 150,at 160 

Osborn v. Osborn, 174 Mass. 399, at 400 

Jefferson v. Jefferson, 168 Mass. 456 

Lyster v. Lyster, 111 Mass. 327, at 328 and 329 "Extreme cruelty" means personal violence, or such acts or conduct as show actual suffering or great personal danger, while 

Burlen v. Shannon, 3 Gray, 387, at 390 

Hill v. Hill, 12 Mass. 150 

Warren v. Warren, 3 Mass. 321 "cruel and abusive treatment" means such conduct which injures or endangers, or creates a reasonable apprehension of injury or danger to the libellant's life, limb or health. But in order to amount to extreme cruelty, there must be proof of personal violence intentionally inflicted. 

Lyster v. Lyster, 111 Mass. 327, at 329 

Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198 

Warren v. Warren, 3 Mass. 321

Cruel and abusive treatment, which injures or endangers or creates a reasonable apprehension of injury or danger to life, limb or health, but does not amount to extreme cruelty, for want of proof of acts of personal violence, is not admissible under the allegations in a former libel. 

Lyster v. Lyster, 111 Mass. 327, at 330 

See Holt v. Holt, 117 Mass. 202 

(III) Statutory Provisions 

Gen. Laws, c. 208, s. 1, provides in part that: "A divorce from the bond of matrimony may be decreed for... cruel and abusive treatment. . . ."

A statute declaring the causes for which divorces may be granted is ordinarily to be given a prospective operation only and does not authorize a divorce for a specified cause which occurred before the statute was enacted. 

Burt v. Burt, 168 Mass. 204

F-2

DIVORCE (IV) What Constitutes (A) Preliminary Considerations  

Cruel and abusive treatment is such conduct toward the libellant by the libellee as will cause the libellant injury by actual personal violence, or the reasonable apprehension of it, or such course of treatment as endangers the libellant's life, limb or health, and renders cohabitation unsafe. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51 

Cowles v. Cowles, 112 Mass. 298

Peabody v. Peabody, 104 Mass. 198 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373

Whether cruel and abusive treatment is created is not to be determined by a particular act, acts, word or words of the libellee standing alone, nor is his conduct to be judged by dismembering it and viewing its separate parts, but all acts, words and conduct of the libellee are to be looked at as a whole and taken together to determine whether they constitute cruel and abusive treatment. 

The test is whether under the circumstances existing at the trial it is probable that the libellant with safety to life, limb and health, can continue to cohabit with the libellee. 

In judging the existence of conduct amounting to cruel and abusive treatment consideration should be given to the station in life of the parties and their habits, training and refinement. What might disturb a person of refinement will not affect one of grosser sensibilities. 

Pidge v. Pidge, 3 Met. 257

The statute among other causes provides that a divorce may be decreed for cruel and abusive treatment. 

It was held in Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373, that cruelty as a ground for divorce must be of such a character as shall cause injury to life, limb or health or create a danger of such injury or a reasonable apprehension of such danger upon the parties if they continue to live together. This is broad enough to include mere words, if they create reasonable apprehension of personal violence, or tend to wound the feelings to such a degree as to affect the health of the party or create a reasonable apprehension that it may be affected.

Freeman v. Freeman, 238 Mass. 150, at 159 and 160 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50, at 52

Where there was no evidence of physical violence, that during the libellant's sickness she lacked no attention "except her husband's attention personally," that her health was impaired "because of the alienation of his affections" . . . such constitutes no evidence to warrant the granting of the petition." 

Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 593

The commission by the husband of a disgusting act in the presence of his wife which injured her health, was not cruel and abusive treatment within the statute in the absence of evidence that the act was done with the intention of injuring her. 

W. v. W., 141 Mass. 495

Language may be so irritating and so frequently used as to permit the granting of a divorce because of cruel and abusive treatment when injury to health results from it, but where there is no such purpose, although the libellant's health was seriously affected, a divorce cannot be granted on this ground. 

Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 594 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50

Neither words nor acts which do not involve physical violence, inflicted on the other party, are sufficient to constitute cruel and abusive treatment unless it is shown that the language was uttered or these acts were committed with a malicious intent and for the purpose of injuring the libellant. 

Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 594

Acts or words are sufficient to constitute cruel and abusive treatment within Gen. Laws, c. 208, where the acts are committed or the words are spoken with a malevolent motive or an intention to injure or to cause suffering to the libellant, if it is found that injury or the danger of injury to the libellant's life, limb or health or a reasonable apprehension thereof, is thereby caused.

Distinguished from Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592 These findings are sufficient to sustain the libel,—a deliberate communication to his wife, who at the time was ignorant of his infected condition, of a venereal disease which he had contracted through illicit sexual intercourse. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, at 54

The acts of the libellee toward his wife, and treatment of her, when he knew that he was suffering from a venereal and infectious disease that could be communicated by contact with her person, by which she was made "ill much of the time," warranted the judge in ruling as a matter of law that the libellant had made out a case. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, at 56

Application of physical force to the body of the libellant by the libellee with the purpose of inflicting suffering and not for the sake of self-protection of the libellee is cruel and abusive within the literal and most narrow interpretation of the words. 

Meader v. Meader, 252 Mass. 132

A series of acts of personal violence, a menace to the safety of life, limb, or health, or any determined threats of serious bodily hurt, have always been a ground for divorce. 

Actual, personal violence, or conduct causing a reasonable apprehension of it, or such a course of treatment as endangers life, limb, of health, and renders cohabitation unsafe. 

Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198

DIVORCE 

However, mere want of congeniality, or incompatibility of temper, and the consequent wranglings of the parties, will not justify a charge of cruelty on the part of either. 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50

The conduct of one of the parties must at least be such as to render cohabitation intolerable to the other. 

Yet, there must have been such treatment as to destroy the peace of mind and happiness of the injured party, and to endanger the health or utterly defeat legitimate objects of the marriage. 

Mere austerity of temper, petulance of manner, rudeness of language, a want of civil attention and accommodation, even occasional sallies of passion, if they do not threaten bodily harm, do not amount to legal cruelty. 

Kenley v. Kenley, 2 How. (U. S.) 751 

Personal violence may amount to cruel and abusive treatment and on the contrary it may not create such result. However, it may arise from mere words. 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373

Whether the conduct of the libellant amounts to a justification for the acts of the libellee or barred a divorce was for the trial judge. 

Linnell v. Linnell, 249 Mass. 51, at 54 

Freeman v. Freeman, 238 Mass. 150, at 160

Where a husband has been sentenced to the state prison for a maximum term of years and a minimum term of years, under a statute authorizing a prison commission to parole a prisoner after the expiration of the minimum term upon certain conditions and to rearrest him if the conditions are violated prior to the expiration of the maximum term, the wife may obtain a divorce under Gen. 

Laws, c. 208, s. 2, giving her the right to a divorce where her husband is sentenced to state prison for five years or more. 

Oliver v. Oliver, 169 Mass. 592

But generally a sentence to imprisonment in a reformatory does not present a ground for divorce under these statutes. 

Unsoeld v. Unsoeld, 216 Mass. 594
