DIVORCE 

Conviction and imprisonment without the state is not a cause for divorce. 

Leonard v. Leonard, 151 Mass. 151

Divorce on the ground of extreme cruelty will be denied where there is no actual violence, unless the treatment, or abuse, or neglect, or bad conduct complained of be such as damages health, or renders cohabitation intolerable and unsafe, or unless there are threats of mistreatment of such flagrant kind as to cause reasonable and abiding apprehension of bodily violence, so as to render it impracticable to discharge marital duties. 

(2) Single Acts of Cruelty 

A single act of violence is sufficient cruelty and abusive treatment if there is a likelihood of repetition. 

As was said in French v. French, 4 Mass. 587: . . when force and violence are once used without provocation, the woman is unsafe. Such a husband ought not to have power over his wife."

But proof of a single act of violence does not create cruel and abusive treatment unless there is apprehension by the libellant of a repetition of such acts. 

Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198

A solitary instance of ill treatment usually is insufficient if during a long cohabitation, unless its nature is so serious as to create reasonable apprehension of danger to libellant's personal safety. (3) Intention, Willfulness, Malice and

Motive Neither words nor acts which do not involve physical violence, inflicted on the other party, are sufficient to constitute cruel and abusive treatment within the meaning of the statute, unless it is shown that the language was uttered or these acts were committed with a malicious intent and for the purpose of injuring the libellant. 

Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 594

So, where her husband "stayed away from her longer than he had ever in four years and went out many evenings;" that when she spoke to him about this he said "he had been going... with a F-7

girl in Boston;" that she became unhappy, could not sleep, "had extreme attacks of vomiting;" that "she expostulated with him and told him of her suffering" and he said he could not give up the girl; that she was worried, became sick and has not completely recovered her health. There was no evidence to support a finding that the acts of the husband were committed with such motive, and there was nothing to indicate that the confession of his guilt and his other statements were made with the purpose of injuring his wife, Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 593 and 594 and the libel should be dismissed for there is nothing to show an intent. 

Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 593 and 594

The conduct of the libellee must have been wilful and with a malevolent motive and not done accidentally, or unintentionally. 

W. v. W., 141 Mass. 495 

Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198

The libellee must have intended to injure the libellant by the cruel and abusive treatment.

Ordinary intention, willfulness, or malice is a necessary element of the cruel treatment which the law recognizes as a ground for divorce, Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592 

W. v. W., 141 Mass. 495 

Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198 notwithstanding that the act complained of injuriously affected the health of the other spouse. 

See also Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass., 50, at 52, where in denying a husband a divorce on the ground of cruel treatment, although the proof showed that his health had been injuriously af- F-8

Though the libellant was affected injuriously in his health to some extent by her acts and words, she had no purpose to harm him in this manner, but in part was moved by what seemed to her good motives, and by the desire for his success in life, and in part by her own nervous condition, she being in reality strongly attached to him, and her feelings being affectionate."

In Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, it was said, at page 53: "Acts or words are sufficient to constitute cruel and abusive treatment within the purview of ... Gen. Laws, c. 208, s. 1, where the acts are committed, or the words are spoken with a malevolent motive or an intention to injure or to cause suffering to the libellant, if it is found that injury or the danger of injury to the libellant's life, limb or health, or reasonable apprehension thereof, is thereby caused." 

(4) Permiting Cruelty by Third Person 

In Holt v. Holt, 204 Mass. 25, the court said at page 26: "Undoubtedly if the assault were in any degree participated in or encouraged or even afterwards approved by the husband, it would have been material evidence of cruelty on his part, in view of the duty of protection owed to a wife by her husband, it would perhaps have been as strong evidence against him as if he had himself committed the assault. But he cannot be held answerable for the act of a third person, even if one with whom his relations were as close and intimate as was alleged to be the case, here, unless he is shown to have made the act his own, either by procurement or previous assent or by acquiescence or subsequent approval and adoption." 

(B) Acts of Violence 

Continued acts of personal violence producing physical pain or bodily injury and a fear of future danger are recognized as suffi- F-9

cient cause for divorce in nearly all jurisdictions. 

Jefferson v. Jefferson, 168 Mass. 456

French v. French, 4 Mass. 587 

"[The] application of physical force to the body of the libellant by the libellee with the purpose of inflicting suffering and not for the sake of self-protection of the libellee [is] conduct [amounting to] cruel and abusive [treatment] within the literal and most narrow interpretation of the words [of the statute].” 

Meader v. Meader, 252 Mass. 132 

Katz v. Katz, 274 Mass. 77 .. there may be personal violence which does not amount to what is regarded as cruelty; and that there may be cruelty without personal violence. And in every case the character and condition of the parties is to be taken into consideration; and the practical judgment of the court or jury must be exercised in each particular case." 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373, at 380

In French v. French, 4 Mass. 587, the court said: 

"... when force and violence are once used without provocation, the woman is unsafe. Such a husband ought not to have power over his wife.” (1) Chastisement "The beating of [one's] wife was not lawful.... Beating or striking a wife is held to be unlawful in New York. There is no authority in its favor in this Commonwealth. Beating or striking a wife violently with the open hand is not one of the rights conferred on a husband by the marriage, even if the wife be drunk or insolent.” 

Comm. v. McAfee, 108 Mass. 458, at 461 (2) Reasonable Apprehension of Bodily Harm

It is essential in every libel for divorce for cruel and abusive treatment to prove reasonable apprehension of personal harm, physical or mental, to the libellee if the cohabitation of the parties continues. 

As was said in Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198, at 206: "The question before them was, whether the libellee had inflicted blows upon the libellant, on a single occasion, which F-10

DIVORCE 

were such as to constitute extreme cruelty. The instruction that there must be personal violence, intentionally inflicted, and that it must be of such a character as to endanger the life, limb or health, or as to create a reasonable apprehension of such danger, was correct." 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373

Slight acts of violence usually are not sufficient to cause apprehension. (C) Mere Words 

Cruelty as a ground for divorce must be of such a character "as shall cause injury to life, limb or health, or create a danger of such injury or a reasonable apprehension of such danger upon the parties continuing to live together." 

Freeman v. Freeman, 238 Mass. 105, at 160 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373

This is broad enough to include mere words, if they create a reasonable apprehension of personal violence, or tend to wound the feelings to such a degree as to effect the health of the party, or create a reasonable apprehension that it may be affected. 

Freeman v. Freeman, 238 Mass. 105, at 160 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50, at 52 

Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373

No physical violence is necessary to create cruel and abusive treatment. The same may result from mere words. Words sometimes wound more deeply that blows.

It was held in Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373, where the libel alleged that the libellee had "treated the libellant with extreme cruelty, and bruised and beat the person of the libellant and threatened to take her life," that cruelty as a ground for divorce must be of such a character "as shall cause injury to life, limb or health, or create a danger of such injury or to reasonable apprehension of such danger upon the parties continuing to live together. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, at 53 

Freeman v. Freeman, 238 Mass. 105, at 160 

Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198

F-11

DIVORCE 

In Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass.

373, it was said, at pages 380 and 381: where a divorce is sought on the ground of cruelty, whether it be cruel and abusive treatment, or cruelty in neglecting or refusing to provide suitable maintenance for the wife, a reasonable construction of the statute requires that it shall appear to be at least, such cruelty as shall cause injury to life, limb, or health, or create a danger of such injury or a reasonable apprehension of such danger upon the parties continuing to live together. "This is broad enough to include mere words, if they create a reasonable apprehension of personal violence, or tend to wound the feelings to such a degree as to affect the health of the party, or create a reasonable apprehension that it may be affected. "If it be supposed that this interpretation of the statute does not sufficiently provide for a class of cases where, though the abusive language or conduct of one party does not affect the health of the other, yet it makes the life of the other so wretched and intollerable that a divorce ought to be granted on account of the cruelty, we think such supposed cases cannot actually exist. For deeply wounded sensibility and wretchedness of mind can hardly fail to affect the health. 

And where there is not this evidence of injured feeling, we can see no ground for granting a divorce that is not uncertain and dangerous, and that would not authorize divorces for slighter causes than the legislature apparently contemplated." 

In Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, the cruel and abusive treatment consisted in part, of scolding, nagging and swearing, and the frequent use of loud and exasperating language directed to the libellant. 

Angry words, coarse and abusive language, or grossly intemperate habits might bring greater sufferings upon a refined and delicate woman than a single act of violence upon her person. 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373, at 379

Pidge v. Pidge, 3 Met. 257 

F-12

DIVORCE 

The court does not have to wait until the mischief is done but may grant a divorce when the words uttered show a likelihood of actual danger of bodily harm or mental suffering. 

(2) Malevolent Motive Essential 

Language may be so irritating and so frequently used as to permit the granting of a divorce because of cruel and abusive treatment when injury to health results from it, but where there is no such purpose—although the libellant's health was severely affected-a divorce cannot be granted on this ground. 

Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 594

There may be such an habitual or frequent use of exasperating language as to warrant the granting of a divorce when injury to health follows. 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50, at 52 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373

But when cruel and abusive treatment is charged, and the proof consists merely of words spoken, and these words contain no threat of actual violence, the purpose and intent of speaking them may be considered. 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50, at 52 

W. v. W., 141 Mass. 495

So, in Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50, where, after their marriage the parties had lived together pleasantly for many years and then the libellee wife began to use toward the libellant occasional expressions, which increased in frequency until during the last year or two of cohabitation they became common, such as "fool," "idiot," "know-nothing," "no ambition," and "vile wretch."

The libellant was a school teacher in Boston. The language used irritated him, but he suppressed his feelings. He lost sleep, and became affected nervously, in consequence of the libellee's said language and conduct, so that his school work was disturbed to some extent. But he kept on with his work. 

The libellant, on April 3, 1893, separated from the libellee, and refused to live with her. He made ample provision for her separate support. She insisted that she should be allowed to live with him, and on one occasion she went to his room in the school- F-13

DIVORCE 

house, and on several occasions to his sleeping apartments, for the purpose of persuading him to permit her to live with him. She wrote and sent letters to him, asking him to allow her to come to him. He refused. On one occasion he told her he would call a policeman to eject her from his apartments if she did not leave. 

The libellant was kind to the libellee while they lived together. 

There was nothing in his conduct which justified her language and conduct toward him. The libellee had no purpose to harm or injure the libellant, but in part was moved by what seemed to her to be good motives, and by a desire for his success in life, and in part by her nervous condition. 

The court said, at page 52: "The facts found did not require the final step of granting an absolute divorce. Though the libellant was affected injuriously in his health to some extent by her acts and words, she had no purpose to harm him in this manner, but in part was moved by what seemed to her good motives, and by a desire for his success in life, and in part by her own nervous condition, she being in reality strongly attached to him, and her feelings being affectionate." 

(D) Conduct Exciting Fear of Harm  

Actual violence is no longer a necessary element of cruelty as a ground for divorce; any conduct justifying a reasonable apprehension of bodily harm is sufficient. 

There must exist, however, a probability that future harm will ensue.

In Hill v. Hill, 2 Mass. 150, the court said: "Threats of violence, without an actual assault, are not a legal cause for divorce. The wife's remedy in such case is by exhibiting articles of the peace against her husband." 

But courts will interfere on the ground that conduct exciting fear or harm is cruelty to prevent future harm rather than to punish the offender for what has already been done. 

In Linnell v. Linnell, 249 Mass. 5, where the libellee attempted to strike him with a mirror in the presence of his son; she kicked him, called him vile names, accused him of murdering his wife F-14

DIVORCE and of attempting to kill her; she accused him of various misdeeds and threatened to do him injury; that on another occasion, she kicked him and he was obliged to restrain her by force; he offered her some money which she refused and struck him in the face with her fist; that he started to go out of the room and she threw a heavy vase striking him in the back of the head; that she administered cruel and excessive punishment to his daughter (ten years old, of a former marriage); threatened the child with violence if she talked to her father and punished her so severely as to cause black and blue marks on her legs and neck. . . . He went home to get the keys to a trunk; as he stepped out of his room, he heard a shot and felt the sting of a bullet, he looked up and his wife was standing about fourteen feet away from him with a gun levelled at him; she threatened to kill him, the court said, at page 55: "If the libellee did not intend to shoot the libellant when she discharged the pictol, still her act might well have been found to constitute cruel and abusive treatment." (2) Threats As a rule words of menace importing actual danger of bodily harm may justify the granting of a divorce. 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373

Threats of bodily violence, while not acts of violence in themselves, may be cruel and abusive treatment, according to the circumstances. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51

But empty threats uttered in anger do not constitute ground for divorce in the absence of any attempt to carry them out. 

Hill v. Hill, 2 Mass. 150

In Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, the libellee's conduct was cruel and abusive treatment where in part of compelling her on one occasion and attempting to compel her on various other occasions by verbal threats and by force to have relations with him when he knew that she reasonably feared contracting a venereal disease from him.

F-15

DIVORCE 

(E) Conduct Causing Mental Suffering 

It was formerly thought that actual bodily harm, or apprehension thereof, must be shown to authorize granting a divorce on the ground of cruelty. 

Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198 

Hill v. Hill, 2 Mass. 150

Any unwarranted conduct by either spouse which causes the other mental suffering of sufficient degree constitutes such cruelty as will authorize a divorce, Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373 as where a wife renders her husband's living with her unbearable by bemeaning him and refusing to attend to his household duties. 

Any justifiable conduct on the part of either the husband or the wife, which so grievously wounds the mental feeling of the other, or so utterly destroys the peace of mind of the other as to seriously impair the bodily health or endanger the life of the other, or such as in any other manner endangers the life of the other, or such as utterly destroys the legitimate ends and objects of matrimony, constitutes extreme cruelty under the statutes although no physical or personal violence may be inflicted, or even threatened. 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373

So, there is sufficient mental suffering to create cruel and abusive treatment where the wife learns from the husband of his infatuation with another woman, his preference for this other woman above his wife; and his determination to continue in his relations with the other and in neglect and disregard toward his wife and children. . . which knowledge and its heartless communication causes his wife great mental suffering, so keen that her physical health is seriously impaired. . . The husband being informed by the family physician that his conduct is the cause of the failure in health of his wife, and is told that still greater injury to her physical health would follow if he persisted in his course, and the husband declared that he did not care, and would do worse, if his wife did not yield to his wish for a separation, persisted in his of fensive presence that he will make it unbearable for his wife to live with him, banged doors, beat the furniture and made the home resound with his voice to add emphasis to his statement.... F-14

DIVORCE 

His wife may, with reason, fear actual physical violence at his hands, if she does not step aside and further his wishes in this matter. His purpose, in so speaking and acting with his wife, being to obtain the separation he desires, not in order to cause her pain, but in order through her pain, if need be, and regardless of her feelings, mental or physical to attain his end. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, at 53 and 54 

Reasons for Rule. (1) Mental anguish, wounded feelings, constantly aggravated by repeated insults and neglect, are as bad as actual bruises of the person; and that which produces the one is not more cruel than that which causes the other. (2) Little patience is found with the insistence of the once semi-barbaric rule that afforded an avenue of escape to the injured wife only where physical violence was inflicted upon her. 

(2) Degree of Suffering 

Conduct causing mental pain to constitute cruelty must be such as to produce impairment of health or create a reasonable apprehension of that result.

In determining the question (1) whether the treatment could reasonably be expected seriously to injure the health of the person complaining, the effect and probable consequence of the misconduct upon such person is determinative, rather than whether it could be reasonably expected to endanger the health of a person of ordinary intelligence and strength. 

A court will look to the effect that actually has resulted, or that may be reasonably apprehended, rather than to the character of such acts and conduct, in deference to the view that while they might constitute very extreme cruelty in one case, they might constitute much less in another. 

Where, however, the conduct of a spouse is calculated permanently, to destroy the peace of mind and happiness of the other so as utterly to destroy the objects of matrimony, a divorce may be granted on the ground of cruelty. 

(3) Abuse of Children and Others 

Abuse of libellee's children standing by itself is not cruel and abusive treatment, but with other circumstances it may constitute it, particularly this may be so where the abuse of the children was F-17

DIVORCE 

done intentionally to cause mental suffering to the libellee, which caused the intended result. 

Linnell v. Linnell, 249 Mass. 5 (4) Adultery and Lewd Association (5) Attempts to Entrap (6) False Accusations (a) Adultery (b) Other Crimes (c) Insanity.

Probably our courts would determine it cruel and abusive treatment and grant a divorce to a wife where the husband treated her as a menial in the presence of servants, asserted that she was under the influence of designing and wicked persons, circulated reports that she was of unsound mind, kept her in constant fear that he intended to resort to legal proceedings to test her sanity and deprive her of her liberty, affecting her health, and rendering her life intolerable and burdensome. 

Russell v. Russell, 37 Pa. Super. 348 (d) Physical Incapacity (7) Profanity-Vile Language

Profane, obscene and insulting language, habitually indulged towards a person of a sensitive nature and refined feelings, may, doubtless, in some cases, amount to extreme cruelty. But this, as a general rule, would be more readily recognized, when used by the husband to the wife, than by the wife to the husband. 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50

However, mere rudeness of language, petulence of manners, austerity of temper, or an occasional sally of temper which does not injure or threaten to injure the health of the complaining party does not constitute legal cruelty. 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50 (8) Unnatural Acts (a) Masturbation

The practice of masturbation in the voluntary presence of the wife is not cruelty, although her health may be injured by its effect on her feelings, when she is not compelled to participate in it. 

W. v. W., 141 Mass. 495 (b) Sodomy

F-18

DIVORCE (9) Compelling Abortion 

When the libellee compels the libellant by acts or threats to undergo a surgical operation against her will as a result of which she is ill for a long period, such conduct is cruel and abusive treatment. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, at 55 (F) Conduct Imposing Hardship or Privation 

(1) Failure to Provide Necessaries 

In Peabody v. Peabody, 104 Mass.

195, it was said, at pages 197 and 198: "It may be, that, under some circumstances, a sudden and continued refusal to provide the necessaries of life to a wife, who is left thereby, with her children, to her own earnings, would be regarded, within the meaning of the statute, as gross and cruel; as where, from the previous habits, or mode of life, or state of health, or incapacity to labor from any cause, such conduct would cause injury to health, or danger of such injury, or reasonable apprehension thereof." 

(2) Failure to Provide Medical Care 

Where a husband negligently or willfully refuses to provide for a wife necessary medicines and medical attendance when able to do so, the wife is entitled to a divorce on the ground of cruelty, especially when such conduct is coupled with other misconduct. 

But the failure of a wife to care for her sick husband is not always such cruelty as to entitle the husband to a divorce. 

Bonney v. Bonney, 175 Mass. 7 (3) Compelling Wife to Labor 

(4) Involving Husband in Difficulties 

(G) Conduct Directly Injuring Health (1) Communication of Disease 

In Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, where the cruel and abusive treatment by the libellee consisted, in part, of his forcibly kissing the libellant against her will when he had an infected throat which emitted a peculiar odor making the act disagreeable and dangerous and knowing that she realized the disagreeableness and danger and when the libellant had a venereal disease, so that the libellant's fear from having intercourse with him, so that this caused F-19

DIVORCE 

a marked detrimental effect on the libellant physically and mentally, making her ill much of the time, causing her much mental anguish, and keeping her in a state of nervousness, anxiety and fear, the court said, at page 56: "The acts of the libellee toward his wife, and treatment of her, when he knew that he was suffering from a venereal and infectious disease that could be communicated by contact with her person, by which she was made 'ill of the time,' warranted the judge in ruling as matter of law that the libellant had made out a case."

It is cruel and abusive treatment where the libellee, knowing that he is therewith afflicted, deliberately communicates to his wife, who at the time is ignorant of his infected condition, a venereal disease known as gonorrhea, which he had contracted through illicit sexual intercourse. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, at 54

Especially is this so when it was not until after the libellee had left the libellee and gone away with another woman that she consulted a physician and was informed of the nature of this disease from which she was suffering, and that a radical cure is rarely affected and recurrent attacks were probable and the libellant's health was and would continue to be impaired by the disease and the nervous strain thereby caused. 

Curtiss v. Curtiss, 243 Mass. 51, at 54 

(2) Sexual Excess 

Under special circumstances abuse of sexual intercourse may create cruel and abusive treatment when it results in injury to health of the other spouse. 

S. v. S., 192 Mass. 194 (H) Habitual Intemperance (I) Refusal to Cohabit

In the absence of proof that the health of the libellant has either been injured or threatened, the refusal of the libellee to cohabit is not cruel and abusive treatment. 

So, the utter denial of sexual intercourse on the part of a wife is not cruel and abusive treatment entitling the husband to a divorce, neither is is a cause for annulling the marriage. F-20

Desertion does not amount to cruelty. 

Southwick v. Southwick, 97 Mass. 327

(V) What Does Not Constitute 

A spouse may be guilty of drunkenness or other vices; his habits or disposition, his indifference, neglect, or desertion may cause mental worry and injury to his wife's health; but these acts standing by themselves are not enough to make out a case of cruel and abusive treatment. 

Armstrong v. Armstrong, 229 Mass. 592, at 594

If, in a libel for divorce for extreme cruelty and cruel and abusive treatment, it appears that, though the libellant was affected injuriously in his health to some extent by his wife's acts and words, she had no purpose to harm him in this manner, but in part was moved by what seemed to her good motives and by a desire for his success in life, and in part by her own nervous condition, she being in reality strongly attached to him and her feelings being affectionate, the decision of the justice dismissing the libel will be accepted as final. 

Freeborn v. Freeborn, 168 Mass. 50 

In Bonney v. Bonney, 175 Mass. 7, where the libellee wife failed to stay at home and take care of her sick husband, the libellant, or to consent to him having a nurse or housekeeper so to do, the libellant was financially able to procure a servant, nurse or housekeeper to wait on him, but the libellee said if he would do so she would leave him, and there was nobody else in the family to administer medicines except the libellee and she gave the libellant medicine when she was there, but she did not remain at home all the time, went to theatre and dances and was at work also, the court said at page 8: "But the libellant was not dependent solely upon his wife. 

He was under the care of a physician and had the money with which to procure proper food and nursing. . . . [he] did... when he got up from his sick bed, by boarding with F-21

DIVORCE 

the occupants of another tenement in the same. house; and he afterwards went to Jamaica in search of health. If he was not content with the care his wife, gave him while he was sick in bed his remedy was to hire a nurse, even if his wife wrongly threatened to leave his tenement if he did so. was no pretence that this could not have been done through the physician in attendance. There "... the fact that the libellant's health was temporarily injured by the libellee's failure to comply with the doctor's orders as to the libellant's diet and medicines is not sufficient. 

Her action in that respect may in one sense be said to be cruel, and the libellant may be said to have been abused by her. But it is not such cruel and abusive treatment as under the circumstances of the libellant will cause injury to his health or create danger of such injury, or reasonable apprehension of such danger, if the parties: continue to live together; and nothing less will make out a case of divorce on this ground." 

Lyster v. Lyster, 111 Mass. 327, at 328 and 329 

Bailey v. Bailey, 97 Mass. 373, at 380 and 381 

In Ford v. Ford, 104 Mass. 198, it was found' that blows inflicted upon the libellant, on a single occasion, did not constitute extreme cruelty.

GENERAL STATEMENT 

Every person must have a domicile somewhere. 

Ness v. Commissioner, 1932 A. S. 1037, at 1039 

Feehan v. Tax Comm. 237 Mass. 169, at 171

Domicil of origin or domicil acquired remains until new one is acquired. 

Ness v. Commissioner, 1932 A. S. 1037, at 1039 

Hallett v. Bassett, 100 Mass. 167, at 170

Native domicil is not so easily changed as acquired domicil and more easily reverts. 

Ness v. Commissioner, 1932 A. S. 1037, at 1039 

But see: Otis v. Boston, 12 Cush. 44, at 50

To establish a change of aumicil, fact and intent must concur. 

Ness v. Commissioner, 1932 A. S. 1037, at 1039 

Comm. v. Bogigian, 265 Mass. 531, at 538 

Tax Coll. v. Hanchett, 240 Mass. 557, at 558-560 

Babcock v. Slater, 212 Mass. 434, at 436 

Whately v. Inhabitants, 196 Mass. 393, at 394

A domicil once existing cannot be lost by mere abandonment even when coupled with the intent to acquire a new one, but continues until a new one is in fact gained. 

Ness v. Commissioner, 1932 A. S. 1037, at 1039 and 1040 

Shaw v. Shaw, 98 Mass. 158 

Borland v. Borland, 132 Mass. 89

That is, an existing domicil cannot be lost without another being gained.

DOUBLE JEOPARDY

DOUBLE JEOPARDY DOUBLE JEOPARDY A. DEFINITIONS SECTION 1 

Autrefois acquit (formerly acquitted) A plea made by a defendant indicted for a crime or misdemeanor, that he has formerly been tried and acquitted of the same offence.

Autrefois convict (formerly convicted) A plea that the defendant has been indicted for a crime or misdemeanor, that he has formerly been tried and convicted of the same. "The maxim that no person shall be tried twice for the same offence, stated in other words means, where one has been convicted and punished by a court of competent jurisdiction, all other proceedings for the same offence are barred to the end that the defendant shall not be punished again for the same matter.” 

Comm. v. McCan, 277 Mass. 199, at 201

Jeopardy is the peril in which a prisoner is put when he is regularly charged with a crime before a tribunal properly organized and competent to try him. 

A person is in legal jeopardy when he is put upon trial, before a court of competent jurisdiction, upon indictment or information which is sufficient in form and substance to sustain a conviction, and a jury has been charged with his deliverance. 

Cooley, Const. Lim. (4th Ed.), 404

Jeopardy is the peril and danger to life and liberty in which a person is put when he has been regularly and sufficiently charged with the commission of a crime; has been put upon his trial before a tribunal properly organized and competent to try him for the offense charged; and a jury has been duly impanelled from persons competent to sit upon the trial, and duly sworn to try the cause, and charged with due deliverance. 

Wharton's Crim. Law, 12 Ed., Vol. 1, page 541 1

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

In Commonwealth v. Roby, 12 Pick., 496, it was said at 501: "This plea of a former conviction, like that of a former acquittal, is founded upon that great principle and fundamental maxim of jurisprudence, that no man shall be twice put in jeopardy for the same offense. This is one of the ancient and well-established principles of the common law sanctioned and enforced, in different forms of words, in most of the constitutions of the several states and in that of the United States. In the latter, it is thus expressed, 'Nor shall any person be subject for the same offense, to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb.' This is an ancient phrase, known in the law, and without endeavoring to seek for its origin, in times when dismemberment was actually inflicted as a punishment for offenses, it may now be taken to be an expression descriptive of the class of punishments denounced by law against those offences coming under the denomination of felony. . . . This clause in the constitution, then, may be considered equivalent to a declaration of the common law principle, that no person shall be twice tried for the same offence." 

B. DISTINCTIONS SECTION 2 1. Distinguished from Preliminary or Summary Proceedings 

In Commonwealth v. Rice, 216 Mass. 480, it was held that an alleged plea of former jeopardy, filed as a bar to an indictment in the Superior Court for larceny for the sum of $20, which alleges that the defendant was tried for the same offense before a judge of the Municipal Court of Boston, who, after finding the defendant guilty, withdrew that finding and ordered him to recognize for his appearance in the Superior Court, must be overruled upon demurrer; because on the allegations of the plea it appears that such action of the judge was a proper exercise of his discretionary power, and the subjection of the defendant to trial in the Superior Court in such a case is no infringement of any right under the Constitution of the United States or that of this Commonwealth.

A preliminary examination of one arrested on suspicion of crime is not a trial; and his discharge by the magistrate is not an acquittal. 2

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

Commonwealth v. Rice, 216 Mass. 480 

Collins v. Loisie, 262 U. S. 426, at 429

In Commonwealth v. Brown, 167 Mass. 144, it was held that the pendency of a previous indictment, the verdict upon which has been set aside on the defendant's motion and the indictment placed on file, is no defense to a subsequent indictment for the same offense. 

In Comm. v. Cody, 165 Mass. 133, the court said, at 136: "But the pendency of an indictment is no ground for a plea of abatement to another indictment in the same court for the same cause. 

Commonwealth v. Berry, 5 Gray, 93 

Commonwealth v. Drew, 3 Cush. 279 "Nor is it ground for plea in bar." 

Commonwealth v. Berry, 5 Gray, 93

In Commonwealth v. Harris, 8 Gray, 470, it was held that where a complaint had been made to a justice of the peace who had concurrent jurisdiction of such offense with the court of common pleas and such justice of the peace had listened to a plea of not guilty and evidence, and considered the defendant guilty, so ordering him to be held for the court of common pleas, such hearing was not a defense to subsequent indictment for the same offense.

In Bassing v. Cady, 208 U. S. 386, it was held that the finding of an indictment, followed by arraignment, pleading thereto, repeated continuances, and eventually dismissal at the instance of the prosecuting officer on the ground that there was not sufficient evidence to hold the accused, did not constitute prior jeopardy. 

In Post v. U. S., 161 U. S. 583, it was said, at page 587: "The submission of a bill of indictment by the attorney for the government to the grand jury, and the examination of witnesses before them, are both in secret, and are no part of the criminal proceedings against the accused, but are merely to assist the grand jury in determining whether such proceedings shall be commenced; the grand jury may ignore the bill, and decline to find any indictment; and it cannot be known

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

whether any proceedings will be instituted against the accused until an indictment against him is presented in open court." 

SECTION 3 C. CONSTITUTIONAL PROVISIONS 

Amendment 5 of the Constitution of the United States provides in part: "... nor shall any person be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb."

Though the phrase, "life or limb," as used in the United States constitution, if strictly construed, would apply only to crimes involving the deprivation of the use of a part of the accused's body, the U. S. courts have construed the phrase in its liberal sense, and so it has been held to embrace all cases wherein there is an attempted second prosecution for a felony or misdemeanor on which the defendant had been previously placed in jeopardy and has been acquitted or convicted. 

Cross v. North Carolina, 132 U. S. 138 

In re Snow, 120 U. S. 206

Fox v. Ohio, 5 How. (U. S.) 439 Ex parte Lange, 18 Wall. (U. S.) 163

SECTION 5 E. PROCEEDINGS IN WHICH FORMER JEOPARDY IS A DEFENSE 1. General Statement 

The plea of former jeopardy may be availed of only in criminl prosecutions, but includes misdemeanors as well as felonies. 

Commonwealth v. Churchill, 5 Mass. 174

However, such proceedings must be regularly conducted criminal prosecutions within the proper channels set forth for governmental prosecutions, and so it has been held that voluntary appearance in court or before a magistrate and confession of a public offense, followed by the imposition and payment of a fine, where no written complaint or information is filed, is in effect, an ex parte proceeding where the Commonwealth is not represented, and is no bar to a prosecution in regular form. 

State v. Bartlett, 181 Iowa 436 

2. Imposition of Heavier Penalty 

It was held in Ex parte White, 14 Pick 90, that where a statute provides that if any person should be convicted at the same time of three distinct larcenies, he should be punished as a common and notorious thief, by confinement to hard labor for a term not less than three years nor more than fifteen years, this statute did not violate the Constitutional provision as to double jeopardy. The court said, at page 92: "The effect of the statute is, to consolidate the three so as to make one aggravated crime, that of being a notorious thief, punishable by one sentence, and that going much beyond the aggregate of the three punishments, if imposed severally.

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

"It may be regarded as a punishment of the last three offenses, which, if it stood alone, would be a simple larceny, but enhanced and aggravated by the two previous convictions, is regarded by the law as a highly aggravated crime. This is conformable to the general principle and policy of this class of statutes, inflicting increased penalties upon second and third offenses. The increased punishment is not regarded as an additional punishment for the prior offense, which would be unjust; but the prior conviction is regarded as giving a character of increased aggravation to the subsequent offence." 

A person is not twice put in jeopardy for the same offense by a law punishing more severely for a second offense, nor is the increase of punishment by reason of the first offense cruel and unusual. 

Moore v. Missouri, 159 U. S. 673

In the above cited case, the court said, at pages 676 and 677: "The increased severity of the punishment for the subsequent offense is not a punishment for the same offense for the second time, but a severer punishment for the subsequent offense, the law which imposes the increased punishment be ing presumed to be known by all persons, and to deter those so inclined from the further commission of crime; and we are unable to see how the statute which imposes such increased punishment violates the provision of our constitution. . . . The fact that the indictment charged a former conviction of another and entirely different offense is not, in fact, charging him with an offense with respect of the former case in hand. The averments as to the former offense go as to the punishment only."

SECTION 6 F. WHEN JEOPARDY ATTACHES 

1. 

General Statement 

Generally speaking, it may be said that jeopardy attaches when a person has been placed on trial before a court of competent jurisdiction under a valid indictment, has been arraigned and has pleaded, and a proper jury has been impanelled to hear the evidence. 

Commonwealth v. Hart, 149 Mass. 7 

Commonwealth v. Tuck, 20 Pick. 356

DOUBLE JEOPARDY SECTION 7 G. ESSENTIALS OF FORMER JEOPARDY 1. General Statement 

Legal jeopardy of a defendant in a criminal prosecution requires that he shall have been placed upon trial: a. Upon a valid indictment or complaint b. Before a court of competent jurisdiction

C. After he has been arraigned d. After he has pleaded to the indictment or complaint and e. When a competent jury has been impanelled and sworn. 

In Commonwealth v. Cabot, 241 Mass. 131, the court said, at page 153: "When a former acquittal is pleaded in bar, two kinds of matters are involved, those of record consisting of the former proceedings of the acquittal, and those of fact which involve the identity of the offense and of the person alleged to have been guilty." 

Commonwealth v. Merrill, 8 Allen, 545 

Commonwealth v. Roby, 12 Pick., 496 

a. Upon a Valid Indictment or Complaint 

Where an indictment is insufficient in form or substance and no judgment can be rendered upon it, no jeopardy arises because such indictment is deemed to be a nullity, wholly inoperative and void, and upon which no punishment can be awarded. 

Commonwealth v. Roby, 12 Pick., 496

So, it has been held that where the first indictment did not allege the necessary criminal intent of the defendant, upon which indictment he was acquitted, such acquittal would not be a bar to a subsequent indictment against the same defendant for the same offense but which properly alleges criminal intent. 

Commonwealth v. Bakeman, 105 Mass. 53

In Commonwealth v. Call, 21 Pick. 509, where a special verdict was rendered finding the defendant guilty of an offense alleged but not finding him guilty in the county where it is alleged to have been committed, it was held that such a verdict would not operate as an acquittal but the accused could be again put on trial.

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

In Commonwealth v. Farrell, 105 Mass. 189, where, after a jury had been impaneled to try the defendant on his plea of not guilty to an indictment, and he was then held to withdraw that plea and file a plea in abatement for misnomer which was tendered and the indictment quashed, it was held that the defendant could not object to being tried on a new indictment for the same offense on the ground that he had been once put in jeopardy.

However, where there has been a prior conviction by judgment before a justice of the peace and a performance of the sentence pursuant to the judgment, such conviction will constitute a bar to indictment for the same offense, although the complaint on which the justice proceeded was so defective that his judgment might have been reversed by a writ of error by the defendant. 

Commonwealth v. Loud, 3 Met. 328

In Commonwealth v. Chesley, 107 Mass. 223, the court said, at pages 224 and 225: "The record in the present case showed that the former acquittal was by reason of a variance and so could not be a defense to this indictment. The offense for which the defendant was here tried and convicted was not the offense described in the former indictment, or there could have been no variance." 

Commonwealth v. Wade, 17 Pick. 395 

In Commonwealth v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496, the court, in dealing ith elements of prior jeopardy, said, at page 501: "So where the indictment was insufficient, in form or substance, and no judgment could be rendered upon it [the defendant was not in jeopardy] because it is deemed as a nullity, wholly inoperative and void and upon which no punishment could be awarded." 

b. Before a Court of Competent Jurisdiction 

A conviction in an inferior court of a misdemeanor does not constitute former jeopardy so as to bar subsequent prosecution for a felony arising out of the same transaction. 

Commonwealth v. McCan, 277 Mass. 199, at 205

In the above cited case, the court said, at page 202: "The present indictment, on the contrary, charges a felony of high degree, the maximum punishment permissible there-

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

for being imprisonment in the State prison for life.... It is a crime beyond the final jurisdiction for trial of any save the Superior Court under our system of distribution of powers among the several courts. If a complaint of that nature were lodged in the Municipal Court, or if evidence. showing the commission of that crime appeared on a trial, that court would have no jurisdiction to punish therefor; in either event the proper course for that court, provided there appeared to be probable cause to believe that such crime had been committed, would be to bind the person who appeared to be guilty over for the action of the Superior Court." 

In Commonwealth v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496, the court said, at page 501: "Thus, where the court before which the former trial took place had no jurisdiction of the offense, the party cannot be deemed in law to have been put in jeopardy, because no valid and binding judgment could have been rendered by such court."

An acquittal by a jury, in a court of the United States, of a defendant who is there indicted for an offense of which that court had no jurisdiction, is no bar to an indictment against him, for the same offense, in a state court. 

Commonwealth v. Peters, 12 Met. 387

In the above cited case, the court said, at pages 396 and 397: "It being clear that the indictment against the defendant, in the district court of the United States, for the same assault charged in this indictment, was not within the jurisdiction of that court, we may presume that the acquittal there was upon that ground, and not upon the merits. But whether it was so in fact, or not, it is equally clear that no legal judgment could have been rendered on a conviction in that court, and therefore, that an acquittal there is no bar to this indictment." 

In instances where the lower court has discretionary power as to whether or not it shall assume jurisdiction to pronounce sentence after hearing evidence, if such court chooses to convict or acquit, such conviction or acquittal will be a bar to a subsequent indictment for the same offense in a court of superior jurisdiction. 

Commonwealth v. Goddard, 13 Mass. 455

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

So, where a defendant pleaded in bar to an indictment for an assault and battery a former conviction before a justice of the peace, of the same offense, and the record showed that the justice first ordered the defendant to recognize for his appearance and afterwards revoked that order, and sentenced him to pay a fine, the plea in bar was held to be sufficient. 

Commonwealth v. Goddard, 13 Mass. 455

Before a person can be said to have been put in jeopardy in life or limb the court in which he was acquitted or convicted must have had jurisdiction to try him for the offense charged. 

Grafton v. U. S., 206 U. S. 333 

c. After He Has Been Arraigned 

Where there has been the finding of an indictment, followed by arraignment and a pleading thereto, but no subsequent action has been taken by the court, and the prosecuting officer declined to prosecute because of insufficient evidence, there has been no prior jeopardy that is a bar to a subsequent indictment for the same offense. 

Bassing v. Cady, 208 U. S. 386 d. After He Had Pleaded to the Indictment or Complaint 

The mere pleading to an indictment or complaint is not of itself, jeopardy, and so, if no further action is taken by the prosecution, such indictment and pleading thereunder will not be a bar to a subsequent indictment for the same offense. 

Bassing v. Cady, 208 U. S. 386 

e. When a Competent Jury Has Been Impanelled and 

Sworn 

However, jeopardy may attach to a defendant by a trial without a jury in instances where he has no legal right to demand a jury, such as where the trial is had in an inferior court having proper jurisdiction but not providing jury trials. 

Commonwealth v. Cunningham, 13 Mass. 244

SECTION 8 H. TERMINATION OF PROCEEDINGS AFFECTING JEOPARDY 1. General Statement 

In Commonwealth v. Murphy, 174 Mass. 369, the court said, at page 371: 10

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

"By jeopardy is meant, we think, lawful jeopardy from the commencement of the proceedings until their termination by a proper judgment, or acquittal, or what the law regards as such. It has been held, in numerous cases that where, either for want of jurisdiction or from some defects in the indictment, or from some error in the course of the proceedings, the verdict has been set aside or the judgment has been arrested on a writ of error brought by the defendant, or on a motion made by him, and he has been tried again, he was not thereby put in jeopardy a second time and his constitutional rights were not abridged."

When an original indictment is quashed, adjudged bad on demurrer, or when judgment thereon is arrested for a defect therein, it is held that the accused has not thereby been in jeopardy. 

Commonwealth v. Gould, 12 Gray 171, at 173 

2. Preliminary Matters 

The disposition of the case upon preliminary matters such as motion to quash or pleas in abatement are not sufficient to create jeopardy. 

Commonwealth v. Taylor, 113 Mass. 4 

3. Preliminary Hearings a. To Determine Probable Cause and Bind Over to Su perior Court

A preliminary hearing to determine probable cause for the purpose of binding the defendant to be tried before the Superior 

Court does not create jeopardy.

Where an indictment has been found for the same offense as that described in a pending complaint against the same defendant in the district court, it is the custom, in this Commonwealth, for the district court not to try the complaint, Klous v. Judges of Municipal Court, 251 Mass. 292 and no constitutional right of the defendant is violated by such custom. 

Klous v. Judges of Municipal Court, 251 Mass. 292

So, where the defendant was indicted in the Superior Court for an offense for which he had been tried in the Municipal Court, found guilty, and then the judge had withdrawn his finding and 11

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

declined jurisdiction and had ordered the defendant to recognize for his appearance in the Superior Court, the defendant's plea of former jeopardy was not a bar to prosecution on such indictment. 

Commonwealth v. Rice, 216 Mass. 480

In Commonwealth v. Sullivan, 156 Mass. 487, where there was a complaint in a district court charging the defendant with keeping a common nuisance, a tenement used for the selling, and keeping for sale of intoxicating liquors, the record stated that the de fendant was discharged because it did not appear that there was probable cause to believe him guilty. The court said, at page 489: "It is well settled that a district court or a trial justice may either try and acquit, or convict, a person charged with the offense of keeping a tenement for the illegal keeping or illegal sale of intoxicating liquors, or may examine the case for the purpose of determining whether there is probable cause to believe him guilty, and, if so, may order him to recognize for his appearance before the Superior Court.... Whether in a particular case the court took jurisdiction, or merely conducted a preliminary examination, must be determined from the record of its proceedings. "In the present case, the record states that the defendant is discharged because 'it does not appear that there is probable cause to believe defendant guilty.' This language indicates that the court did not assume to take final jurisdiction, but was simply doing the preliminary duty of determining whether the defendant should be held for appearance before a higher tribunal . . . such a record does not show an acquittal which will bar conviction on an indictment in the Superior Court."

In Commonwealth v. Hamilton, 129 Mass. 479, where it was held that neither the judgment of a magistrate, upon a complaint of which he has concurrent jurisdiction with the Superior Court, that the defendant be discharged for want of probable cause to believe him guilty, nor his judgment that there was probable cause to believe the defendant guilty, and that he recognize for his appearance in the Superior Court, can be pleaded in bar to a subsequent indictment for the same offense, the court said, at page 481: 12

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

"It is clear, from an inspection of the record of the proceedings before the trial justice, that he took jurisdiction in each case only for the purpose of making preliminary examination to determine whether to order [the defendant] in the first case, and both defendants in the second case, to recognize for appearance at the Superior Court. Any conclusion arrived at on such an examination is not conclusive as to the guilt or innocence of a party charged, and is not a bar to a subsequent indictment for the same offense.” 

A complaint to a justice of the peace upon which the defendant "is found guilty of the offense charged against him" and "ordered to recognize for his personal appearance in the court of common pleas," is no bar to an indictment for the same offense. 

Commonwealth v. Marcy, 14 Gray 82 

Commonwealth v. Golding, 14 Gray 49 

Commonwealth v. Boyle, 14 Gray 3 

Commonwealth v. Harris, 8 Gray 470 

4. Quashing or Dismissing Indictment or Complaint 

Ordinarily, the quashing or dismissal of an indictment or complaint will not create jeopardy.

When an original indictment is quashed, adjudged bad on demurrer, or when judgment thereon is arrested for a defect therein, the accused has not been in jeopardy and may be tried again for the same offense. 

Commonwealth v. Gould, 12 Gray 171, at 173

So, where after a jury had been impanelled to try the defendant on his plea of not guilty to an indictment, and he was allowed to withdraw that plea and file a plea in abatement for misnomer which was sustained and the indictment quashed, it was held that such defendant could not object to being tried on a new indictment for the same offense on the ground that he had been once put in jeopardy. 

Commonwealth v. Farrell, 105 Mass. 189

But if the indictment or complaint is valid and is dismissed without the defendant's consent, after jeopardy is attached, he cannot be prosecuted again for the same offense. 

Commonwealth v. Hart, 149 Mass. 7 13

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

In the above cited case the court said, at page 8: "In general, a person put upon trial for a crime is thereby put in jeopardy, and cannot be again tried for the same of fense. Of the exceptions to this rule it is necessary to refer only to the one upon which the Commonwealth relies,—when a prosecution is terminated during the progress of a trial by the entry of a nolle prosequi by the Commonwealth's attorney, with the consent of the defendant. The general right of a defendant on trial to insist upon a termination of the trial which will bar another prosecution is admitted; but it is claimed that the attorney for the Commonwealth has a right to enter a nolle prosequi during a trial, and leave with the defendant his right of a verdict; and that if the defendant does not insist upon the right, but accepts his discharge without a verdict, there will be no bar to another prosecution. It would seem that after the termination there would be nothing before the court upon which a verdict could be rendered, and that the court could do nothing except to discharge the defendant. The true rule would seem to be, that, after a trial has commenced, the Commonwealth's attorney, though he has the power, has not the right to terminate the prosecution without a verdict; and his refusal of record to further prosecute the indictment has the effect of and amounts to an acquittal of the defendant, unless it is done with his consent." 

Commonwealth v. McCormack, 130 Mass. 61 

Commonwealth v. Scott, 121 Mass. 33 

Commonwealth v. Tuck, 20 Pick. 356 

Commonwealth v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496

A nolle prosequi can be entered only by a prosecuting attorney, and not by the court, and if the court discharges the defendant, because of lack of evidence, such discharge would operate as an acquittal. 

Commonwealth v. Hart, 149 Mass. 7 14

DOUBLE JEOPARDY Nolle Prosequi 

а. (I) 

Before Trial 

Power to enter a nolle prosequi is absolute in the prosecuting officer from the return of the indictment up to the beginning of the trial, except possibly in instances of scandalous abuse of authority. 

Comm. v. Dascalakis, 246 Mass. 12, at 18

A nolle prosequi or other form of dismissal of the indictment or complaint entered before the defendant is put on trial will not bar a subsequent prosecution for the same offence. 

Comm. v. Galligan, 156 Mass. 270 

Comm. v. Cutler, 9 Allen, 486 

Bacon v. Towne, 4 Cush. 217 

Comm. v. Tuck, 20 Pick. 356 

(II) After Beginning Trial 

After a trial has commenced, the Commonwealth's attorney, though he has power, has not the right, to terminate the prosecution without a verdict; and his refusal of record to further prosecute the indictment has the effect of, and amounts to, an acquittal of the defendant, unless it is done with his consent. 

Comm. v. Hart, 149 Mass. 7, at 8 

Comm. v. McCormick, 130 Mass. 61 

Comm. v. Scott, 121 Mass. 33 

Comm. v. Tuck, 20 Pick. 356 

Comm. v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496

After a jury is empanelled the defendant acquires a right to have that tribunal pass upon his guilt by verdict and thus secure a bar to another prosecution for the same offense. It follows that a nolle prosequi cannot be entered after the jury has been empanelled without the express or implied consent of the defendant. 

Comm. v. Dascalakis, 246 Mass. 12, at 18 

Comm. v. Adams, 127 Mass. 15, at 19 

Comm. v. Kimball, 7 Gray, 328

A nolle prosequi without the consent of the defendant after the trial has commenced and before verdict has the effect of 15

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

acquittal and bars a subsequent prosecution for the same offense. 

Comm. v. Dascalakis, 246 Mass. 12, at 19 

Comm. v. Hart, 149 Mass. 7

But the entry of a nolle prosequi or other form of dismissal with the consent of the defendant will not bar a subsequent prosecution for the same offense. 

Comm. v. Hart, 149 Mass. 7 (A) Where Less Than All of Several Counts of Indictments Are Nol Prossed

In Comm. v. Dunster, 145 Mass. 101, it was said at page 102: "Where a complaint or indictment contains several counts each charging an offence, it is within the power of the prosecuting officer, before the jury are empanelled, to enter a nolle prosequi as to either count. So, where two offenses are improperly charged in one count, he may enter a nolle prosequi as to one of them, and where, as in the exceptional case of burglary, both breaking and entering with intent to steal and larceny are properly charged in one count, he may enter a nolle prosequi as to either of the charges. And, generally, where an offense is set out with aggravating circumstances, which enlarge the offence, he may enter a nolle prosequi as to the aggravation, and obtain a conviction for the lesser offence which is well charged. 

Comm. v. Holmes, 119 Mass. 195 

Jennings v. Comm., 105 Mass. 586 

Comm. v. Cain, 102 Mass. 487 

Comm. v .Mead, 10 Allen, 396

Comm. v. Briggs, 7 Pick. 177 

Comm. v. M'Monagle, 1 Mass. 517 "But in all these cases, the matter upon which the nolle prosequi operates is a distinct and independent charge, and, when entered, the nolle prosequi leaves an offence formally as well as substantially charged, being the same offence which is formally charged in the original complaint or indictment. The prosecuting officer cannot, by means of a 16

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

nolle prosequi, put the defendant upon trial for an offence differing from any offence with which he is formally charged in the complaint or indictment."

It is not competent for the prosecuting officer, by entering a nolle prosequi as to a part, to amend a complaint in the material allegation of time so that the defendant is put to trial in the Superior Court on appeal upon an offence differing legally from that for which he was tried in the District Court. 

Comm. v. Dunster, 145 Mass. 101, at 103

When a former conviction is a bar to the whole of an offence set out in a complaint, the prosecuting officer cannot defeat this defence by entering a nolle prosequi as to a part of the offence, any more than he can do so by confining his proof to facts not included in the former complaint. 

Comm. v. Dunster, 145 Mass. 101, at 103

But the prosecuting officer has power, in the absence of the issue of former jeopardy, to enter a nolle prosequi as to the whole substantive part of the indictment. or any 5. 

Comm. v. Clifford, 254 Mass. 390, at 393

Discharge of Jury Before Verdict а. General Statement 

If the defendant consents to the discharge of the jury during trial, he cannot thereafter contend that he has been in jeopardy. 

Comm. v. Campopiano, 254 Mass. 560, at 562 b. 

Comm. v. Hart, 149 Mass. 7 

Comm. v. Sholes, 13 Allen, 554 

Comm. v. Bowden, 9 Mass. 494

Reasons (I) 

General Statement 

The reasons which create the propriety of discharging a jury before verdict are either, where there is no probability that the jury will agree and return a verdict, where the defendant has by his own conduct, interfered with the fairness of the trial, and 17

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

where before the jury can agree upon a verdict, an adjournment of the court is compelled by law or the urgencies of the situation. 

In U. S. v. Perez, 9 Wheaton 579, the court, in speaking of discharge of a jury before they arrive at a verdict, said at page 580: "The prisoner has not been convicted or acquitted, and may again be put upon his defence. We think that in all cases of this nature, the law has invested courts of justice with the authority to discharge a jury from giving any verdict, whenever, in their opinion, taking all the circumstances into consideration, there is a manifest necessity for the act, or the ends of public justice would otherwise be defeated. They are to exercise a sound discretion on the subject and it is impossible to define all the circumstances which would render it proper to interfere."

So, in Lovato v. New Mexico, 242 U. S. 199, it was held that the accused was not placed in double jeopardy merely because after a demurrer to the indictment, which had been entertained after a plea of not guilty had been entered and not withdrawn, was overruled and the jury, which had been empanelled and sworn, was dismissed and the accused was forthwith arraigned and required to plead, and this having been done, and both sides again announcing themselves ready for trial, the same jury previously empanelled was sworn and the trial proceeded. 

Generally speaking, it may be said that if it is impossible to proceed with the trial or to proceed without manifest injustice to the defendant or to the Commonwealth, the jury may be discharged and the defendant again be put on trial for the same offence. 

Comm. v. Purchase, 2 Pick. 521

U. S. v. Perez, 9 Wheat. (U. S.) 579 

In Comm. v. McCormick, 130 Mass. 61, the court said, at page 62; "From the necessity of the case, however, there must be many exceptions to the rule. . . . in short, whenever the case cannot be proceeded with by reason of some physical or 18

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

moral necessity arising from no fault or neglect of the government. When such is the case, the trial may be stopped, and the defendant will not be protected from being afterward tried upon the same indictment." (II) 

Absence of Accused 

Death, Disability or Illness (A) Of Accused

If, after the jury is empanelled and charged with the prisoner and progress is made in the trial, the prisoner becomes ill, the jury may be dismissed, and the defendant may again be put on trial before another jury.

(B) Of Judge 

The discharge of the jury because of the illness of the judge is not a bar to a subsequent trial of the defendant for the same offence. 

Comm. v. McCormick, 130 Mass. 60, at 61 (C) 

Of Counsel 

See Comm. v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496, at 502 (D) Illness of Juror

Where the trial comes to an end because of the sickness or death of a juryman, the defendant may be again placed on trial for the same offence. 

Comm. v. McCormick, 130 Mass. 61, at 62 

In Comm. v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496, the court said, at page 502: "So, after the jury is empanelled and charged with the prisoner, and progress made in the trial, if through the death or sudden sickness of a juror, the illness of the prisoner, or other case of urgent necessity, the progress of the trial is interrupted, another jury may be empanelled, and the prisoner again put upon his trial."

"It is manifest that we have no means of determining, as did the trial judge, the effect which the statement of counsel might reasonably have had upon the minds of the jurors. 

If the judge, acting impartially, as we must assume he did, believed that the statement of counsel was likely to result in an unjust verdict, we cannot say that his action was without justification. Of course, he would not exercise the power vested in him to act arbitrarily or without good cause to believe that the action he took was necessary to prevent great injustice either to the Commonwealth or to the defendant. 

The power of the court is always to be used alike for the protection of the public and for the security of the defendant in his right to an impartial trial." (X)

6. Acquittal or Conviction a. 

General Statement 

The acquittal or conviction that may be pleaded in a bar of a subsequent indictment for the same offence must be an acquittal or conviction on the merits.

G. L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 263, s. 7, protects a defendant from answering on a second indictment or complaint for a crime of which he had been acquitted on the facts and merits. 

Comm. v. Walsh, 255 Mass. 317, at 320 

It was said in Comm. v. Cabot, 241 Mass. 131, at page 153: "An acquittal is a bar to a subsequent conviction for an offence upon which a defendant properly could have been convicted thereunder because it was embraced in the crime. 

Comm. v. Bosworth, 113 Mass. 200 

Wood v. Southwick, 97 Mass. 354, at 356 

Comm. v. Clair, 7 Allen, 525 

Comm. v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496 "If the judge against the objection of a defendant wrongfully directs a verdict when there is in fact evidence justifying a conviction of the offence charged or of some crime embraced therein, the enormous limitation in the verdict will not impair the legal effect of the acquittal in proceedings in which the defendant has in truth been put in jeopardy. If the evidence did not have the effect described, it would have supported an indictment for a distinct crime, the verdict of acquittal, even though no limitation is expressed therein, could not be pleaded in defence to a subsequent indictment. 

The question of former jeopardy is not determined by reference alone to the form of verdict, and the inclusion of the 22 22

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

reasons for the direction of the verdict does not prevent the defendant from fully availing himself of it as a defence in subsequent criminal proceedings. When a former acquittal is pleaded in bar, two kinds of matters are involved, those of record consisting of the former proceedings and the acquittal, and those of fact which involve the identity of the defence and of the person alleged to have been guilty." 

Comm. v. Merril, 8 Allen, 546 

Comm. v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496

In Comm. v. Squire, 1 Pick. 258, at 256, the conviction or acquittal of a party, thus charged with the minor larceny, must be a bar to a subsequent indictment charging the same larceny with aggravating circumstances. b.

Acquittal 

(I) General Statement 

The effect of dismissing a complaint without a trial is like that of quashing or entering a nolle prosequi of an indictment. 

By neither of these is the defendant acquitted of the offence charged against him, but he is only exempted from liability on that complaint or indictment. 

Comm. v. Bressant, 126 Mass. 246 

(II) 

Acquittal in Lower Court as Bar to Subsequent Indictment

In Comm. v. McCan, 277 Mass. 199, the court said, at page 202: "The present indictment, on the contrary, charges a felony of high degree, the maximum punishment permissible therefor being imprisonment in the State prison for life. . . . It is a crime beyond the final jurisdiction for trial of any save the Superior Court, under our system of distribution of powers among the several courts. If a complaint of that nature were lodged in the Municipal Court, or if evidence showing the commission of the crime appeared on a trial, that court would have no jurisdiction to punish therefor; in either event the proper course for that court, provided there appeared to be probable cause to believe that such crime had been committed, would be to bind the person who appeared 23

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

to be guilty over for the action of the Superior Court." 

In Comm. v. Roby, 12 Pick. 496, the court said, at page 501: "Thus, where the court before which the former trial took place had no jurisdiction of the offence, the party cannot be deemed in law to have been put in jeopardy, because no valid and binding judgment could have been rendered by such court." 

(III) 

Acquittal on Indictment as Bar to Prosecution in Lower Court

It was said in Comm. v. Squire, 1 Met. 258, at pages 264 and 265: "Larcenies, by our statute, are of various grades, and are punished with greater or less severity, according to the aggravation of the offence; and these different grades of offences are punished under the provisions contained in different and distinct sections of the statute. But we know very well that in larcenies, indictments are often found, charging the inferior grade of crimes, and omitting the circumstances of aggravation when all the facts existing in the case would, if disclosed to the jury bring the case within the higher grade of larcenies. Would it be a defence to such indictment on the trial before the petit jury, that the defendant committed the offence, but with certain aggravating circumstances not charged? It seems to us not, and that when the offence charged in the indictment, and the offence actually committed, are both merely larcenies, the greater offence includes the less, and evidence, proving the greater offence, will support an indictment for the smaller offence." (IV) Direction of Verdict to Acquit Inasmuch as the Commonwealth has no right of appeal in criminal prosecutions, a direction of a verdict of acquittal on the merits of the case is a bar to a subsequent prosecution for the same offence. 

Comm. v. Hart, 149 Mass. 7, at 9 at page 153: 

As was said in Comm. v. Cabot, 241 Mass. 131, "If the judge against the objection of a defendant wrongfully directs a verdict when there is in fact evidence justify- 24

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

ing a conviction of the offence charged or some crime embraced therein, the erroneous limitation in the verdict will not impair the legal effect of the acquittal in proceedings in which the defendant has in truth been put in jeopardy. 

The question of former jeopardy is not determined by reference alone. Another form of verdict and the inclusion of the reasons for the directions of the verdict does not prevent the defendant from fully availing himself of it as a defence in subsequent criminal proceedings."

But if a verdict of acquittal is directed because of a variance or defective indictment such directed verdict will not operate as a bar to a subsequent prosecution. 

Comm. v. Campapiano, 254 Mass. 560, at 562 

Comm. v. Chesley, 107 Mass. 223

G. L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 263, s. 8 (V) Acquittal by Jury G. L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 263, s. 7, provides: 

"A person shall not be held to answer on a second indictment or complaint for a crime of which he has been acquitted upon the facts and merits; but he may plead such acquittal in bar of any subsequent prosecution for the same crime, notwithstanding any defect in form of substance of the indictment or complaint on which he was acquitted." 

But where a defendant is indicted on more than one count, all counts charging the same crime in different forms, an acquittal on one count will not operate as a bar to a verdict of guilty on another count, even though all counts pertain to the same offence. 

Comm. v. Walsh, 255 Mass. 317, at 320 

In the last cited case the court said, at page 320: "The courts charge in different forms of statement perjury committed before a master in the hearing on one case; and upon the allegations in the first and second counts it must be assumed that the evidence relating to the second count was admissible and would have justified a conviction on the first count. Where all the facts necessary to sustain the count on which a verdict of guilty was returned are consistent 25

DOUBLE JEOPARDY 

with those necessary to sustain a count on which the jury returned a verdict of not guilty, even if not necessarily included in them, the defendant suffers no harm by the acquittal. 

Comm. v. Lowry, 158 Mass, 18 "The jury had the right to apply the evidence to one of the counts and having exhausted its force by finding the defendant guilty on that count, were justified in returning a verdict of not guilty on the other." C. 

Comm. v. Dow, 217 Mass. 473 

Comm. v. Edds, 14 Gray, 406

Conviction 

(I) 

General Statement 

A former conviction is a bar to a subsequent prosecution for the same offence. 

Comm. v. Dunster, 145 Mass. 101, at 103

The Constitution of Massachusetts carries no provision permitting the pleading of a prior conviction to bar a subsequent prosecution for the same offence. Nor is this right accorded by any of the provisions of G. L. (Ter. Ed.) c. 263 which pertains to pleading prior acquittals. But this is not to be construed as permitting two prosecutions for the same offence, for the cases have in dicta stated as an accepted principle of law, that a prior conviction will bar a subsequent prosecution for the same offence. 26 20

DUE CARE AND CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE

MA RAO 200

DUE CARE AND CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE DUE CARE AND CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE A. DEFINITIONS 1. Due Care 

Due care means that care for his own safety required by law. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458

The conventional definition of due care as the kind and degree of care that persons of ordinary prudence would exercise in the same circumstances of place, time, and attendant conditions in its practical application to the trial of cases is not an abstraction. 

It is practical, specific, definite. It is descriptive of conduct with reference to the cause of action on trial, not with reference to unrelated matters. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 459

It is conceivable for a plaintiff in an action for negligence to be wanting in due care with respect to an indifferent matter and be in the exercise of due care with respect to the cause of the injury inflicted or through the negligence of the defendant.

Negligence which does not contribute to the injury is immaterial and irrelevant. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 459 

Marble v. Ross, 124 Mass. 44, at 48

Due care and contributory negligence on the part of a person killed or injured through the negligence of another are correlative terms; one states his essential positive duty with reference to his own safety and the other his failure in performance of that duty; both imply conduct touching the proximate cause of his injury. They relate to the causal connection between his conduct and his injury, with respect to the tortious conduct of the defendant. 8. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458 

Want of

Want of due care is negligence on the part of a person injured or killed through the negligence of another in respect to the cause of the injury or death and is itself conduct having a share in bringing on the harm. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458

A-1

DUE CARE AND CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE 2. Contributory Negligence 

Contributory negligence is want of due care by the person injured, touching the cause of his injury resulting from the negli gence of another. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458

Contributory negligence means violation of the duty to care for one's own safety which exists at least in those cases where a person who has sustained an injury seeks to fasten liability for that injury upon some other person. 

O'Connor v. Hickey, 268 Mass. 454, at 458

EASEMENTS E. CREATION AND EXISTENCE 3. Express Grant, Covenant or Reservation g. Covenant or Contract 

In Bronson v. Coffin, 108 Mass. 175, at 180, the court in an opinion by Gray, J., said: "Words sounding in covenant only may operate by way of grant of an easement, wherever it is necessary to give them that effect in order to carry out the manifest intention of the parties."

Rajewski v. MacBean, 273 Mass. 1, at 5 

In Hogan v. Barry, 143 Mass. 538, the court said: "There is no doubt that an easement may be created by words sounding in covenant. If the seeming covenant is for a present enjoyment of a nature recognized by the law as capable of being conveyed and made an easement . . . and if the deed discloses that the covenant is for the benefit of adjoining land conveyed at the same time, the covenant must be construed as a grant . . . 

Rajewski v. MacBean, 273 Mass. 1, at 5 

See also: Ladd v. Boston, 151 Mass. 585

A covenant intended for the benefit of adjoining land conveyed must be construed as a grant of an easement, and when the clause conveying it appears in the granting part of the deed, it is controlled by the habendum which usually creates in the grantee a title in fee in the land conveyed and an easement in fee in the right of way.

Rajewski v. MacBean, 273 Mass. 1, at 5 

Parsons v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 216 Mass. 269, at 271 

Hogan v. Barry, 143 Mass. 538, at 539 

Pratt v. Sanger, 4 Gray 84, at 86

When a right of way is granted but its exact limits are not defined in the deed, the grantee is entitled to a convenient way within the land specified adapted to the convenient use and enjoyment of the land granted for any useful and proper purpose for which it might be used considering its location and all circumstances. 

Rajewski v. MacBean, 273 Mass. 1, at 5 

Dunham v. Dodge, 235 Mass. 367, at 371 

Lovejoy v. Lovett, 124 Mass. 270 

Johnson v. Kinnicutt, 2 Cush. 153, at 157
