If the limits of the way are not fixed by the deed, the practical location and use of it by the grantee acquiesced in by the grantor may operate as an assignment of the right and be deemed to be that which was intended to be conveyed. 

Rajewski v. MacBean, 273 Mass. 1, at 6 

Willard v. Stone, 253 Mass. 555, at 563

Bannon v. Angier, 2 Allen, 128

Such a way is not necessarily confined to the purposes for which the dominant estate was used at the time of the grant but is a right of way for every reasonable use to which the dominant estate may be devoted.

Rajewski v. MacBean, 273 Mass. 1, at 6

6. Obstruction and Disturbance a.

General Statement b. Actionable Obstructions (I) General Statement 

Usually, whether respective owners of the servient or dominant estate have the right to build over and upon the way is a question of construction to ascertain the intention of the parties in creating the way and giving effect to that indication if it can be done consistently with established rules of law. 

Crocker v. Cotting, 181 Mass. 146, at 150 and 151

There is no rule that determines once and for all whether the parties have or have not the right to build over a way. 

Crocker v. Cotting, 181 Mass. 146, at 151

In some cases it has been held that a way could be built over. 

Burnham v. Nevins, 144 Mass. 88 

Gerrish v. Shattuck, 132 Mass. 235 

Atkins v. Boardman, 2 Met. 456

In other cases it has been held that it could not. 

Attorney General v. Williams, 140 Mass. 329 

Brooks v. Reynolds, 106 Mass. 31 

Schwoerer v. Boylston Market, 99 Mass. 285

In each case the question has been one of construction, what the parties to "the convention" intended. 

Atkins v. Boardman, 2 Met. 457

The rights of the [parties] depend upon the construction to be given to the [instrument creating the way]. 

Crocker v. Cotting, 181 Mass. 146, at 151 

Gerrish v. Shattuck, 132 Mass. 235

In Burnham v. Nevins, 144 Mass. 88, it is said, at pages 92 and 93: "The extent of the easement claimed must be determined by the true construction of the grant or reservation . . . aided by any circumstances surrounding the estate and the parties which have a legitimate tendency to show the intention of the parties."

Speaking generally, if a right of way is created, and nothing more appears from the deed or the attendant circumstances, the owner of the servient tenement may build over the way, or do anything else so long as he does not interfere with or obstruct the right of passage over the soil. J-1

EASEMENTS 

Crocker v. Cotting, 181 Mass. 146, at 151 

Burnham v. Bevins, 144 Mass. 88 

Atkins v. Boardman, 2 Met. 457

Where the way is created by way of reservation the right or easement over the granted premises will be limited to that expressly reserved. 

Crocker v. Cotting, 181 Mass. 146, at 151 

Gerrish v. Shattuck, 132 Mass. 235 

Atkins v. Boardman, 2 Met. 456

If a grantor intends to reserve any right over the tenement granted, it is his duty to reserve it expressly in the grant. 

Crocker v. Cotting, 181 Mass. 146, at 151 citing Englis! cases

In the absence of anything in the [instruments creating the way] showing whether the way was to be kept open and could be covered over, the court is obliged to resort to the attending circumstances for aid in their construction, and taking these into account, to ascertain the intention of the parties whether the way should be an open way or could be built upon or over. 

Crocker v. Cotting, 181 Mass. 146, at 152 and 153

So, where a way created by deeds to the abutters was originally designed as a passageway in the rear of lots intended for dwelling purposes, the grantor retaining the fee, and there being when some of the deeds were given a building immediately abutting on the way with windows in the second, third and fourth stories opening upon it, the way was shown by the attending circumstances to have been granted as an open way, and it could not be arched over by the owners of the fee. 

Crocker v. Cotting, 181 Mass. 146, at 152 and 153

EMINENT DOMAIN G. EXERCISE OF POWER

2. Necessity and Extent of Appropriation Exhaustion or Further Exercise of Power 

Compliance with Statute 4. a.

General Statement b. Street Widening

In Walker v. City of Medford, 272 Mass. 161, the petition was for the assessment of damages for the alleged taking of land of the petitioner. The board of aldermen of the defendant city, ordered that Main Street be widened as a public way, and further ordered that certain described parcels of land including that of the petitioner be taken for the purpose of widening. Section 1 of Gen. Laws, c. 79, requires that the order of taking "shall contain a description of the land taken . . . and shall state the interest therein taken and the purpose for which such property is taken.” 

The court held that the order for taking must show on its face the specific purpose to which the land appropriated to public uses is to be devoted. It is equally important that the accompanying provision requiring a statement in the order of the interest taken shall be observed. Otherwise the purpose of the statute to secure uniformity in the method of taking real estate by eminent domain would be in part defeated. The taking is invalid because of the failure of the board of aldermen to comply with this essential mandate of the statute. Petition dismissed. 

5. Who May Object to Exercise of Power

Equitable Replevin

EQUITABLE REPLEVIN EQUITABLE REPLEVIN Gen. Laws, (Mass.) c. 214 provides: 

SECTION 3. The supreme judicial and superior courts shall have original and concurrent jurisdiction in equity of the following cases: (1) Suits to compel the re-delivery of goods or chattels taken or detained from the owner, and so secreted or withheld that they cannot be replevied. 

Gen. Laws, c. 204, secs. 13 and 14, conferred concurrent jurisdictoin on the Probate Court in the settlement of the estates of deceased persons.

COLLECTION OF CASES 

Luciano v. Caldrone, 255 Mass. 270

Mortgagee after demand and lapse of ten days can compel sheriff to deliver up stock of goods which he had attached. Bill must allege that goods have been so concealed or controlled that they cannot be replevied. 

Tuttle v. Corey, 245 Mass. 196

Conservator compelled return of personal property and money procured from the ward by fraud and undue influence. 

Mitchell v. Weaver, 242 Mass. 331 at 336 and 377

Probate Court has jurisdiction to order testator's agent to deliver securities to executor. 

Puffer v. Hazzard, 240 Mass. 195

Money and personal property given by an insane person may be recovered from one who procured the same by fraud or with knowledge of the insanity and from other persons who later received the money or property with knowledge of the original fraud or insanity. 1

EQUITABLE REPLEVIN 

Lloyd v. Imperial Machine Co., 224 Mass. 574

A bill founded on the plaintiff's possession of certain property cannot be amended into equitable replevin so as to give the plaintiff that possession which he did not have at the time of the bringing of the original bill. 

So, a bill in equity to enforce the payment of the principal sums and unpaid interest coupons attached to negotiable bonds, which were procured from the plaintiff by fraud and deceit, cannot be amended so as to make it a bill of equitable replevin. 

Nor can a bill of equitable replevin be retained to compel the defendant to pay the amount due to the plaintiff for the purchase or other acquisition of the property sought to be replevied. 

Homrich v. Robinson, 221 Mass. 308

Police compelled to return diamonds to owner from whom they had been stolen even before trial of thief. 

Herman v. Conn. Mutual Life Ins. Co., 218 Mass. 181 

The assignee of a life insurance policy has the title and right of possession to the same. He may compel its delivery by the insured and even by a third person who is innocently but without right holding the policy as security through the fraud of the insured or his agent, unless facts are established creating an estoppel. 

Herrick v. Dennett, 203 Mass. 17

Gift inter vivos prevented administrator from compelling delivery of negotiable bonds which had belonged to intestate. 

Nelson v. Peterson, 202 Mass. 369

Administrator obtained delivery of wearing apparel and $500.00 in money withheld by defendant as having been given to him by intestate. 

Patterson v. Patterson, 197 Mass. 112

A party to a divorce proceeding may by bill in equity, but not by petition in the divorce proceeding, compel the other party to re turn personal property which is unlawfully detained and concealed and which cannot be reached to be taken by replevin or other process at law. The Court said at page 117: "Upon the finding

EQUITABLE REPLEVIN 

that the property belongs to the petitioner, and the admission in the answer that it is held and detained by the respondent against her will, there is no doubt that the Court of equity, upon a bill brought by the wife against her husband, might grant her relief." 

Hodgkins v. Bowser, 195 Mass. 141

The owner of a race horse may compel its delivery by a person secreting the horse outside the Commonwealth and which cannot be replevied at law and may recover damages against another person to whom custody of the horse was wrongfully given. 

Kershaw v. Merritt, 194 Mass. 113

Wife compelled delivery of wedding presents belonging to her consisting of silver, cutlery, bric-a-brac and china, which were pledged wrongfully by her husband in whose possession she left them, to an innocent third person for value. 

Pels v. Millen, 192 Mass. 13

A bill of equitable replevin was maintained where the defendant had possession of a certain machine belonging to the plaintiff, the plaintiff attempted to obtain possession of it by writ of replevin and the defendant concealed, secreted and withheld essential parts of the machine from the officer, so that the writ could not properly be served. 

Frankel v. Frankel, 173 Mass. 214

Equitable replevin may be maintained between husband and wife. Husband was ordered to return money obtained from wife by fraud and coercion, which was her separate property, even though the money was in the bank in his own name. 

Lombard v. Morse, 155 Mass. 136

Husband may compel savings bank deposits and realty obtained from him by his wife through fraud, while he was insane, shortly before and in contemplation of marriage. Their ultimate marriage does not affect the husband's right to maintain the suit. 

Davis v. Sullivan, 141 Mass. 76

A decree ordering the defendant to forthwith surrender and deliver to the plaintiff, her agent or attorney, each and every article

EQUITABLE REPLEVIN 

of personal property mentioned in the plaintiff's bill is properly entered upon evidence that the plaintiff is the owner of certain jewelry which she lent to the defendant, relying upon his promise to return the same, and although the defendant claimed he had disposed of the jewelry and they were beyond his control, such were not the facts. 

Holden v. Phelps, 135 Mass. 61, at 62 and 63

Where a savings bank treasurer, without authority, has sold and assigned mortgages to persons who have paid full value for them, such person can be compelled to reassign those mortgages to the bank. 

Holden v. Hoyt, 134 Mass. 181

The owner of a promissory note and mortgage securing it may compel their surrender by a person holding them under a fraudulent transfer. At Page 185: "The specific possession of the mortgage, even if obtainable by a writ of replevin, would not be an adequate protection, since purchasers might rely on the record. 

The remedy by replevin is at best of limited utility in such a case, either as to the mortgage or note, and is attended with the burden of giving a bond to the defendant in double the appraised value of the property replevied. In most instances it probably would be found available by reason of the difficulty of obtaining the articles without a breach of the peace." 

Holden v. Upton, 134 Mass. 177

Receivers of a savings bank compel surrender of note by person who had possession of such note through abuse of power of bank's treasurer.

Brigham v. Home Ins. Co., 131 Mass. 319 

Trustee in bankruptcy obtained delivery of existent life insurance policy which was bankrupt's property. 

Fuller v. Percival, 126 Mass. 381

A receiver of a partnership may compel the surrender of a promissory note fraudulently issued by one partner and delivered to the defendant who had knowledge of the fraud. The rule would be otherwise if the note had been negotiated to an innocent purchaser for value without notice of the fraud.

EQUITABLE REPLEVIN 

McNeil v. Ames, 120 Mass. 481

A purchaser at a sale on execution of a leasehold estate cannot compel the lessee, whose interest in the lease has been sold at that sale, to deliver up to such purchaser the counterparts of his lease and subleases which are recorded. And the fact that the lessee continues to claim the rent does not give the purchaser any additional rights to equitable replevin, for the purchaser's rights are fully protected by a suit of law. A judgment in his favor for the rent would be conclusive, and would afford him the same relief that he can obtain by a suit in equity. 

Pierce v. Lamson, 5 Allen 60

A mortgage compelled a mortgagor to surrender and deliver up the mortgage which was entrusted to the mortgagor for the purpose of having it recorded and which he wilfully and fraudulently omitted and neglected to do. At pages 61 and 62: "One of the most ancient heads of chancery jurisdiction is that which gives specific relief to persons having a right to the possession of deeds and other written instruments, by a decree of their surrender and delivery by those who wrongfully retain and withhold them. 

The remedy at law is inadequate in the present case, because it furnishes no means by which the plaintiff in one suit can recover his deed (mortgage) and at the same time restrain the defendant, in whom the apparent title to the premises described in the (mortgage) stands on the record, from conveying the premises to an innocent purchaser without actual notice of the previous (mortgage) to the plaintiff, and thus depriving the plaintiff of the estate to which he is entitled." 

Sears v. Carrier, 4 Allen 339

An administrator may compel delivery of promissory note which the defendant fraudulently induced the intestate to endorse and deliver to him for the reasons that (1) the administrator has a right to the specific securities belonging to the estate, (2) the notes if filed in court to obtain judgments cannot be recovered in replevin at law, (3) the notes themselves are important evidence in such suits that the administrator shall bring thereon, and (4) the administrator needs the notes to enable him to settle the estate without incurring the expense, delay and trouble of bringing suits.

EQUITABLE REPLEVIN 

Maxham v. Day, 16 Gray 213, at 219

Equitable replevin will lie to compel the delivery of jewelry be longing to the plaintiff and which the defendant is wearing on his person solely for the purpose of keeping it beyond an action of replevin at law, for no replevin can be made at law if it is neces sary for the officer in serving the process to commit an assault. 

Fish v. French, 15 Gray 520

Mortgagee required to cancel mortgage given without consideration. 

Travis v. Tyler, 7 Gray 146, at 147

The owner of real estate cannot be compelled to deliver up a deed which he gave to the plaintiff and later took back to get his wife's release of dower, unless the owner has secreted ΟΙ withheld the deed so that it cannot be replevined at law. 

Strickland v. Fitzgerald, 7 Cush. 530

Equitable replevin is a mere substitute for a writ of replevin of property which is so secreted that it cannot be reached by the ordinary replevin process.

Therefore, a bill in equity which seeks equitable replevin need only allege that the plaintiff is the owner of the property and that the defendant illegally and unjustly detains the property under such circumstances that the plaintiff cannot replevin the same at law as the defendant is secreting and withholding the same. 

Pool v. Lloyd, 5 Met. 525, at 528

Where a defense at law will give the plaintiff adequate protection on a promissory note he cannot maintain a bill for equitable replevin. 

Clapp v. Shepard, 2 Met. 127, at 131

In order to maintain a bill in equity for equitable replevin the plaintiff must show that he has a legal right to maintain an action of replevin at law, and that such an action at law could not be effectually prosecuted by reason of the concealment of the property by the defendants. So, an equitable assignee cannot in his own name maintain a bill for equitable replevin.

EQUITABLE REPLEVIN 

Clapp v. Shepard, 23 Pick. 228, at 231 "An equity court has jurisdiction of all suits to compel the redelivery of any goods or chattels whatsoever taken and detained from the owner thereof, and secreted or withheld so that the same cannot be replevied. Notes and other securities for debts, are goods and chattels within the true meaning of this rule. "It is sufficient for the plaintiff to aver, that the note in question has been concealed by the defendant, so that it cannot be replev-: ied, to entitle him to relief in equity. "It is no objection, that the plaintiff might bring an action of, trover for the tortious taking of the note, or that the defendant might be used on the note in assumpsit; for the intention of the rule (G. L. c. 214, s. I, cl. 3) is to provide a remedy in equity in cases where the party has a right to maintain an action of replevin, and is deprived of the benefit of that remedy by wrongful act of: the defendant. "The plaintiff is bound to set forth, as correctly as he can, his title notes or goods which are the subject matter of the equitable replevin." 

Mills v. Gore, 20 Pick. 28

In suit by a person named as grantee in a deed against the owner or grantor the plaintiff is required to prove delivery of that deed to him or to some third person so that the plaintiff has a right to its possession. When the plaintiff does not prove delivery of the deed the Court cannot order these papers to be restored for any purpose whatever.

The plaintiff's demand for the deed and the defendant's refusal to deliver it, conclusively prove that it is being detained and withheld within the meaning of the statute. The plaintiff is not bound to try an experiment which might prove ineffectual by suing by a writ of replevin and causing a new demand to be made by an officer.

EQUITABLE REPLEVIN 

Gibbens v. Peeler, 8 Pick. 254

When a defendant refuses to produce promissory notes, claim ing them as his own property, the notes are withheld, so that they cannot be found, within the meaning of the statute. 

They cannot be replevied, for unless exposed, an officer cannot take possession of them; he has not the power to extort them from the pocket of the defendant, nor can he, by arresting the person of the defendant, compel him to deliver them up. 

It is not necessary to lay a foundation for equitable replevin, that writ of replevin should first be taken out, and the officer should return on it that he cannot obtain possession of the goods or papers. It is enough that it shall appear to the court by the facts stated in the bill, admitted or proved, that the goods or papers sought to be delivered up were so controlled by the defendant that an attempt to replevin them would probably be fruitless.

So, when there is a demand for promissory notes before filing of the bill and a refusal to deliver or even to show them, the case is brought clearly within the provision of the statute because promissory notes are of a nature to be concealed in the pocket of the defendant so that they cannot be found, and be invisible so that they cannot be replevied.

After the bill is brought a formal offer by the defendant to produce the notes to any officer, so that they might be taken upon a writ of replevin does not defeat the bill for the equitable replevin. 

The right of action exists at the time of the filing of the original bill, it is a vested right which cannot be defeated by a subsequent act of the defendant.

EQUITY, PLEADING, PRACTICE AND PROCEDURE C. DISCLAIMER 

A disclaimer is a renunciation of title, right of possession and all claim to any of the subject matter involved in the suit. 

Oakham v. Hall, 112 Mass. 535, at 539

Whether a disclaimer is a proper pleading in this Commonwealth is open to doubt because disclaimer is excluded from Gen. Laws, c. 214, s. 13, which provides that: tebe “A defence to a suit in equity shall be made by demurrer, plea or answer.”

However, a disclaimer is really in the nature of an answer. 

1. Effect of 

A disclaimer operates like a release and creates an estoppel against the defendant's afterward claiming the property, possession or interest in the subject matter set forth in the bill. 

As was said in Oakham v. Hall, 112 Mass. 535, at 539 and 540: "If [the disclaimer is] not falsified, it defeats the action. But the demandant is thereupon entitled to the possession of the land, and the party pleading the disclaimer is forever estopped by the judgment from denying his right of possession. "If, however, the plea is falsified, the tenant is nevertheless bound by his disclaimer, and the demandant may have judgment against him. "The judgment upon a disclaimer, whether for or against the demandant, is conclusive in his favor upon title, as between the parties. "So at common law, a disclaimer in a writ of entry operates to extinguish whatever estate, adverse to the demandant, the tenant may have had in fact at the time of pleading the disclaimer. 66 ....When two persons are joined in a writ of entry, a disclaimer by one is said to enure 'as a release, to pass all his estate to his co-tenant”.” 

2. When Improper a. 

When the defendant formerly asserted some right, title or interest in any of the matters referred to in the bill even though he now claims no present interest therein. b. When the bill alleges that the defendant is pretending to have or asserting some interest in any of the matters alleged in the bill. $1

C. When the defendant is charged with liability arising. from his personal fraud or misconduct. 8. 

When Proper

If a disclaimer is proper pleading in this Commonwealth, there is only one instance when it may be used with safety, namely, when the defendant has no interest in any of the subject matters alleged in the bill, has never previously claimed any interest and no charge of personal fraud or misconduct is made against him in the bill. 

4. Offer of Decree or Judgment

Under General Laws, c. 231, s. 74, where damages are sought to be recovered, a defendant may make an offer of judgment or an offer for a decree which will effect a judgment.

D.

DEMURRER 1. Definitions, Function and Essentials a. Definitions

A demurrer in equity is an attack upon the legal sufficiency of the plaintiff's bill of complaint. 

A demurrer is an objection that the bill, against which it is directed, is insufficient in law to support the suit and that the demurrant [defendant] should not therefore be required to further plead.

A demurrer is a claim by a defendant that the plaintiff's case, taken just as he states it in his bill of complaint, gives him no right to any relief in equity. 

A demurrer in equity is an assertion by the defendant that because of some defect of form or of substance, the plaintiff is not entitled to any relief upon the case stated in his bill of complaint.

A demurrer in equity is an allegation of the defendant, which, admitting the truth of the matters of fact properly alleged in the bill of complaint, insists that those facts, as matter of law, are insufficient for the plaintiff to oblige the defendant to answer and to proceed further in the suit. The import of the demurrer is that the defendant will not proceed, but will wait the judgment of the court whether he is bound to do so.

A demurrer is an allegation that the defendant will go no further because the plaintiff in his bill of complaint has not shown sufficient matter against him. 

The meaning of "demurrer" is that, admitting the allegations of the bill to be true, they are not sufficient to maintain the suit. b. Function

The function of a demurrer in equity is to sweep away a defective bill of complaint.

Also its function is to specifically point out the defects in the plaintiff's bill of complaint so as to afford the plaintiff the opportunity of curing those defects by amendment, C. General Statement 

A demurrer is a part of the proceeding in equity by which the suit is put at issue and the order sustaining it eliminates from the bill the matter to which the demurrer is directed.

Technically, the demurrer should not be classed among pleas in equity, because the demurrer neither affirms nor denies any matter of fact, and is not, therefore, strictly a plea of any class, but rather an excuse for not pleading. The demurrer merely advances a legal proposition and causes the suit to rest or pause. It forms an issue of law, admitting the facts, so far as well pleaded in the bill, for the purposes of taking the preliminary opinion of the court, whether there is anything in the bill of complaint which calls upon the defendant to answer or plead.

The demurrer lies only for defects which appear upon the face of the bill of complaint and extraneous or collateral facts cannot be considered in its determination, even though such facts are stated in the demurrer. 

It is not proper to set out facts in the demurrer, but the demurrer must stand or fall by the facts properly alleged in the bill.

The determination of a demurrer is based upon the sufficiency of the allegations of the bill taken as true and not upon any prayer or prayers for relief. 

Although in equity pleading the demurrer admits the facts well pleaded in the bill of complaint for the purpose of determining their legal efficiency, yet, as a rule of evidence, the demurrer does not admit any fact or anything else. The hearing of the merits of the suit has no concern with the demurrer. 

The demurrer can raise only questions of law as to the suf ficiency of the facts properly alleged in the bill. 

A question of fact is not to be determined by demurrer, but should be raised by answer or plea and settled by proper proof. 

New York Co. v. New Jersey Co., 137 U. S. 445

New Jersey v. New York, 6 Peters (U. S.) 323 

A demurrer neither asserts nor denies any matters of fact, it merely, in effect, advances a legal proposition, namely, that the bill of complaint is insufficient to enable the plaintiff to maintain the suit in equity.

The demurrer admits the truth of the properly pleaded allegations in the bill but denies the plaintiff's right to relief in whole or in part.

A demurrer in effect is an allegation that even if the facts as stated in the plaintiff's bill of complaint are taken to be

true, yet their legal consequences are not such as to put the defendant to the necessity of answering those facts or proceeding further in the suit. 

The causes for which demurrers may be filed have been grouped: 

(I) The frame of the bill. 

(II) The matter contained in the bill. And 

(III) The case made out by the bill. 

Other classifications or causes for demurrer have been stated to be: (A) Want of jurisdiction of the court. (B) Want of interest or right of the plaintiff. (C) Nonjoinder of parties. 

(D) Misjoinder of parties. 

(E) Misjoinder of causes of action. And (F) Absence of obligation of the defendant to the plaintiff. 

The demurrer attacks the bill in two ways. Either as to its form or substance. 

As to Form.

Unless the defect in the bill as to form is of a serious nature it is not advisable to take advantage of such defect. Ordinarily, the standing of the defendant will be prejudiced in the eyes of the court because of the apparent unwillingness of the defendant to fairly meet the plaintiff's case on its merits. 

As to Substance.

When the substance of the bill is defective the defendant should demur, and if the defect goes to an essential of the plaintiff's case, the time and expense of a hearing on the merits may be saved.

All demurrers, whether as to form or substance, must distinctly specify the grounds of the defect or insufficiency of the bill of complaint.

There are certain matters which must be raised by demurrer or they are deemed to be waived. Particularly, is the defence of the plaintiff's having an adequate remedy at law. 

Pothier v. Doucette, 1931 A. S. 1607 Nelson v. Belmont, 1931 A. S. 173 

Baskes v. Cushing, 270 Mass. 230

Radway v. Selectmen of Dennis, 266 Mass. 329

Reynolds v. Grow, 265 Mass. 578 

Wickwire Spencer Steel Corp. v. United Springs Co., 247 Mass. 565, at 569 

Creely v. Bay State Brick Co., 103 Mass. 514 

Dearth v. Hide & Leather Bank, 100 Mass. 540 

Lyons Milling Co. v. Goffe, 46 F. (2d) 241, at 245

If the adequacy of the law remedy is not seasonably raised by demurrer there is no reason why a court of equity cannot determine the case upon law principles. 

Donohue v. White, 247 Mass. 479 

Stratton v. Hernon, 154 Mass. 310, at 313

The court's action in overruling a demurrer is open on later appeal from the final decree, even though no interlocutory appeal was taken at the time. 

Harrell v. Sonnabend, 191 Mass. 310 d. Kinds

Demurrers are either general or special. 

(I) General 

A general demurrer is one which merely states in broad terms that the bill presents no case for equitable relief, without assigning any other ground. 

Billings v. Mann, 156 Mass. 203

Matters raised by the general demurrer may be further classified: (A) An attack upon the propriety of the subject matter for a relief in equity, or if discovery is sought, to the discovery only or to both. (B) To the jurisdiction; to the person of the plaintiff; or to the matter of the bill. 

(II) Special 

A special demurrer is one which assigns specific objections to the bill, the special causes of demurrer. 

All merely formal objections must be taken by special demurrer; specific objections will not be considered or noticed under a general demurrer. 

Billings v. Mann, 156 Mass. 203 e. Use Confined to Bills

The use of a demurrer in equity is confined to defending against bills, that is, in equity a demurrer lies only to the bill of complaint and never to any other pleading. So, in equity, there is no such thing as a demurrer to a disclaimer; or to a plea or to another demurrer or to an answer or to a replication.

(Additional Material, Page 7) D. DEMURRER 1. Definitions, Functions and Essentials f. When Demurrer Required I. General Statement (Continued) 

be The long established rule in equity is to forbid recourse to the extraordinary remedies of equity where the right asserted fully protected by law. 

Matthews v. Rodgers, 284 U. S. 521, at 525 

Deweese v. Reinhard, 165 U. S. 386, at 389 may 

N. Y. Guaranty Co. v. Memphis Water Co., 107 U. S. 205, at 214 The want of equity jurisdiction, if obvious, may and should be objected to by the court of its own motion. 

Matthews v. Rodgers, 284 U. S. 521, at 524 

Twist v. Prairie Oil Co., 274 U. S. 684, at 690

In other cases, this jurisdictional requirement may be treated as waived if the objection is not presented by the defendant in limine [at the beginning].

Duignan v. United States, 274 U. S. 195, at 199

A demurrer improperly filed to a pleading other than to a bill of complaint may upon hearing be treated as if the suit had been set down for hearing on the bill and the pleading to which the demurrer is addressed. 

Banks v. Manchester, 128 U. S. 244 (Demurrer to answer.) (I) Waiver of Irregularity

If demurrer to a disclaimer, plea, answer or replication is argued on its merits the irregularity is waived and the court may deal with the demurrer as if it is a proper mode of attacking the particular pleading. 

Barry v. Abbott, 100 Mass. 396 

1. When Demurrer Required (I) General Statement 

There are certain objections to a bill of complaint which can be taken only by demurrer, among these are attacks upon: (A) Form of the bill. (B) Defects curable by amendment. (C) Plaintiff's adequate remedy at law. (D) Multifariousness. 

(E) Misjoinder of parties. 

For grounds of demurrer generally see page 14 et seq.

(II) Effect of Failure to Demur 

Matters of form and technicalities are waived unless seasonable objection is made.

Cobb v. Rice, 130 Mass. 231 

Nelson v. Ferdinand, 111 Mass. 300 

Pingree v. Coffin, 12 Gray 288 

Pinch v. Anthony, 10 Allen 470

Objections based upon the adequacy of the law remedy and multifariousness are waived by failing to demur. 

Ryan v. Annelin, 228 Mass. 591 

Crocker v. Dillon, 133 Mass. 91, at 92 

(III) Defects Cured by Subsequent Pleadings, Proof or Proceedings 

Ryan v. Annelin, 228 Mass. 591 

Crocker v. Dillon, 133 Mass. 91, at 92 

Cobb v. Rice, 130 Mass. 231 

Nelson v. Ferdinand, 111 Mass. 300 

Pinch v. Anthony, 10 Allen 470 

Pingree v. Coffin, 12 Gray 288 

2. Effect of 

Unlike a demurrer at law the demurrer in equity does not submit the suit to final determination upon the pleadings. 

However, the filing of a demurrer has certain effects. 

It amounts to a general appearance of the demurrant; 

Thames & Mersey Ins. Co. v. United States, 237 U. S. 

19, at 24 and 25 except when the demurrer raises the question of jurisdiction over either the party or the subject matter. 

Mass. Grange v. Benton, 272 Mass. 525 

Gunter v. Arlington Mills, 271 Mass. 314 

Black v. Alercrombie, 267 Mass. 316 

Rothstein v. Commissioner, 258 Mass. 196 

Pond v. Simpson, 251 Mass. 25

General I. Co. v. New York etc. Co., 271 U. S. 228 Robertson v. Railroad Labor Board, 268 U. S. 619 

3. Right to Demur a. Who May Demur

The right to demur to a bill is confined to such defendants as are affected by the defects in the bill. b. When There are Several Defendants

A demurrer by one defendant does not enure to the benefit or prejudice of the other defendants. In other words, no defendant is affected by a demurrer unless he is a party to the same.

4. Time to Demur

Supreme Judicial Court Equity Rule No. 7 (1926) provides in part: "The day of appearance shall be the return day of the writ or subpoena, when personal service shall be made on the defendant, or he shall have had personal notice of the suit; or the return day of any order issued under the third or fourth rule, when no personal service shall be made. And, if the defendant does not appear and file his answer, plea, or demurrer within twenty-one days after the day of appearance, the plaintiff may enter an order to take his bill for confessed. .... 99 or 

Superior Court Rule No. 25 (1932) provides in part: "A defendant.... within twenty-one days, such other period as may be prescribed by statute, or .by the terms of the subpoena, after the return day of the subpoena, file his demurrer, plea or answer." ....

However, the court may permit a defendant to file a demurrer even after the time set forth in the rules of court or after an answer to the merits has been filed. 

Keown v. Keown, 231 Mass. 404 a. Demurrer May Come Too Late

The objection that the plaintiff has a plain and complete remedy at law, or that the bill is multifarious, should be made without delay at the earliest opportunity or it may come too late. 

Perry v. Pye, 215 Mass. 403, at 403 

Cobb v. Fogg, 166 Mass. 466 

Dearth v. Hyde & Leather Bank, 100 Mass. 540 

5. Form of Demurrer a. General Statement 

In point of form no precise words are necessary to constitute a demurrer.

A pleading which is in substance a demurrer, though very informal, will be considered as such, regardless of its name. 

So, the character of the pleading "is commonly to be determined by the nature of its averments and not by the name attached to it."

Rothstein v. Commissioner, 258 Mass. 196 (Motion to dismiss treated as demurrer to jurisdiction.) 

Corey v. Tuttle, 249 Mass. 135 (Motion to compel election between suits, treated as plea in abatement.) 

White v. E. T. Slattery Co., 236 Mass. 28, at 31 

Comm. v. Wakelin, 230 Mass. 567, at 571 

Merriam v. Currier, 191 Mass. 133, at 141 

By Gen. Laws, c. 214, s. 13 the "demurrer .... need not contain a protestation or concluding prayer" and by Statute of 1921, c. 431 the "demurrer need not be accompanied by a certificate that it is not intended for delay."

The demurrer may be to the whole bill or parts thereof. 

The proper practice is to demur separately to the various portions of the bill.

A demurrer may be sustained which merely attacks the form of the bill. 

Christiansen v. Dixon, 271 Mass. 475

So, when a bill, which properly can contain the material facts and arguments relied on by the plaintiff in a brief, concise and summary manner, sets out such discursive, argumentative and at irrelevant length the grounds for relief and details of facts and evidence, the bill is obnoxious to the statute (G. L. c. 214, s. 12) and in contravention to the rule of equity pleading thereby established. 

Christiansen v. Dixon, 271 Mass. 475 

Taylor v. Neal, 260 Mass. 427, at 439 b. Grounds Must be Specific

A defendant may include in his demurrer as many grounds as he wishes but he must separately set out each ground. 

Specific defects must be distinctly pointed out in a demurrer, if it is intended to claim them, so as to give the plaintiff an opportunity to amend before the case is taken to the Supreme 

Judicial Court. 

Billings v. Mann, 156 Mass. 203, at 205 

Windram v. French, 151 Mass. 547, at 552

A demurrer that goes to the whole ground of the plaintiff's case, is sufficient if it avers the cause of the demurrer in the general words of the statute, but when reliance is placed upon omissions in the form or statement of the bill, such omissions must be definitely pointed out. 10

Parker v. Simpson, 180 Mass. 334, at 340 

Conant v. Warren, 6 Gray 562 

Wright v. Dame, 1 Met. 237, at 241

The requirement that the demurrer should specify each ground assigned as a defect in the bill is for the purpose of informing the plaintiff of the particular points raised against the case stated by the bill. 

The test of the sufficiency of the specifications of the grounds of demurrer is whether the court is enabled to clearly ascertain and determine the objections raised. 

C. General Demurrers 

A general demurrer is one directed to the defects in substance of the bill and need assign only the ground that the bili is without equity. 

Frisbee v. Prussian Nat. Ins. Co., 223 Mass. 159 

Washington v. Eames, 6 Allen 417

So, a general demurrer reaches defects in the substance of the bill only and not in its form. 

The function of the general demurrer is to make the bill of complaint more definite and certain, but it also serves to determine the question whether any cause of action is stated, or whether the plaintiff is entitled to any relief. 

Parker v. Simpson, 180 Mass. 334, at 340

Defects in the form of the bill will not be considered under a general demurrer for want of equity. Such objections must be specifically pointed out. 

Billings v. Mann, 156 Mass. 203

A general demurrer is "a denial in form and substance, of the right of [the plaintiff] to have his case considered in the court of equity, [and also is] an admission that all the allegations of [the bill], which [are] properly pleaded, [are] true." 

Griffing v. Gibb, 2 Black, (U. S.) 519, at 523

The general demurrer only admits facts that are well pleaded, and such admission extends not only to what is expressly alleged in the bill, but also to whatever can by fair and reasonable intent be implied from the express allegations thereof. 

(I) When Proper 

A general demurrer is proper only when the bill in its entirety show a want of equity. That is, states no case entitling the plaintiff to any equitable relief. 11

A general demurrer must be overruled if one clause in the bill is not demurrable because its substance is proper for equitable relief. 

Wellington v. Rugg, 243 Mass. 30

Also, a general demurrer to the whole bill cannot be properly sustained if any part of the bill shows that the plaintiff is entitled to equitable relief. 

Parker v. Simpson, 180 Mass. 334, at 340

So, a general demurrer to the whole of a bill, which contains some matters relievable and others not, is bad, unless the bill is multifarious. 

Robinson v. Guild, 12 Met. 323 

Dimmock v. Bixby, 20 Pick. 368 

d. Special Demurrers 

A special demurrer sets forth specifically on the record before the court the objections intended to be raised to the plaintiff's bill of complaint. It is preferable practice to precede a special demurrer by a general demurrer. 

e. Demurrers ORE TENUS 

Demurrer ore tenus is the assignment at the time of the hearing of grounds in addition to those stated in the written. demurrer.

That is, demurring ore tenus is orally assigning at the time of the hearing, new causes for demurrer besides those stated in the written demurrer.

Grounds not specified in the written demurrer may be relied on ore tenus, but at the risk of costs in favor of the plaintiff, even though the demurrer ore tenus is sustained. 

Derby v. Derby, 248 Mass. 310 

Wright v. Dame, 1 Met. 237

Such new causes for demurrer may prevail even though the grounds assigned in the written demurrer are overruled. But there are three essential conditions precedent to the right to demur ore tenus: (I) There must have been filed a written demurrer, which is on record. (II) The scope of the demurrer ore tenus must be coincident with the written demurrer on record. 

That is, the demurrer ore tenus must be co-extensive with the written demurrer and must apply to the same parts of the bill. 12

If the original demurrer attacks the bill as a whole, the demurrer ore tenus must do likewise and if the written demurrer was confined to certain portions of the bill, the demurrer ore tenus must be equally restricted. (III) The subject matters of the demurrer ore tenus must not have been previously adjudicated, such as where a plea has been filed and disallowed. 

But see: Crease Babcock, 2 Met. 525, at 531. 

f. Partial Demurrers 

A demurrer may be made to part of the bill. 

If such demurrer is overruled the same defence may be again made in the answer, provided there are some new facts to support it. 

Turner Falls v. Miller's Falls, 189 Mass. 263

A waiver or withdrawal of a partial demurrer is not a waiver of the defence and so the same matter may be set up in the answer. 

Turner Falls v. Miller's Falls, 189 Mass. 263 (Laches.) g. 

Combining Demurrer with Answer

Under Supreme Judicial Court Rule No. 9, (1926) a de murrer may be combined with an answer. 

Richards v. Richards, 270 Mass. 113

Eastman Marble Co. v. Vt. Marble Co., 236 Mass. 138 

Finneran v. Graham, 198 Mass. 385, at 387 

Hobson v. Satterlee, 163 Mass. 402 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262, at 268 

O'Hare v. Downing, 130 Mass. 16, at 18 and 20 

O'Loughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass. 600 

Young v. Gilles, 113 Mass. 34 

Lee v. Kane, 6 Gray 495

Livingston v. Story, 11 Pet. (U. S.) 351 

But under Superior Court Rule No. 28 (1932) the demurrer must be combined, or filed simultaneously, with the answer. 

When a demurrer is combined in the answer it has the same standing as if it were filed separately, as to preliminary hearing and disposition. 

Parks v. Smith, 155 Mass. 26, at 30 

O'Hare v. Downing, 130 Mass. 16 

Fisher v. Frapie, 125 Mass. 472 13

h. Motion Instead of Demurrer 

There is no such thing as a motion to dismiss known to equity practice in this Commonwealth. i. Waiver of Informality 

The plaintiff waives all informality of the demurrer by joining issue and setting the same down for hearing. 6. 

Colt v. Leonard, 118 Mass. 380

Grounds of Deniurrer a. General Statement 

The grounds of demurrer must be as to matters which appear on the face of the bill without the introduction of testimony or evidence.

The grounds or causes for demurrer may relate to: 

(I) The jurisdiction of the court. 

(II) The character or number of parties. Or, (III) The form or substance of the bill. 

The grounds chiefly alleged by demurrer are: (A) The plaintiff's bill does not state a case for equit able relief. (B) Plaintiff's lack of interest in the subject matter of the bill. (C) Lack of necessary parties. 

(E) Misjoinder of parties (D) Multifariousness of the bill. 

(F) Statute of Frauds. 

(G) Statute of Limitations. 

(H) Laches.

There are also grounds of demurrer directed to defects in form which are too numerous to set forth here. b. 

Matters of Substance (I) General Statement 

As distinguished from defects in form, the main grounds of demurrer attacking the substance of the bill are that: (A) There is no jurisdiction in equity because the plaintiff has a plain, adequate and complete remedy at law. (B) The plaintiff has no title or interest in the subject matter of the suit. (C) From the bill it appears that there is no responsi sibility on the part of the defendant. 14

(D) Statute of Frauds. 

(E) Statute of Limitations. 

(F) Laches. 

Stuart v. Joyce, 201 Mass. 301

Snow v. Boston Blankbook Co., 153 Mass. 456 Maxwell v. Kennedy, 8 How. (U. S.) 210 

To a bill for discovery only, the main grounds of demurrer are that: (1) The plaintiff has a complete means at law for discovery by filing interrogatories which could be filed in the original action at law. () The plaintiff has no title or interest in the subject matter of any suit or action. (3) No other suit or action is pending or is about to be brought to which the discovery is material. (4) The discovery sought relates to matters which are not material or competent in evidence in the main suit or action. (5) The discovery sought relates to privileged matters, such as confidential communications, incriminating evidence or seeking to expose the defendant to a penalty or forfeiture. (6) The discovery sought relates entirely to the defendant's title or case. (7) The defendant is a mere witness and not a party to the original suit or action. 

(II) Want of Jurisdiction 

If the allegations of the bill fail to show jurisdiction, either as to the subject matter or parties, the proper manner of objecting to the want of jurisdiction, is by demurrer. 

May v. Parker, 12 Pick. 34

The ground of demurrer may be that the court in which the suit is brought has no jurisdiction over the parties, subject matter, or particular case.

So, a demurrer is the proper mode to raise the want of jurisdiction, because the relief desired will require the performance of acts outside this Commonwealth and therefore complete justice cannot be administered. 

Guntner v. Arlington Mills, 271 Mass. 314 (Bill to prevent taking water in lake in New Hamp- 15

shire creating a nuisance and fire hazard, and restoring former condition of lake.) 

Kansas etc. Co. v. Topeka etc. R. R., 135 Mass. 34

Ordinarily, such want of jurisdiction is waived unless it is seasonably raised by demurrer.

Reilly v. Selectmen, 266 Mass. 503 Weiscopf v. Commissioner, 258 Mass. 199 

Rothstein v. Commissioner, 258 Mass. 196

Eastman Marble Co. v. Vt. Marble Co., 236 Mass. 138, at 148 Demurrer is not the only manner by which the question of jurisdiction may be raised.

The court itself may take notice of it and dismiss the bill whenever the objection appears on the face of the pleading or becomes apparent during the hearing. 

Where the facts stated in the bill show jurisdiction and those facts are denied, then objection cannot be made by demurrer and should be made by plea. 

(III) Want of Equity 

A bill is demurrable on this ground whenever the plaintiff has a plain, complete and adequate remedy at law. 

Skolnick v. Greenburg, 230 Mass. 359 

Also the bill is demurrable on this ground, not only if it shows that the plaintiff has such a full remedy at law, but also if the bill fails to show that he is without such remedy. 

Jones v. Newhall, 115 Mass. 244

Where the subject matter of the bill is not cognizable by any court of justice, as where the matter is of a political nature and is therefore a matter for negotiation or treaty by the executive department of the government, a demurrer will lie. 

Foster v. Neilson, 2 Pet. (U. S.) 253 

But a bill is not demurrable on this ground where an accounting as to a trust fund of a voluntary association is sought. 

Donovan v. Danielson, 244 Mass. 432 

(IV) Want of Title, Interest or Liability (A) General Statement 

It is not indispensable that all the parties to the bill should have an interest in all the matters complained of; it is enough if each party is connected with one another. 

Lovejoy v. Bailey, 241 Mass. 134, at 151 16

Ginn v. Almy, 212 Mass. 486, at 493 

Goram v. Davis, 209 Mass. 229, at 248 and cases collected 

But see Mesisco v. Giuliano, 190 Mass. 352

Davis v. Peabody, 170 Mass. 397 

Sylvester v. Boyd, 166 Mass. 445 

Ricker v. Brooks, 155 Mass. 400, at 403 

Keith v. Keith, 143 Mass. 262 

(B) Of Plaintiff 

It is necessary that each plaintiff have an interest in the subject matter of the suit. 

Strachan v. Beacon Oil Co., 251 Mass 479 

(C) Of Defendant 

Each defendant must be so related to the whole or a material part of the subject matter of the suit as to make his presence more than a mere matter of form. 

Warecki v. United States Fidelity Co., 270 Mass. 233 

Zimmerman v. Finkelstein, 230 Mass. 17 (V) 

Triviality of Subject Matter 

When it appears from the face of the bill that the matter to which the bill relates is insignificant or of small or trifling nature the court may refuse to take jurisdiction and dismiss the suit. The matter may properly be raised by demurrer. 

(VI) Statute of Frauds 

When it sufficiently appears by the bill that the alleged agreement between the parties was not in writing as required by the Statute of Frauds, such defence may be made by demurrer. 

Linsky v. Exchange Trust Co., 260 Mass. 15, at 18 

Southwick v. Spevak, 252 Mass. 354 

Miller v. Burt, 196 Mass. 395 

Ohrend v. Odiorne, 118 Mass. 261, at 269 

(A) Part Performance 

When it appears from the face of the bill that although the original agreement was within the Statute of Frauds, the plaintiff has performed the agreement in such part and to such an extent that the defendant cannot set up the Statute of Frauds, then such a defence cannot be asserted by demurrer. 17

In Davis v. Downer, 210 Mass.

573, the court said at page 576: "Where a person has been induced to make expenditures upon land, to construct improvements thereon or to change his situation materially in reliance upon the performance of the oral agreement and in expectation of the rights to be acquired thereby, refusal to carry out the agreement is not merely deprivation of the rights it was intended to confer, which alone is within the statute of frauds, but is in addition 'an infliction of an unjust and unconscientious injury and loss.' In such case, the party is held, by force of his acts or silent acquiescence, which have misled the other to his harm, to be estopped from setting up the statute of frauds." 

Curran v. Magee, 244 Mass. 1, at 5 and cases collected 

Mason v. Albert, 243 Mass. 433, at 437 

Tracy v. Blinn, 236 Mass. 585, at 587 and 588 

Peoples Express, Inc. v. Quinn, 235 Mass. 156, at 159 

Traveler Shoe Co. v. Koch, 216 Mass. 310 

Williams v. Carty, 205 Mass. 396 

Harrell v. Sonnabend, 191 Mass. 310 

Gross v. Milligan, 176 Mass. 566 

Low v. Low, 173 Mass. 580, at 582 

Potter v. Jacobs, 111 Mass. 32 

Glass v. Hulbert, 102 Mass. 24, at 35 

(VII) Statute of Limitations 

Advantage can be taken of the statute of limitations by demurrer if the same appears from the face of the bill. 

Coffey v. Rady, 267 Mass. 301 by Monahan v. Harvard Brewing Co., 241 Mass. 286 

Fogg v. Price, 145 Mass. 513, at 516 

Sawyer v. Boston, 144 Mass. 470, at 472

The time limited by the statute of limitations does not begin to run against a breach of trust, when there is a fiduciary duty to disclose the facts on which the cause of action rests, until the facts have, or ought to have, been discovered. 

Old Dom. Copper Co. v. Bigelow, 203 Mass. 159, at 201 

Atlantic Nat. Bank v. Harris, 118 Mass. 147 

(VIII) Laches 

Laches is not, like limitation, a mere matter of time, but rather a question of the inequity of granting relief to the plaintiff. 

Galliher v. Cadwell, 145 U. S. 368 18

The lapse of time which might induce the application of the doctrine of laches is not a determined period, and depends upon the circumstances of the particular case. One principle pervades all cases involving the defense of laches, and that is not only must there be a seemingly necessary delay on the part of the plaintiff in bringing or prosecuting his suit, but that, by reason of some change in the condition or relations of the property or parties occurring during the period of delay, it would be inequitable to permit the claim of the plaintiff to be enforced. 

Halstead v. Grinnan, 152 U. S. 412

Galliher v. Cadwell, 145 U. S. 368 

Laches is negligence or omission reasonably to assert a right. 

It exists when the omission to assert the right has continued for an unreasonable and unexplained lapse of time, and under circumstances where the delay has been prejudicial to an adverse party, and when it would be inequitable to enforce the right.

Laches may be a cause for demurrer but only if they are shown by the face of the bill. 

Von Arnim v. Am. Tube Works, 188 Mass. 515, at 518 

Sawyer v. Cook, 188 Mass. 163, at 168 

Doane v. Preston, 183 Mass. 569

It has been thought that a demurrer could not be filed as to laches even though they appear from the face of the bill, on the ground that laches are a conclusion of fact. 

Fogg v. Price, 145 Mass. 513, at 516

But the Massachusetts decisions hold that a demurrer will lie in clear cases. 

Fogg v. Price, 145 Mass. 513, at 516 

Williams v. Hart, 116 Mass. 513 

Plymouth v. Russell Mills, 7 Allen 438

So, when the bill shows upon its face that the plaintiff, by reason of lapse of time and of his own laches, is not entitled to relief, the objection may be taken by demurrer. 

Tetreault v. Fournier, 187 Mass. 58 

Snow v. Boston Blank Book Co., 153 Mass. 456, at 458 

Codman v. Rogers, 10 Pick. 111, at 119 

Hammond v. Hopkins, 143 U. S. 224 

Sullivan v. Portland etc. R. R., 94 U. S. 806, at 812

In Tetrault v. Fournier, 187 Mass. 58, it was alleged that the delay (ten years) of the plaintiff in bringing the suit was 19

due to the negligence and misconduct "of the plaintiff's attorneys." It was held that the allegation was too general a one to put the defendant to the burden of a trial. 

See: Rolikatis v. Lovett, 213 Mass. 545, at 548

Equity aids the diligent and refuses relief to those who slumber upon their rights.

Von Arnim v. Am. Tube Works, 188 Mass. 515, at 518 

Sawyer v. Cook, 188 Mass. 163, at 168

Independently of any statute of limitations, courts of equity uniformly decline to assist a person who has slept upon his rights, and shows no excuse for his laches in asserting them. 

A court in equity said Lord Camden has always refused its aid to state demands, where the party slept upon his rights, and acquiesced for a great length of time. Nothing can call forth this court into activity, but conscience, good faith and reasonable diligence; when these are wanting, the court is passive, and does nothing. Laches and neglect are also discountenanced, and therefore, from the beginning of this jurisdiction there was always a limitation to suits in this court. 

Sawyer v. Cook, 188 Mass. 168 

Tetreault v. Fournier, 187 Mass. 58 

Snow v. Boston Blank Book Co., 153 Mass. 456, at 458 

Codman v. Hopkins, 10 Pick. 111, at 119 

Hammond v. Hopkins, 143 U. S. 224

Mere delay, provided it does not extend beyond the period of the statute of limitations, does not of itself amount to laches. 

Calkins v. Wire, 267 Mass. 52 

Stewart v. Finkelstein, 206 Mass. 28, at 36 

Moore v. Dick, 207, at 212

Laches is not mere delay, but delay that works disadvantage to another. 

Calkins v. Wire, 267 Mass. 52 (Stockholder guilty of laches, 5 years after illegal agreement and 32 years after director's vote.) 

Mascari v. Mascari, 255 Mass. 92, at 98 

Cooke v. Barrett, 155 Mass. 413, at 414 

Boston Roll. Mills v. Cambridge, 117 Mass. 396, at 401

The defence of long and unexplainable delay, when accompanied by a full knowledge of the facts, or of information which should put a party upon his inquiry, if shown by the bill, may be raised by demurrer. 

Von Arnim v. Am. Tube Works, 188 Mass. 515, at 518 

Sawyer v. Cook, 188 Mass. 163, at 168 20

But where the plaintiff relied upon the defendant who has deliberately kept the plaintiff in ignorance of the true state of affairs, no unreasonable delay or want of diligence exists on the plaintiff's part.

Von Arnim v. Am. Tube Works, 188 Mass. 515, at 519 

Doane v. Preston, 183 Mass. 559 

Dumphy v. Traveller, 146 Mass. 495 

Loring v. Palmer, 118 U. S. 321, at 324

Laches has little, if any, application where plaintiff seeks to protect vested legal right as distinguished from establishment of executive right.

(IX) Multifariousness 

Multifariousness is the misjoinder of legally distinct and equitably inconsistent demands. 

Saltman v. Nesson, 201 Mass. 534, at 539 

Bliss v. Parks, 175 Mass. 539, at 543

The matters must not only be separate, but each of itself must be of such a character as to entitle the plaintiff to relief. 

Saltman v. Nesson, 201 Mass. 534, at 539

Multifariousness in the bill may be attacked by demurrer. 

Crawford v. Nies, 220 Mass. 61, at 63 

Perry v. Pye, 215 Mass. 403, at 409 

Cobb v. Fogg, 166 Mass. 466, at 475 and 476

As to multifariousness, it was said in Shields v. Thomas, 18 How. (U. S.) 253, at 259: "There is, perhaps, no rule established for the conducting of equity pleadings, with reference to which (whilst as a rule it is universally admitted) there has existed less of certainty and uniformity in application, than has attended this relating to multifariousness. "This effect, flowing perhaps inevitably, from the va riety of modes and degrees of right and interest entering in to the transaction of life, seems to have led to a conclusion rendering the rule almost as much an exception as a rule, and that conclusion is, that each case must be determined by its peculiar features. 22

"Thus Daniell, in his work on Chancery Practice, vol. 

1, p. 384, quoting from Lord Cottenham, says: 'It is impossible, upon the authorities, to lay down any rule or abstract proposition, as to what constitutes multifariousness, which can be made universally applicable. The cases upon which the subject are extremely various, and the court, in deciding upon them, seems to have considered what was convenient in particular cases, rather than to have attempted to lay down an absolute rule.' "Continuing his opinion, the learned justice in the above case said: 'Justice Story, in his compilation upon equity pleading, defines multifariousness in a bill to mean distinct and independent matters, and thereby confounding them.' "Justice Story closes his review of the authorities upon this defect in the bill with the following remark: "The conclusion to which a close survey of the authorities will conduct us, seems to be, that there is not any positive inflexible rule as to what, in the sense of a court of equity, constitutes multifariousness, which is fatal to a suit on demurrer'." 

Harrison v. Perea, 168 U. S. 311, at 319

There is no inflexible rule by which to determine whether a bill is multifarious. Whether objection shall be sustained on this ground must be decided largely by the circumstances of each case. 

Spear v. H. V. Greene Co., 246 Mass. 259, at 269 

Cosmopolitan Tr. Co. v. Mitchell, 242 Mass. 95 at 123 

Coram v. Davis, 209 Mass. 229, at 249 and 250 

Bliss v. Parks, 175 Mass. 539, at 543 

Robinson v. Guild, 12 Met. 323, at 328

The scope of a bill to set aside a fraudulent conveyance does not become multifarious merely because it follows all the ramification of the vicious project, and thereby includes divers persons of varying degrees of culpability against whom the issues may not be identical and towards whom different kinds or degrees of relief may be necessary. If the scheme is comprehensive the pleadings must be likewise extensive. The unity of the plan embraces all the parts. 

Hutchins v. Nickerson, 212 Mass. 122 

Swift Co. v. U. S., 196 U. S. 375, at 396 

Harrison v. Perea, 168 U. S. 311

U. S. v. Am. Bell Tel. Co., 128 U. S. 315 Walker v. Powers, 104 U. S. 

23

A demurrer for this cause will hold only where the plaintiff claims several matters of a different nature, and not where one general right is claimed by the plaintiff, although the defendants may have separate and distinct rights. 

Dimmock v. Bixby, 20 Pick. 368, at 377

A bill which prays for relief and directions as to conflicting claims of creditors, and as to the order in which they are to be paid ought not to be joined for two branches of the bill are founded on distinct rights. 

Dimmock v. Bixby, 20 Pick. 368, at 377

But where the part of the bill as to directions to an executor or trustee in the execution of his trust, remains alone because the debtors have been eliminated from the bill, either by dismissal or inability to obtain service, because the debtor or debtors are not within the jurisdiction of the court, a bill may be retained and the demurrer overruled because the multifarious effect has been eliminated. 

Dimmock v. Bixby, 20 Pick. 368, at 377

Multifariousness does not exist where there is a recital of the details of a fraudulent scheme and the joining of all the conspirators as parties defendant in the bill brought to enforce rights against partners who are the primary debtors where the other defendants are alleged to have combined with those partners in a fraudulent endeavor to deprive the plaintiff of his rights against each partner. 

Lovejoy v. Bailey, 214 Mass. 134, at 151

In the last cited case the averments of the bill were not multifarious where the plaintiff sought to avoid the effects of one scheme of fraud participated in by all the defendants except one partner who had absconded and could not act. 

The objection of multifariousness is one to which there is no inflexible rule, and the question must be determined largely by the circumstances of each particular case. 

Lovejoy v. Bailey, 214 Mass. 134, at 151 

Bliss v. Parks, 175 Mass. 539 (Where the bill sought to enforce a general right with which all the matters charged were connected and to which all the parties were so related so that he could not be said to be unduly burdened by being joined in the same suit.)

Nor is it indispensable that all the parties to the bill should have an interest in all the matters complained of. It is enough 24

if each party has an interest in some of the matters and they are connected with one another. 

Lovejoy v. Bailey, 214 Mass. 134, at 151 

Ginn v. Almy, 212 Mass. 486, at 493 

Coram v. Davis, 209 Mass. 229, at 248 

Mesisco v. Giuliano, 190 Mass. 352

Davis v. Peabody, 170 Mass. 397 

Sylvester v. Boyd, 166 Mass. 443 

Ricker v. Brooks, 155 Mass. 400, at 403 

Keith v. Keith, 143 Mass. 262 (X) Parties 

(A) Capacity 

If the legal incapacity of the plaintiff appears from the face of the bill, the objection may be by demurrer. Such is the case of a minor or foreign executor or administrator. 

(B) Nonjoinder-Lack of Necessary 

If there has been an omission or any necessary party, either as a plaintiff or defendant, and such fact appears from the face of the bill it may be raised by demurrer. 

But a demurrer must be overruled for want of parties when they are not shown to be necessary by the allegations 

Lyman v. Bonney, 101 Mass. 562 of the bill, even though upon a hearing it may appear that they were necessary. 

Bowker v. Torrey, 211 Mass. 282, at 283

It is usually the duty of the court to take notice itself of the defect due to the absence of a necessary party and refuse to pass any decree affecting him, and if necessary will dismiss the bill. 

Lyman v. Bonney, 101 Mass. 562

But not all parties are necessary to the proceedings. 

Zimmerman v. Finkelstein, 230 Mass. 17

The proper mode of taking advantage of nonjoinder of parties in equity is by demurrer, plea or answer. 

Warecki v. United Fidelity etc. Co., 270 Mass. 233 

Jewell v. Tucker, 139 Mass. 566, at 577

The failure to join as parties persons referred to under an allegation that the "other persons acted in concert and participated with the defendants" affords no ground for dismissing the bill when the defendants are answerable for their own misconduct as under a prayer for an accounting and repayment, 25

even though the defendants are not responsible for independent illegal acts of the unnamed parties. 

Todd v. Old Colony etc. R. R., 3 Allen 18, at 20 

Von Armin v. Am. Tube Co., 188 Mass. 515, at 519 

Bay State Co. v. Lawson, 188 Mass. 502, at 505

Such an instance arises when a conspiracy is alleged as each individual conspirator is liable for all acts committed in pursuance of the conspiracy. 

(C) Misjoinder 

The proper way to take advantage of misjoinder of either plaintiff or defendant, is by demurrer. 

Yaskill v. Thibault, 273 Mass. 266 

Stevens v. Rockport Granite Co., 216 Mass. 486 

Lyman v. Bonney, 101 Mass. 562

One test of misjoinder is whether there is or will be any difficulty in framing a decre which will dispose of the whole case. 

Parker v. Simpson, 180 Mass. 334, at 341

Another test is whether the bill is multifarious. 

Parker v. Simpson, 180 Mass. 334, at 341

It is necessary that rescission should apply so far as practicable to the whole transaction in order that justice can be done to all parties, and it is proper that those who are interested in any of the property should be parties to the bill, so that the court may have the whole case before it, and that all persons entitled to any of the property should be bound by the result. In this way the rights of all the parties may be adjusted and preserved in one suit. 

Parker v. Simpson, 180 Mass. 334, at 341

So, there is no misjoinder where parties who are interested join to set aside various contracts all being parts of one entire scheme or fraud. 

Parker v. Simpson, 180 Mass. 334, at 341

And an administrator and heir may properly join in setting aside conveyances obtained by the defendant from the testate by undue influence. 

Parker v. Simpson, 180 Mass. 334, at 341 

(XI) Res Judicata-Former Decree or Judgment 

When it appears from the face of the bill that a final decrer or judgment was rendered by a court of competent jurisdiction concerning the subject matter set forth in the bill, such former decree or judgment may be raised by demurrer. 

New York Central etc. R. R., v. Stuart, 260 Mass. 242 26

(XII) 

Another Suit Pending 

A demurrer will lie because of the pendency of related action at law or suit in equity, if the pendency appears on the face of the bill.

Consol. Ord. Co. v. Marsh, 227 Mass. 15 

Lewenstein v. Forman, 223 Mass. 325, at 328 

Sanford v. Wright, 164 Mass. 85 

(XIII) Prematureness 

Where a bill on its face appears to be prematurely brought a demurrer will be fatal, but if the prematureness appears on hearing, the court is bound to dismiss, but may, if plaintiff is entitled to relief, grant it. 

(XIV) Fraud-Unclean Hands 

When it appears from the face of the bill that the plaintiff himself has been guilty of fraud in the transaction upon which he relies for relief, the plaintiff's fraudulent conduct may be raised by demurrer, as a ground for a dismissal of the bill. 

(XV) Invalidity of Transaction (A) Foreign Law 

If the parties desire to put themselves in a position where the effect of the foreign law upon the rights of the parties is to be raised or settled by demurrer, that foreign law must be set forth with adequate particularity in the bill. 

Without such particularity of allegation in the bill, the defect in the plaintiff's case does not appear on the face of the bill.

A demurrer deals only with defects appearing on the face of the bill. If resort must be had to extraneous matters to determine the issue, demurrer is not the appropriate pleading. 

It has been said that what the laws of the state of New York "is of course a question of fact in this jurisdiction, and cannot be considered upon demurrer to a bill which contains no allegations as to the New York laws." 

Richards v. Richards, 270 Mass. 113 

Peters v. Equitable Life, 200 Mass. 579, at 588 

In Keown v. Keown, 230 Mass. 313, at 316 it was held that law of a sister State should have been set out in the bill as a fact before being susceptible of consideration on demurrer. 

In Hanna v. Lichtenhein, 225 New York 579, at 582 the court said: "No court is to be charged with the knowledge of foreign laws; but they are well understood to be facts, which must like other facts, be proved before they can be re- 27

ceived in a court of justice. .... They are admitted by demurrer. .... Foreign Law is a question of fact and must be proved as such." 

Richards v. Richards, 270 Mass. 113 

Nashua Savings v. Anglo-Am., 189 U. S. 221, at 228 

Liverpool & Gt. West. v. Phenix, 129 U. S. 397, at 445

However, a general averment of a transaction in a foreign state might be sufficient where the defendant did not move for further specifications as to this averment. Even though the demurrer is of general nature the court usually holds that there is enough in an averment to warrant a trial on the facts in the absence of any challenge of the adequacy of the foreign law but on demurrer the allegations as to foreign law should be present. 

Richards v. Richards, 270 Mass. 113

C. Defects in Form or Frame of Bill 

Defects in form or frame of bill may be raised by demurrer. 

Christianson v. Dixon, 271 Mass. 475 d. Demurrers to Discovery

Demurrers may be made to the discovery. 

7. Hearing and Determination a. Setting Down for Hearing

Demurrers should be set down for hearing. 

A demurrer should be set down for hearing, if insisted upon, otherwise it is waived. 

b. What Considered (I) General Statement 

A demurrer may be based entirely upon facts stated in the bill. It cannot invoke in its support any fact whatever which is not contained in the bill, excepting those facts of which the court takes judicial notice 1911ume e bebin
