French v. Lawrence, 190 Mass. 231, at 231 

Chenery v. Holden, 16 Gray 125 

Lee v. Robeson, 12 Gray 280 

Richards v. Richards, 9 Gray 313

A demurrer is an admission of the fact, submitting the law arising on that fact to the court. That is, the demurrer admits the facts set forth, and challenges their sufficiency in law upon which to maintain the action. 

It is an admission by the defendant of the facts charged by proper pleading in the plaintiff's bill of complaint but denies the right to any decree in the plaintiff's favor under the law applied to such facts.

The office of the demurrer is to admit the facts as alleged in the bill, but declare them insufficient on which to predicate the suit or right to relief in equity.

In other words, a demurrer admits all the material facts stated in the bill, but alleges that those facts in law and all inferences to be drawn therefrom, do not constitute a cause of action and submits that question, and that question alone, to the judgment of the court. 

A demurrer is only a technical admission and does not involve any confession. 

Although the demurrer admits all material allegations it does not admit matters which are immaterial or anything that is not well pleaded.

So arguments and conclusions of law are never deemed admissions.

In considering questions raised by a demurrer the allegations of the bill must be taken to be true. 

Bancroft v. Canane, 271 Mass. 191 

Willett v. Herrick, 242 Mass. 471, at 477 

Granara v. Italian Cath. Cem., 218 Mass. 387, at 392

So, all the material allegations of the bill and its amendments, if any, that are material and well pleaded, must be taken as admitted to be true on the demurrer. 

Von Armin v. Am. Tube Works, 188 Mass. 515, at 516

Also, allegations of the petition of an intervener in an equity suit must be taken as true on demurrer. 29

Cole v. Wells, 224 Mass. 504 

Rice v. Merrill, 215 Mass. 419

Louisville etc. R. R., v. Palmes, 109 U. S. 244 

On demurrer to a bill for relief against a suit on a written contract in which by mutual mistake an agent bound himself instead of his principal, all the allegations of the bill with reference to the existence of such mistake are admitted. 

Eustis Co. v. Saco Brick Co., 198 Mass. 212 (A) 

Information and Belief

As to an allegation that the plaintiff is informed, believes and alleges a certain fact the demurrer does not admit the fact, but admits only that the plaintiff is so informed and believes. 

(B) Arguments, Inferences and Conclusions of Law

Althought the demurrer admits the truth of every fact well pleaded in the bill it does not admit the truth of any arguments nor statements or inferences of law, nor does the demurrer admit the accuracy of legal deductions or inferences based upon facts stated in the bill. 

Thompson v. National Bank, 106 Mass. 128 

Chicot County v. Sherwood, 148 U. S. 529

Pullman Car Co. v. Missouri etc. Rlwy. Co., 115 U. S. 

587, at 596 So fraud being a conclusion of law is not admitted by demurrer. 

United States v. DesMoines Co., 142 U. S. 510, at 544 

Fogg v. Blair, 139 U. S. 118

Also the legal construction of an agreement or written contract is not admitted by the demurrer. 

Duane v. Merchants Co., 227 Mass. 466 

Thompson v. National Bank, 106 Mass. 128 

Lee v. Robeson, 12 Gray 280

Equitable Life Ins. Co. v. Brown, 213 U. S. 25 

Chicot County v. Sherwood, 148 U. S. 529

Interstate Land Co. v. Maxwell Co., 139 U. S. 569 Pennie v. Ries, 132 U. S. 464 

Mosher v. St. Louis etc. Co., 127 U. S. 390 

Pullman etc. Co. v. Missouri, 115 U. S. 587

Louisville v. Palmes, 109 U. S. 244 

Oakes v. Ames, 99 U. S. 35 

Dillon v. Barnard, 21 Wall. (U. S.) 430 30

(C) 

Inconsistencies Between Allegations and Exhibits 

In inconsistency between allegations and exhibits in or annexed to the bill are determined in favor of the exhibits. 

So, by demurring the statements contained in the exhibits are deemed to be true and where inconsistent with the allegations of the bill, the latter are disregarded. 

Dakota v. Price, 169 U. S. 45 

(D) Extent of Admission 

Although a demurrer is said to admit the truth of all material allegations stated in the bill, such admission relates only to facts stated in the bill and no assumption of fact not alleged in the bill can be made in the plaintiff's favor. 

Eldredge v. Mutual, 217 Mass. 444 

However, this admission is for purposes of determining the sufficiency of the allegations alleged in the bill and is not an absolute admission. 

The demurrer's only office is to raise issue of law upon facts stated in the bill; so that the demurrer cannot perform the office of an answer in admitting the facts alleged. 

The admission made by the demurrer is not for the purpose of trial on the merits. It is only for the determination of the sufficiency of the bill. 

Mere averments or legal conclusions are not admitted by the demurrer until the facts and circumstances are set forth to sustain the allegations.

After the overruling of the demurrer the facts must be proved by the plaintiff at the trial, the fact that the defendant did demur is not admissible in evidence. 

(1) Judicial Knowledge Contrary to 

Fact Admitted by

While a demurrer admits the truth of the material allegations of fact in the pleading, it does not admit arguments, legal conclusions, or inferences not supported by facts and circumstances therein set forth, nor the construction of statutes or facts that are immaterial or against common knowledge. 

Although a demurrer admits every well pleaded allegation of fact alleged declaration or bill 

Arizona v. California, 283 U. S. 423, at 452 

Griffin v. Gibb, 2 Black (U. S.) 519, at 523 yet, a court may take judicial notice concerning matters of common knowledge even if the contrary is alleged in the bill. 81

EQUITY PLEADING. PRACTICE AND PROCEDURE 

Arizona v. California, 283 U. S. 423, at 452 (Bill alleged Colorado River has never been, and is not now a navigable river, court took judicial notice from evidence of history to the contrary.) 

(2) Against Whom Admission Operates 

For purposes of the demurrer the admission operates only against such of the defendants as file the same. 

c. Rules Governing Determination (I) Demurrer Too Broad 

If the demurrer is too broad, such as if it goes to the whole bill and a part of the bill is good, a part only being bad and demurrable, the whole demurrer should be overruled. This is the invariable rule.

Granara v. Italian Cath. Cemetery, 218 Mass. 387 

Whitmore v. International etc. Co., 214 Mass. 525 

Bowker v. Torrey, 211 Mass. 282 

White v. Curtis, 2 Gray 467 

Robinson v. Guild, 12 Met. 323

Dimmock v. Bixby, 20 Pick. 368 

Boston etc. Co. v. Boston etc. R. R. 16 Pick. 512 Stewart v. Masterson, 131 U. S. 151 Livingston v. Story, 9 Pet. (U. S.) 632 

(A) Exceptions

Where the bill entitles the plaintiff to some of the relief he seeks, the demurrer to the whole bill must be overruled, even though the other relief sought is not a proper subject for equity. 

Granara v. Italian Cath. Cem., 218 Mass. 387 at 388 

Dimmock v. Bixby, 20 Pick.

368 

(II) Demurrer Too Narrow 

Where the demurrer is too narrow it cannot be sustained for grounds or causes not alleged therein. 

(III) Joint Demurrer 

A joint demurrer must be good as to all defendants who are parties thereto, otherwise it will be overruled. 

(IV) Demurrer Overruled by Plea or Answer 

Formerly, a defendant who demurred, and then filed a plea or answer without awaiting decision on his demurrer, by his own act overruled his demurrer, since he had destroyed the principal reason for it. 82

This rule, because of the growth of the right to demur and plead or answer at the same time, appears to be obsolete in this Commonwealth. 

Fogg v. Price, 145 Mass. 513

But where the defendant saves his rights upon the overruling of the demurrer by exceptions or appeal, when a special appeal from the interlocutory decision is necessary, Norton v. Lilley, 210 Mass. 214, at 218 

Harrell v. Sonnabend, 191 Mass. 310 

McCullum v. Lambie, 145 Mass. 234 his subsequent answering and trying the case on the merits, under the order of the court, does not deprive him of the benefit of the demurrer on an appeal. He could not stop the proceedings by pressing the appeal from the overruling of the demurrer to a hearing before trying the merits. 

Knox v. Springfield, 273 Mass. 109 

Weil v. Boston Elevated, 216 Mass. 545 

O'Connell Petr., 174 Mass. 253, at 262 

Fuller v. Chapin, 165 Mass. 1, at 2 

Bennett v. Clemence, 3 Allen 431 (V) Abandonment, Waiver or Withdrawal

The filing of an answer simultaneously with, or on the same day as, a demurrer does not waive or overrule the demurrer. 

Stratton v. Hernon, 154 Mass. 310, at 313

But when no disposition has been made of the demurrer and the case proceeds to a hearing, it is not confined to a hearing on the demurrer, the practice is to hear the questions of law raised by the demurrer, and the questions of fact raised by the answer at the same time. 

Stratton v. Hernon, 154 Mass. 310, at 313

However, a defendant who proceeds to trial on the merits, waives his demurrer. 

Old Colony Trust Co. v. Nat. etc. Bureau, Inc., 1931 

A. S. 451, at 453

A demurrer is waived by going to hearing on the merits before the court or a master without insisting upon a preliminary hearing of the demurrer. 

Luciano v. Caldarone, 255 Mass. 270 

Berenson v. Vogel Co., 253 Mass. 185, at 187 

Fairbanks v. Nehall, 222 Mass. 598

Atty Gen. v. Onset Ass'n., 221 Mass. 342 33

EQUITY PLEADING. PRACTICE AND PROCEDURE 

Torrey v. Parker, 220 Mass. 520 

Gargano v. Pope, 184 Mass. 571 

Driscoll v. Smith, 184 Mass. 221 

Parker v. Nickerson, 137 Mass. 487 

Crocker v. Dillon, 133 Mass. 91 

Creely v. Bay State Co., 103 Mass. 514

This is true whether the demurrer was contained in a separate document or included in the answer 

Lucano v. Caldarone, 255 Mass. 270 

Torrey v. Parker, 220 Mass. 520, at 525 

Driscoll v. Smith, 184 Mass. 221, at 223

The mere setting the case down for hearing or reference to a master, without objection by the demurring party, is a waiver of the demurrer. 

Fairbanks v. Newhall, 222 Mass. 598

Atty. Gen. v. Onset Ass'n., 221 Mass. 342 

But where the defendant insists at all stages upon his demurrer, it is not waived, even though he is compelled to try his case upon the merits.

DeVeer v. Pierson, 222 Mass. 167 

It has been said that the object of a demurrer is to excuse the defendant from answering, and therefore, if the defendant proceeds to answer, the reason for the demurrer no longer exists; and it has been said that if an answer shows a defence to the bill as originally drawn, or as subsequently amended, it prevents a subsequent demurrer to the amended bill. 

Fogg v. Price, 145 Mass. 513

But where the defendant is compelled to go to trial on the merits, by order of the court, saving all his rights on the demurrer, it is not waived, and in DeVeer v. Pierson, 222 Mass. 

167, a decree having been entered on the master's report without disposing of the demurrer, the full court acted upon it, apparently under the power given it by St. 1913, c. 716, (G. L. c. 231, s. 124), although that statute was not cited.

By proceeding with the hearing on the merits a defendant waives his demurrer to the bill because of multifariousness. 

Vaughan v. Bridgham, 193 Mass. 392, at 397

Submitting the case on an agreed statement of facts is a waiver of all objections to procedure, unless such objections are expressly reserved also. 

Russell v. Loring, 3 Allen 121, at 125 34

8. 

Disposition of Suit on Demurrer a. General Statement 

An order sustaining or overruling a demurrer is not final, unless in terms or effect it dismisses the bill. 

Upon the sustaining or overruling of a demurrer the proper practice is to draw a decree to that effect. 

Nelson Theatre Co. v. Nelson, 216 Mass. 30, at 33

All appeals in equity are from decrees. However, in few instances review of the judge's action upon demurrers have been heard by the Supreme Judicial Court on a bill of exceptions. 

Worcester v. Tupper, 210 Mass. 380 

Norton v. Lilley, 210 Mass. 214 

Mayberry v. Sprague, 207 Mass. 508 

Bearse v. Mabie, 198 Mass. 445, at 455

If the demurrer is sustained, the defendant need not answer the bill unless amended and if not amended the defendant may have it dismissed for want of prosecution.

There is practically no distinction between law and equity as to the effect of an adjudication of a judgment or decree for the defendant upon the sustaining of a demurrer. 

Keown v. Keown, 231 Mass. 404

If the demurrer is overruled, the defendant is required to answer the allegations of the bill. 

Forbes v. Tuckerman, 115 Mass. 115, at 119 b. Sustaining the Demurrer 

(I) General Statement 

The demurrer should be sustained if any of its grounds is good.

If the demurrer is sustained, the plaintiff is usually permitted to amend his bill, if it is amendable; but if the defect cannot be cured by an amendment the bill should be dismissed. 

Ginn v. Almy, 212 Mass. 486

A special demurrer assigning, among others, a special ground as a defect, although overruled in other respects, may be sustained as to that special ground. 

Cashman v. Bean, 226 Mass. 198, at 200, 201 and 204

The decree sustaining the demurrer need not specify the particular ground.

However, the decree may lack value as an adjudication if the ground is not specified, as where it is sustained on a ground going to the merits. 

Montogomery v. Richards, 1931 A. S. 1269

Mezoff v. United Kosher Butchers, 1931 A. S. 165, 35

(II) To Part of the Bill 

If the demurrer is sustained to a part only of the bill, then the plaintiff may maintain his suit as to the remaining portions of the bill.

Powder Co. v. Powder Works, 98 U. S. 126 (III) Leave to Amend 

Upon the hearing of a demurrer, where the defect can be remedied, the court, instead of sustaining the demurrer usually gives the plaintiff leave to amend his bill. 

Johnson v. Union Ins. Co., 127 Mass. 555 

Bank of Newburyport v. Stevenson, 7 Allen 489

Lea v. Robeson, 12 Gray 280 

Riddle v. Whitebill, 135 U. S. 621

National Bank v. Carpenter, 101 U. S. 567 

Also, upon the sustaining of a demurrer the usual practice is to permit the plaintiff a reasonable time within which to amend his bill for the purpose of supplying the defects or alleging new grounds for relief. 

Cummings v. Ayer, 188 Mass. 292, at 293 

Moran v. Dunphy, 177 Mass. 485 

Bank of Newburyport v. Stevenson, 7 Allen 489, at 491

But the permission to amend the bill is within the discretion of the judge who sustained the demurrer. 

Fay v. Boston etc. Rlwy. Co., 196 Mass. 329, at 336

However, other members of the court may, in their discretion, allow amendments in form or substance at any time before the entry of the final decree. 

Fay v. Boston etc. Rlwy. Co., 196 Mass. 329, at 330 

Cummings v. Ayer, 188 Mass. 292 

Bank of Newburyport v. Stevenson, 7 Allen 489, at 491

After a demurrer has been sustained and the bill amended, the court may restrict the second demurrer to the amendment itself. 

Lynn Safe Deposit & Trust Co. v. Andrews, 180 Mass. 527 (A) Application for Leave to Amend

A plaintiff to whose bill a demurrer has been sustained, may apply for leave to amend at any time before final decree. 

Fay v. Boston etc. Rlwy. Co., 196 Mass. 329, at 330 

Cummings v. Ayer, 188 Mass. 292 

Bank of Newburyport v. Stevenson, 7 Allen 489 36

United States v. Atherton, 102 U. S. 372 

National Bank v. Carpenter, 101 U. S. 567 (B) Failure to Amend Within Time Limited.

If the plaintiff fails to amend his bill within the time limited by the court the defendant may have the bill dismissed for want of prosecution.

However, the court may in its discretion permit additional time for the plaintiff to file the amendment. 

(C) Effect of Amendment 

When a demurrer is sustained with leave to amend within a stated time and the plaintiff presents an amendment which is denied because it does not remove the valid grounds for demurrer and a decree is entered dismissing the bill, the proper practice is to allow the amendment and permit the defendant to demur again. 

Corbett v Gallagher, 225 Mass. 480, at 482

On the other hand, if the demurrer is sustained, subject to the exception or appeal of the plaintiff, his subsequent amendment of his bill makes moot the law question thus saved, and he can have no benefit from it. 

Cole v. Wells, 224 Mass. 504, at 512 

Cook v. Castner, 9 Cush. 266, at 273 

(D) Amendment After Appeal 

Where a demurrer is sustained on the ground of multifariousness and the plaintiff appeals but subsequently amends, by the amendment the plaintiff waives his appeal because the amended bill relates back to the filing of the original bill. 

Cole v. Wells, 224 Mass. 504, at 512 

(IV) Judgment or Final Decree Based upon Sus taining of Demurrer

When a bill is dismissed on a demurrer the final decree ought to contain the words, "that the bill is dismissed without prejudice", so as to show that the bill was not dismissed on its merits. 

Christiansen v. Dixon, 271 Mass. 475

A bill that cannot be maintained on demurrer need not be retained for an accounting. 

Downing v. Brennan, 232 Mass. 535 (A) Effect of A judgment on sustaining a demurrer for defect is not a bar to a new suit where proper allegations are made. 

Capaccio v. Merrill, 222 Mass. 308 to 37

(III) Overruling Partial Demurrer 

When a demurrer to part of the bill has been overruled the court usually orders the defendant to file an answer within a certain specified time. 

O'Hare v. Downing, 130 Mass 16 (IV) Renewing Demurrer or Questions Presented Thereby

Usually the court restricts the defendant's right to a second demurrer to the amendment filed by the plaintiff to his bill and will not permit the defendant to renew the questions presented by his former demurrer. 

However, if the court makes no such restriction the defendant may again present the grounds raised by his former demurrer. (A) Presenting Same Question

When the court restricts the defendant, he may present the the same questions in his second demurrer. 

(V) Final Decree Based Upon 

The reasons stated which influence the judge in overruling a demurrer are not part of the decision of the suit itself. 

Lundin v. Post Pub. Co., 217 Mass. 213, at 219 d. Reservation of Questions Raised by Demurrer 

The court may reserve the questions raised by demurrer for the Supreme Judicial Court upon a report. 

Also, the court may order the demurrer to be heard at the same time as the hearing on the merits. 

Stratton v. Hernon, 154 Mass. 310, at 313

It is not an unusual practice for the court to hear questions of law raised by the demurrer and the questions of fact raised by a plea or answer at the same time. 

Stratton v. Hernon, 154 Mass. 310, at 313 

Virginia v. West Virginia, 206 U. S. 290 

Kansas v. Colorado, 185 U. S. 125 (1) Duty of Judge to Pass Upon

When the judge is of the opinion that many of the questions raised by the demurrer can be better considered at the hearing on the merits he may properly overrule the demurrer without prejudice to the rights of the defendant to raise questions at the hearing upon the merits. 

Glover v. Waltham Laundry Co., 235 Mass. 330, at 332 

Saltman v. Nesson, 201 Mass. 534, at 537 and 538 38

It is a bar, however: 1. 

Where the demurrer is based on the merits. 

Old Dom. Copper Co. v. Bigelow, 203 Mass. 159, at 205 

2. Where leave to amend was given and the plaintiff refused or neglected to do so.

Capaccio v. Merrill, 222 Mass. 308 Correla v. Supreme etc. Fraternity, 218 Mass. 305 (1) Res Judicata 

The effect of sustaining the demurrer without specification of the causes which that action rested, is to leave in doubt the causes adjudged sufficient. In appropriate circumstances a decree entered upon sustaining a demurrer is as conclusive of the merits of the cause of action alleged in the bill as one entered after a decision founded on a hearing of the evidence. 

It may bar another suit under the doctrine of res judicata. 

Mezoff v. United Kosher Butchers, 1931 A. S. 165, at 

166 

Keown v. Keown, 231 Mass. 404, at 408

Capaccio v. Merrill, 222 Mass. 308 

Old Dom. Cop. etc. Co., v. Bigelow, 203 Mass. 159

When conditions warrant, it is permissible to show by oral evidence the precise ground on which a decree in a former suit rested, in order to determine whether it ought to have the effect of res judicata.

Mezoff v. United Kosher Butchers, 1931 A. S. 165, at 

166 

Newburyport Bank v. Puffer, 201 Mass. 41, at 49

C. Overruling the Demurrer  

If the demurrer is overruled, the defendant is required to plead or answer to the bill. 

(II) Answer After Demurrer Overruled 

When the demurrer is overruled the court should order the filing of an answer within a certain time. 

O'Hare v. Downing, 130 Mass 16 

Forbes v. Tuckerman, 115 Mass. 115

When the answer is filed with the demurrer and the demurrer is overruled, no order to answer is necessary. 

O'Hare v. Downing, 130 Mass 16

The court upon overruling a demurrer, may order answer to be filed notwithstanding a claim of appeal from the decree overruling the demurrer. 

Forbes v. Tuckerman, 115 Mass. 115 39

(II) Disposition of Demurrer not Necessary Be fore Hearing Merits If the court desires it may deal with the facts first and the grounds of demurrer later. 

For, although a defendant has a right to have his demurrer considered and determined by the court, the time of its consideration and determination is within the sole discretion of the court.

The court can overrule the demurrer and permit the defendant to raise the same legal questions in his answer and bring them up at the hearing on the merits. 

Cram v. Cram, 262 Mass. 509, at 513 

Glover v. Waltham Laundry Co., 235 Mass. 330, at 332 and 339 

Saltman v. Nesson, 201 Mass. 534 

Stratton v. Hernon, 154 Mass. 310, at 313 (III)

Advantages of Hearing Facts First 

The modern tendency as shown by Superior Court Rule No. 

28 (1932) is to bring the parties to a speedy hearing on the merits and all questions of law, and not to allow separate hearings at any stage of the case which may unduly delay its termination. 9.

Striking out the Demurrer A motion to strike out a demurrer which is not in form substantially in accordance with the statute may be allowed. 

10. Review by Supreme Judicial Court a. On Appeal (I) Truth of Allegations in the Bill

For the purposes of appeal from the sustaining of the demurrer the allegations of fact in the bill must be taken as true. 

Hutchins v. Nickerson, 212 Mass. 118, at 121 b. On Bill of Exceptions

Although the better practice in equity of procuring review by the Supreme Judicial Court is by an appeal, yet, the same may also be accomplished by bill of exceptions. 

Gen. Laws, c. 231, ss. 113 and 114 

11. Forms

The defendant, not waiving his right to answer to the merits, demurs to the plaintiff's bill of complaint and assigns the following causes of demurrer: 40

1. The bill of complaint [as amended] does not state facts entitling the plaintiffs, or either of them, to relief in equity. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

2. The plaintiff has not stated in his bill [as amended] such a cause as entitles him to any relief in equity against this defendant.

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

3. It does not appear that the plaintiffs, or either of them, have sustained any damages. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

4. It does not appear that the plaintiffs, or either of them. are entitled to recover the profits, if any, derived by the defendants, or any or either of them from the use of the name. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

5. There is an absence of necessary parties. 

6. The plaintiffs are improperly joined as plaintiffs in this suit. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

7. The bill of complaint [as amended] is multifarious. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

8. The causes of action, if any, of the two plaintiffs are improperly joined. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

9. The plaintiff has been guilty of laches. 

10. The plaintiff does not allege that he was the owner of the land described in the plaintiff's bill. 

11. The plaintiff's bill is not a bill to redeem from the mortgage mentioned in the plaintiff's bill. 

12. There has been a foreclosure of the equity of redemption of the land described in the plaintiff's bill. 

Dennett v. Atkins, 232 Mass. 301, at 302 

13. It does not appear that either the word "Page" or the word "Shaw" has been used by the defendants, or any or either of them, in a manner not authorized by the plaintiffs. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 41

14. It does not appear that any property received by Page and 

Shaw, Inc., for any name or for any goodwill is affected with a trust in favor of the plaintiffs, or of either of them. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

15. It does not appear that any profits have been derived by the defendants, or by any or either of them, from the use of them, or by any of them of the name "Page" or of the name "Shaw" in a manner not authorized by the plaintiffs. 

Page v. Fage & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

16. It appears that the phrase "Page and Shaw" is a trademark and trade name owned by the defendant Page & Shaw, Inc., and that neither of the plaintiffs is entitled to object to any use thereof, and particularly that neither of the plaintiffs is entitled to object to such use thereof as is alleged in the bill of complaint. 

Page v. Page & Shaw Co., 240 Mass. 505, at 511 

17. The bill is impertinent for gross prolixity contrary to the provisions of Section 12 of Chapter 214 of the Gen eral Laws. 

Christiansen v. Dixon, 271 Mass. 475 

18. The bill is so improperly verbose and grossly argumenta tive as to be incapable of direct and specific traverse of its material allegations by the defendants in their answers and they ought not in equity to be required to plead further to it. 

Christiansen v. Dixon, 271 Mass. 475 42

EQUITY PLEADING, PRACTICE, & PROCEDURE 

PLEAS E. 1. 

Nature, Object and Function a. Definitions 

A plea in equity is in the nature of a special answer, to avoid a general answer, under a rule that, if one answers at all, he must answer fully; and the plea is permitted when it puts the matter upon some one point which is decisive of the suit. 

A plea in equity is in effect an answer which reduces the issue between the parties to a single point. 

The office of a plea in equity is to present some one single and well-defined ground of defense, which if sustained, will dispose of the case and avoid the expense and delay of a hearing.

The object of a plea is to bring the matter presented by the bill to an issue on a single point, which may save the defendant from answering in whole or in part, and save the expense of going into the evidence at large. The general rule permits a single plea only, and several pleas will not be allowed unless they present well-defined issues not interwoven with the alleged equities of the bill, which can be determined separately, without regard to such equity, and without injustice to the complainant.

The proper function of a plea in equity is to interpose some ground of conclusive defense, which may determine the suit without the necessity of an exhaustive hearing on the merits of the case under the several different defenses which may be appropriately made by answer. A defendant by such a plea rests his entire defense on it. 

b. Distinctions 

(I) Distinguished from Demurrer The functions of a plea in equity practice is to present a single issue of fact as a defense which operates as a bar to the plaintiff's right to maintain the suit, while a demurrer raises a question of law and is directed to the sufficiency of the bill of complaint.

A demurrer raises a question of law, while a plea raises an issue of fact.

A plea is the defendant's special answer by matter of fact, to the plaintiff's bill of complaint. It is distinguished from 51

a demurrer, which opposes matter of law to the bill of complaint. 

It was said in Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303, at 314, 315 and 316 that: "....the proper office of a plea is not, .... like a demurrer, admitting those allegations, to deny the equity of the bill; but it is to present some distinct fact, which of itself creates a bar to the suit, or to the part to which the plea applies, and thus to avoid the necessity of making the discovery asked for, and the expense of going into the evidence at large. "The distinction between a demurrer and plea dates as far back as the time of Lord Bacon by .... whose Ordinances for the Administration of Justice in Chancery, 'a demurrer is properly upon matter defective contained in the bill itself, and no foreign matter; but a plea is of foreign matter to discharge or stay the suit, ....' "....Lord Redesdale .... says: 'A plea must aver facts to which the plaintiff may reply, and not in the nature of a demurrer, rests on facts in the bill.' "In other words, a plea which avers that a certain fact is not as the bill affirms it to be, sets up matter not contained in the bill. That an objection to the equity of the plaintiff's claim, as stated in the bill, must be done by demurrer and not by plea is so well established that it has been constantly assumed and therefore seldom stated in the judicial opinions." 

National Bank v. Ins. Co., 104 U.S. 54, at 76 

R. I. v. Mass., 14 Peters (U.S.) 210, at 258 and 262 

(II) Distinguished From Answer 

The plea presents some distinct fact which of itself creates a bar to the suit while an answer meets all the material allegations of the bill. 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303, at 314

A plea sets up facts not apparent on the face of the bill without replying to the allegations of the bill, while an answer must respond to the material allegations of the bill, even though it also sets up additional averments of defense. 

(III) Distinguished From Disclaimer 

A plea asserts some distinct fact concerning which there is a controversy, while a disclaimer eliminates any controversy concerning the rights asserted by the plaintiff. 52

C. General Statement 

The proper office of a plea is to set forth some single fact or point of law, the establishment of which will defeat the suit or the part of it to which the plea applies. 

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503, at 507 

E. S. Parks Shellac Co. v. Jones, 265 Mass. 108, at 110 

Eastman Mar. Co. v. Vt. Mar. Co., 236 Mass. 138, at 148 

Hancock v. Carlton, 6 Gray 39, at 53, 54, and 63 

Crease v. Babcock, 10 Met. 525, at 543 and 544 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 132 

Chapin v. Coleman, 11 Pick. 330, at 336 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303, at 314

A plea is a device which settles the suit upon some single issue of fact or point of law by which the defendant is excused from answering the material allegations of the bill and thus avoids general discovery. 

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303, at 314 and 315

The office of a plea is to bring forward a single ground of defense a fact or point of law-which does not appear on the face of the bill and which, if established as true, is sufficient to defeat the suit without hearing all the evidence. 

The function of the plea is to present a single issue of fact which, when proved, will operate as a bar to the plaintiff's right to maintain the suit. The fact put in issue by the plea must constitute in itself a complete defense to the bill, or to that part of the bill to which it is pleaded. The advantage of the plea, if sustained, is that the defendant will be relieved from making a complete answer to the bill and so will not be required to reveal the facts otherwise incident to a full discovery.

The plea may be in one or two different forms. It may specifically deny the existence of some one essential fact without which the plaintiff cannot maintain his suit, although the other allegations in the bill may be true; or the plea may consist in putting in issue some extraneous fact, not alleged or referred to in the bill, the existence of which constitutes in itself a complete reply and defense to the matters alleged in the bill of complaint.

If the matter alleged in the plea appears on the face of the bill then the defendant should file a demurrer and not a plea. 

But it sometimes happens that a bill,-which, if all the particulars of the case were disclosed, would be open to a de- 53

murrer is so artfully drawn as to avoid showing on the face of it a cause for demurrer. 

In such a case the defendant is compelled to resort to a plea by which he may allege matter which, if it appeared on the face of the bill, would be a good cause of demurrer. 

The plea is divided into two parts: 

First: Whether the allegations if true constitute a legal defense; and

Second: Whether the allegations of the plea are true in fact. (I) Must Be Confined to Single Point

A plea ought not to contain more than one defense. 

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503, at 507 

Berenson v. Franch, 262 Mass. 247 

Chapin v. Coleman, 11 Pick. 330 

R. I. v. Massachusetts, 14 Peters (U. S.) 210, at 259 

United States v. Bell Tel. Co., 30 Fed. Rep. 523

If one point will put an end to the whole cause it is important to the administration of justice that it should be pleaded. 

Crease v. Babcock, 10 Met. 525

It was said in the last cited case at pages 543 and 544: "A plea in equity is a well established mode of defense, and is very useful in a suitable case, where the defense depends upon a single fact or point, the establishment of which answers the whole equity of the bill, and thus tends to shorten the proceedings. It is more particularly beneficial when the defendant pleads some single fact, which may be traversed and put in issue, and tried by evidence not depending upon the defendant's answer by way of discovery. a plea in equity is required to be a decisive fact, answering the whole equity of the bill. "But such plea must be made in precise and accurate language, in terms so plain and unequivocal that the fact may be put in issue, so if found true it must decide the case. But if the matter, as pleaded, may be found true and yet the defendant be in any form liable, the plea is bad."

Although the matters raised by the plea must be confined to a single point it is the issue only that must be single. 54

So, many facts may be proved and a variety of circumstances may be shown if they all tend to establish the single point or issue. 

Berenson v. French, 262 Mass. 247, at 255

It was said in Rhode Island v. Massachusetts, 14 Peters (U. S.) 210, at 259: "It is a general rule that the plea ought not to contain more defenses than one. Various facts, therefore, can never be pleaded in one plea, unless they are conducive to a single point on which the defendent means to rest his defense." 

If a plea only is put in, it must be of some matter of fact, which, if true, is an entire bar to the suit. 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 133

Although a plea like a demurrer or an answer may be to the whole of the bill, or only to part of it, yet the cases are comparatively few where a plea can apply to a part and not to the whole of the bill. However, such a case arises when the claim of the plaintiff is divisible in its nature, and one part of it is open to some special defense which does not apply to the rest.

The plea must of course be of some fact, which if proved will be a bar to the entire suit, or at least to an entire substantive part of the suit, and in the latter case if it does not go to the whole suit, the defendant must answer or demur to the residue. 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 132

A defendant may plead to part, answer to part, and demur to part, where his case requires it; and he may do this by separate documents or join them all in one, but in some form he must meet the whole substance of the bill. 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 132 and 133 

(II) Double Pleas 

When seasonable objection is made, the plea cannot contain two or more distinct points or issues. When the plea contains two or more distinct points or issues it is termed double and is defective.

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503, at 507 Rhode Island v. Massachusetts, 14 Peters (U. S.) 210 

If two defenses could be brought forward by plea, the same reason would justify any number of defenses by plea and the advantage of the plea would not be obtained. 

United States v. Bell Tel. Co., 30 Fed. Rep. 523 55

However, more than one reason can be given in a plea tending to the same point or issue, such as jurisdiction. 

Ellis v. Hunt, 228 Mass. 39

But, there are instances when double pleas have been permitted, particularly when they do not lead to diverse or inconsistent issues. 

Homrich v. Robinson, 221 Mass. 308 

Bailey v. Hemmenway, 147 Mass. 326 

Gormley v. Bunyan, 138 U. S. 623

The presentation and trial of a double plea without objection operates as a waiver of the defect of the plea and its impropriety.

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503, at 507 

and cases cited 

(III) Burden of Proof 

The burden of proof upon a pure or affirmative plea is upon the defendant, while the burden of proof on a negative plea is upon the plaintiff. The burden of proof rests upon the party who has the affirmative of the issue. So, when the affirmative issue rests upon the plaintiff at the outset by the necessary allegations of his bill, the defendant by his plea does not assume the burden of proving any of those necessary allegations even though he sets up any or all of them in the plea. The burden of proof does not shift as to those necessary allegations but remains upon the plaintiff throughout. 

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503, at 511 

Berenson v. French, 262 Mass. 247, at 254 (Burden of proving waiver was on the defendant.) 

Prunier v. Schulman, 261 Mass. 417, at 418 and 419 

Torrey v. Adams, 254 Mass. 22 

d. When Necessary 

Pleas in equity as at law are in effect in abatement or in bar. 

The difference between a plea which effects an abatement and one that creates a bar is that the former goes to the form of the bill or process, while the latter goes to the cause of action. 

Whiton v. Balch, 203 Mass. 575 (I) (A) Pleas which effect an abatement of a suit are:

Jurisdiction 

(1) Lack of, as to subject matter (2) 

Defective, as to parties 56

Lack of interest in the subject-matter of the suit 

Multifariousness 

(B) 

Death of party (C) (D) (E) (F) (G) (II) Objections to the form of the bill or process Pendency of another suit for the same cause Want of necessary parties Pleas which will bar the suit are based on some fact or law which is a complete defense to the plaintiff's claim and goes to the existence of the cause of action. 

In this class are included: 

(A) Estoppel 

(B) 

Former Judgment (C) Fraud (D) Laches (E) (F) (G) Purchaser for value without notice Release Res Judicata 

Cutter v. Cutter, 226 Mass. 196 e. 

(H) Statute of Frauds 

(I) 

Statute of Limitations (J) Title in the Defendant 

(K) Waiver 

When Pleas Proper 

The plea is proper when a defendant does not wish to submit himself to full discovery and is willing to risk his defense upon a single point of fact which, if established, would be a complete termination of the plaintiff's right to maintain the suit. 2. 

Crease v. Babcock, 10 Met. 525, at 543 

Kinds or Classes a. Affirmative or Pure Pleas 

An affirmative or pure plea is one which sets up some fact outside of the bill as a defense to it. 

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503, at 511

The affirmative or pure plea sets up some matter not raised by the bill, such as confession and avoidance, release, statute of limitations, purchase for a valuable consideration and former adjudication. 

b. Negative Pleas 

A negative plea is one which extracts from the bill some essential and conclusive fact or issue, without which the bill 57

cannot be maintained and specifically denies that particular fact or issue in the hope of defeating the bill upon a preliminary hearing of that fact or issue. The negative plea by denying the existence of such fact must raise a complete defense to the whole suit. 

Crease v. Babcock, 10 Met. 525, at 544 

United States v. California, 148 U. S. 31 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303, at 314 

Rhino v. Emery, 79 Fed. 483 

c. Anomalous Pleas 

Some pleas are called anomalous. No exact definition can be given of an anomalous plea, but cases in which the bill anticipates a defense and alleges matter in avoidance of it, the plea may take a third form called an anomalous plea, by setting up the affirmative defence and denying the matter alleged in avoidance of it. The anomalous plea is somewhat analogous to the negative plea. 

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503, at 511 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303 

3. Filing of а. 

Right To 

Any defendant before or at the time that he answers to the merits of the allegations of the bill may file a plea. However, only those parties who are named in the suit have such right. Minors, lunatics and others under disability cannot personally file a plea, but must do so through their lawful representatives.

All, or any two or more defendants may file a joint plea, but the disposition of such plea as to those defendants will not affect the other defendants. b. Time of 

(I) Rules of Court (A) Supreme Judicial Court Supreme Judicial Court Equity Rule 7 (1926) provides in part that: "The day of appearance shall be the return day of the writ or subpoena, when personal service shall be made on the defendant, or he shall have had personal notice of the suit; or the return day of any order issued under the third or fourth rule, when no personal service shall be made. And, if the defendant does not 58

appear and file his answer, plea, or demurrer within twenty-one days after the day of appearance, the plaintiff may enter an order to take his bill for confessed." (B) Superior Court Superior Court Rule 28 (1932) provides that: "The defendant, at any time before the bill is taken for confessed, or afterwards by leave of court, may demur, plead or answer to the bill; and he may demur to part, plead to part, and answer as to the residue. "The court may give leave to a defendant to file a demurrer or plea, reserving his answer. In the absence of such leave, the defendant must (a) file at the same time his demurrer, plea and answer, or such of them as he may desire, and shall have no right without leave of court to file another of such pleadings after filing any one of them, or (b) include in his answer any special matter by way of demurrer and plea, or either of them, describing such matter clearly as by way of demurrer or plea as the case may be in which case and not otherwise he shall have the same benefit therefrom as if he had pleaded the same or demurred to the bill. "If a plea or demurrer shall be filed, with leave to reserve the answer, and the plea or demurrer shall be overruled or disproved, no other plea or demurrer shall be received without leave of court, but the defendant shall within ten days answer the bill. "If, upon an issue on a plea, the facts pleaded be determined for the defendant, they shall avail him only as far as in law and equity they ought to avail him." 

4. Form and Sufficiency a. General Statement 

A plea is required to state in its entirety a decisive fact answering the whole or part of the equity of the bill. 

But such plea must be made in precise and accurate language in terms so plain and unequivocal that the fact may be put in issue, and so that if found true it must decide the case. 

But if the matter, as pleaded, may be found true, and yet the defendant be in any form liable, the plea is bad. 

Crease v. Babcock, 10 Met. 525, at 544 1 59

The plea, to operate as a bar to maintaining the bill, should state directly, positively and fully the facts and circumstances which constitute the defense claimed. 

Hancock v. Carlton, 6 Gray 39, at 53

A plea is bad which merely alleges a conclusion of law without setting forth the facts or circumstances leading to that conclusion. 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303, at 315 

b. Formal Parts 

(I) Oath General Laws, c. 214, s. 13 provides in part that: .a plea, shall not be made under oath..... and it need not contain any saving of exceptions to the bill, or a prayer to be dismissed or for costs." 

(II) Seal 

General Laws, c. 214, s. 13 provides in part that: "... a plea, shall not be made... under seal, ...." c. Requisites Every plea, whether affirmative or pure, negative or anomalous, must present but one issue of fact. If it raises two or more issues, it is tainted with duplicity and is fatally defective. 

R. I. v. Mass., 14 Peters (U.S.)210, at 259

So, the statute of limitations and a release, or other matter in abatement or bar, are two distinct defenses, which cannot be joined in the plea.

So, also, several distinct pleas cannot be filed raising distinc issues, although such procedure is permitted at law. 

In such an instance, the defendant should present his several defenses by way of an answer to the whole bill. 

There have been instances where pleas tainted with duplicity have been allowed and considered as in Parker v. New England Trust Company, 215 Mass. 226 four distinct defenses were claimed in the plea and all were sustained. 

However, the filing of several pleas or several grounds in one plea may be permitted by the court. 

The plea may refer only to a part of the bill. 

The original or copies of exhibits which are to be relied upon in support of the plea should be annexed to it. d. Combining with Answer

Under Supreme Judicial Court Equity Rule 9 (1926) a plea may be put in the answer. 60

Under Superior Court Rule 28 (1932) in the absence of leave of court, the defendant must either file the plea at the same time as the answer, or include in his answer any special matter by way of .... plea, .... describing such matter clearly as by way of .... plea in which case and not otherwise, he shall have the same benefit therefrom as if he had pleaded the same to the bill. ....9

A plea inserted in an answer has the same standing as though filed separately. 

Parks v. Smith, 155 Mass. 26, at 30 

O'Hara v. Downing, 130 Mass. 16 

Fisher v. Fraprie, 125 Mass. 472

These rules of the Supreme Judicial and Superior Courts have removed any uncertainty that formerly existed as to the effect of inserting a plea in the answer, filing the plea simultaneously with the answer or filing the answer after the plea. 

Richards v. Richards, 270 Mass. 113 

Luciano v. Caldarone, 255 Mass 270

Eastman Marble Co. v. Vermont Mar. Co., 236 Mass. 

138, at 151 

Finneran v. Graham, 198 Mass. 385 

Craig Silver Co. v. Smith, 163 Mass. 262, at 268 

Fogg v. Price, 145 Mass. 513 

O'Hare v. Downing, 130 Mass. 16, at 18 and 20 

O'Laughlin v. Bird, 128 Mass. 600 

Hancock v. Carlton, 6 Gray 39 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303 

5. Grounds For a. General Statement 

The effect of pleas in equity being the same as at law, namely, an abatement or a bar to the suit, may be classified as attacking fundamental essentials as follows: 

(I) Jurisdiction (II) Parties (III) Process (IV) Substance of the Bill 

It was said by Chief Justice Rugg in White v. E. T. Slattery Company, 236 Mass. 28, at 30 and 31: "A plea in abatement goes to the form of the writ; a plea in bar goes to the cause of action. 61

"Any fact which impeaches the form of the [process], the timeliness of the action, the capacity of the parties, or such like matter not attacking the foundation of the cause of action, properly may be pleaded in abatement, such as misnomer or any misdescription of the parties; non-joinder of necessary parties; the bringing of the [suit] in the wrong county; pendency of prior suit between the same parties for the same cause; that the plaintiff is not owner of or for any reason is not entitled to prosecute the cause of action either for his own benefit or that of another; temporary inhibition operating on the plaintiff, coverture, the disability of being an Indian, of being an alien enemy, infancy, or other disability of the plaintiff, must be taken advantage of by plea in abatement. "Certain matters like non-existence of corporation made party to the action, non tenure in real actions, that the action is prematurely brought, that the party is alien enemy in real actions may be pleaded, either in abatement or in bar. "The question whether a matter is in abatement or in bar is to be decided, not by the form in which it is presented, but by its substance. If it is essentially in bar of the action, it will be so treated and considered even though cast in the form of a plea in abatement." b. Jurisdiction

Objection to the jurisdiction of the court may properly be raised by plea when the defect of jurisdiction depends upon some fact not appearing on the face of the bill. When such defect appears from the face of the bill it should be raised by demurrer. 

Livingston v. Story, 11 Pet. 351, at 393

So, a plea may properly raise the question of the court's jurisdiction, either as to the subject-matter of the bill or as to the parties. If the objection relates to the parties only it is necessary that the objection to the jurisdiction should be seasonably pleaded, or it will be considered waived, as hereinafter stated.

The question of jurisdiction may be divided into two parts. 

First, lack of jurisdiction; and second, the excess of jurisdiction. 

Locomobile Co. of America v. Comm., 232 Mass. 16, at 

22 and 28 

Durat v. Simmons, 231 Mass. 313, at 318 

Kirby v. Donovan, 228 Mass. 86, at 90 62

Ashley v. Justices, 228 Mass. 63, at 82

The terms "lack of jurisdiction" and "excess of jurisdiction" are frequently interchanged, but there exists a technical distinction between them.

Lack of jurisdiction, sometimes called want of jurisdiction, usually refers to the jurisdiction over the person of the defendant or the absence of the right to invoke the aid of the equity court because the law court has concurrent jurisdiction. While excess of jurisdiction relates to the court's power to entertain the suit and attacks its right to assume jurisdiction over the same.

As to lack of jurisdiction, this objection may be waived, but if intended to be relied upon, must be asserted without delay and at the earliest opportunity. It is too late to raise this objection at the hearing on the merits. 

Baker v. Langley, 247 Mass. 127

A waiver of this objection results from the filing of a general appearance, demurrer, pleading to the merits or proceding with a hearing on the merits. 

Humphrey's case, 226 Mass. 143 

Gaff v. Cornwallis, 219 Mass. 226 

Pierce v. Equitable Life Ass. Co., 145 Mass. 56 

Walling v. Beers, 120 Mass. 548 

Harkness v. Hyck, 98 U. S. 476 

Creighton v. Kerr, 20 Wall. (U. S.) 551 

But see: Enfield v. Woods, 212 Mass. 547

As to excess of jurisdiction, the question can be raised at any time, Hill v. Moore, 224 Mass. 163, at 166 

Ensign v. Faxon, 224 Mass. 145, at 151 

Welch v. Boston, 208 Mass. 326 and may even be raised by the court of its own motion. 

Carroll v. Berger, 255 Mass. 132, at 134 and 135 

Boston Bar Association v. Casey, 227 Mass. 46, at 50 and cases cited 

Humphrey's Case, 226 Mass. 143 

Ensign v. Faxon, 224 Mass. 145, at 151 

Parkhurst v. Almy, 222 Mass. 27, at 32

Fourth National Bank v. Mead, 216 Mass. 521 

Comm. v. N.Y.C. & H. R. R.R., 206 Mass. 417, at 427 

Mercier v. Chace, 9 Allen 242, at 244 

Jochumsen v. Bank, 3 Allen 87 and cases cited 

Smith v. Rice, 11 Mass. 507, at 513 63

C. Parties 

Defect arising from the parties sued, or an absence of necessary parties, or a misjoinder or nonjoinder of parties or a want of proper interest in the plaintiff, as well as the incapacity of the parties, is the proper subject of a plea. When the objection is apparent on the face of the bill the correct practice is to raise such objections by demurrer. But when it does not thus appear the objection should be presented by plea. 

The plea not only should point out the defect in the parties but should also disclose the proper parties by name or description, if such information is within the knowledge of the defendant.

Case v. Minot, 158 Mass. 577 

d. Process

Defect in the process by which the defendant is made a party or brought to court may be raised by plea. 

e. Substance of the Bill 

When the substance or scope of the bill has a complete defence in the proof or disproof in a single fact or issue, a plea asserting or denying the particular fact is proper. The following are under this classification as affirmative pleas: (I) Confession and Avoidance (II) 

(III) 

Defendant as Becoming Purchaser for 

Value without Notice of Plaintiff's Claim 

Laches of the Plaintiff 

(IV) 

Payment 

(V) Release (VI) Statute of Frauds (VII) Statute of Limitations and as negative or anomalous pleas:

(VIII) 

Denial of Plaintiff's title, such as that the Plaintiff is not an heir or devisee. (IX) Denial of Relation and on which the bill is predicated, such as that the defendant is not a fiduciary, co-partner, corporation, executor or trustee. 

f. Pendency Of Another Suit For the Same Cause (I) Other Suit in Equity 

The plaintiff cannot prosecute two suits in equity for the same cause. The court will require the plaintiff to elect the suit with which he will proceed, instead of dismissing the one in which the plea is filed. 

Lewenstein v. Forman, 223 Mass. 325 

Sanford v. Wright, 164 Mass. 85 64

(II) Other Suit at Law 

The pendency of a bill in equity is not usually sufficient to sustain a plea in abatement to an action in law; 

Powers v. Heggie, 268 Mass. 233, at 239

Mattel v. Conant, 156 Mass. 418 

Colt v. Partridge, 7 Met. 570, at 576

See: ABATEMENT, pages 48 and 49 

and the converse is also true that the pendency of an action at law will not sustain a plea in equity without first giving the plaintiff an opportunity to discontinue or to elect between his law action and the suit in equity. If the plaintiff elects to continue with his suit in equity, he must discontinue his law action, for the court will not permit the defendant to be vexed by two suits for the same cause at the same time in the same jurisdiction. 

Sanford v. Wright, 164 Mass. 85

However, the court in dealing with the defendant's plea may order the equity suit dismissed unless within a stated time the plaintiff shall dismiss or discontinue his law action. 

Spear v. Coggan, 223 Mass. 156

Where the pendency of the prior action in law appears on the face of the bill advantage can be taken by demurrer, but the court will usually give the plaintiff a reasonable opportunity to elect between his law action and suit in equity. 

Spear v. Coggan, 223 Mass. 156

To raise this question a plea is the proper practice as “a motion to require the plaintiff to elect" is unknown to equity practice and is improper.

Corey v. Tuttle, 248 Mass. 135 (III) Foreign Suit 

A suit pending at law or in equity in a foreign jurisdiction is not ground for a plea to a suit begun in this Commonwealth, even if the parties are the same or the subject-matter and relief asked are identical. 

Holt v. Silver, 169 Mass. 435 

Radford v. Folsom, 14 Fed. 97 

g. Res Judicata 

When the plea rests upon the doctrine of res judicata, the bar of a judgment in another suit for the same cause of action between the same parties or those in privy with them, it extends not only to that which was pleaded or litigated in the earlier suit, but also to that which might have been pleaded G5

or litigated; and if the second suit is upon a different cause of action the bar of the earlier judgment is limited to that which was actually litigated and determined. 

Eastman Marble Co. v. Vermont Marble Co., 236 Mass. 

138, at 148 On such a plea the plaintiff may show that the decree for the defendant was entered solely on the ground that the action had been prematurely brought, such as that the purchase was made on credit which had not expired when the former suit or action had begun.

See: ABATEMENT, pages 53 and 54 h. Multifariousness 

If multifariousness does not appear from the face of the bill in which instance it would be a cause for demurrer, and if it can only be developed by presenting facts ether than those alleged in the bill, then such facts may be set up in a plea and relied upon as the defence of multifariousness. i. 6. Supporting Plea a. When Necessary to Accompany by Answer 

There are three instances in which a plea must be accompanied and supported by an answer: 

Grant v. Phoenix Life Ins. Co., 121 U. S. 105 (I) When the Bill Anticipates the Defence and States Facts to Avoid It 

If a plea is affirmative or pure, as where it sets up a release and then the plaintiff anticipating this defence alleges in his bill that the release was obtained from him by fraud and sets out the facts tending to prove such fraud and asks for discovery as to them, the defendant, if he pleads a release, should also in his plea deny the fraud and answer fully as to the facts charged in the bill in support of the fraud, not, confine his answer to the plaintiff's original claim, but of the alleged fraud in obtaining the release. 

Chapin v. Coleman, 11 Pick. 331 

66

So, also when the plaintiff anticipates that the defendant will claim that he is a bona fide purchaser for value without notice of the plaintiff's title or claim. If the plaintiff anticipates this defence and has charged the defendant with notice, setting forth the facts upon which he relies as evidence of notice, the defendant's plea must be supported by an answer to that part of the bill fully replying as to the facts upon which the plaintiff charges him with notice. 

Were the rule otherwise, the defendant, by a fraudulent release or purchase for consideration, could prevent a plaintiff from discovery of the facts and the defendant's fraud in obtaining the release or notice in acquiring the property. 

This rule applies to any ground set out in the bill by way of defeating anticipated defences. (II)

When the Bill Sets Forth Facts or Circum stances as Being Within the Defendant's 

Knowledge, Which Facts Are Necessary of Discovery to Establish the Plaintiff's Title. 

Whenever a bill, by way of proving the plaintiff's title, alleges any facts or circumstances as being within the defendant's knowledge, a plea denying the plaintiff's title must be accompanied by an answer and discovery as to such facts and circumstances. For example, when the bill asserts the title of the plaintiff as a partner or heir at law and avers that certain facts as to the plaintiff's title are within the defendant's knowledge. The defendant's plea, which denies the existence of the plaintiff's title as partner or heir, must be accompanied by an answer as to these facts and circumstances which are alleged to be within his knowledge and which he is required to disclose. 

(III) When the Bill Charges Fraud or Con spiracy

Whenever the bill specifically charges fraud or conspiracy, a plea to that part of the bill must be accompanied by an answer explicitly denying the fraud and conspiracy and replying categorically to the facts upon which the charge is founded. 7. 

Withdrawing, Waiving or Abandoning Plea

The plea may be expressly withdrawn, waived or abandoned, or any one of these things may be done constructively or by implication. Certain things have been held to effect a withdrawal, waiver or abandonment, such as: a. Filing an Answer Subsequent to the Plea b. Proceeding to a Hearing on the Merits of the Case 

Without Regard to the Plea 67

But other matters have been held not to constitute a withdrawal, waiver or abandonment, such as: c.

Arguing the Propriety of Issues and Temporary Injunction After a Plea has been Filed to the Jurisdiction of the Court 

Reynolds v. Missouri, Kansas & Texas Ry., 224 Mass. 379, at 388 

8. Determination and Disposition of Plea a. General Statement 

A replication to the plea is unnecessary. So also, a special replication, denying part of the matter of the plea and reasserting the substance of the bill, is inadmissible. 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 132

If the plaintiff insists that the plea is insufficient to bar the suit, whether true or not, the course is for the plaintiff to move to set it aside for insufficiency, which is much in the nature of a demurrer. 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 132 

Gen. Laws, c. 214, s. 14

Also, a plea is not demurrable. 

If the plea is insufficient in law the plaintiff should set the case down for hearing upon the sufficiency of the plea. If the plea is determined to be sufficient as matter of law the plaintiff may then be permitted by the court to take issue upon the plea and the truth of the facts set up in the plea will be heard

If the plea is determined insufficient as matter of law, the court may allow the defendant to make answer to the merits of the bill. 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 132 

Nougue v. Clapp, 101 U. S. 551 

Rhode Island v. Massachusetts, 14 Peters (U. S.) 210

If the plaintiff without attacking the sufficiency of the plea as matter of law takes issue on the plea, he admits its sufficiency in law as a reply to the bill and the hearing on the plea is limited as to whether or not the facts stated therein are true. b. Determining Sufficiency or Truth 

(I) Setting Aside or Striking Out 

If the plea is attacked by the plaintiff as being insufficient as matter of law, he should not move to set it aside or strike 68

it from the record, the proper practice is to set the case down for hearing upon the insufficiency of the plea. 

Dorsey v. Corkery, 227 Mass. 498, at 500 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 132 

(II) Setting Case Down for Hearing 

A case may be set down for hearing upon the plea for two purposes: 

First: Attack upon the sufficiency of the plea as matter of law.

This is in the nature of a demurrer to the plea and the hearing is confined to argument of counsel. If the court rules that the plea is sufficient its order is that the plea is "allowed" otherwise it is "overruled." 

As was said in Dorsey v. Corkery, 227 Mass. 498, at 500: "The plaintiff by setting the plea down for argument admitted the truth of all the facts stated in the plea. The inquiry thereupon is substantially the same as on a demurrer in an action at law. If held sufficient in point of law, the plea is overruled and the cause proceeds as if no such plea had been filed; but if held sufficient the plaintiff may take issue upon it, and if found for the defendant will determine the suit."

Duncan v. N. E. Power Co., 225 Mass. 155 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303 

Kennedy v. Creswell, 101 U. S. 641, at 644

Second: Hearing upon the truth of the facts set forth in the plea, which if found to be so, requires the entry "plea sustained," otherwise "plea disproved."

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503 

Berenson v. French, 262 Mass. 247 

Prunier v. Schulman, 261 Mass. 417

Westervelt v. Library Bureau, 118 Fed. 824, at 825 

The court can refuse to set down the case for hearing upon the sufficiency of the plea as matter of law and may postpone consideration of the attack upon the plea until the hearing of the merits of the case, but must save the benefit of the plea and its attack upon it to the respective parties. The court may also order the plea to stand for an answer or may overrule the plea without a hearing and give leave to the defendant to set up the same defences in the answer. 69

Superior Court Rule 28, (1932) 

Hancock v. Carlton, 6 Gray 39 

Pearce v. Rice, 142 U. S. 28 

Chisholm v. Johnson, 84 Fed. 384 

(A) Effect of 

When a plea is set down for argument upon its insufficiency the facts well pleaded are, for the purpose of the argument, taken to be true. This is the effect of the plaintiff's attack upon the plea for insufficiency as matter of law. 

Dorsey v. Corkery, 227 Mass. 498, at 500 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303

The hearing is then conducted substantially the same as on a demurrer, no facts are put in issue but the truth of all matters pleaded is assumed. 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303

Rhode Island v. Massachusetts, 14 Peters (U. S.) 210 

Hughes v. Black, 6 Wheaton (U. S.) 453, at 472

The sole question is whether as matter of law the facts alleged in the bill, which are not denied in the plea, are suf ficient to maintain the suit. 

Cole v. Wells, 224 Mass. 504, at 512 

Davidson v. Johnson, 16 New Jersey Eq. 112

If the plea is set down for hearing upon its merits the defendant is required to prove the facts set forth in his affirmative plea and the plaintiff is required to prove the facts set forth in the negative plea.

Reilly v. Selectmen of Blackstone, 266 Mass. 503 

Farley v. Kittson, 120 U. S. 303

This second hearing involves the introduction of evidence and the proof of facts and is not confined to argument of law. 

By setting the case down for hearing on the truth of the plea the plaintiff waives any question of the insufficiency of the plea. 

(III) Matters Considered 

When the plea is set down for hearing upon its sufficiency, the merits of the plaintiff's claim are not examined. The sole question before the court is the sufficiency of the plea to bar the suit. The allegations of the plea are taken to be true. 

Steads v. Course, 4 Cranch (U. S.) 403, at 413 70

Disposition of Suit

A fact found at the hearing on a plea is not open again on the answer. Such finding stands as to that fact throughout the case.

Tansey v. McDonnell, 142 Mass. 220

If the plea is held insufficient as matter of law, it is overruled and the cause proceeds as if no such plea had been filed. 

Newton v. Thayer, 17 Pick. 129, at 132

Supreme Judicial Court Equity Rule 10 (1926) provides that: "If a plea is overruled the defendant must answer within ten days or the bill will be taken for confessed." 

Prunier v. Schulman, 261 Mass. 417, at 419

But the court may allow an answer or other pleading to be filed under this rule. 

Prunier v. Schulman, 261 Mass. 417, at 419

Under Superior Court Rule 28, (1932) the plea must be filed with or as a part of the answer, but the court may allow the plea to be filed separately and may also permit additional pleadings after the plea has been overruled. 

Under the original equity practice when the plea was disproved on the facts the bill was taken for confessed, Kennedy v. Creswell, 101 U. S. 641 and also, when the plaintiff set the case down for hearing on the issues of fact raised by the plea without first having a determination of the legal sufficiency of the plea, if the truth of the plea is established, the bill was dismissed, regardless of whether the plea was insufficient as matter of law. 71

Dorsey v. Corkery, 227 Mass. 498

But under modern practice a defendant whose plea is overruled as matter of law or disproved as matter of fact, may be allowed to answer.

Supreme Judicial Court Equity Rule 10, (1926)

If the plea is held sufficient the plaintiff may take issue upon it and the fact will be tried in the usual way and if found for the defendant will determine the suit and the bill will be dismissed.
