H. 

CUSTODY AND MANAGEMENT OF ESTATE * 4. Engaging in Business a. General Rule

As a matter of law the estate of the testator will not be liable for debts incurred by executors or administrators in conducting the business as a financial adventure without proper authority. The liability descends upon the representative who has contracted such debts while carrying on the business without proper authority, and he in turn has no right of indemnity against the estate. 

Donnelly v. Alden, 229 Mass. 214 b. 

Limitations of Rule (I) General Statement 

There are three methods by which an executor or administrator can preserve his right of indemnity against the estate: (A) By applying to and receiving authority from the probate court; (B) By conducting the business in accordance with testamentary directions given in the will; (C) By conducting the business with the sanction of all partics interested in the estate, including creditors. 

Donnelly v. Alden, 229 Mass. 214 

Hines v. Levers and Sargent Co., 226 Mass. 109 

Gen. Laws, c. 195, s. 7 

(II) Authority from Court 

Gen. Laws, c. 195, s. 7, provides: "The probate court, upon such notice as it considers reasonable, may authorize an executor or administrator to continue the business of the deceased for the benefit of the estate for a period not exceeding one year." 

Donnelly v. Alden, 229 Mass. 114 

Hines v. Levers and Sargent Co., 226 Mass. 109 

(III) Testamentary Direction 

Where trustees who are authorized to carry on a business, contract debts, they are not only liable personally for the payment of them but the creditors may also resort to the trust fund, subject however to the rules of equity, as applicable to the facts and circumstances which may exist in any particular case. 

Mason v. Pomeroy, 151 Mass. 164

Leon Aronson assisted the editor in the preparation of this part of the main topic.

H. 4. - 1

(IV) Consent of All Parties Concerned 

An executor or administrator who, in a particular transaction, acts in good faith under the direction of all parties interested in the estate, in continuing and managing the business for the benefit of the estate, is to be protected when rendering his accounts in the probate court. He may prosecute or defend suits, compromise claims against the estate and business; and the personal representatives or creditors by whose request or assent it has been done, will not be permitted to charge him with maladministration. 

Poole v. Munday, 103 Mass. 174 

c. Liability for Debts (I) Where Continuance of Business Authorized A) General Statement 

Where executors or administrators carry on the business under the proper authority and contract debts, they are personally liable to the creditors for the payment of such debts, (unless there is a stipulation in the contract that the creditors will look only to the estate) but the executor or administrator has a right to be indemnified out of the estate. 

Howe v. Richardson, 186 Mass. 259 

(B) What Assets Liable 

Where the executor or administrator is authorized to carry on the business, all transactions relative to this venture, such as debts incurred, involve only the business assets, or the assets that were in the business at the time of the incurring of such debts, plus any assets that may have added during the continuance of the business. 

Mason v. Pomeroy, 151 Mass. 164 

(II) Where Continuance of Business Unauthorized 

If an executor or administrator carries on the business without proper authority, he does not bind the assets of the estate. All debts contracted by him while engaged in carrying out the business, even though it be for the purpose of enriching and benefiting the estate, become his personal debts, nor has he a right of indemnity against the estate. 

The burden is on all persons dealing with such administrator or executor, to ascertain from the probate records whether or not such representative has been authorized to carry on the business of the deceased. "As a matter of law the estate of the testator will not be liable for debts incurred by the executor or administrator in conducting the business as a financial adventure. Actual 

---

knowledge of all the facts is not necessary to charge the firm with notice of them." 

Hines v. Levers & Sargent Co., 226 Mass. 214 

Donnelly v. Alden, 229 Mass. 109 

(III) Where Business Carried on by Legatee 

If a testator bequeaths his business to a legatee who complies with the terms of the will and carries on the business for his personal benefit, the executor assumes no liability in allowing him to carry on the business, unless such liability can be fixed by the doctrine of estoppel.

American Tube Works v. Tucker, 185 Mass. 236 

d. Partnership 

Upon the death of one of the members of a partnership the firm is dissolved, and the representative has no more right to engage in the business of the partnership than he has to engage in an individual enterprise with the business carried on by the deceased as an entrepreneur (single owner). (I) Right to Become Partner with Survivor of Firm In the absence of an agreement of all the partners, the executors of a deceased partner have no right to become partners with the survivors of the firm, nor to interfere with the partnership business, save to represent the deceased for all purposes of accounting. 

In Washburn v. Goodman, 17 Pick. 519, there were four partners, including one T, under the name of Goodman, Saville and Kent. These three whose names constituted the firm designation, were the active members, and they took a lease of the premises used by the partnership, in their three names. T died and his administrator seeks to have the lease accounted for as partnership property and also seeks interest on T's share of the capital stock. 1 

It was said at page 525: "In regard to the stock belonging to the company at the dissolution by the death of T, it was rightfully in possession of the surviving partners, subject to disposition by sale, they being jointly accountable to the administrator of T for the amount of his interest therein... therefore in the settlement of the account it was right to charge the stock on hand at the death of T [to the surviving partners]. 

At page 526, it was further said, "The lease was taken by the active partners in their individual names, but for the use of the firm of which T was one. 

He therefore had a joint interest in it, and we see no reason why he should not have his proportion of its value,above what was paid by the lessor.' 

---

(II) Title to Firm Property (A) Rights Limited to Accounting 

If the deceased was a member of a partnership, the title to the firm property vests only in the surviving partner or partners, and the only interest which accrues to the administrator is the right to an accounting for the share of the deceased in the partnership assets after a final settlement of the partnership affairs. 

In Hewitt v. Hayes, 204 Mass. 586, at 591, it is said: "It follows that upon the death of W, B as the sole surviving partner at once became the owner of all the partnership property, and charged with the duty of winding up the affairs of the firm, turning its assets into money, and applying such money to the payment of its debts. . . . For this purpose he [surviving partner] was entitled to demand and receive from the defendants, the executors of the will of his deceased partner, whatever property of the firm might come into their hands." 

Hutchinson v. Nay, 183 Mass. 355 

Thayer v. Badger, Administrator, 171 Mass. 279 

In Bush v. Clark, 137 Mass. 111, it is said, at page 112: "When a partnership is dissolved by the death of one of the partners, the survivor becomes the owner of the personal property of the partnership. The representatives of the deceased partner have certain rights as against the survivor; the chief of these being the right of the representatives to have an account of the property, of the collection and application of it, and to receive any balance which may become due as the deceased's share of the net proceeds. The survivor is under corresponding obligations. It is his duty to collect the property, pay the debts, and pay the representatives whatever becomes due as the share of the deceased. But he holds the legal title to the property, pending the settlement of partnership business, and not as trustee. At law, his title is so absolute that, if he sues for a debt due the partnership, a debt due from him separately to the defendant may be set off. 

Holbrook v. Lackey, 13 Met. 132 "The property and assets of the firm were held by the defendant [surviving partner] as trust property. After paying the debts, it was his duty to account for and pay over to the plaintiff his share. If he used the property for his own benefit he is chargeable for all profits. If he has mingled the money of the firm with his own or neglected unreasonably to settle his accounts, he is properly chargeable with interest." 

H. 4.4

In Freeman v. Freeman, 136 Mass. 260, it was said at pages 

263 and 264: "This duty of sale is not limited to a disposition of so much of the partnership property as is required to pay debts. 

The surviving partner is bound to wind up the partnership and ordinarily to make sale of all the personal assets, and not only to pay the debts of the firm, but to distribute to the representatives of the deceased partner the share to which they may be entitled. This duty of the surviving partner may not be strictly that of a trustee, but it is analogous; and he is not allowed to derive a distinct and independent personal advantage, either directly or indirectly, from the use of the partnership assets, but he must manage and dispose of them with a single eye to the advantage of the partnership estate which he is to administer. This rule is universal in its application to fiduciary relation. It extends also to the duty of a surviving partner and he is bound to act in perfect fairness and good faith, according to the highest standards of honor, and with reasonable care and diligence, with reference to the decedent's interest. That which was partnership property before the dissolution continues to be so afterwards; and a sale of the whole personal property will ordinarily be enforced by a court of equity, and an amount ordered of profits made since the dissolution. The surviving partner is not allowed to divide this property in specie, or to take it himself at a valuation, or to have its value ascertained otherwise than by sale; but he must turn all the assets into an available and distributable form, so far as this can be done." 

Bush. Clark, 127 Mass. 111 

Dunlap v. Watson, 124 Mass. 305, at 307 

Bowen v. Richardson, 113 Mass. 293

Shearer v. Shearer, 98 Mass. 107, at 114 

In Dunlap v. Watson, 124 Mass. 305, it was said at pages 306 and 307: "It is clear that the services rendered in closing up the business was only that which was due from the defendant under the partnership agreement. In a qualified and limited sense the partnership is said to continue between the parties until its affairs are fully closed up, and the obligations of each to contribute his services without compensation continucs, unless changed by a new agreement." 

Schenkel v. Dana, 118 Mass. 236 

Washburn v. Goodman, 17 Pick 519 

Story on Partnership (6th ed.) sec. 325, at 321, and notes.

---

In Schenkel v. Dana, 118 Mass.

236, it was said at pages 238 and 239: "There is no occasion in this case to question the general rule of law relied on, that upon the dissolution of an ordinary mercantile partnership by death, the surviving partner is not entitled as a matter of law, in the absence of a special agreement, to be paid for his personal services in winding up the business and disposing of the assets. But this rule, in its practical application to the final settlement of partnerships must in equity be largely varied by the nature of the business carried on, the capital employed, the state of the accounts with the deceased partner, the necessity of continuing the business for the purpose of realizing the most from the assets and especially by the fact that such continuance is known and assented to by the legal representatives of the deceased partner. 

It is not the case where property of the deceased partner is used wrongfully without the knowledge or consent of his personal representatives. The defendant is to be regarded more like a trustee who has managed an estate for the benefit of another with his approval, and who is entitled to compensation when the cestui que trust seeks to avail himself of the benefits of such management. "Under the general rule above stated, all that can be required of the surviving partner is that he proceed at once to wind up the partnership and account with the legal representatives of the deceased partner. In the absence of any agreement he is entitled to no pay for his personal services in the strict discharge of this duty. But if, with the assent of the administrator of the deceased partner, he employs extra labor to finish existing contracts; if he enters upon new contracts, employing the machinery and property of the firm therein; then, to the extent of his personal services devoted to such extra work, he is entitled to compensation." 

In Leland v. Newton, 102 Mass. 350, it was said, at page 351: "When one of two co-partners dies the survivor should settle the estate, and account to the personal representatives of the deceased." 

(B) Statutory Provisions 

Acts of 1922, c. 486, s. 42, provide:

When any partner retires or dies, and the business is continued under any of the conditions set forth in section forty-one (1) (2) (3) (5) (6) or section thirty-eight (26) without any settlement of accounts as between him or his estate and the person or partnership continuing the H. 4.-6

business, unless otherwise agreed, he or his legal re sentatives as against such persons or partnership may the value of his interest at the date of dissolution ascertained, and shall receive as an ordinary creditor an amount equal to the value of his interest in the dissolved partnership with interest, or, at his option or at the option of his legal representatives, in lieu of interest, the profits attributable to the use of his right in the property of the dissolved partnership as against the creditors or the representatives of the retired or deceased partner, shall have priority on any claim arising under this section. (C) Propriety of Charges and Credits In Account of Surviving Partner 

(1) Personal Compensation 

Winding Up Business for The general rule is that where a partnership is dissolved by death of one of the partners the partner who winds up the business is not entitled to pay in the discharge of that duty, in the absence of special agreement to be paid for such services. But if, with the assent of the administrator of the deceased partner, he employs extra labor to finish existing contracts; if he enters upon new contracts, employing the machinery, patents, and property of the firm therein; then, to the extent of his personal services devoted to such extra work, he is entitled to compensation. 

Magullion v. Magee, 241 Mass. 360, at 370 (a) Where Profits Accrue 

During Continuance of Business Whole profits earned in the liquidation of a commercial partnership as a general rule belong to the firm without deduction for the services of the liquidating partner, under the rule in this Commonwealth the right to charge profits with compensation for the liquidating partner depends upon the particular facts of each case. 

Magullion v. Magee, 241 Mass. 360, at 370 

Thayer v. Badger, 171 Mass. 279

Ruta v. Coolidge, 146 Mass. 167 (2) Employment of Counsel 

The surviving partner is authorized to obtain advice as to his duties and to employ and pay counsel out of the assets, if necessary to collect and preserve them for the benefit of himself and the H. 4. - 7

estate. The right to charge for such services is analogous to that of executors, administrators and trustees. 

Loring v. Wise, 226 Mass. 231 

Hampden Trust Co. v. Leary, 186 Mass. 577, at 579 

Budley v. Sanborn, 159 Mass. 185, at 189 

Forward v. Forward, 6 Allen 494, at 497

He was not empowered to employ counsel to assert or protect his private interests adversely to the personal representatives or heirs of the deceased partner; such legal services should be borne by him individually. 

Magullion v. Magee, 241 Mass. 360, at 372 

Urann v. Coates, 117 Mass. 41, at 44 

Blake v. Pegram, 109 Mass. 541

Cases on how far surviving partner can employ counsel: 

Magullion v. Magee, 241 Mass. 360, at 371 and 372 

Loring v. Wise, 226 Mass. 231 

Hampden Trust Co. v. Leary, 186 Mass. 577, at 579 

Dudley v. Sandborn, 159 Mass. 185, at 189 

Forward et al v. Forward et al, 6 Allen 497 

(3) Liability of Surviving Partner for Profits or Interest 

In Robinson v. Simons, 146 Mass. 167, at pages 175, 176, and 

177, it was said: "If the accounts could have been settled at the death of the intestate, his representatives would have been entitled to receive the above-named amount of capital standing to his credit unless this was impracticable. "As a general rule, where a surviving partner continues to use the capital of a deceased partner in the business, the representatives of the latter, in the absence of any agreement to the contrary, have the election to demand either interest on the capital used or the profits earned by its use, the latter being accretions to the fund owned by them. There is, however no inflexible rule governing all cases, but each case depends upon its own circumstances and equities. "The rule which is to be applied must be deduced, in almost every case, from the particular circumstances of that very case; and Lord Eldon fully recognized the justice of making allowance for the skill and services of the surviving partners. "In most of these cases the rule applied was, that the profits should be divided according to the capital, after making allowances for profits earned by the personal activity, attention to business, skill, and services of the surviving partners. 

---

"We think a just rule to be deduced from the authorities is that, where there are no circumstances which render its application inequitable, the profits should be divided according to the capital, after deducting such share of them as is attributable to the skill and services of the surviving partner. 

When his good faith and fairness are not impeached, the most that the representatives of the deceased partner can justly demand is that he should account to them for their capital and, in addition, for whatever it has earned. This involves the necessity of inquiring how much of the profits is attributable to the services and skill of the surviving partners, and how much to the capital invested in the business. The latter portion of the profits shows what the capital has earned, and should rightfully be divided among the owners of the capital in proportion to their shares of the capital. It is clear, that, in applying this rule, any withdrawal or subtraction by the representatives of the deceased partner of any part of their capital would diminish pro tanto [to that extent] the proportion of the profits to which they are entitled." 

A liquidating partner is chargeable with interest on money overdrawn in excess of his share, and already due to the partnership for which he assumed responsibility and his proportion of the net loss.

In Crabtree v. Randall, 133 Mass. 552, at page 554, it was said: "As, if he mingles the funds of the firm with his own he may be obliged to pay interest thereon, it is equally reasonable he should do so when they consist of debts and liabilities due from him."

In Washburn v. Goodman, 17 Pick. 519, it was said at page 526. "As to interest: The survivors became indebted to Tucker's estate for the capital, on his death. Time should be allowed them to settle the affairs, collect and pay debts, after which they ought to be charged with interest. Eighteen months were allowed, during which time they are not charged with interest. We think the time fixed by the master for interest to commence is reasonable.”

If a partner dies a right to wind up the partnership concern and to collect the assets is by law vested in the surviving partner. 

Before the court will interfere and appoint a receiver, some breach or neglect of duty on his part must be established. H. 4. - 9

e. 

Compensation Amount of Fees 

(I) 

General Statement 

What was a reasonable fee for the services of an executor or administrator is a question of fact for the Probate Court. 

Taylor v. Trefrey, 1933 A. S. 783, at 784

An executor should not be allowed for services performed by others whom he employs. 

Taylor v. Trefrey, 1933 A. S. 783, at 784 

Bailey v. Crosby, 226 Mass. 492 

Newell v. West, 149 Mass. 520 

Blake v. Pegram, 101 Mass. 592, at 599 and 600

Lyman v. Conkey, 1 Met. 319 Statutory Provisions 

(III) 

Extra Allowances 

May v. Skinner, 149 Mass. 375 

Urann v. Coates, 117 Mass. 41 

(IV) Effect of Testamentary Provisions 

Provision for award by heirs.—Where the will provided that the executor's and trustee's compensation should be such as a majority of the heirs should award him, the executor was entitled only to the amount by the heirs, and not to a reasonable compensation under the statute. 

Bailey v. Crosby, 226 Mass. 492 

Fernald v. Gooch, 202 Mass. 408 

Little v. Little, 161 Mass. 188

Manning v. Am. Bd. of Foreign Missions, 8 Met. 566 (V) 

Effect of Agreement 

Usually in his account an executor may charge such fee as he and the beneficiaries have by special agreement agreed upon. 

Taylor v. Trefrey, 1933 A. S. 783, at 784 ("Fee as executor by special agreement.") 

Newell v. West, 149 Mass. 520

But a subsequent agreement for an additional fee, after one agreement has been made, is usually without consideration and unenforceable. 

Taylor v. Trefrey, 1933 A. S. 783, at 784

So, when the executor rests his claim to extra compensation upon a talk in which the sole beneficiary expressed her satisfaction with a total charge which included the extra fee by the accountant, and upon two unsealed writings signed by her in 1931, in the first of which she assented to that fee and in the second of which she agreed to it, Taylor v. Trefrey, 1933 A. S. 783, at 784 

Bailey v. Crosby, 226 Mass. 492 

Newell v. West, 149 Mass. 520, at 521 

Bowker v. Pierce, 130 Mass. 262 but no consideration whatever is shown for any such assent or agreement, and he is under duty as the salaried president of the corporation, the accountant owed a duty, as executor of the will, for the compensation which might be allowed him by the Probate Court, to use all reasonable efforts to liquidate the estate. 

The anxiety of the beneficiary to convert the stock into money did not justify an additional charge or furnish any consideration for her promise to allow one. 

Taylor v. Trefrey, 1933 A. S. 783, at 784 

Boston Bar. Assoc. v. Hale, 197 Mass. 423, at 437

The rule may be otherwise if the writings are assignments of a share of the estate. 

Taylor v. Trefrey, 1933 A. S. 783, at 784 

Security Bank of N. Y. v. Callahan, 220 Mass. 84, at 88 and 89

(b) Non-payment of Execution on Judgment 

Against Executor or Administrator in Official Capacity 

A failure to pay an execution issued on a judgment obtained against an executor or administrator in his official capacity, or to show sufficient goods or estate of the deceased to satisfy it, is prima facie a breach of the executor's or administrator's bond, and unless the affirmative defence which is initiated by a representative is made out, executors and administrators and their sureties are liable. 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 550 and 551 (A settlement made by executor personally for a sum less than the claim allowed by insolvency commissioners while appeal pending is based on valid consideration.) 

Harmon v. Sweet, 221 Mass. 587

The liability on the bond, therefore, is not absolute upon the prima facie breach, but is subject to the entry of a final decree in insolvency, although no recovery could be had on the bond before such a decree was entered, for the executor or administrator would be entitled to have an action on the bond continued until the question of the insolvency of the estate is ascertained, at least when the proceedings in insolvency are prosecuted with diligent 

Chamberlain v. Barrows, 1933 A. S. 547, at 550 and 551 

McKim v. Roosa, 183 Mass. 510, at 513

FIRES FIRES A. CITIES AND TOWNS 

1. Liability a. Negligence of Firemen 

A fireman is a public officer for whose negligence the city or town is not responsible. 

Deveney's Case, 223 Mass. 270 (Dependent) 

Woods v. Woburn, 220 Mass. 410 

Shelton v. Sears, 187 Mass. 455 

Fisher v. Boston, 104 Mass. 87

B. CONTRACTS 

1. Performance a. 

Instances Which Excuse Or Relieve (I) Work on Articles or Structures 

It is well settled that when work is to be done under a contract on a chattel or building which is not wholly the property of the contractor, or for which he is not solely accountable, as where reare to be made on the property of another, the agreement on des is upon the implied condition that the chattel or buildig shall continue in existence, and the destruction of it without the fault of either of the parties will excuse performance of the contract, and leave no right of recovery of damages in favor of either against the other: 

Butterfield v. Byron, 153 Mass. 517, at 519 

Gilbert & Barker Manuf. Co. v. Butler, 146 Mass. 82 

Eliot National Bank v. Beal, 141 Mass. 566, and cases there cited 

Lord v. Wheeler, 1 Gray 282 

b. Instances Which Do Not Excuse Or Relieve (I) Furnishing Labor and Materials or Construction of Chattels or Buildings 

It is well established law, that, where one contracts to furnish labor and materials, and construct a chattel or build a house on land of another, he will not ordinarily be excused from performance of his contract by the destruction of the chattel or building, without his fault, before the time fixed for the delivery of it. 

Butterfield v. Byron, 153 Mass. 517, at 519 

Wells v. Calnan, 107 Mass. 514 

Adams v. Nichols, 19 Pick. 275

Dermott v. Jones, 2 Wall. (U. S.) 1

When no provision is contained in the lease or agreement of tenancy that the landlord will change the premises to comply with fire hazard law or warrant that the premises will continue to be fit or usable for any particular purpose, then the failure of the landlord to make such alterations will not be a defense to an action for rent or use and occupation.

Particular Persons (A) General Statement

F. REAL PROPERTY 

1. Mortgages 

2. Sales a. Risk of Loss 

(I) Oral Agreement of Purchase 

Where the agreement of sale is oral and before it is executed by the delivery of the deed the house is destroyed by fire, the purchaser may recover back any deposit or purchase money which he has paid to the seller. As no deed has been given at the time of the fire the house is at the risk of the seller and the loss is his loss. 

The purchaser is not bound to accept a deed of the land only after the destruction of the building and he has a right to recover the purchase money or money paid on a consideration which has failed. 

Thompson v. Gould, 20 Pick. 134

But if the purchaser has occupied the premises up to the time of the fire intending to complete the sale, he is liable for rent as a tenant at will. 

Gould v. Thompson, 4 Met. 224

G. SALES 

1. Loss by Destruction of Chattel a. General Statement 

In Goddard v. Binney, 115 Mass. 450, the plaintiff agreed to build a buggy for the defendant and deliver it at a certain time. 

The defendant gave directions as to the style and finish of the buggy, and it was built in compliance with his directions and was

FIRES 

marked with his monogram. Before the buggy was finished the defendant caled to see it and in response to an inquiry of the plaintiff, asking if he might sell the buggy, replied that he, the defendant, would keep it. When the buggy was finished the plaintiff notified the defendant and sent him a bill for it. The defendant retained the bill and promised to see the plaintiff about it. 

The buggy was afterwards destroyed by fire while in the plaintiff's possession. The court said at pages 455 and 456: "It is well settled that as between the immediate parties, property in personal chattels may pass by bargain and sale without actual delivery. "If the parties have agreed upon the specific thing that is sold and the price that the buyer is to pay for it, and nothing remains to be done but that the buyer should pay the price and take the same thing, the property passes to the buyer, and with it the risk of loss by fire or any other accident. "The appropriation of the chattel to the buyer is equivalent, for that purpose, to delivery by the seller. "The assent of the buyer to take the specific chattel is equivalent for the same purpose to his acceptance of possession. "The property may well be in the buyer, though the right of possession, or lien for the price is in the seller. "There could in fact be no such lien without a change of ownership. No man can be said to have a lien, in the proper sense of the term, upon his own property, and the seller's lien can only be upon the buyer's property. It has often been decided that assumpsit for the price of goods bargained and sold can be maintained where the goods have been selected by the buyer, and set apart for him by the seller, though not actually delivered to him, and where nothing remains to be done except that the buyer should pay the agreed price. In such a state of things the property vests in him, and with it the risk of any accident that may happen to the goods in the meantime." 

Morse v. Sherman, 106 Mass. 430 

Macomber v. Parker, 13 Pick. 175, at 183 b. When on Seller

FIRE INSURANCE X. ACTIONS ON POLICY 

7. Parties a. Plaintiff h. Tenants in Common

Plaintiffs are the owners as tenants in common of a dwelling house which was damaged by fire. The question is: Can T. W. R. join with his co-owner, W. R.? It was held that the parole evidence showing that W. R. was acting for T. W. R. and intended to insure the interests of both plaintiffs was erroneously admitted. 

The record does not show any objection was made to its admission. But the introduction of this evidence does not take away the rights of the parties. The plaintiffs, therefore, cannot recover in this action, but W. R., on a proper amendment can recover to the extent of his interest. If this is done, a new trial as to amount of damages, is ordered.

Ritson v. Atlas Assurance Co., Ltd., 272 Mass. 73

FIXTURES AS BETWEEN A CONDITIONAL VENDOR AND PUR- CHASER FROM SUBSEQUENT MORTGAGEE WHO FORECLOSED. 

Gardner v. Buckley & Scott, Inc., 1932 A. S. 1367

Oil Burner and Oil Storage Tank Connected with Steam Heating 

System Were Personalty and Did Not Pass to Buyer

Purchaser at Foreclosure Sale. 

On May 20th, 1931, the plaintiff became the owner of a single dwelling house which contained an oil burner and oil storage tank. The plaintiff knew nothing of the circumstances attending their installation. The defendant claims the ownership of the burner and tank under a rental agreement or conditional bill of sale entered into on September 21, 1928, with a former owner of the house.

No notice of this rental agreement or conditional bill of sale was recorded in the registry of deeds.

Shortly after the execution of the agreement of rental or sale, the burner and tank were installed and connected with the steam system already in the house. 

The burner weighed 150 pounds, was five feet long and stood eighteen inches above the floor. It rested at one end on two iron legs which stood three feet outside of the steam boiler of the heating system and in front of it, and, at the other end, inside the boiler on an iron cradle resting on the floor.

The aper ture through which it passed into the steam boiler was closed by bricks, uncemented, placed around the burner and made air tight by a coating of asbestos over bricks and tubing. This asbestos coating was brittle. It could be broken by a kick, and be removed without damage to the building or boiler. The ash pit door and the grates of the steam boiler were removed to permit this adjustment. A single gas pipe dropped from the gas supply pipe of the house on the cellar ceiling to the burner. It could be removed by unscrewing at either end. A wire running through a galvanized conduit from a special cutout box on the house meter board connected the house electric supply with the burner. It could be removed at either end. The asbestos coating, the gas pipe and the electric wire were the only attachments of the burner to the real estate. 3

FIXTURES 

997 The oil storage tank was steel and cylindrical, weighed 175 pounds and was set upon the concrete cellar floor, resting on four steel legs and not fastened to the floor. It was connected with the burner by a pipe, which was not attached to the building and was removable by unscrewing. A fill pipe ran from the tank to outside the house through a hole drilled in the concrete cellar wall. This was removable by unscrewing. 

About May 7th, 1929, the former owner mortgaged the premises, which conveyed the land and buildings "together with all furnaces, heaters, gas and electric fixtures and all other fixtures of every kind now or hereafter installed in and about said premises, all of which it is agreed shall constitute and be treated as part of said realty." The mortgagee had no notice of the rental or sale agreement nor did the defendant have notice of the mortgage. 

The trial judge saw an oil burner of the type in question which, with a model fire box with brick and asbestos, was set up in court. 

The trial judge found, among other things, that the burner was a stock burner that would fit in any house where a burner of that size was needed, that it rested on but was not attached to the floor, and that it bore a plate with trade name upon it, but that neither the burner nor tank bore anything stating it to be the property of the defendant. He found and ruled, as mixed law and fact, that neither tank nor burner ever became part of the real estate, that both remained personal property; and he ruled that Gen. Laws, c. 184, s. 13, as amended, does not apply to either burner or tank as installed under the "rental or sale agreement." 

It was said, at pages 1370, 1371, 1372, and 1373: "The plaintiff's title depends upon whether the mortgagee, from whom he obtained his deed, had a right superior to that of the defendant in the burner and tank. "The mortgagee's right depends upon whether that equipment had become part of the real estate and lost its character as personal property. "If, at any time the mortgage was executed, this equipment was in fact and law part of the realty, title, in the absence of notice to the mortgagee of the agreement, passed by the

Southbridge Savings Bk. v. Mason, 147 Mass. 500.

The factors [which determine whether the property is realty or personalty] are well stated in 

Stone v. Livingston, 222 Mass. 192 [These factors are whether:] [a] The identity of the chattels had been lost; [b] [the chattels] could be removed without material injury to the real estate or to themselves; [c] [the chattels] were not specially designed for use upon the premises, were not peculiar in their pattern; and [d] [the chattels], when put in, were not intended to become part of the real estate, and were not annexed with an eye to a permanent increase in the value of the premises or to the readier adaptation of the premises for letting to tenants.

Gen. Laws, c. 184, s. 13, as amended by Statutes of 1929, c. 

261, does not apply [where the articles have not been wrought into or attached to the real estate but remain separable]. 

Lancaster Iron Works, Inc. v. Otter River Brick Co., 277 

Mass. 102

Mass. 289, at 391

This statute does not require that the articles shall be both wrought into and attached to the real estate, so as to require physical incorporation of the chattels with the real estate. 

Greene v. Lampert, 274 Mass. 386

There must be something more than [that the chattels are] annexed to the real estate by some tenuous connections. . . . There

FIXTURES 

must be something in the connection to indicate a bonding intended to secure permanent rather than temporary relationship between realty and the article in question. 

Sealing necessary to obtain a tight junction should not necessarily determine whether an attachment is or is not within the statute. 

Morrison v. Segal, 270 Mass. 292 (Stoves were personal property, although joined to real estate.)

The statute, Gen. Laws, c. 184, s. 13, is negative in nature. It enables a conditional vendor, by giving the notice for which it provides, to avoid a loss which otherwise might come to him from the operation of the law laid down in Clary v. Owen, 15 Gray, 522. 

Commercial Credit Corp. v. Gould, 275 Mass. 48 

Waverly Co-operative Bank v. Haner, 273 Mass. 477

Chattels which have never lost their character as personal property cannot be held against a conditional vendor by mortgagee, purchaser or grantee of the real estate where they are placed, unless they fall within the classes incorporated within Gen. Laws, c. 184, s. 13, as amended by Statutes of 1929, c. 261, and have been wrought into the real estate or attached to it in some manner intended to be permanent.

8. Valua

General Statement b. Market Value

In Gaucher v. Solomon, 279 Mass. 296, where the defendant sold real estate to the plaintiff, the defendant told the plaintiff that he, the defendant, had been in the real estate business long enough "to know what it was" and that the property was worth and had the market value of $18,000 and that he could get that amount for it, that he had dealt in real estate some time and knew what he was talking about. 

The court said, at page 298: "It has long been settled that false statements concerning the market value of property are held to be matters of opinion, judgment, or seller's talk, and do not afford any ground. for a claim of damages either in an action for false representations, or by way of recoupment in an action to recover the purchase money.""

Good Will 

In Reinherz v. Am. Piano Co., 254 Mass. 411, the court said, (a) false and fraudulent representation respecting the value of good will (is) manifestly a declaration of opinion, or, if not such, (is) within the protection of representations classified as dealers' talk. 

Deming v. Darling, 148 Mass. 504 "No sensible person could understand that the value of the good will sold, with its limitations, (is) other than problematical." e. Shares of Stock

In Butler v. Martin, 247 Mass. 169, where the defendant who was president, general manager and majority stockholder in active control of the business of a corporation, falsely represented

FRAUD to the plaintiff, who bought shares of its stock, that: (1) the corporation "had dollar for dollar in assets; that (2) the assets were enough to make the stock worth $130 a share; that (3) the stock was valued at $130 per share; (4) the stock was worth $130 as shown by the assets." 

The court said, at page 171: "The defendant's representation that the stock was worth $130 a share should be considered in connection with his knowledge, full management, and control of the corporation's affairs, and the statement, that he "had dollar for dollar in assets," and the finding, that he knew, "or ought to have known" that the machinery valued in the certificate of condition at $24,677.29 was in real value worth only $7500."

PARTICULAR SUBJECTS OF REPRESENTATION 

7. Value a. 

General Statement b. Market Value

Prima facie, a statement to an experienced dealer in an article as to the market value of the article he is asked to buy is dealer's talk on a subject about which the seller has a right to assume that the buyer will make up his mind for himself, the means of information being equally open to both. 

Lilienthal v. Suffolk Brewing Co., 154 Mass. 185, at 188 

Deming v. Darling, 148 Mass. 504 

Poland v. Brownell, 131 Mass. 138 

Manning v. Albee, 11 Allen, 520 at 522

But it may be otherwise where the buyer reasonably surrenders his judgment to the seller. 

Lilienthal v. Suffolk Brewing Co., 154 Mass. 185, at 188 

Whiteside v. Brawley, 152 Mass. 133

C. Extrinsic Facts Affecting Value 8. Cost of Property 

In Medbury v. Watson, 6 Met. 246, where the plaintiffs, wishing to purchase a tannery for the purpose of carrying on a joint business in the making and vending of leather, inquired of the defendant, if he could inform them where they could purchase such an establishment; that the defendant, intending to deceive and defraud them and to induce them to purchase a tannery in W., belonging to one T. and to give a much greater sum for it than it was worth, falsely asserted and affirmed to them, that he knew of such a tannery as they wanted, belonging to T. who was ready to sell it, and that it could be purchased for $4,000; being the same sum which said 

T. paid one J. for it; and that he would aid the plaintiffs in mak- 1

FRAUD 

ing the purchase; at the same time knowing that T. paid only $3,000 for it, and that it was not worth that sum at the time when T. purchased it, nor at the time of his (the defendant's) making this representation. The defendant wrongfully and deceitfully encouraged them to make the purchase, and pay for it a much larger price than it was worth, namely $4,000; and that the plaintiffs, confiding in his false assertions and affirmations, and believing them to be true, and being ignorant of the value of the property, made the purchase.

The court said, at pages 259-261: "But in actions on the case for deceit, founded upon false affirmations, there has always existed the exception, that naked assertions, though known to be false, are not the ground of action, as between vendor and vendee; and in regard to affirmations and representations respecting real estate, the maxim of caveat emptor has ever been held to apply. 

When therefore, a vendor of real estate affirms to the vendee that his estate is worth so much, that he gave so much for it, that he has been offered so much for it; such assertions, though known by him to be false, and though uttered with a view to deceive, are not actionable. They are the mere affirmations of the vendor, on which the vendee cannot safely place confidence, and will not excuse his neglect in not examining for himself, and ascertaining what the facts are, and what credit is to be given to the assertions. "But even this is qualified by one of the more ancient decisions. As when a vendor had falsely affirmed as to the amount for which the estate rented, and had induced a person to give a higher price for the estate in consequence of such false affirmation respecting the rent, there an action was held to lie, on the ground that it was a matter within his own knowledge, and the tenant might not disclose the amount of rent paid by him. 

Elkins v. Tresham, 1 Lev. 102 (Eng.): 1 Sid. 146 (Eng.) 

"And so fraudulent misrepresentations of particulars in relation to the estate, which the buyer has not equal means of knowing, and where he is induced to forbear inquiries that he otherwise would have made, are not to be viewed in the 2

FRA UD light of assertions gratis dicta; and therefore, when damage ensues, the party guilty of the fraud will be liable for the injury sustained. . . . the cases cited are those of false affirmation of the vendor to the vendee, where the maxim caveat emptor applies, and not those resting upon the false representations of a third person with regard to the value of the property. And the distinction between the two cases is marked and obvious. 

In one, the buyer is aware of his position, and he is dealing with the owner of the property whose aim is to secure a good price, and whose interest it is to put a high estimate upon his estate, and whose great object is to induce the purchaser to make the purchase; while in the other, the man who makes the false assertions has apparently no object to gain; he stands in the situation of a disinterested person, in the light of a friend who has no motive nor intention to depart from the truth, and who thus throws the vendee off his guard, and exposes him to be misled by the deceitful representations. [The action] would not have support . . ., if the false representations had been made by the vendor to the vendees. But the representations were made by a third person, apparently disinterested, and who proposed to aid the plaintiffs in making the purchase, and to procure the estate for them for a price which he stated he knew that it cost, and which he affirmed it was worth. Such false affirmations and representations, having been made by a third person, with the intent to defraud, . . . are actionable."

General Laws, Chapter 109A Acts of 1924, Chapter 147 Fraudulent Transfers of Real and Personal Property 

Uniform fradulent conveyance law.

Section 1. In this chapter "Assets" of a debtor means property not exempt from liability for his debts. To the extent that any property is liable for any debts of the debtor, such property shall be included in his assets. Definitions. "Conveyance" includes every payment of money, assignment, release, transfer, lease, mortgage or pledge of tangible or intangible property, and also the creation of any lien or incumbrance. "Creditor" is a person having any claim, whether matured or unmatured, liquidated or unliquidated absolute, fixed or contingent. "Debt" includes any legal liability, whether matured or unmatured, liquidated or unliquidated, absolute, fixed or contingent. Insolvency.

Section 2. (1) A person is insolvent within the meaning of this chapter when the present fair salable value of his assets is less than the amount that will require to pay his probable liability on his existing debts as they become absolute and matured. (2) In determining whether a partnership is insolvent within the meaning of this chapter there shall be added to the partnership property the present fair salable value of the separate assets of each general partner in excess of the amount probably sufficient to meet the claims of his separate creditors, and also the amount of any unpaid subscription to the partnership of each limited partner, provided the present fair salable value of the assets of such limited partner is probably sufficient to pay his debts, including such unpaid subscription. FRAUDULENT CONVEYANCES 

(a) When in exchange for such property or obligation, as a fair equivalent therefor, and in good faith, property is conveyed or an antecedent debt is satisfied, or (b) When such property or obligation is received in good faith to secure a present advance or antecedent debt in amount not disproportionately small as compared with the value of the property or obligation obtained. Conveyances

Section 4. Every conveyance made and every obligation incurred by a person who is or will be by insolvent. thereby rendered insolvent is fraudulent as to creditors without regard to his actual intent if the conveyance is made or the obligation is incurred without a fair consideration. Conveyances business.

Section 5. Every conveyance made without fair consideration when the person making it is engaged by persons in or is about to engage in a business or transaction, for which the property remaining in his hands after the conveyance is an unreasonably small capital, is fraudulent as to creditors and as to other persons who become creditors during the continuance of such business or transaction, without regard to his actual intent. Conveyances by a person about to incur debts.

Section 6. Every conveyance made and every obligation incurred without fair consideration when the person making the conveyance or entering into the obligation intends or believes that he will incur yond his ability to pay as they mature is fraudulent as to both present and future creditors. debts be- Conveyances made with intent to defraud.

(I) Statute with Penalty 

In Commonwealth v. Novak, 272 Mass. 113, the defendant was prosecuted on a complaint under Gen. Laws, c. 271, s. 1, which alleged that the defendant did unlawfully win by playing Poker $650. The defendant contended that the statute was contrary to the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution of the United States. Held that the statute does not deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, nor deny to any person within the jurisdiction of the Commonwealth the equal protection of its laws. The statute was enacted to prevent gambling, and the Legislature had the power to pass the statute in order to accomplish this purpose and as far as possible suppress the evil by providing that the defendant "shall forfeit double the value of such money" won by gaming.

(II) Fraudulent Conveyance C. Particular Persons 

(1) Husband and Wife

In Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, where the donor was indebted to the plaintiff in the sum of $1,620 for room, board and care of his mother-also the mother of the plaintiff, and being in good health, he went with his wife, the defendant, to two savings banks and transferred deposits therein, aggregating $3,971.68 in amount, from his name "to the joint name of himself and his wife with the right of survivorship." At that time the donor had no other property except his clothing. 

The judge found "that this transfer was made without consideration and was a gift to his wife; that the gift was not made with any intent to hinder, delay or defraud creditors and that this transfer did not make Michael insolvent." 

The court said, at page 456: "On these findings the transfer of the savings bank deposits was not a fraudulent conveyance within the provisions of Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 109A, dealing with such conveyances, but it would have been a fraudulent conveyance if the deceased was rendered insolvent thereby. (s. 4) "By statutory definition in Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.) c. 109A, a person is insolvent within the meaning of this chapter when the present fair salable value of his assets is less than the amount that will be required to pay his probable liability on his existing debts as they become absolute and matured (s. 2(1)), and the assets of a debtor as here used means property not exempt from liability for his debts. (s. 1)" 

The court said further, at page 458: "If the 'fair saleable value' of such interests of the deceased at the time they were created by the transfer was not less than the amount of his indebtedness the transfer would not render him insolvent. Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 109A, s. 2. 

Though these interests became of little value to him by reason of his death less than four months after the transfer, leaving his wife surviving, we cannot say on the basis of facts found

GIFTS 

and matters of common knowledge that the judge would have been plainly wrong in finding that at the time of the transfer they were worth not less than the amount of his indebtedness. "If such a tenancy was created the deceased, at any time during the joint lives of himself and his wife, could have severed the tenancy and withdrawn his share of each deposit and his wife could have withdrawn only her share thereof. 

Bernatavicius v. Bernatavicius, 259 Mass. 486 

Marble v. Treasurer & Receiver General, 245 Mass. 504, at 509 "His interests in such deposits were liable for his debts. 

See Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 167, s. 14; c. 214, s. 3(7); c. 223, ss. 102-105; c. 236, s. 1;

R. H. White Co. v. Lees, 267 Mass. 122 

Ames v. Chandler, 265 Mass. 428, at 433 

Hayden v. Binney, 7 Gray, 416 "And they could have been found to have had a value at the time of the transfer not less than the amount of his indebtedness." 

The court said, at page 459: "Even if the contracts with the banks created such a joint ownership of the deposits with right of survivorship as was considered in 

Johnson v. Nourse, 258 Mass. 417, at 419 and 420 

Marble v. Treasurer & Receiver General, 245 Mass. 504 where, during the joint lives of the husband and wife, either of them could have withdrawn the whole or any part of these deposits on his or her individual receipt and disposed of the money on his or her individual account, ... the transfer did not render the deceased insolvent. At any time during the joint lives of the deceased and his wife the deposits, if not previously withdrawn, could have been attached in a suit against the deceased and, since the wife could show no superior title thereto, could have been held for his indebtedness."

R. H. White Co. v. Lees, 267 Mass. 112 

Samuels v. Charles E. Fogg Co., 258 Mass. 402, at 406

(B) Husband and Wife 

The husband donor makes a present gift to his wife, not of the deposits themselves but of such interests therein as are implied fro mthe terms of deposit upon which they were held by the banks. Such a gift is effected by the banks entering into new contracts of deposits with the donor and his wife, in substitution for the prior contracts of deposit with the donor, if the donor intends that result. 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 456 and 457 

Chippendale v. North Adams Savings Bank, 222 Mass. 499

This is true even if the savings bank books were never delivered to the wife. 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 456 and 457 

Barnes v. Chandler, 277 Mass. 395 

Rockefeller v. Davenport, 277 Mass. 105 

Holyoke National Bank v. Bailey, 273 Mass. 551 

Perry v. Leveroni, 252 Mass. 390 

Battles v. Millbury Sav. Bk., 250 Mass. 180, at 187 and 188 And the incapacity of a married woman to contract with her husband (see Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 209, s. 2); 

Boland v. McKowen, 189 Mass. 563, at 565 would not stand in the way of such a gift, for no contract between the deceased and his wife would be required. 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 456 and 457 

Brown v. Brown, 174 Mass. 197 (2) Tenancy by Entirety

The interests of the husband, donor, and his wife, donee, in each savings bank deposit, implied from the terms of deposit, obviously constitute some kind of joint ownership with right of survivorship. 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 457

Joint ownership of real or personal property with a right of survivorship created by a transfer to husband and wife is pre-

GIFTS 

sumably a tenancy by entirety, though an ordinary joint tenancy or some other form of joint ownership by them could be created if the intention to do so clearly appeared. 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 457 

Ames v. Chandler, 265 Mass. 428, at 431 and 432 

Woodard v. Woodard, 216 Mass. 1, at 2 

Hoag v. Hoag, 213 Mass. 50, at 53 and 54

The language of the contracts of deposit, that each deposit is transferred by the deceased "to the joint name of himself and his wife with the right of survivorship" is apt for the creation of a tenancy by entirety. 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 457

These words taken in their natural sense describe a tenancy in a deposit such that, as in the case of a tenancy by entirety, nothing could be drawn from the deposit "except upon the joint order or receipt of the two during their joint lives." 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 457 

Marble v. Treasurer & Rec. Gen., 245 Mass. 504, at 509

If husband and wife take by contracts with the banks the transaction is not open to the objection that a husband cannot convey to himself and his wife an estate by entirety. 

Ames v. Chandler, 265 Mass. 428, at 430 and 431 

Brown v. Brown, 174 Mass. 197 

Gen. Laws (Ter. Ed.), c. 209, s. 3

The interests of the husband donor in the deposits, if he is a tenant by entirety, are liable for his debts. 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 457 

Licker v. Gluskin, 265 Mass. 403, at 406 and 407 

Raptes v. Pappas, 259 Mass. 37 

Phelps v. Simons, 159 Mass. 415

The interest of the donor husband in each deposit is the entire income thereof during his life with the possibility of absolute title thereto if he should survive, while his wife's interest is merely the possibility of absolute title if she survives. 

Splaine v. Morrissey, 1933 A. S. 455, at 457 

Licker v. Gluskin, 265 Mass. 403, at 406 

Raptes v. Pappas, 259 Mass. 37, at 39 

Phelps v. Simons, 159 Mass. 415, at 418

Presumptions and Burden of Proof General Statement Capacity to Make or Take Gift (D) Relation of Parties 

In Ryder v. Donovan, 1933 A. S. 779, where in 1901 a husband died, intestate, leaving his widow, the plaintiff, then fiftythree years old, and their only child, then nineteen years old, the administrator of his estate settled his final account and turned over to them cash and corporate stock upon which they received dividends until the corporation was liquidated in 1929, besides dividends in liquidation in 1929. The daughter worked for the corporation for some years prior to 1929. In addition, the husband left them real estate which they sold in 1924. The plaintiff had one third, and the daughter two thirds, of the estate. 

The daughter and her mother lived together at all times. 

Their chief interest and concern in life was the welfare of each other. There was never any fraud, concealment or want of harmony between them. Soon after the death of the husband father, the daughter, with the consent of her mother, took charge of all their business affairs. Practically all the money received from the estate, from the sale of property derived from the father, and from the income of investments, was deposited in the name of the daughter. Almost all investments, whether in savings banks, stocks, bonds, real estate or jewelry, were made in her name. 

The income of all investments was used by her to defray the living expenses of herself and her mother and no record of payments was kept. There was no agreement that the mother should have any specific interest, legal or equitable, in any of the investments made. The mother apparently knew everything that was done, and was perfectly satisfied with whatever her daughter did.

In 1929, the daughter became seriously ill with cancer. The

GIFTS 

plaintiff knew that the daughter was about to die, knew that by an earlier will the daughter had given her entire estate for the benefit of the plaintiff for life with remainder to charity, suggested the making of the daughter's last will for the purpose of extending the benefit of the remainder to certain relatives in addition to charity, and never asked any accounting or division of the property known to the plaintiff to be standing in the name of the daughter. The daughter's last will, executed in 1929, appointed the defendants executors, and gave the entire estate to trustees for the benefit of the plaintiff for life, with power in the trustees to use the principal for her support if needed, and with remainder to various persons and charities. The daughter died May 15, 1920.

Thereafter, with the intention of benefiting at her own death one or more of her relatives and prospective legatees who have been closely associated with her since the death of her daughter, the plaintiff, then eighty-two years old, brought this suit for an accounting of the property of the plaintiff received many years ago by the daughter. 

Justice Lummas said, at page 782: "We think the proper inference is that the plaintiff made a gift of the property to her daughter. The relations of the plaintiff and her daughter, the natural expectation that the daughter would be the survivor, the acquiescence of the plaintiff for so many years in a use of the property that renders impossible the untangling and division of it on any certain basis, Simon v. Sleinis, 270 Mass. 465, at 470 and the failure of the plaintiff even when the death of her daughter was imminent to ask any accounting or to make any claim lead us to the conclusion that the plaintiff made a gift to her daughter of all the plaintiff's property turned over to the daughter."

GOOD WILL 

A. 1. 

DEFINITIONS 

Massachusetts

GOOD WILL 

The words "good will," like many other trade terms, may have different meanings dependent upon the connection in which they are used and the purpose intended to be accomplished. They may mean only the advantages of a particular location for attracting business and the expectation that former customers will continue to resort there. 

Martin v. Jablonski, 253 Mass. 451, at 456 and 457 

Bassett v. Percival, 5 Allen, 345, at 347

They may include in addition to these factors all that goes with a business in excess of its mere capital and physical value, such as reputation for promptness, fidelity, integrity, conduct of its affairs, solicitude for the welfare of customers and other intangible elements which contributed to successful commercial adventure. 

Martin v. Jablonski, 253 Mass. 451, at 456 and 457 

Angier v. Webber, 14 Allen, 211, a! 215

When the nature of good will as a part of a transaction has been the subject of discussion and mutual understanding between the parties, the particular sense in which those words were used may be shown by parol. 

Martin v. Jablonski, 253 Mass. 451, at 456 and 457

The practice of dentistry, which depends for its success on personal qualities and professional skill, has no good will that arises merely from the place where it is carried on. 

Wightman v. Wightman, 223 Mass. 398 

In , the court said, at page 297: "In a mercantile partnership the sale of the good will conveys an interest in a commercial business, the trade of which may be largely, if not wholly, dependent upon locality, and the right which the vendee acquires under such 1

GOOD WILL 

a purchase is the chance of being able to retain the trade connected with the business where it has been conducted. 

Webster v. Webster, 180 Mass. 310, at 316 

Bassett v. Percival, 5 Allen, 345 "But in a partnership for the practice of dentistry, the personal qualities of integrity, professional skill and ability attach to and follow the person not the place." 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175

Good will is the advantage or benefit which is acquired by an establishment beyond the mere value of the capital stock, funds or property employed therein, in consequence of the general public patronage and encouragement which it received from constant or habitual customers on account of its local position, or from celebrity or reputation for skill or affluence or punctuality, or from other accidental circumstances or necessities, or even from ancient partialities or prejudices. 

Munsey v. Butterfield, 133 Mass. 492, at 494 

As was said by Chief Justice Bigelow in Angier v. Webber, 14

Allen, 211, at 215, in language applied to a sale by one member of a firm to another, but equally applicable to a sale to a stranger, (Goodwill is) "the benefit or advantage which had accrued to the firm, in addition to the value of their property, derived from their reputation for promptness, fidelity and integrity in their transactions, from their mode of doing business, and other incidental circumstances, in consequence of which they had acquired general patronage from constant and habitual customers."

In Griffith v. Kirley, 189 Mass. 522, it was said, at page 527: "Under such a sale the good will which has been sold 'is nothing more than the probability, that the old customers will resort to the old place'. 

To hold otherwise would be to hamper a man in his future actions as to his lawful business in a matter in which he has made no covenant, and would be wholly unreasonable." 2

GOOD WILL 

In Rosenberg v. Adelson, 234 Mass.

488, it was said, at page 490: "The probability that the old customers will resort to the old place,' that the concern will continue to receive the patronage which has been built up by reason of its location, the quality of the goods and service there furnished, the skill and solicitation of the former owner, is the essence of that good will." 

2. United States

Good will is only an incident as connected with a going concern or business having locality or name, and is not susceptible of being disposed of independently. 

De La Vergne Co. v. German Inst., 175 U. S. 40 

Metropolitan Bk. v. St. Louis Dispatch Co., 149 U. S. 436

As was said in the last cited case, at page 446: "Undoubtedly, good will is in many cases a valuable thing, although there is difficulty in deciding accurately what is included under the term. It is tangible only as an incident, as connected with a going concern or business having locality or name, and is not susceptible of being disposed of independently. Mr. Justice Story defined good will to be 'the advantage or benefit, which is acquired by an establishment, beyond the mere value of the capital, stock, funds or property employed therein, in consequence of the general public patronage and encouragement which it receives from constant or habitual customers, on account of its local position, or common celebrity, or reputation for skill or affluence, or punctuality or from other accidental circumstances or necessity, or even from ancient partialities or prejudices'." 

Story, Partnership, sec. 99

In Menendez v. Holt, 128 U. S. 514, the court said, at page 522: "Good will was defined by Lord Eldon, in Cruttwell v. 

Lye, 17 Ves. 335, at 346, to be 'nothing more than the probability that the old customers will resort to the old place,' but Vice-Chancellor Wood in Churton v. Douglas, Johns (H. R. V.) 174, at 188, says it would be taking too narrow a view of what is there laid down by Lord Eldon, to

GOOD WILL 

confine it to that, but that it must mean every positive advantage that has been acquired by the old firm in the progress of its business, whether connected with the premises in which the business was previously carried on, or with the name of the late firm, or with any other matter carrying with it the benefit of the business. "It may be that where a firm is dissolved and ceases to exist under the old name, each of the former partners would be allowed to obtain 'his share' in the good will, so far as that might consist in the use of trademarks, by continuing such use in the absence of stipulations to the contrary; but when a partner retires from a firm, assenting to or acquiescing in the retention by the other partners of possession of the old place of business and the future conduct of the business by them under the old name, the good will remains with the latter as of course." "Good will" consists largely of reputation for competence, honesty, and fair dealing, but its value is in attracting customers. and not in securing credit. Payments made by a store to its former creditors for purpose of restoring the store's credit ratings held not in the nature of purchase of "good will." 

Harris Co. v. Lucas, 48 F. (2d) 187, at 189 "Good will" is the favor which the management of a business wins from the public. 

Seneca Hotel v. U. S., 42 F. (2d) 343, at 344

The good will of a business comprises these advantages which may enure to the purchaser from holding himself out to the public as succeeding to an enterprise which has been conducted in the past with the name and repute of his predecessor. 

Knoedler v. Boussod, 46 Fed. 465, at 466 

3. Other Jurisdictions a. Alabama "Good will," as applied to cafe business, is lure of a place for the public seeking such service, arising from name, location reputation, service, general atmosphere, including the effect of a crowd of pleased customers, and the habit of going there. 

Collas v. Brown, 211 Ala. 443

GOOD WILL 

b. Georgia

Good will is the advantage which is acquired by an establishment beyond a mere value of the property employed therein, in consequence of the general public patronage and encouragement received from habitual customers from local position, reputation, or other accidental circumstances. C. 

Armstrong v. Atlantic Ice Corp., 141 Ga. 464 

Illinois

The good will in a partnership may be defined as every possible advantage acquired by the firm in carrying on its business, whether connected with premises, name or other matter. 

Farwell v. Huling, 132 Ill. 112, at 119 d. Louisiana "Good will" is the favor which the management of a business wins from the public and the probability that old customers will continue their patronage and resort to the old place, and is not attached exclusively to the person but chiefly to the place of business. 

Rapides Grocery v. Grant, 174 La. 1083

Liquidators of Nicholson Pub. Co. v. Upton, 152 La. 270 

Good will is an advantage or benefit which is acquired by business establishments beyond the mere intrinsic value of the capital stock. It is the general public patronage and encouragement which a business receives from its customers on account of its local position. It is the subject of value and price, and of bargain and sale, though intangible. But in order to be conveyed, mention of it must be made in the act of sale. 

Vonderbank v. Schmidt, 44 La. Ann. 264 e. Maine "Good will" is the probability that the old customers will resort to the old place.

Kennebec Water Dist. v. Waterville, 97 Me. 185 

f. Michigan "Good will" indicates that value which inheres in fixed and favorable consideration of customers arising from established and well-conducted businesses.

GOOD WILL 

"Good will" of business is based on prospective profits to result from voluntarily continued patronage of public. 

Colton v. Duvall, 254 Mich. 346 

Chittenden v. Witbeck, 50 Mich. 401 g. New York

There cannot be a "good will," strictly so called, of a business which depends for its existence upon the professional qualities of the person who carries it on. 

Masters v. Brooks, 117 N. Y. Supp. 585, at 589 "The good will is property which may go to enhance the value of that to which it is legitimately incident. It has relation to the place where business has been conducted.” h. 

Meier v. Wilkins, 44 N. Y. Supp. 274, at 278 

North Carolina

The good will of a trade or business exists in a professional as well as a commercial business, subject to the qualification that it has no local existence, but attaches to the person of the professional man, and when sold the vendor may not thereafter solicit his former customers to deal with him, and not with his vendee. It does not, however, include a covenant by the vendor not to re-engage in the same business in the same locality in competition with his vendee. 

Faust v. Rohr, 166 N. C. 187 

i. Vermont 

The good will of a business is not the business, but is one result springing out of it. It would be too narrow to construe the word "business" to be the good will of the business. j. 

McGowan v. Griffin, 69 Vt. 168 

Wisconsin

Good will varies with the custom of the general trade and the character or methods of the particular business. An early definition by Lord Eldon is "the probability that the old customers will resort to the old place." This involved the ancient idea that good will inhered in the premises where the business was con-

GOOD WILL 

ducted. This is too limited for modern kinds or methods of business. The habit of people to purchase from a certain dealer or manufacturer, which is the foundation for any expectation that purchasers will continue, may depend on many things besides place. Confidence in the quality of the goods, in the facilities of the establishment to fill orders promptly, or in the personal integrity or skill of a dealer or manufacturer, familiarity of the public with a designating name for the product, and probably many other circumstances, might be mentioned as illustrative. The good will is a sort of beaten pathway from the seller to the buyer, usually established and made easy of passage by years of effort and expense in advertising, solicitation and recommendation by traveling agents, exhibition tests, or displays of goods, often by acquaintance with local dealers who enjoy confidence of their own neighbors, and the like. B. 

Rowell v. Rowell, 122 Wis. 1

DISTINCTIONS 

Distinguished from "going value" or "going concern value.”

In Des Moines Gas Co. v. Des Moines, 238 U. S. 153, it was said, at pages 163 and 164: "The element of 'good will' as applied to the ordinary merchant or manufacturer dealing with the public generally is not considered in estimating the 'going value' of complainant's plant. It cannot be considered in a public utility like the one in question in this case, because the complainant has a monopoly of the business in which it is engaged in the city of Des Moines, and those who desire to use its product must buy of it. But there is a great difference even in a monopoly which has a business already developed and one that must develop it. (Where the business of a plant is already developed.) There is no question that such a plant has a 'going value,' because it is a money maker from the start. 

And at page 165: "That 'good will,' in the sense in which that term is generally used as indicating that element of value which inheres in the fixed and favorable consideration of customers, arising 7

GOOD WILL 

from an established and well-known and well-conducted business, has no place in the fixing of valuation for the purpose of rate making of public service corporations of this character, was established in 

Willcox v. Consolidated Gas Co., 212 U. S. 19, at 52 

'Going value,' or 'going concern value,' i. e., the value which inheres in a plant where its business is established, as distinguished from one which has yet to establish its business, has been the subject of much discussion in ratemaking cases.
