GOOD WILL GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS 

Nature

D. 1. a. 

General Statement 

An agreement never to engage in the business of manufacturing or selling a certain kind of machine, even though unlimited in time and space, is valid if it is coupled with the sale of a business and is necessary to give the purchaser what he has bought, and therefore such an agreement can be implied as a necessary part of the sale of the good will of a business. b. 

Marshall Engine Co. v. New Marshall Engine Co., 203 

Mass. 410, at 424

Adherence to Business, Name, Place or Property 

A person who sells the good will of a small grocery store in the south end of Boston may set up a small grocery store in the north end of the same city. Customers of small grocery stores are those living in the immediate neighborhood, and a similar store in another locality would not affect the rights acquired by the purchaser of the good will of the first store. 

Wightman v. Wightman, 223 Mass. 398 

Marshall Engine Co. v. New Marshall Engine Co., 203 

Mass. 410 

Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 493 

Gordon v. Knott, 199 Mass. 173 

George G. Fox Co. v. Glynn, 191 Mass. 344 

Griffith v. Kirley, 189 Mass. 522 

Moore v. Rawson, 185 Mass. 264 

Wilcox v. Consolidated Gas Co., 212 U. S. 19

A person cannot use his own name in a competing business after selling good will with the right to use that name. 

Gaines v. Hake, 247 Mass. 88 

Rosenberg v. Adelson, 234 Mass. 488 

But see: Batchelder v. Batchelder, 220 Mass. 42

In Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 493, it was said, at pages 498, 499 and 500: "The right to use the firm name, for the purpose of designating the business carried on by a purchaser as a continua-

GOOD WILL 

tion of that done by the old firm, passes with a sale of the good will. This is an exclusive right. The limitations upon its exercise are only such as are necessary to protect the rights of the partners or others. Such a limitation is expressed in 

R. L. c. 72, s. 5. The purchaser has no right to use the name in such a way as to indicate that the business is then being conducted by persons who have no connection with it. Each member of the old firm, like everybody else, has a right to use his own name in a new business, either alone, or with the names of others who are associated with him. But after a sale of the good will, no one but the purchaser can lawfully use the firm name as an indication that his business is a continuation of that of the old firm. 

Lothrop Pub. Co. v. Lothrop, Lee & Shepard Co., 191 

Mass. 353, at 355 "A convenient way of using the firm name by a purchaser of the good will, if rights of third persons are involved, is by advertising as the successor to the former firm. The statute permits this. 

Martin v. Bowker, 163 Mass. 461 

Sohier v. Johnson, 111 Mass. 238 

See also:  "Such a use of the name implies that the business continued by the successor retains the valuable and attractive features which it possessed under the former proprietor. 

It implies that everything that enters into the good will of the business continues in it, so far as it can in any business which is wound up by legal proceedings in the life-time of the partners. .. "It often happens, on the dissolution of a partnership and the formation of a new one which purchases the good will and continues the business, that the former firm name is continued, without anything to indicate a change in the partnership. All that this legitimately means, or can mean, is that the new firm is the successor to the old one, continuing the same kind of business and enjoying its good will. 

If it purported to mean that there had been no change in 10

GOOD WILL 

the partnership, it would be, to that extent, a fraud upon the public. A purchaser of the good will of a business sold by order of a court gets a right to the exclusive use of the firm name in the only way in which such a name can ever be used legitimately, as between a new firm or a new proprietor and the public, namely, to show a direct succession to the business, with all its valuable features." 

(I) Dentist's Practice 

In the practice of dentistry the "good will," i. e., the personal qualities of integrity, professional skill, and ability attach to the person and not the place. 

Shong v. Shee, 254 Mass. 366 (Physician) 

Wightman v. Wightman, 223 Mass. 398, at 402 

Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 492 

, at 298 

 (II) 

Distinctive Visual Appearance 

In George G. Fox Co. v. Glynn, 191 Mass. 344, it was said, at page 349: "This good will is connected with and dependent upon the use of the name 'Creamalt' and the combination of features in the manufacture of the bread which give it a distinctive visual appearance unlike that of any other bread on the market. These indicate the place of manufacture of the loaves as they are sold, and give them a peculiar value in the market. The right to have the benefit of the reputation of its products, which are designated as above, is important to the plaintiff, and it is a right of property which the courts will guard as carefully as it would visible, tangible property." 

Again, at page 351: "The foundation of the plaintiff's right is the fact that the combination of name, size, shape and condition of surface, producing a peculiar visual appearance, were all adopted by the plaintiff when not in use by any one else, and are such a combination as no one else needs to use. 

The shape 11

GOOD WILL 

is found to be unusual, and uneconomical for cutting. The general right of the defendants, to use any size or shape or condition of surface that they choose does not give them a right to adopt a combination of these, which will mislead the public, to the plaintiff's detriment and their own advantage."

C. Termination

So far as dependent upon locality or name, good will may become extinct or rendered less valuable by the termination of the right to continue to occupy the premises, or the loss of the right to do business under the name theretofore used. 

Webster v. Webster, 180 Mass. 310 

2. Ownership 3. Valuation

No rigid and unvarying rule for the determination of the value of good will has been laid down by the courts. 

Moore v. Rawson, 185 Mass. 264

Elements of value. The length of time that the firm has been in existence, the nature and character of its business, the fact whether it had been successful or unsuccessful, the average amount of the net profits, the probability of the continuance of the business under the same name without competition from the retiring partner, are some of the elements that may enter into the value of good will. 4. 

Moore v. Rawson, 185 Mass. 264

Miscellaneous Matters 

It has been doubted whether the good will of professional men or firms, which is supposed to be entirely personal, depending upon the trust and confidence which persons may repose in their integrity and ability, is the subject of sale and transfer. Such should be limited in time. 

Batchelder v. Batchelder, 220 Mass. 42 

Martin v. Bowker, 163 Mass. 461 

Russia Cement Co. v. LePage, 147 Mass. 206 12

GOOD WILL E. SALE, TRANSFER OR OTHER DISPOSITION 

1. 

General Statement 

The sale of good will bars the opening of a competing business. 

Marshall Eng. Co. v. New Marshall Eng. Co., 203 Mass. 410 

Old Corner Book Store v. Upham, 194 Mass. 101 

United Shoe Machine Co. v. Kimball, 193 Mass. 351 

Anchor Elec. Co. v. Hawkes, 171 Mass. 101 

Gamewell Co. v. Crane, 160 Mass. 50 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175

A barber, who sold to the plaintiff a barber shop, including good will, and agreed "not to engage in the barber business either as an owner or part owner, for a term of five years," was enjoined from working not only as proprietor, member of a partnership or shareholder, but also as an employee or voluntary assistant in the barber shop three hundred feet from the plaintiff's shop. 

Ruggiero v. Salome, 248 Mass. 237

Where a person sells to another all his property used in the business, and its interest and good will, and agrees in writing not in any manner to do anything which should in any wise impair or injure said interest or good will, such a stipulation in relation to the good will is not an undue restraint of trade. The doctrine is now well settled that a partial restriction on carrying on a trade or business in a particular locality is not open to any objection on the ground of illegality, as violating the rules of sound public policy. 

Angier v. Webber, 14 Allen, 211

However, where the plant and good will of a newspaper were mortgaged and thereafter sold subject to the mortgage, and the purchaser consolidated the newspaper with another under a similar but not identical name, and in the course of carrying on business gradually used up the mortgaged plant and substituted a new plant, and continued business for eight years, the good will of the newspaper was not the same good will which was conveyed, hence there was no plant or good will, upon which the mortgagee could foreclose. 

Metropolitan Nat. Bank v. St. Louis Dispatch Co., 149

U. S. 436 13

GOOD WILL 2. Sale of Property to Which Good Will is Incident 

If the property, business, or rights to which a good will adheres are sold or otherwise transferred, the good will, although not specifically mentioned, passes to the tranferee as an incident thereto. 

Fairfield v. Lowry, 207 Mass. 352 

Good will may be impliedly included in transfer of business. 

Canadian v. Canadian, 268 Mass. 561

The sale of labels, bottles and cases possessed by company's customers indicated that purchaser was to continue the bottling business. 

Canadian v. Canadian, 268 Mass. 561 

Lothrop Pub. Co. v. Lothrop & Co., 191 Mass. 353

Russia Cement Co. v. LePage, 147 Mass. 206 

Hoxie v. Chaney, 143 Mass. 592 

Sohier v. Johnson, 111 Mass. 238

Where plaintiff had built up a very large foreign trade, and for some time carried on such trade as defendant's agent and thereafter defendant took a transfer, not only of all the assets of the business and of the plaintiff's leasehold estate in the business premises, but also of the good will, of which plaintiff was called in the assignment the beneficial owner, and plaintiff's personal knowledge of the business was great, his experience in it large and his acquaintance both with the traveling salesmen, through whom sales were generally made, and with probable purchasers extensive, and where the plaintiff, according to part of his evidence, specified his good will as consisting of his files of letters from customers, plaintiff's knowledge, experience, acquaintance and ability, it might well be found to constitute what the parties to the agreement called a good will, even though plaintiff, before the transfer of the business, could not have copied for his own future use the accounts, letters or names of customers with whom he had dealt as defendant's agent, since it might well have been contemplated that plaintiff, because of his personal knowledge, experience and acquaintance with trade, could secure merchandise from other sources and become so 14

GOOD WILL 

troublesome a competitor with defendant as to make all the difference between a profit and a loss in the latter's business. 

Gordon v. Knott, 199 Mass. 173

In an action on an agreement to sell a milk route, evidence was admissible to show that the term, "right and good will of supplying customers" meant in the trade the right of supplying milk to customers pointed out by seller. 

Page v. Cole, 120 Mass. 37, at 39

One who voluntarily sells his interest in a business, together with the good will, impliedly agrees that his relations to the business are ended, and that all the advantages belonging to it as a going concern are to pass to the purchaser, and that he himself will not do anything to interfere directly with it as property having a good will which will be valuable to the purchaser. One selling in such a way puts himself in the attitude of retiring from business, so far as his activity would directly affect that which fairly might be considered as belonging to the business at the time of the sale and giving it value for his successor. 

Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 493, at 497

The sale of the practice and good will of a physician within certain limits is the legitimate subject matter of a contract, and carries with it the implied covenant, as in other sales, that the vendor will not himself do anything to disturb or injure the vendee in the enjoyment of that which he has purchased. 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175 

In Martin v. Jablowski, 253 Mass. 451, the court said, at page 455 "It is the law of this Commonwealth that a sale by one partner to another of all his right, title and interest in and to the entire assets of the firm includes a sale of good will. 

It has also been 'assumed that a case where there was such an implied sale of good will stood on the same footing as an express sale and grant of it' so far as concerns the right of such vendor to engage in competing business. 

Marshall Eng. Co. v. New Marshall Eng. Co., 203 Mass. 410, at 421 15

GOOD WILL 

"It was laid down in Old Corner Book Store v. Upham, 194 Mass. 101, at 105 that, 'In each case where the good will of a business is sold and the vendor sets up a competing business it is a question of fact whether, having regard to the character of the business sold and that set up, the new business does or does not derogate from the grant made by that sale.' "In most cases which have arisen in this court the sale has been held to be of such nature and under such circumstances as to preclude the vendor from engaging in competing business.

6. 

Competition by Former Owner a.

In Absence of Restrictive Covenant 

(I) Engaging in Similar Business 

(A) 

Voluntary Sales  

The doctrine is established that one who voluntarily sells his business, or his entire interest in a partnership, together with the good will, precludes himself from setting up a competing business which will derogate from the good will which he has sold. 

Rosenberg v. Adelson, 234 Mass. 488 

Batchelder v. Batchelder, 220 Mass. 42 

Fairfield v. Lowry, 207 Mass. 352 

Marshall Eng. Co. v. New Marshall Eng. Co., 203 Mass. 410 (Covenant will be implied) 

Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 493 

Gordon v. Knott, 199 Mass. 173 

Old Corner Book Store v. Upham, 194 Mass. 101 

Hutchinson v. Nay, 183 Mass. 355 

Munsey v. Butterfield, 133 Mass. 492 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175 

Angier v. Webber, 14 Allen, 211

This does not necessarily prevent him from engaging in a similar business, provided the new business is so conducted as not to injure the original business which he has sold. 

Fairfield v. Lowry, 207 Mass. 352 

Bassett v. Percival, 5 Allen, 345

Reason for rule.—The implication, upon the sale of the good will of a business, of a covenant not to engage in a similar business in competition with the buyer is based upon the ground that it is necessary to protect the purchaser in his purchase of the good will. 

Marshall Eng. Co. v. New Marshall Eng. Co., 203 Mass. 410 17

GOOD WILL

The object to be obtained is the protection of the purchaser, and the agreement is to be construed as if the seller had expressly covenanted to render the old practice secure by not competing himself under conditions by which it might be either impaired or destroyed. 

Distinction between Massachusetts and English doctrine.- 

The difference between the law which has been established in England and that which has been established in Massachusetts is that in England a competing business can always be set up by anyone who has sold his good will, and the purchaser gets nothing more than a right to have the seller refrain from soliciting customers of the old firm, whereas in Massachusetts no competing business can be set up if it derogates from the grant of the good will of the old business. 

Whether a business subsequently established by the seller derogates from a grant of good will depends upon the extent of the business sold. 

Marshall Eng. Co. v. New Marshall Eng. Co., 203 Mass. 410. 

Illustrations: (a) Where one who had been for many years an employee and later a partner in a book store, whose customers were largely of a certain religious denomination, sold his interest in the business to the remaining partners, his subsequent formation of a corporation to carry on a similar business among the same customers and the establishment of a place of business about five minutes walk from that of the old concern derogated from his prior grant. 

Old Corner Book Store v. Upham, 194 Mass. 101 (b) Plaintiff had built up a very large foreign trade, and for some time carried on such trade as defendant's agent, and thereafter defendant took a transfer not only of all the assets of the business and of plaintiff's leasehold estate in the business premises, but also of the good will of which plaintiff was called in the assignment the beneficial owner. Plaintiff's personal 18

GOOD WILL 

knowledge of the business was great, his experience in it large, and his acquaintance both with the traveling salesman through whom sales were made and with probable purchasers extensive. 

It was held that, after the transfer of such good will, plaintiff could not derogate from his grant by engaging in a competing business of the same kind, selling the same goods, and endeavoring to deal with the same customers. 

Gordon v. Knott, 199 Mass. 173 (c) Where a defendant sells his interest in the good will of a dental business, and afterward resumes practice in the same city and sends out circulars to former patients, giving the name of the old firm, with the street and number, and announces that, having opened an office in the city, he solicits their custom, he has broken his implied covenant to refrain from competition. 

 (d) Where the seller transferred a small grocery store with his good will, the contract of sale cannot be construed as imposing any personal restraint upon the seller or as restricting his right to transact a similar business at another place at a subsequent time. 

Bassett v. Percival, 5 Allen, 345 (Which case, although in apparent conflict with later Massachusetts decisions, is explained in Old Corner 

Book Store v. Upham, 194 Mass. 101, on the ground that the new business did not derogate from the sale of the good will of the old business.) 

(2) Soliciting Old Customers 

Where the sale of partnership property is made not by the owner of the property but by a decree of the court, the general rule is that there is no implied covenant on the part of either partner that he will not solicit trade from the former customers of the firm, but on the contrary either of the members of the old firm stands with reference to a purchaser at such a sale as though the partnership had never existed. In such a case either partner is at liberty to enter on a competing business and to solicit trade from the customers of the old firm. 

Griffith v. Kirley, 189 Mass. 522 19

GOOD WILL 

Where a seller, who has been carrying on an insurance business, sells it to the buyer without agreeing not to engage in the same business again, he cannot derogate from the effect of the sale by attempting to deprive the buyer of any part of the business sold to him. But the seller still can engage in the same business himself, although he would not be allowed to solicit business from the former customers of himself, or so conduct his own business as to injure the business which he had sold to the buyer. 

Fairfield v. Lowry, 207 Mass. 352

A sale upon the dissolution of a partnership has been held to be similar to a forced judicial sale and to give the partners the right to solicit old customers. 

 (B) Involuntary Sales (1) 

General Statement 

Where a sale of a partnership assets is forced upon the survivor by the administrator of a deceased partner, the surviving partner is not in the position of a sole trader who has voluntarily parted with the good will of his business. He is not bound to retire from the business. Such a sale is like a sale of the good will of a sole trader by his trustee or assignee in bankruptcy. 

Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 493 

Griffith v. Kirley, 189 Mass. 522 

Hutchinson v. Nay 187 Mass. 262 

See: Webster v. Webster, 180 Mass. 310 (Where a partnership agreement, which provided for a sale of the property and assets as it appeared by the books of the firm upon the termination of the partnership, was construed as showing that the parties must have understood that, as the partnership had come to an end by its own limitation, they were all at liberty to do any kind of business and to gain such advantage as they could from their relations to the former business.) 

Holbrook v. Nesbit, 163 Mass. 120 

A sale of the good will of a partnership, under a decree of the court, when the affairs of the partnership are wound up by 20

GOOD WILL 

reason of the death or bankruptcy of one or of all of the partners, carries with it everything of advantage belonging to the existing business relative to the continuance of it, but leaves the several members of the firm at liberty to start a new business of the same kind which will come into competition with the business of the purchaser. 

Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 493 

(II) Engaging in Identical Business 

The sale of a business and its good will precludes the former owner from attempting to set up again the identical business, or from representing the new business in which he is engaged as a continuation of the old. 

The principles involved are those involved in cases of unfair competition. 

(III) Interference with Premises (IV) Trade-Marks, Trade Names, and Unfair Compe tition

A person cannot make a trade-mark of his own name, and thus debar another having the same name from using it in his business, if he does so honestly, and without any intention to appropriate wrongfully the good will of a business already established by others of the name. Every one has the absolute right to use his own name honestly in his own business for the purpose of advertising it, even though he may thereby incidentally interfere with and injure the business of another having the same name. But although he may thus use his name, he cannot resort to any artifice or do any act calculated to mislead the public as to the identity of the business, firm or establishment, or of the article produced by them, and thus produce injury to the other beyond that which results from the similarity of name. 

Canadian Club Beverage Co. v. Can. Club. Corp., 268 

Mass. 561, at 568 and 569 

Robert Burns v. Wm. J. Burns Int. Det. Agency, 235 

Mass. 553, at 556 and 557 

Lothrop Pub. Co. v. Lothrop, Lee & Shepard Co., 191 

Mass. 353, at 355 21

GOOD WILL 

George G. Fox Co. v. Glynn, 191 Mass. 344, at 349 

Messer v. The Fadettes, 168 Mass. 140, at 143 (Dissenting opinion.) 

Dover Stamping Co. v. Fellows, 163 Mass. 191 

Noera v. Williams Mfg. Co., 158 Mass. 110 

Covell v. Chadwick, 153 Mass. 263, at 267 

Russia Cement Co. v. LePage, 147 Mass. 206 

Gilman v. Hunnewell, 122 Mass. 139

While this is the general rule, it is also true that one may so sell or part with the right to use his own name as a description or designation of a manufactured article as to deprive himself of the right to use it as such, and confer this right upon another. 

Russia Cement Co. v. LePage, 147 Mass. 206, at 209 

Jacobs v. Beecham, 221 U. S. 263 

Howe Scale Co. v. Wyckoff, 198 U. S. 118, at 140 

Brown Chemical Co. v. Meyer, 139 U. S. 540, at 542 

Menendez v. Holt, 128 U. S. 514, at 523 

McLean v. Fleming, 96 U. S. 245

The general rule is that the trade-marks are assignable. 

Kidd v. Johnson, 100 U. S. 617

However, where the personal skill of an artist or artisan may so far enter into the value of a product that a trade-mark bearing his name would, or at least might, imply that his personal work or supervision was employed in the manufacture, it would be a fraud upon the public if the trade-mark should be used by other persons, and for this reason such a trade-mark is unassignable. 

No such inference can be drawn where all that the purchasers would reasonably understand is that goods bearing the trademark are of a certain standard kind or quality, or are made in a certain manner, or after a certain formula, by persons who are carrying on the same business that formerly was carried on by the person whose name is in the trade-mark. 

Thus, where the assignee of the trade-marks "A. N. Hoxie's 

Mineral Soap," and "A. N. Hoxie's Pumice Soap," used them to denote soaps made according to the formulas of A. N. Hoxie, 22

GOOD WILL 

and not to denote that they were made by said Hoxie, he could maintain a bill in equity to restrain an infringement of the trademarks. 

Where one Hoxie sold to one Pegram "the following goods and chattels, namely: All my right, title, and interest in and to all and singular the partnership property belonging to the firm of A. N. Hoxie & Co. (consisting of A. N. Hoxie and Frank R.

Pegram), meaning hereby to sell and convey to said Pegram all my interest in the entire assets of said firm, wherever the same may be situated," it was held that these terms were broad so that, even though the trade-marks and the good will of the firm were not expressly mentioned, both were included within their meaning Pegram therefore became the owner of the trademarks, and his firm was entitled to their exclusive use. 

The court does not interfere to prevent the public from being misled, but "for the purpose of protecting the owner of a trade or business from a fraudulent invasion of that business by somebody else." If what is done tends to mislead the public, it naturally diverts customers from the shop of the person entitled to use the firm name, and so injures his business. 

Holbrook v. Nesbitt, 163 Mass. 120, at 125

In Costa v. Costa, 222 Mass. 280, the firm name was L. J. & 

M. Costa. After the dissolution of the firm, the defendant continued the business in the name of L. J. Costa, and not in the name of L. J. & M. Costa. This did not deprive the plaintiff, the widow of a former member of the partnership, of the right to be paid for the good will. 

In C. H. Batchelder & Co., Inc. v. Batchelder, 220 Mass. 42, the new corporation, having brought a suit to enjoin the defendant from carrying on the business in his own name after they had purchased the good will of that business, could not recover, where it appeared that the defendant did not intend to transfer the right to use his name beyond the business life of the corporation then formed by him. The new corporation's purchase from 23

GOOD WILL 

the receiver of the good will of the first corporation gave it the right only to do business as the successor of the first corporation and did not give it the right to use in its business the name of the defendant, who, having refused to consent to its use, had the right under 

R. L. c. 72, s. 5 to resume his business in his own name, if he refrained from unfair competition. The use of the defendant's name, having been limited to the first corporation, was not a transferable right or asset which the plaintiff corporation could take over and use against the defendant's protest. 

Fairfield v. Lowry, 207 Mass. 352 

Lodge v. Weld, 139 Mass. 499

If the defendant never has represented his goods as having been made by the plaintiff and has informed customers and instructed his employees to inform them that he was not in any way connected with the plaintiff company, he cannot be charged with unfair competition, where it appears that the plaintiff, without the assent of the defendant and against his written protest, has appropriated his name as the principle part of its corporate designation. b. 

Economy Food Products Co. v. Economy Gro. St. Corp., 1932 A. S. 1957, at 1959 

Highland Dye Works v. Anteblian, 270 Mass. 209, at 212 

Carney Hospital v. McDonald, 227 Mass. 231, at 233 and 234

Restrictive Covenants (I) 

General Statement 

One who has sold his good will may covenant not to engage in competition with the purchaser in such a way as to derogate from the value of his grant, and if the restrictive covenant is no 24

GOOD WILL 

broader than necessary for this purpose it is valid; otherwise it is void as being a contract in restraint of trade. 

Marshall Eng. Co. v. New Marshall Eng. Co., 203 Mass. 410 (A) Remaining Partner

Where a business with its good will was sold to a partnership with a restrictive covenant and subsequently, after the partnership had been dissolved, one partner purchased the entire interest of the other, such other partner need not be a party to the suit, as he had no interest which could be affected by a decree. 

Marshall Eng. Co. v. New Marshall Eng. Co., 203 Mass. 410 

Old Corner Book Store v. Upham, 194 Mass. 101 

Jenkins v. Eliot, 192 Mass. 474 (B) Extent as to Territory Where a dentist sold his practice carried on at Church Street, Boston, those who subsequently acquired the practice so sold were held entitled to an injunction prohibiting the seller from practicing in Boston only, although the former practice had included some patients from other cities. 

Foss v. Roby, 195 Mass. 292 

(II) Assignment by Purchaser 

In Myott v. Greer, 204 Mass. 389 the defendant sold to the plaintiff an express business together with the good will. The plaintiff then assigned the same to a corporation. Thereupon, the assignee corporation ceased to do business. Afterward, the plaintiff resumed business in his personal capacity, but the good will never was reconveyed to him. The defendant, soon after selling his business to the plaintiff, had set up an express business in violation of the covenant not to engage in the express business within twenty miles of the town for a period of ten years. 

Therefore the plaintiff, the assignor, brought a suit in equity to restrain the defendant from carrying on an express business in violation of his covenant. Held, that the plaintiff could not maintain the suit, because the corporation and not he was the owner of the good will of the business and without owning such 25

GOOD WILL 

good will he could not enforce the covenant not to engage in a competing business. 

The court said, at page 392: "The corporation is the owner of that good will, and it is the corporation only as the owner of that good will that has a right to enforce the covenant. The fact that the corporation is not now doing business is of no consequence. That was true in the case of 

Marshall Eng. Co. v. New Marshall Eng. Co., 203 Mass. 410 where it was held that a receiver of the corporation not carrying on its business could stop the grantor of the good will assigned to the corporation from conducting a competing business. In that way alone could the creditors of the corporation represented by the receiver realize the full value of the good will owned by the corporation." 7. 

Remedies of Parties a. Seller's Remedies b. 

Purchaser's Remedies 

(I) 

General Statement 

If the vendor interferes with the good will he has sold, the vendee may have an action at law, or a more complete remedy in equity by injunction to compel the defendant to the performance of his agreement. 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175 (II) Damages Where the damages in their nature are such as not to be susceptible of proof or exact computation, and the injury caused by the acts of the defendant is a constantly recurring one, for which multiplied suits at law would afford but an imperfect remedy, the plaintiff is entitled to relief in equity. 

Angier u. W ebber, 14 Allen, 211

Where the plaintiff, having suffered damages as a result of the breach of the contract for the sale of a business including the good will, applies for an injunction, he is entitled, in addition to his injunction, to a decree for such money damages as he has 26

GOOD WILL sustained from the defendant's breach of contract. 

In an action for false representations in the sale of the defendant's interest in the stock and good will of a firm of which he was a member, the measure of damages is the difference between the actual value of the interest at the time of the purchase and its value if it had been what it was represented to be. 

Morse v. Hutchins, 102 Mass. 439 

Injunction

In a contract of sale of a business and its good will, there is an implied covenant that the vendor will not interfere with the enjoyment of what he has sold; if he does, such interference may be restrained by injunction.

F. 1. 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175 

Augier v. Webber, 14 Allen, 211 

But see: Myott v. Greer, 204 Mass. 389

PARTICULAR PERSONS 

Bakers

Where bakers sold their business and their personal property connected with that business and made a contract not to engage or interfere in the business in that town for five years, they were liable if one of them drove a bread cart in that town on his former routes and supplied his former customers with bread, acting as the hired servant of a baker in another town. 

Boutelle v. Smith, 116 Mass. 111 

2. Boot and Shoe Manufacturers 

Where by a dissolution of a boot and shoe manufacturing concern under the terms of a partnership agreement, which contained no provision as to winding up the business, one of the partners is forced by the other partners to retire, and the remaining partners refuse the retired partner an accounting, and, forming a new partnership, continue the business using the retired partner's share in the property and good will of the old firm as part of their working capital, the remaining partners must account to the retired partner, not only for his share of the partnership property including the good will, but also for his share in all actual profits 27

GOOD WILL 

derived from the property, or must pay him interest on his share of the capital if he so elects. 

Moore v. Rawson, 185 Mass. 264 

3. Dentists

A dentist, who, after the insanity of his employer, carried on practice in the same office on his own account, was not responsible concerning good will even though he used the furniture, instruments and machinery of his former employer. 

Wightman v. Wightman, 223 Mass. 398 

4. Partners

The right to use a name on a medicine may be assigned to an outgoing partner or a successor in business, as an incident to its good will. 

Brown Co. v. Meyer, 139 U. S. 540

When a partner retires from a firm, assenting to or acquiescing in the retention by the other partners of possession of the old place of business and the future conduct of the business by them under the old name, the good will remains with the latter, including the firm's trade-marks. 

Brown Co. v. Meyer, 139 U. S. 540

Although sale by one partner to another included good will, the former could compete with the latter. 

Martin v. Jablonski, 253 Mass. 451

Good will of partnership should be included in accounting between surviving and liquidating partner and executrix of deceased partner.

Rutan v. Coolidge, 241 Mass. 584 

Taking the assets and continuing the business at the same location under the same or similar name of the firm renders the continuing partner accountable for the value of the good will. 

Costa v. Costa, 222 Mass. 280

Where continuing partner uses the assets and name of the firm after termination of partnership, he is responsible to the retiring partner for good will. 

Hutchins v. Page, 204 Mass. 284 28

GOOD WILL 

A retiring partner on termination of the partnership may require his copartners to account for the property of the partnership including the good will which they wrongfully appropriated to their own use. They will be held to account to the retiring partner for the good will in the same way as if they had purchased it or sold it to a stranger. 

Moore v. Rawson, 185 Mass. 264

If after the death of one or two partners engaged in the teaming business the survivor carries on the business on his own account and in his own name and solicits business from the customers of the old firm he is not liable to account to the administrator of his deceased partner for the value of the good will. 

Hutchinson v. Nay, 183 Mass. 355

A remaining partner is entitled to an injunction against a retiring partner where they were partners in business in a certain town, dissolved their partnership by consent, the remaining partner agreed to assume the debts of the firm, and the retiring partner agreed in writing to sell to the remaining partner all his interests in the assets and good will of the firm for a certain sum and "not to manufacture or sell or become engaged in said business, either for myself or others, hereafter in the town of D., under the forfeiture of $1,000 to be paid to said (remaining partner) in case of breach of these conditions." 5. 

Ropes v. Upton, 125 Mass. 258 Physicians

If a physician covenants never to practice his profession in a certain city so long as a purchaser of his professional business engages in practice there, provided, however, that he shall have the right to do so at any time after five years by paying the purchaser $2,000, "but not otherwise," that sum is not to be treated as liquidated damages to be paid upon a breach of the agreement, or as a penalty, but is the price fixed for what the contract permits the seller to do if he pays, and is recoverable by the purchaser upon the seller's engaging in practice there after five years without paying. 

Smith v. Bergengren, 153 Mass. 236 29

GOOD WILL 

A contract by a physician for the sale of his "practice and good will" in a specified town is not void as against public policy. 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175

An agreement by the physician of a country village, transferring his practice and good will to another physician for a certain sum, and guaranteeing "that no other physician, for the space of four years, will establish himself in this place as a competitor, unless the increased population of the place would warrant it, or unless the purchaser should commit some act, which shall forfeit to him the confidence of the community," and agreeing, in case any such competitor shall establish himself there within that time, contrary to the above provisions, to repay the sum paid, is not void as being in restraint of trade, nor too uncertain and insensible to support an action. 

Gilman v. Dwight, 13 Gray 356 

6. Soap Manufacturer 

A soap manufacturer, who had acquired trade-marks for his soap, entered into a partnership to which he contributed the good will and implements of his business. On dissolution of the partnership, he conveyed to his former partner by a bill of sale all his interest in the entire assets of the firm, of which, it was decided, the trade marks were a part. 

7. Teamsters 

Where the surviving teamster of a partnership carries on the business in his own name at the old stand with only slight changes, for nearly two years, and then sells the good will of the business, he need not accour to executor or administrator of his former partner, as the goo will sold is his own and not that of the former partnership. 

Hutchinson v. Na, 187 Mass. 262 

If after the death of one of two teamsters of a prtnership the surviving teamsterarries on the busi ess on his own count and in his own nam and solicits business from the custome.. of the old firm, he not liable to acount to the administrator of his deceased par her for the value of the good will.

PARTICULAR TRADES AND OCCUPATIONS 

Bedding

A purchaser promised to pay in instalments for a business plant and property, in consideration of its sale and delivery, and the performance of three particular covenants and agreements by the seller, the first of which was a general agreement, without any limitation of space, that for and during the period of five years he would not either directly or indirectly continue in, carry on, or engage in that business or any business of which that might form any part. Held, that the covenant was void as being in restraint of trade, and that, not being severable from the rest of the consideration, no action would lie on the promise for instalments of the price. 

Bishop v. Palmer, 146 Mass. 469 

2. Book Store

Sale of good will prevented competition. Derogation of grant was question of fact. Corporation formed by vendor enjoined unless independent body. 3. 

Old Corner Book Store v. Upham, 194 Mass. 101 

Butchering Business

A firm carrying on a butchering business and dealing in tallow, bones, grease and hides, on real estate used as a farm and fertilizer factory which has become in equity partnership property, has a good will attached to the real estate and fixtures which any of the partners on the winding up of the partnership has the right to have sold, so that the partnership may obtain the benefit of it, but such sale conveys no exclusive right to solicit trade from former customers of the old firm, and leaves the -31

GOOD WILL 

members of the old firm as free to enter a competing business and to solicit trade as though the partnership never has existed. 

'Griffith v. Kirley, 189 Mass. 522 4. Dentistry 

Partnership for practice of dentistry has no good will, but agreement not to compete is enforceable. 

5. Druggist Supplies 

Where a partnership for the sale of druggist supplies was formed and the stock belonged to the defendant and upon termination of the partnership the defendant sold to the plaintiffs "the property and assets" of the firm, there was no sale of good will beyond that, if any, which pertained to the ownership of the goods, and each partner was at liberty to gain such advantage as he could from his relations to the former business. 

Webster v. Webster, 180 Mass. 310

A contract is valid which provides that a sum is to be paid for breach of the agreement purchasing a drug store, the property therein and the good will of the business. 

Smith v. Brown, 164 Mass. 584 

6. Electrical Supplies 

In connection with the sale of the good will of a business, the vendor will be bound by any covenant which is reasonably necessary for the preservation and protection of the property which he sells. 

Anchor Elec. Co. v. Hawkes, 171 Mass. 101, at 106 and 107 

7. Express Business 

An express business was conveyed to a corporation. Original vendee of good will cannot restrain competition after selling the same to a corporation. Good will may be transferred by unsealed instrument. Assignment of good will by corporation is valid even though directors are minors. 

Myott v. Greer, 204 Mass. 389 32

GOOD WILL 

8. Grocery Store

The vendor sold good will of a business and opened a similar business across the street. There was no clause in the agreement preventing the vendor from engaging again in a similar business. 

Whenever such is the intent of the parties, it is carried into effect by an express stipulation, which if not in undue restraint of trade, may be valid and binding. 

Bassett v. Percival, 5 Allen, 345 

9. Ice Business 

Where the purchaser seeks to rescind, he cannot do so by merely returning the physical property if the sale also included good will which cannot be restored. 

Handforth v. Jackson, 150 Mass. 149 

10. Fire Alarm Co. 

A clause of a contract is void, as being in restraint of trade, because the stipulation seems to be something more than is reasonably necessary to protect the plaintiff in the enjoyment of the property it bought. 11. 

Gamewell Fire Alarm Tel. Co. v. Crane, 160 Mass. 50

Milk Route 

Where a person agrees to sell and another to purchase a milk route in certain towns, delivery to be made on a day named, in an action by the seller against the buyer for breach of the agreement, in refusing to take the route and pay the consideration, if it appears that after the agreement, and before the day fixed for delivery, the owner bargained with a third person to purchase the latter's milk route, intending to run the same after the purchaser took his route and that the route of the third person comprised a portion of the same territory which the seller was intending to deliver and that the seller had promised not to disturb any of the customers of the route which he was selling, the buyer is under no obligation to complete the purchase and a verdict should be directed for him. 12. 

Munsey v. Butterfield, 133 Mass. 492

Millinery 

In a millinery business where there was a sale of the business and good will to a partnership and later a sale of partner's 33

GOOD WILL 

interest to remaining partner, the latter may prevent competition by original vendor. Retiring partner need not be party to suit. 

Jenkins v. Eliot, 192 Mass. 474 13. Partnership It was said in Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 493, at pages 497 and 498: "The first question of importance relates to the manner. of estimating the value of the good will, and particularly its value in reference to the right to use the firm name. 

An answer to the question requires a consideration of what is fairly included in the good will, in view of the situation of the parties and the implications involved in the terms of the contract. Sometimes very little, if anything, is meant, beyond what is included in a sale of the good will under a judicial decree in settling the business of a partnership. 

But usually, in this Commonwealth, there is an implied agreement not to set up a competing business that will directly interfere with the business to be carried on by the purchaser of the good will. In England, a competing business may be set up by the seller of the good will; but he is not permitted to solicit business from the customers of the old firm." 

Webster v. Webster, 180 Mass. 310

In the accounting between surviving and liquidating partner and executrix of deceased partner, the good will of partnership should be included.

Where one partner of a firm of a butchering business to which a good will is attached has taken exclusive possession of the partnership property and is carrying on the business as if he were the purchaser of it, in a suit by one of his partners for an ac counting he may be charged with the value of the good will. 

Griffith v. Kirley, 189 Mass. 522

On the dissolution of a partnership by the death of one of the partners, the good will of the partnership business is a part of the assets of the partnership, and, in the absence of an agreement between the partners on the subject, the executor or administrator of a deceased partner has a right to have it sold in the liquidation of the assets of the partnership. 

If a partnership has established a business sufficiently permanent in character to include not only the patronage of its customers but the elements of locality and a distinctive name, a good will exists which forms an asset of commercial value in an accounting among partners. 

Moore v. Rawson, 185 Mass. 264

Where the defendant owned all the stock in trade of a partnership and the agreement among the partners provided that, upon the termination of the partnership by limitation, the defendant should sell to the plaintiffs "the property and assets" of the firm and the defendant did so, there was no sale of good will beyond that, if any, which pertained to the ownership of the goods, and each partner was at liberty to gain such advantage as he could from his relations to the former business. 14.

Printing Where the defendant, although he had covenanted with the plaintiff, on the dissolution of the firm of a printing business of which they had been members, not to engage in or interfere with that business for a limited time, nevertheless joined a new partnership of the same type of business, he was held liable for all 35

GOOD WILL 

injury occasioned to the plaintiff by the establishment of the new partnership.

Dean v. Emerson, 102 Mass. 480 15. Shoe Cutter Manufacturing 

A contract made between citizens of this Commonwealth, by which one of them agreed, for a good consideration, never to "set up, exercise or carry on the trade or business of manufacturing and selling shoecutters at any place within the Commonwealth of Massachusetts" is illegal, as being in restraint of trade; although the manufacture of shoecutters is an art which can only be carried on by persons instructed in the same, and at the time of making the above contract the person so promising was ig norant of said art, and his said promise was made as a part of an agreement of partnership with one who was skilled and actually engaged in carrying on the same, and to take effect at the expiration of the partnership, and although at that time only three other persons were engaged in the business. 

Taylor v. Blanchard, 13 Allen, 370

Brown, 164 Mass. 584 (A contract is valid which provides that for the consideration of the promisee's "taking from me my lease of an apothecary shop in I., . my promise herein being the chief inducement leading him to take said lease, and to purchase the property therein, and in said shop and the good will of the business, I hereby agree with said A. under a penalty of one thousand dollars (to be forfeited and paid said A. or his legal representatives, in the event of my committing any breach of this agreement) not to engage directly or indirectly, or become in any manner interested, in the drug business within at least two miles of said apothecary shop, whose lease said A. takes from me, without first obtaining the written consent of said A. thereto."

Although the sum named is a penalty, substantial damages may be awarded.) 

Gamewell Fire Alarm Tel. Co. v. Crane, 160 Mass. 50 (A clause of a contract is void, as being in restraint of trade which provides that: "Said C. further agrees not to engage in the business of manufacturing or selling fire alarm or police telegraph machines and apparatus, and not to enter into competition with said G. Company, either directly or indirectly, for the period of ten years next ensuing after the date of this agreement." because "The stipulation seems to us to be something more than is reasonably necessary to protect the plaintiff in the enjoyment of the property it bought, even if that should be adopted as the test, upon which we express no opinion.") 

Smith v. Bergengren, 153 Mass. 236 (If a physician covenants never to practice his profes- 43

GOOD WILL 

sion in a certain city so long as a purchaser of his professional business engages in practice there, provided, however, that he shall have the right to do so at any time after five years by paying the purchaser $2,000, "but not otherwise," that sum is not to be treated as liquidated damages to be paid upon a breach of the agreement, or as a penalty, but is the price fixed for what the contract permits the seller to do if he pays, and is recoverable by the purchaser upon the seller's engaging in practice there after the five years without paying.) 

Handforth v. Jackson, 150 Mass. 149 ("The plaintiff has had the benefit of the good will of the defendant's business, which cannot now be restored.") 

Bishop v. Palmer, 146 Mass. 469 (A purchaser promised to pay in instalments for a business plant and property, in consideration of its sale and delivery, and the performance of three particular covenants and agreements by the seller, the first of which was a general agreement, without any limitation of space, that for and during the period of five years he would not either directly or indirectly continue in, carry on, or engage in that business or any business of which that might form any part. Held, that the covenant was void as being in restraint of trade, and that, not being severable from the rest of the consideration, no action would lie on the promise for instalments of the price.) 

 (A manufacturer, who had acquired trade-marks in two kinds of soap manufactured by him, entered into a partnership with another, under articles in writing by which he contributed the good will of the business he was carrying on, with the tools, implements, and fix tures. On the dissolution of the partnership, he conveyed to his former partner, by a bill of sale, "the 44

GOOD WILL 

following goods and chattels, namely: All my right, title, and interest in and to all and singular the partnership property belonging to the firm, meaning hereby to sell and convey all my interest in the entire assets of the firm." Held, that the trade-marks became, by the articles of copartnership, a part of the property of the firm; and that they passed by the bill of sale. Held, also, on a bill in equity by the purchaser under the bill of sale to restrain the seller from making and selling said two kinds of soap, from using wrappers bearing the trade-marks, and from doing matters tending to injure and impair the good will of the business, that the plaintiff was entitled to an injunction, except as to the making and selling the soap.) 

Munsey v. Butterfield, 133 Mass. 492 (Where a person agrees to sell and another to purchase a milk route in certain towns, delivery to be made on a day named, in an action by the seller against the buyer for breach of the agreement, in refusing to take the route and pay the consideration, if it appears that after the agreement, and before the day fixed for delivery, the owner bargained with a third person to purchase the latter's milk route, intending to run the same after the purchaser took his route and that the route of the third person comprised a portion of the same territory which the seller was intending to deliver and that the seller had promised not to disturb any of the customers of the route which he was selling, the buyer is under no obligation to complete the purchase and a verdict should be directed for him.) 

Ropes v. Upton, 125 Mass. 258 (A remaining partner is entitled to an injunction against a retiring partner where they were partners in business in a certain town, dissolved their partnership by consent, the remaining partner agreed to assume the debts of the firm, and the retiring partner agreed in writing to sell to the remaining partner all his interests 45

in the assets and good will of the firm for a certain sum and "not to manufacture or sell or become engaged in said business, either for myself or others, hereafter in the town of D., under the forfeiture of $1,000 to be paid to said (remaining partner) in case of breach of these conditions.") 

Boutelle v. Smith, 116 Mass. 111 (A. and B., bakers in F., bought of C. and D. their business as bakers in the same town, and their personal property connected with that business, and made a contract with them whereby C. and D. agreed "that they will not or either of them hereafter engage in the business of bakers in the town of F., and will not directly or indirectly engage in any business or do any act that shall interfere with the business thus purchased for the sale of bread on the several bread routes heretofore connected with said business," for five years. Held, also, that C. and D. were liable, if one of them drove a bread cart in F. on his former routes and supplied his former customers with bread, acting as the hired servant of a baker in another town.) 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175 (A contract by a physician for the sale of his "practice and good will" in a specified town is not void as against public policy.) (In a contract of sale of a business and its good will, there is an implied covenant that the vendor will not interfere with the enjoyment of what he has sold; if he does, such interference may be restrained by injunc tion.) 

Dean v. Emerson, 102 Mass. 480 (The defendant, having covenanted with the plaintiff on the dissolution of a firm for the manufacture of daguerreotype materials, of which they had been members, "not, directly or indirectly, to enter into, or carry on, or in any way be interested in, or furnish to any 46

person or persons information in regard to," that business within certain limits, nevertheless formed with a third person a new partnership within said limits for that business, had the whole financial charge of the new partnership, travelled about the country, visiting the customers of the old firm, and introducing the goods of the new partnership, and received a commission on all sales. Held, that these facts warranted a finding that the defendant was liable for all the injury occasioned to the plaintiff by the establishment of the new partnership.) GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

A.

DEFINITIONS GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

Gross negligence is such conduct as results from the addition to ordinary carelessness of an utter disregard of the dictates of prudence, culminating in complete neglect of safety. · Manning v. Simpson, 261 Mass. 494 (Crossing path of oncoming automobile on slippery road at increased speed.) 

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65 

Shiear v. Feigelson, 248 Mass. 432 

Burke v. Cook, 246 Mass. 518

Gross negligence is substantially and appreciably higher in magnitude than ordinary negligence. It is materially more want of care than constitutes simple inadvertence. It is an act or omission respecting legal duty of an aggravated character as distinguished from a mere failure to exercise ordinary care. It is very great negligence, or the absence of slight diligence, or the want of even scant care. It amounts to indifference to present legal duty and to utter forgetfulness of legal obligations so far as other persons may be affected. It is a heedless and palpable violation of legal duty respecting the rights of others. The element of culpability which characterizes all negligence is in gross negligence magnified to a high degree as compared with that present in ordinary negligence. 

Gross negligence is a manifestly smaller amount of watchfulness and circumspection than the circumstances require of a person of ordinary prudence. 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591, and 592 

Mason v. Thomas, 1931 A. S. 133, at 135 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123 

Barry v. Harding, 244 Mass. 588 

Flynn v. Lewis, 231 Mass. 550 

Massaletti v. Fitzroy, 228 Mass. 487 

Cane v. Boston Elevated Ry. Co., 217 Mass. 594, at 598 

Davis v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 214 Mass. 98 

Adams v. Boston Elevated Ry. Co., 214 Mass. 1 

Berry v. Newton & Boston St. Ry., 209 Mass. 100 

Spooner v. Old Colony St. Ry., 190 Mass. 132 

Aiken v. Holyoke St. Ry., 184 Mass. 269, at 271 

Banks v. Braman, 188 Mass. 367, at 369 

Evenson v. Lexington & Boston St. Ry., 165 Mass. 

572, and cases cited 

4 A. L. R. 1185 1

GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

To constitute gross negligence it must appear that the plaintiff's injury was due to something more than simple carelessness, something which has in its elements of "indifference to present legal duty", of "utter forgetfulness of legal obligations so far as other persons may be affected", of "heedless and palpable violation of legal duty respecting the rights of others", of "manifestly smaller amount of watchfulness and circumspection than the circumstances require of a person of ordinary prudence", and of "the omission of even such diligence as habitually inattentive and careless men do not fail to exercise in avoiding danger to their own person or property." 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471 

Dzura v. Phillips, 1931 A. S. 969, at 970 

Bjornquist v. Boston & Albany R. R., 185 Mass. 130

Gross negligence has as an essential to this proof the indifference to present legal duty, and striking disregard of the danger of probable injury. 

Bank v. Satran, 266 Mass. 253

In determining negligence whether the conduct of the defendant amounts to gross negligence, it first must be determined what the ordinary, careful and prudent man would have done under the circumstances and then that conduct must be compared with the conduct of the defendant. If by that comparison the defendant's conduct, having regard to all the facts and circumstances, was a little worse than negligent and did not amount to wilful, wanton or reckless conduct, but the defendant's conduct was between negligence and wilful, wanton and reckless conduct, then it was gross negligence. 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554, at 560

Ordinarily no one element of conduct can be ruled to constitute gross negligence. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471, at 1472 

McKenna v. Smith, 1951 4. S. 819

Gross negligence is usually made up by a combination of circumstances, Dzura v. Phillips, 1931 A. S. 969 but different situations existed in: 

Cook v. Cole, 1931 A. S. 193 

Clay v. Pope Co., 1930 A. S. 1925 

Cannon v. Bassett, 264 Mass. 383

Every act or omission entering into a particular happening must be considered in connection with all the circumstances 2

GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

before the whole can properly be held to be an instance of gross negligence. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471, at 1472

Gross negligence exists when the conduct of the defendant is that of one who recklessly exercised no forethought, no diligence for the safety of the person to whom he owes a duty, when in a situation which the most inattentive and careless person would recognize as pregnant with imminent peril to life, person or property. 

Negligence to be gross must include an element of carelessness so great that the court or jury can say that there was not only absence of due care that he should have exercised, but also a degree of negligence much greater than that which would constitute ordinary negligence. B. 1. 

Renaud v. New York etc. R. Co., 206 Mass. 557 

Martin v. Boston etc. Co., 205 Mass. 16, at 19 

Devine v. New York etc. Railroad, 205 Mass. 416 

Dimauro v. Linwood St. Ry. Co., 200 Mass. 147 

Lanci v. Boston Elevated Ry. Co., 197 Mass. 32 

Manning v. Conway, 192 Mass. 122 

Oulighon v. Butler, 189 Mass. 287 

Dolphin v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry. Co., 189 Mass. 270 

Brennan v. Standard Oil Co., 187 Mass. 376 

Hays-Pitts v. Kimball Co., 183 Mass 262 

Phelps v. New England Ry. Co., 172 Mass. 98

Galbraith v. West End St. Ry. Co., 165 Mass. 572 

Debbins v. Old Colony Ry. Co., 154 Mass. 402

DISTINCTIONS 

Between Ordinary and Gross Negligence Ordinary and gross negligence differ in degree on inattention. 

Cook v. Cole, 1931 A. S. 193, at 196 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 592

Gross negligence differs in degree rather than in kind from ordinary negligence and is materially more want of care than constitutes simple inadvertence and need not amount to such reckless disregard of probable consequences as is equivalent to a wilful and intentional wrong. 

Cook v. Cole, 1931 A. S. 193, at 196 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls, 241 Mass 100; S. C. 238 

Mass. 239 

Cotter v. Petitioner, 237 Mass. 68

GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

But see: Banks v. Braman, 188 Mass. 367, at 370 (Where Knowlton, C. J., says ".... it is different in kind and not degree.") 

2. Between Gross Negligence and Wilful, Wanton and 

Reckless Conduct

Gross negligence is something less than wilful, wanton and reckless conduct, which renders a defendant who has injured another liable to the latter even though guilty of contributory negligence, or which renders a defendant in rightful possession of real estate liable to a trespasser whom he has injured. 

It falls short of being such reckless disregard of probable consequences as is equivalent to a wilful and intentional wrong. 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 592 

4 A. L. R. 1185

CASES INVOLVING

а. Where Gross Negligence Exists 

In Connors v. Boland, 1933 A. S. 657, where the guest on the evening in question was invited by the operator to take a ride; there was testimony that when they started the operator drove his automobile at a speed of about thirty miles an hour which was increased to fifty miles an hour when they were within a third of a mile from the place of accident; that while going down a heavy grade, and where there was a curve to the left, the operator was warned by the guest to slow down; that instead of complying with his request the operator increased the speed of his automobile to sixty miles an hour, and it began to sway; that the automobile struck a fence and "broke down sixty feet of it, and then jumped a deep ravine and embedded itself in the bank of across the ravine. 

The court said, at pages 160 and 161: "To drive a motor vehicle upon the public ways at a speed which would endanger the life or safety of its occupants might be found to be gross negligence even in the absence of other unfavorable conditions. "In the present case, however, apart from the operation of the automobile at a speed of sixty miles an hour, it appears that there was a steep grade and a curve ahead. It is manifest that in these circumstances this automobile was operated with a degree of negligence far greater than the absence of ordinary care. Gross negligence is substantially and appreciably greater than ordinary negligence. It is great negligence, it is the absence of slight diligence, and the want of slight care. It is a heedless and palpable violation of legal duty respecting the rights of others. 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588 "There was abundant evidence of gross negligence in the present case." 4c

The court said, at page 2270: "... it was for the jury to determine . . . whether . . . the defendant's conduct was 'grossly' negligent." 

And at page 2269: 

"We think if one considers all the acts and omissions on the part of the defendant which . . . have entered into the happening which resulted in the injury, he could find that shocking indifference to safe driving which constitutes 'gross negligence' as distinguished from the failure to exercise the care of a reasonably prudent man in driving which can justly be deemed 'negligence'." 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471 

McKenna v. Smith, 1931 A. S. 819

HOSPITALS HOSPITALS A. LIABILITY 

1. Private

In Mahoney v. Harley Private Hospital, Inc., 1932 A. S. 745, where the plaintiff, an infant child, was burnt during the night, while in the exclusive care, charge and control of two nurses acting within the scope of their employment by the defendant, it was their duty to record any happening to the child. No record of the appearance of the bleb was made by the nurses in charge. The nurses were not produced at the trial by the defendant, nor was testimony from them adduced. No record of the hospital covering the time when the burn occurred was put in evidence. The court said, at pages 748 and 749: "... the plaintiff was in the exclusive care and control of the defendant's servants between 10 P. M. of November 12 and 2 A. M. of November 13, 1927; and that a duty was owed to use appropriate care to refrain from injury to hima duty which did not arise solely from contract with [his] mother, but was inherent in the assumption of control by the defendant. 

Lowner v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 175 Mass. 166 "It is equally manifest that something happened between those hours which resulted in the ruptured blister, something about which the nurses should have known and about which they should have made a report. .. No note was made; and no evidence of any statement by them appears, unless it is inferred from the evidence of Dr. L's remarks [that the baby was scalded by a nurse]. No objection was interposed to the introduction of the testimony of his statement [it] cannot now be disregarded. "Hearsay, once admitted, may be weighed with the other evidence, and given any evidentiary value which it may possess. 

Du Pois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394, at 397 

Peterson v. Meekins Packard & Wheat, Inc., 261 Mass. 336, at 339 

Damon v. Carrol, 163 Mass. 404 1-a

HOSPITALS 

"We think an inference possible that Dr. L. had heard scalding while bathing given as an explanation from one or other of the night nurses. Inquiry from them on his part would, at least be justifiable and might be thought to be imperative. "Jurors might well infer that the failure to resort or to record the happening argued a consciousness of fault on the part of the nurses which would imply that the appearance of the bleb was not an inexplicable indication of disease or a result of an innocent event, but a manifestation of injurious action for which one or other or both of them were responsible. .. this was not a case of res ipsa loquitur, i. e., where the happening of the event, in and of itself, was evidence of negligence. The happening of the formation of a blister did not of itself indicate negligence. It could be explained by the existence of the disease, and by other things consistent with due care in the ordinary course of experience. "The mere existence of a burn was not of itself enough to establish liability; . . . the credible testimony with legitimate inferences in the circumstances could be found to exclude all but reasonable findings that a burn existed which had been caused by negligent action of the defendant's servants. "Decisions are not controlling, such as: 

Traverse v. Wing, 260 Mass. 527 

Morris v. Weene, 258 Mass. 178 

Bigwood v. Boston etc. Ry., 209 Mass. 345 

Childs v. American Express Co., 197 Mass. 337" 1-b

E. DISABILITIES AND PRIVILEGE OF COVERTURE 1. At Common Law 

The early common law recognized and upheld the doctrine that for most purposes husband and wife formed a single person, represented by the husband, and as a consequence of this legal merger it has been said "that is, the very being or legal existence of the woman is suspended during the marriage, or at least is incorporated and consolidated into that of the husband. . . . Upon this 

principle, of a union of person in husband and wife, depend almost all the legal rights, duties, and disabilities, that neither of them acquire by the marriage," and "The wife... hath no separate interest in anything during her coverture." Or, as pointedly and accurately stated in Dixon v. Aermican, 181 Mass. 430, at 431, with a reference to the early English authorities, the wife was considered the husband's chattel. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 284

Personal property in her possession upon marriage passed to him, and could be levied upon for his debts, or bequeathed by him to strangers, and he also took during coverture a sole estate in her lands which she could not alien unless he joined, or devise even with his assent, unless when exercising a power granted to her at the creating of the estate, nor derive any benefit or income therefrom by any contract which sh could make separately. 

Nolin v. Pearson. 191 Mass. 283, at 284 

Hawkins v. Providence etc. R. R., 119 Mass. 596 

Bartlett v. Cowles, 15 Gray 445, at 446 

Gerry v. Gerry, 11 Gray 381 

Lowell v. Daniels, 2 Gray 161, at 168 

Ames v. Chew, 5 Met. 320 

Clapp v. Stoughton, 10 Pick. 463, at 468 and 469 

Washburn v. Hale, 10 Pick. 429 

Osgood v. Breed, 12 Mass. 525 

Legg v. Legg, 8 Mass. 99 

Fowler v. Shearer, 7 Mass. 14

Without her consent damages for injury to her person or reputation also might be released by him, or if collected in her lifetime they became his separate property, and as a husband he had the right moderately to chastise his wife, although it was declared by E-1

the Colony in 1641 that she should be free from corporal correction by him. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285 

Kelley v. N. Y. N. H. & H. R. R., 168 Mass. 308, at 311 and cases cited 

Comm. v. McAfee, 108 Mass. 458 

Southworth v. Packard, 7 Mass. 95 

2. Under Statutes Relating to Married Women 

While the common law prevails in this Commonwealth except so far as it may have been modified by statute, it is obvious from this brief reference to some of its provisions that the development of modern society would imperatively call from time to time for the modification or abrogation of many if not all of these archaic conditions. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285

Beginning with the St. of 1842, c. 74, and by subsequent statutory enactments the separate legal existence of a married woman as to her right to hold and dispose of property both real and personal as well as the right to her person has been gradually recognized and established. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285

This remedial legislation has resulted in very largely impairing the unity of husband and wife as it existed at common law. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285 

Bradford v. Worcester, 184 Mass. 557, at 561 

Butler v. Ives, 139 Mass. 202, at 203

It also must be taken as settled that for the purposes of divorce, of separate maintenance and of public charitable relief she may have a separate domicil, and is absolutely entitled to her personal liberty and earnings, with a corresponding liability for her debts and contracts, and for torts committed by her or by her husband under her direction. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285 

Bradford v. Worcester, 184 Mass. 557, at 561 

Shane v. Lyons, 172 Mass. 199, at 200 

Burtis v. Burtis, 161 Mass. 508 

McCarty v. De Best, 120 Mass. 89

Osgood v. Osgood, 153 Mass. 38 E-2 4444~~

If the husband still is recognized as nominally the head of the family, and as such may determine their common residence, for the proper conduct of which he may be responsible under the criminal law, his control over the person or property of his wife has been reduced to a minimum, if it has not entirely disappeared. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 286 

Bradford v. Worcester, 184 Mass. 557, at 561 

Kerslake v. Cummings, 180 Mass. 65, at 68 

Harmon v. Old Colony R. R., 165 Mass. 100

By Gen. Laws, c. 209, s. 6, the disability of coverture, exclusive of suits between the husband and wife, has been removed, and since the first enactment she has been liable to be sued, and might bring suit in the same manner as if sole. In consequence of this broad and comprehensive language she became so far as civil procedure is concerned discovert as to all persons except her husband, and whenever injured in her person or estate a married woman may bring suit in her own name against the wrongdoer for damages suffered, which upon recovery become her exclusive property. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 286 

Harmon v. Old Colony R. R., 165 Mass. 100 

Lombard v. Morse, 155 Mass. 135, at 140

Jordan v. Middlesex R. R., 138 Mass. 425 

Our statute, as we have said, is expressed in the broadest terms. 

It permits a recovery by a married woman not only for injury in any form done to her person or property, but for damages which flow from a wrong suffered from a violation of personal rights. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 289

1. Loss of Consortium

A. Common Law 

At common law and before the enactment of statutes affecting the rights of married women, a husband might maintain an action in his own name alone for an injury to his wife which resulted in his loss of consortium with her 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 269 Mass. 56, at 57 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285 

Kelley v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 168 Mass. 308, at 311

The right of consortium, is a right growing out of the material relation, which the husband and wife have, respectively, to enjoy the society and companionship and affection of each other in their life together. At the common law, the husband had a right to the labor and services of his wife, and in suing for the damages which are person to the husband for an injury to his wife, he was permitted to recover, not only for the expenses of her care and cure, but for his loss of her labor and services and loss of consortium. 

Feneff v. New York Central, 203 Mass. 278, at 279 

Kelley v. N. Y. N. H. & H. R. R., 168 Mass. 309, and cases cited

B. Under Modern Doc trine Most of these common law powers of the husband and limitations upon the wife have faded away under modern statutes, including the right to recover for loss of consortium arising out of actions for personal injuries to the wife. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 269 Mass. 56, at 57 

Bolger v. Boston El. R. Co., 205 Mass. 420 

Feneff v. N. Y. Central R. R., 203 Mass. 278

The husband is not entitled to recover for the loss of his wife's consortium. 

Bolger v. Boston El. Ry., 205 Mass. 420, at 421

It was said in Moore v. Rawson, 199 Mass. 493, at pages 497 and 498: "The first question of importance relates to the manner. of estimating the value of the good will, and particularly its value in reference to the right to use the firm name. 

An answer to the question requires a consideration of what is fairly included in the good will, in view of the situation of the parties and the implications involved in the terms of the contract. Sometimes very little, if anything, is meant, beyond what is included in a sale of the good will under a judicial decree in settling the business of a partnership. 

But usually, in this Commonwealth, there is an implied agreement not to set up a competing business that will directly interfere with the business to be carried on by the purchaser of the good will. In England, a competing business may be set up by the seller of the good will; but he is not permitted to solicit business from the customers of the old firm." 

Webster v. Webster, 180 Mass. 310

In the accounting between surviving and liquidating partner and executrix of deceased partner, the good will of partnership should be included.

Rutan v. Coolidge, 241 Mass. 584 

After termination of partnership, the continuing partner is responsible to retiring partner for good will, where former uses the assets and name of the firm. 

Hutchins v. Page, 204 Mass. 284

Partnership for practice of dentistry has no good will, but agreement not to compete is enforceable. 

Foss v. Roby, 195 Mass. 173 34

GOOD WILL 

Where one partner of a firm of a butchering business to which a good will is attached has taken exclusive possession of the partnership property and is carrying on the business as if he were the purchaser of it, in a suit by one of his partners for an ac counting he may be charged with the value of the good will. 

Griffith v. Kirley, 189 Mass. 522

On the dissolution of a partnership by the death of one of the partners, the good will of the partnership business is a part of the assets of the partnership, and, in the absence of an agreement between the partners on the subject, the executor or administrator of a deceased partner has a right to have it sold in the liquidation of the assets of the partnership. 

If a partnership has established a business sufficiently permanent in character to include not only the patronage of its customers but the elements of locality and a distinctive name, a good will exists which forms an asset of commercial value in an accounting among partners. 

Moore v. Rawson, 185 Mass. 264

Where the defendant owned all the stock in trade of a partnership and the agreement among the partners provided that, upon the termination of the partnership by limitation, the defendant should sell to the plaintiffs "the property and assets" of the firm and the defendant did so, there was no sale of good will beyond that, if any, which pertained to the ownership of the goods, and each partner was at liberty to gain such advantage as he could from his relations to the former business. 14. 

Webster v. Webster, 180 Mass. 310

Printing Where the defendant, although he had covenanted with the plaintiff, on the dissolution of the firm of a printing business of which they had been members, not to engage in or interfere with that business for a limited time, nevertheless joined a new partnership of the same type of business, he was held liable for all 35
