injury occasioned to the plaintiff by the establishment of the new partnership. 

Dean v. Emerson, 102 Mass. 480 15. Shoe Cutter Manufacturing 

A contract made between citizens of this Commonwealth, by which one of them agreed, for a good consideration, never to "set up, exercise or carry on the trade or business of manufacturing and selling shoecutters at any place within the Commonwealth of Massachusetts" is illegal, as being in restraint of trade; although the manufacture of shoecutters is an art which can only be carried on by persons instructed in the same, and at the time of making the above contract the person so promising was ig norant of said art, and his said promise was made as a part of an agreement of partnership with one who was skilled and actually engaged in carrying on the same, and to take effect at the expiration of the partnership, and although at that time only three other persons were engaged in the business. 

Taylor v. Blanchard, 13 Allen, 370

Lothrop, etc. & Co., 191 Mass. 353 (An assignment for the benefit of creditors, made by a publishing corporation having a valuable good will, transferring to a trustee all "the real and personal property and estate and claims of every kind" belonging to the assignor "excepting therefrom such property as is exempt by law from attachment or from being taken on execution," conveys the good will of the assignor's publishing business including the right to use its trade name for the benefit of creditors; and all the more so if the assignment contains a provision authorizing the trustee to carry on in whole or in part the business theretofore conducted by the assignor "the more effectually and to the better advantage to dispose of the stock in trade and other assets" of the assignor; and the trustee can give to a purchaser of the property used in the business and of the good will connected with it a right to use the assignor's name as a designation of the publications that previously have borne its imprint, and to advertise as the assignor's successor in the business so purchased.)

 (On the dissolution of a partnership by the death of one of the partners the good will of the partnership business is a part of the assets of the partnership, and, in the absence of an agreement between the partners on the subject, the executor or administrator of a deceased partner has a right to have it sold in the liquidation of the assets of the partnership.) (Where the survivor of two partners in the teaming business after the death of his partner carries on the business in his own name at the old stand with only slight changes in the personnel of his customers for nearly two years, and then sells the good will of his business with a covenant to remain in the employ of the purchaser for six months and to do all in his power to hold the customers for the purchaser and with another covenant not to engage in the teaming business within the district covered by the old business for five years, he is under no obligation to account for the proceeds in even a nominal sum to the executor or administrator of his former partner, as the good will sold is his own and not that of the former partnership.) 40

Moore v. Rawson, 185 Mass. 264 (A retiring partner on termination of the partnership may require his copartners to account for the property of the partnership including the good will which they wrongfully appropriated to their own use. They will be held to account to the retiring partner for the good will in the same way as if they had purchased it or sold it to a stranger, regardless of the question whether the firm name could have been used without the consent in writing of one of the remaining partners.) (If a partnership has established a business sufficiently permanent in character to include not only the patronage of its customers but the elements of locality and a distinctive name, a good will exists which forms an asset of commercial value in an accounting among partners.) (Where by a dissolution under the terms of a partnership agreement, which contained no provision as to winding up the business, one of the partners is forced by the other partners to retire, and the remaining partners refuse the retired partner an accounting, and, forming a new partnership, continue the business using the retired partner's share in the property and good will of the old firm as part of their working capital, the remaining partners must account to the retired partner, not only for his share of the partnership property including the good will, but also for his share in all actual profits derived from the property, or must pay him interest on his share of the capital if he so elects. The court in its discretion may allow the remaining partners in accounting for the actual profits to deduct from the net profits such a sum as if found to be attributable solely to their skill and services in conducting the business.)

Company for a period of five years. .

The A. Company brought a bill in equity to restrain H. from competing with it contrary to article 6. Held, that the stipulation of article 6. was valid.) 42

Smith v. Brown, 164 Mass. 584 (A contract is valid which provides that for the consideration of the promisee's "taking from me my lease of an apothecary shop in I., . my promise herein being the chief inducement leading him to take said lease, and to purchase the property therein, and in said shop and the good will of the business,-I hereby agree with said A. under a penalty of one thousand dollars (to be forfeited and paid said A. or his legal representatives, in the event of my committing any breach of this agreement) not to engage directly or indirectly, or become in any manner interested, in the drug business within at least two miles of said apothecary shop, whose lease said A. takes from me, without first obtaining the written consent of said A. thereto."

Although the sum named is a penalty, substantial damages may be awarded.)

Handforth v. Jackson, 150 Mass. 149 ("The plaintiff has had the benefit of the good will of the defendant's business, which cannot now be restored.")

Palmer, 146 Mass. 469 (A purchaser promised to pay in instalments for a business plant and property, in consideration of its sale and delivery, and the performance of three particular covenants and agreements by the seller, the first of which was a general agreement, without any limitation of space, that for and during the period of five years he would not either directly or indirectly continue in, carry on, or engage in that business or any business of which that might form any part. Held, that the covenant was void as being in restraint of trade, and that, not being severable from the rest of the consideration, no action would lie on the promise for instalments of the price.) 

 (A manufacturer, who had acquired trade-marks in two kinds of soap manufactured by him, entered into a partnership with another, under articles in writing by which he contributed the good will of the business he was carrying on, with the tools, implements, and fixtures. On the dissolution of the partnership, he conveyed to his former partner, by a bill of sale, "the 44

GOOD WILL 

following goods and chattels, namely: All my right, title, and interest in and to all and singular the partnership property belonging to the firm, meaning hereby to sell and convey all my interest in the entire assets of the firm." Held, also, on a bill in equity by the purchaser under the bill of sale to restrain the seller from making and selling said two kinds of soap, from using wrappers bearing the trade-marks, and from doing matters tending to injure and impair the good will of the business, that the plaintiff was entitled to an injunction, except as to the making and selling the soap.) 

Munsey v. Butterfield, 133 Mass. 492 (Where a person agrees to sell and another to purchase a milk route in certain towns, delivery to be made on a day named, in an action by the seller against the buyer for breach of the agreement, in refusing to take the route and pay the consideration, if it appears that after the agreement, and before the day fixed for delivery, the owner bargained with a third person to purchase the latter's milk route, intending to run the same after the purchaser took his route and that the route of the third person comprised a portion of the same territory which the seller was intending to deliver and that the seller had promised not to disturb any of the customers of the route which he was selling, the buyer is under no obligation to complete the purchase and a verdict should be directed for him.) 

Ropes v. Boutelle v. Smith, 116 Mass. 111 (A. and B., bakers in F., bought of C. and D. their business as bakers in the same town, and their personal property connected with that business, and made a contract with them whereby C. and D. agreed "that they will not or either of them hereafter engage in the business of bakers in the town of F., and will not directly · or indirectly engage in any business or do any act that shall interfere with the business thus purchased for the sale of bread on the several bread routes heretofore connected with said business," for five years. Held, also, that C. and D. were liable, if one of them drove a bread cart in F. on his former routes and supplied his former customers with bread, acting as the hired servant of a baker in another town.) 

Dwight v. Hamilton, 113 Mass. 175 (A contract by a physician for the sale of his "practice and good will" in a specified town is not void as against public policy.) (In a contract of sale of a business and its good will, there is an implied covenant that the vendor will not interfere with the enjoyment of what he has sold; if he does, such interference may be restrained by injunction.) 

Dean v. Emerson, 102 Mass. 480 (The defendant, having covenanted with the plaintiff on the dissolution of a firm for the manufacture of daguerreotype materials, of which they had been members, "not, directly or indirectly, to enter into, or carry on, or in any way be interested in, or furnish to any 46

GOOD WILL 

person or persons information in regard to," that business within certain limits, nevertheless formed with a third person a new partnership within said limits for that business, had the whole financial charge of the new partnership, travelled about the country, visiting the customers of the old firm, and introducing the goods of the new partnership, and received a commission on all sales. Held, that these facts warranted a finding that the defendant was liable for all the injury occasioned to the plaintiff by the establishment of the new partnership.) (A. and B. entered into an indenture in which B. covenanted not to be interested in a certain business within a certain county, and also covenanted not to be interested, for five years in the same business within the United States. Held, that B. was liable for a breach of the first covenant, although the second covenant might be void as in restraint of trade.) 

Angier v. Webber, 14 Allen, 211 (Held, that an injunction should issue to restrain the defendants "from soliciting, doing or obtaining any work, trade, custom or teaming business for or from any of the customers or persons" who had formerly been customers of the partnership, "and from doing anything to impair or injure the said interest and good will in said teaming business.") 

Taylor v. Blanchard, 13 Allen, 370 (A contract made between citizens of this Commonwealth, by which one of them agreed, for a good consideration, never to "set up, exercise or carry on the trade or business of manufacturing and selling shoecutters at any place within the Commonwealth of 

Massachusetts" is illegal, as being in restraint of trade; although the manufacture of shoecutters is an art which can only be carried on by persons instructed in the same, and at the time of making the above contract the person so promising was ignorant of said art, and his said 47

GOOD WILL 

promise was made as a part of an agreement of partnership with one who was skilled and actually engaged in carrying on the same, and to take effect at the expiration of the partnership, and although at that time. only three other persons were engaged in the business.) 

Bassett v. Percival, 5 Allen, 345 (Where the purchaser seeks to rescind he cannot do so by merely returning the physical property if the sale also included good will which cannot be restored.) (A sale of a stock of goods in a store and "the good will of the vendor's trade and all the advantages connected with the store" does not import an agreement by the vendor not to engage again in a similar business. 

Proof that after the lapse of over a year the vendor again engaged in a similar business will not sustain an action to recover back the money paid.) 

Gilman v. Dwight, 13 Gray, 356 (An agreement by a physician of a country village, transferring his practice and good will to another physician for a certain sum, and guaranteeing "that no other physician, for the space of four years, will establish himself in this place as a competitor, unless the increased population of the place should warrant it, or unless the purchaser should commit some act, which shall forfeit to him the confidence of the community," and agreeing, in case any such competitor shall establish himself there within that time, contrary to the above provisions, to repay the sum paid, is not void as being in restraint of trade, nor too uncertain and insensible to support an action.) 48

GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

A. 

DEFINITIONS GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

Gross negligence is such conduct as results from the addition to ordinary carelessness of an utter disregard of the dictates of prudence, culminating in complete neglect of safety. 

Manning v. Simpson, 261 Mass. 494 (Crossing path of oncoming automobile on slippery road at increased speed.) 

Marcienowski v. Sanders, 252 Mass. 65 

Shiear v. Feigelson, 248 Mass. 432 

Burke v. Cook, 246 Mass. 518

Gross negligence is substantially and appreciably higher in magnitude than ordinary negligence. It is materially more want of care than constitutes simple inadvertence. It is an act or omission respecting legal duty of an aggravated character as distinguished from a mere failure to exercise ordinary care. It is very great negligence, or the absence of slight diligence, or the want of even scant care. It amounts to indifference to present legal duty and to utter forgetfulness of legal obligations so far as other persons may be affected. It is a heedless and palpable violation of legal duty respecting the rights of others. The element of culpability which characterizes all negligence is in gross negligence magnified to a high degree as compared with that present in ordinary negligence. 

Gross negligence is a manifestly smaller amount of watchfulness and circumspection than the circumstances require of a person of ordinary prudence. 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 591, and 592 

Mason v. Thomas, 1931 A. S. 133, at 135 

O'Leary v. Fash, 245 Mass. 123 

Barry v. Harding, 244 Mass. 588 

Flynn v. Lewis, 231 Mass. 550 

Massaletti v. Fitzroy, 228 Mass. 487 

Cane v. Boston Elevated Ry. Co., 217 Mass. 594, at 598 

Davis v. Boston & Northern St. Ry., 214 Mass. 98 

Adams v. Boston Elevated Ry. Co., 214 Mass. 1 

Berry v. Newton & Boston St. Ry., 209 Mass. 100 

Spooner v. Old Colony St. Ry., 190 Mass. 132 

Aiken v. Holyoke St. Ry., 184 Mass. 269, at 271 

Banks v. Braman, 188 Mass. 367, at 369 

Evenson v. Lexington & Boston St. Ry., 165 Mass. 

572, and cases cited 

4 A. L. R. 1185 1

GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

To constitute gross negligence it must appear that the plaintiff's injury was due to something more than simple carelessness, something which has in its elements of "indifference to present legal duty", of "utter forgetfulness of legal obligations so far as other persons may be affected", of "heedless and palpable violation of legal duty respecting the rights of others", of "manifestly smaller amount of watchfulness and circumspection than the circumstances require of a person of ordinary prudence", and of "the omission of even such diligence as habitually inattentive and careless men do not fail to exercise in avoiding danger to their own person or property." 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471 

Dzura v. Phillips, 1931 A. S. 969, at 970 

Bjornquist v. Boston & Albany R. R., 185 Mass. 130

Gross negligence has as an essential to this proof the indifference to present legal duty, and striking disregard of the danger of probable injury. 

Bank v. Satran, 266 Mass. 253

In determining negligence whether the conduct of the defendant amounts to gross negligence, it first must be determined what the ordinary, careful and prudent man would have done under the circumstances and then that conduct must be compared with the conduct of the defendant. If by that comparison the defendant's conduct, having regard to all the facts and circumstances, was a little worse than negligent and did not amount to wilful, wanton or reckless conduct, but the defendant's conduct was between negligence and wilful, wanton and reckless conduct, then it was gross negligence. 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554, at 560

Ordinarily no one element of conduct can be ruled to constitute gross negligence. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471, at 1472 

McKenna v. Smith, 1951 4. S. 819

Gross negligence is usually made up by a combination of circumstances, Dzura v. Phillips, 1931 A. S. 969 but different situations existed in: 

Cook v. Cole, 1931 A. S. 193 

Clay v. Pope Co., 1930 A. S. 1925 

Cannon v. Bassett, 264 Mass. 383

Every act or omission entering into a particular happening must be considered in connection with all the circumstances

GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

before the whole can properly be held to be an instance of gross negligence. 

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471, at 1472

Gross negligence exists when the conduct of the defendant is that of one who recklessly exercised no forethought, no diligence for the safety of the person to whom he owes a duty, when in a situation which the most inattentive and careless person would recognize as pregnant with imminent peril to life, person or property. 

Negligence to be gross must include an element of carelessness so great that the court or jury can say that there was not only absence of due care that he should have exercised, but also a degree of negligence much greater than that which would constitute ordinary negligence.

B. 1. 

Renaud v. New York etc. R. Co., 206 Mass. 557 

Martin v. Boston etc. Co., 205 Mass. 16, at 19

Devine v. New York etc. Railroad, 205 Mass. 416 

Dimauro v. Linwood St. Ry. Co., 200 Mass. 147 

Lanci v. Boston Elevated Ry. Co., 197 Mass. 32 

Manning v. Conway, 192 Mass. 122 

Oulighon v. Butler, 189 Mass. 287 

Dolphin v. Worcester Cons. St. Ry. Co., 189 Mass. 270 

Brennan v. Standard Oil Co., 187 Mass. 376 

Hays-Pitts v. Kimball Co., 183 Mass 262 

Phelps v. New England Ry. Co., 172 Mass. 98

Galbraith v. West End St. Ry. Co., 165 Mass. 572 

Debbins v. Old Colony Ry. Co., 154 Mass. 402

DISTINCTIONS 

Between Ordinary and Gross Negligence Ordinary and gross negligence differ in degree on inattention. 

Cook v. Cole, 1931 A. S. 193, at 196 

Learned v. Hawthorne, 269 Mass. 554 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 592

Gross negligence differs in degree rather than in kind from ordinary negligence and is materially more want of care than constitutes simple inadvertence and need not amount to such reckless disregard of probable consequences as is equivalent to a wilful and intentional wrong. 

Cook v. Cole, 1931 A. S. 193, at 196 

Prondecka v. Turners Falls, 241 Mass 100; S. C. 238 

Mass. 239 

Cotter v. Petitioner, 237 Mass. 68

GROSS NEGLIGENCE 

But see: Banks v. Braman, 188 Mass. 367, at 370 (Where Knowlton, C. J., says in kind and not degree.") 2. 

it is different

Between Gross Negligence and Wilful, Wanton and 

Reckless Conduct

Gross negligence is something less than wilful, wanton and reckless conduct, which renders a defendant who has injured another liable to the latter even though guilty of contributory negligence, or which renders a defendant in rightful possession of real estate liable to a trespasser whom he has injured. 

It falls short of being such reckless disregard of probable consequences as is equivalent to a wilful and intentional wrong. 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588, at 592 

4 A. L. R. 1185

C. 1. 

CASES INVOLVING 

a. Automobiles 

Where Gross Negligence Exists 

In Connors v. Boland, 1933 A. S. 657, where the guest on the evening in question was invited by the operator to take a ride; there was testimony that when they started the operator drove his automobile at a speed of about thirty miles an hour which was increased to fifty miles an hour when they were within a third of a mile from the place of accident; that while going down a heavy grade, and where there was a curve to the left, the operator was warned by the guest to slow down; that instead of complying with his request the operator increased the speed of his automobile to sixty miles an hour, and it began to sway; that the automobile struck a fence and "broke down sixty feet of it, and then jumped a deep ravine and embedded itself in the bank of across the ravine. 

The court said, at pages 160 and 161: "To drive a motor vehicle upon the public ways at a speed which would endanger the life or safety of its occupants might be found to be gross negligence even in the absence of other unfavorable conditions. "In the present case, however, apart from the operation of the automobile at a speed of sixty miles an hour, it appears that there was a steep grade and a curve ahead. It is manifest that in these circumstances this automobile was operated with a degree of negligence far greater than the absence of ordinary care. Gross negligence is substantially and appreciably greater than ordinary negligence. It is great negligence, it is the absence of slight diligence, and the want of slight care. It is a heedless and palpable violation of legal duty respecting the rights of others. 

Altman v. Aronson, 231 Mass. 588 "There was abundant evidence of gross negligence in the present case." 4c

The court said, at page 2270: ". . . it was for the jury to determine . . . whether . . . the defendant's conduct was 'grossly' negligent." 

And at page 2269: "We think if one considers all the acts and omissions on the part of the defendant which . . . have entered into the happening which resulted in the injury, he could find that shocking indifference to safe driving which constitutes 'gross negligence' as distinguished from the failure to exercise the care of a reasonably prudent man in driving which can justly be deemed 'negligence'."

Meaney v. Doyle, 1931 A. S. 1471 

McKenna v. Smith, 1931 A. S. 819

In Bruce v. Johnson, 1931 A. S. 2255, the plaintiffs were riding within the cab of a loaded milk truck as guests of its operator; the road was slippery, although he had chains he did not use them, twice the plaintiffs asked the defendant not to drive so fast and he slackened his speed but soon increased it again. A third time as he was approaching an abrupt sharp curve at fifty-five miles an hour, one plaintiff told the defendant not to go so fast as the plaintiffs were scared. The defendant let go the wheel raising both hands from it and said, "A little accident won't hurt you.'

The truck got beyond the control of the defendant, ran into a tree and was damaged beyond repair.

HOSPITALS A. LIABILITY 

1. Private 

HOSPITALS In Mahoney v. Harley Private Hospital, Inc., 1932 A. S. 745, where the plaintiff, an infant child, was burnt during the night, while in the exclusive care, charge and control of two nurses acting within the scope of their employment by the defendant, it was their duty to record any happening to the child. No record of the appearance of the bleb was made by the nurses in charge. The nurses were not produced at the trial by the defendant, nor was testimony from them adduced. No record of the hospital covering the time when the burn occurred was put in evidence. The court said, at pages 748 and 749: "... the plaintiff was in the exclusive care and control of the defendant's servants between 10 P. M. of November 12 and 2 A. M. of November 13, 1927; and that a duty was owed to use appropriate care to refrain from injury to hima duty which did not arise solely from contract with [his] mother, but was inherent in the assumption of control by the defendant. 

Lowner v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 175 Mass. 166 "It is equally manifest that something happened between those hours which resulted in the ruptured blister, something about which the nurses should have known and about which they should have made a report. . . . No note was made; and no evidence of any statement by them appears, unless it is inferred from the evidence of Dr. L's remarks [that the baby was scalded by a nurse]. No objection was interposed to the introduction of the testimony of his statement cannot now be disregarded. [it] "Hearsay, once admitted, may be weighed with the other evidence, and given any evidentiary value which it may possess. 

Du Pois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394, at 397 

Peterson v. Meekins Packard & Wheat, Inc., 261 Mass.

HOSPITALS A. LIABILITY

HOSPITALS 

In Mahoney v. Harley Private Hospital, Inc., 1932 A. S. 745, where the plaintiff, an infant child, was burnt during the night, while in the exclusive care, charge and control of two nurses acting within the scope of their employment by the defendant, it was their duty to record any happening to the child. No record of the appearance of the bleb was made by the nurses in charge. The nurses were not produced at the trial by the defendant, nor was testimony from them adduced. No record of the hospital covering the time when the burn occurred was put in evidence. The court said, at pages 748 and 749: 

the plaintiff was in the exclusive care and control of the defendant's servants between 10 P. M. of November 12 and 2 A. M. of November 13, 1927; and that a duty was owed to use appropriate care to refrain from injury to hima duty which did not arise solely from contract with [his] mother, but was inherent in the assumption of control by the defendant. 

Lowner v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 175 Mass. 166 "It is equally manifest that something happened between those hours which resulted in the ruptured blister, something about which the nurses should have known and about which they should have made a report. . . . No note was made; and no evidence of any statement by them appears, unless it is inferred from the evidence of Dr. L's remarks [that the baby was scalded by a nurse]. No objection was interposed to the introduction of the testimony of his statement [it] cannot now... be disregarded. ... "Hearsay, once admitted, may be weighed with the other evidence, and given any evidentiary value which it may possess. 

Du Pois v. Powdrell, 271 Mass. 394, at 397 

Peterson v. Meekins Packard & Wheat, Inc., 261 Mass. 336, at 339 

Damon v. Carrol, 163 Mass. 404 1-a

HOSPITALS 

"We think an inference possible that Dr. L. had heard scalding while bathing given as an explanation from one or other of the night nurses. Inquiry from them on his part would, at least be justifiable and might be thought to be imperative. "Jurors might well infer that the failure to resort or to record the happening argued a consciousness of fault on the part of the nurses which would imply that the appearance of the bleb was not an inexplicable indication of disease or a result of an innocent event, but a manifestation of injurious action for which one or other or both of them were responsible. "... this was not a case of res ipsa loquitur, i. e., where the happening of the event, in and of itself, was evidence of negligence. The happening of the formation of a blister did not of itself indicate negligence. It could be explained by the existence of the disease, and by other things consistent with due care in the ordinary course of experience. "The mere existence of a burn was not of itself enough to establish liability; . . . the credible testimony with legitimate inferences in the circumstances could be found to exclude all but reasonable findings that a burn existed which had been caused by negligent action of the defendant's servants. "Decisions are not controlling, such as: 

Traverse v. Wing, 260 Mass. 527 

Morris v. Weene, 258 Mass. 178 

Bigwood v. Boston etc. Ry., 209 Mass. 345 

Childs v. American Express Co., 197 Mass. 337" 1-b

E. DISABILITIES AND PRIVILEGE OF COVERTURE 1. At Common Law 

The early common law recognized and upheld the doctrine that for most purposes husband and wife formed a single person, represented by the husband, and as a consequence of this legal merger it has been said "that is, the very being or legal existence of the woman is suspended during the marriage, or at least is incorporated and consolidated into that of the husband. .. Upon this principle, of a union of person in husband and wife, depend almost all the legal rights, duties, and disabilities, that neither of them acquire by the marriage," and "The wife... hath no separate interest in anything during her coverture." Or, as pointedly and accurately stated in Dixon v. Aermican, 181 Mass. 430, at 431, with a reference to the early English authorities, the wife was considered the husband's chattel. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 284

Personal property in her possession upon marriage passed to him, and could be levied upon for his debts, or bequeathed by him to strangers, and he also took during coverture a sole estate in her lands which she could not alien unless he joined, or devise even with his assent, unless when exercising a power granted to her at the creating of the estate, nor derive any benefit or income therefrom by any contract which sh could make separately. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 284

Hawkins v. Providence etc. R. R., 119 Mass. 596 

Bartlett v. Cowles, 15 Gray 445, at 446 

Gerry v. Gerry, 11 Gray 381 

Lowell v. Daniels, 2 Gray 161, at 168 

Ames v. Chew, 5 Met. 320 

Clapp v. Stoughton, 10 Pick. 463, at 468 and 469 

Washburn v. Hale, 10 Pick. 429 

Osgood v. Breed, 12 Mass. 525

Legg v. Legg, 8 Mass. 99 

Fowler v. Shearer, 7 Mass. 14

Without her consent damages for injury to her person or reputation also might be released by him, or if collected in her lifetime they became his separate property, and as a husband he had the right moderately to chastise his wife, although it was declared by E-1

the Colony in 1641 that she should be free from corporal correction by him. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285 

Kelley v. N. Y. N. H. & H. R. R., 168 Mass. 308, at 311 and cases cited 

Comm. v. McAfee, 108 Mass. 458 

Southworth v. Packard, 7 Mass. 95 

2. Under Statutes Relating to Married Women 

While the common law prevails in this Commonwealth except so far as it may have been modified by statute, it is obvious from this brief reference to some of its provisions that the development of modern society would imperatively call from time to time for the modification or abrogation of many if not all of these archaic conditions. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285

Beginning with the St. of 1842, c. 74, and by subsequent statutory enactments the separate legal existence of a married woman as to her right to hold and dispose of property both real and personal as well as the right to her person has been gradually recognized and established. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285

This remedial legislation has resulted in very largely impairing the unity of husband and wife as it existed at common law. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285 

Bradford v. Worcester, 184 Mass. 557, at 561 

Butler v. Ives, 139 Mass. 202, at 203

It also must be taken as settled that for the purposes of divorce, of separate maintenance and of public charitable relief she may have a separate domicil, and is absolutely entitled to her personal liberty and earnings, with a corresponding liability for her debts and contracts, and for torts committed by her or by her husband under her direction. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285 

Bradford v. Worcester, 184 Mass. 557, at 561 

Shane v. Lyons, 172 Mass. 199, at 200 

Burtis v. Burtis, 161 Mass. 508 

McCarty v. De Best, 120 Mass. 89

Osgood v. Osgood, 153 Mass. 38 E-2

If the husband still is recognized as nominally the head of the family, and as such may determine their common residence, for the proper conduct of which he may be responsible under the criminal law, his control over the person or property of his wife has been reduced to a minimum, if it has not entirely disappeared. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 286 

Bradford v. Worcester, 184 Mass. 557, at 561 

Kerslake v. Cummings, 180 Mass. 65, at 68 

Harmon v. Old Colony R. R., 165 Mass. 100

By Gen. Laws, c. 209, s. 6, the disability of coverture, exclusive of suits between the husband and wife, has been removed, and since the first enactment she has been liable to be sued, and might bring suit in the same manner as if sole. In consequence of this broad and comprehensive language she became so far as civil procedure is concerned discovert as to all persons except her husband, and whenever injured in her person or estate a married woman may bring suit in her own name against the wrongdoer for damages suffered, which upon recovery become her exclusive property. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 286 

Harmon v. Old Colony R. R., 165 Mass. 100 

Lombard v. Morse, 155 Mass. 135, at 140

Jordan v. Middlesex R. R., 138 Mass. 425 

Our statute, as we have said, is expressed in the broadest terms. 

It permits a recovery by a married woman not only for injury in any form done to her person or property, but for damages which flow from a wrong suffered from a violation of personal rights. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 289

I. Loss of Consortium 

A. Common Law

At common law and before the enactment of statutes affecting the rights of married women, a husband might maintain an action in his own name alone for an injury to his wife which resulted in his loss of consortium with her 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 269 Mass. 56, at 57 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283, at 285 

Kelley v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 168 Mass. 308, at 311

The right of consortium, is a right growing out of the material relation, which the husband and wife have, respectively, to enjoy the society and companionship and affection of each other in their life together. At the common law, the husband had a right to the labor and services of his wife, and in suing for the damages which are person to the husband for an injury to his wife, he was permitted to recover, not only for the expenses of her care and cure, but for his loss of her labor and services and loss of consortium. 

Feneff v. New York Central, 203 Mass. 278, at 279 

Kelley v. N. Y. N. H. & H. R. R., 168 Mass. 309, and cases cited

B. Under Modern Doc trine Most of these common law powers of the husband and limitations upon the wife have faded away under modern statutes, including the right to recover for loss of consortium arising out of actions for personal injuries to the wife. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 269 Mass. 56, at 57 

Bolger v. Boston El. R. Co., 205 Mass. 420 

Feneff v. N. Y. Central R. R., 203 Mass. 278

The husband is not entitled to recover for the loss of his wife's consortium. 

Bolger v. Boston El. Ry., 205 Mass. 420, at 421

Actions [c]-1

Nor can the wife recover for the loss of her husband's consortium. 

Feneff v. New York Central R. R., 203 Mass. 278

No valid distinction can be drawn between the husband's right to recover for the loss of the wife's consortium, in cases growing out of the negligence of a third party, and the wife's right to recover for loss of the husband's consortium in like cases. Neither can it make any difference that in the case of the wife the loss of consortium is or may be the sole ground of recovery and in the case of the husband it is or may be one of several grounds of recovery. 

Bolger v. Boston El. Ry., 205 Mass. 420, at 421

II. Necessary Nursing and 

Physician's Care

The husband still remains the nominal and legal head of the family and is responsible for the reasonable support of the wife and for affording her necessary nursing and physician's care. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 268 Mass. 56, at 58 

Kenyon v. Vogel, 250 Mass. 341, at 344

The wife may, however, bind her separate estate for services of this nature. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 268 Mass. 56, at 58 

Charron v. Day, 228 Mass. 305

In those circumstances, if properly pleaded, she might recover therefor in an action for personal injuries sustained by her. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 268 Mass. 56, at 58

But in the absence of convincing proof that the wife has bound her separate estates, the husband is presumed to be liable therefor and the wrongdoer is liable for his disbursements and obligations already incurred by him on this account. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 269 Mass. 56, at 57 

Braun v. Bell, 247 Mass. 437, at 440 

Driscoll v. Gaffey, 207 Mass. 102, at 108

The rule is established that if nothing appears the husband is presumed to have incurred such expenses as theretofore have been Actions [c]-2

necessary. The presumption is not absolute; the facts may be proved. 

Cassidy v. Constantin, 269 Mass. 56, at 59

Stated as a principle of law, the measure of damages against a wrongdoer is the same, whether the person injured is a married woman, single woman, or man.

He is bound to make compensation for the injury inflicted. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 268 Mass. 56, at 58

As a practical matter, when the injured person is a married woman the wrongdoer pays either the husband or the wife for the necessary nursing and physicians' care rendered to the wife and so does not escape this part of the consequences of his tort. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 268 Mass. 56, at 58

A. Future Probable Medical Expenses 

The wife, and not the husband, is entitled to recover damages based on proved or estimated future probable medical expenses. 

Cassidy v. Constantin, 269 Mass. 56, at 59

1. Private

HOSPITALS 

In Sheehan v. Strong, 257 Mass. 525, the defendant conducted a private hospital for the care of medical and surgical cases. Various physicians in no way connected with the hospital sent patients there, and had full charge and control of their patients, their diet, care, surgical operations and the exclusive direction and control of the defendant's hospital nurses who attended such patients, the services of the nurses being paid for by the defendant. The plaintiff through her family physician engaged a bed in a ward in the hospital and employed a surgeon, who performed a gall bladder operation on the plaintiff. Neither the physician nor the surgeon had any connection with the hospital. Three days after the operation an abscess formed on the right thigh of the plaintiff at a place where hypodermic injections of pituitrin had been made by a nurse in the defendant's employ while the room was dark after rubbing the plaintiff's thigh with a cold substance and then inserting a hypodermic needle in a different spot from where the cold application was made. 

The question was, whether there was an evidence warranting a finding of negligence. 

It was said at pages 528 and 529: "There was no evidence that the hypodermic needle was infected, or that the abscess was due to an infection. [The surgeon testified that he did not believe the abscess was formed from inserting the hypodermic needle in a place which was not washed or cleaned]. [The plaintiff's family physician] testified that he and [the surgeon] ordered the nurse to inject pituitrin .... that various things might have caused the abscess, such as skin disease that would be carried by an injection through the outer skin, absorbent cotton, or the pituitrin itself (an irritant) meeting with the contents from the gall bladder which coursed through the blood stream of the plaintiff; that no one could say what caused it; that a germ on the skin might cause it, and if the skin was not properly washed the liability of infection would be increased. 66 ....

There was other evidence offered by the plaintiff tending to show that she had jaundice and diabetes, and 1

HOSPITALS 

that an abscess would be more likely to develop if a person was suffering from the latter disease. "Although several physicians testified, none of them were able to express an opinion as to what caused the abscess. "In these circumstances there was nothing to show that any act or omission of the nurse resulted in the formation of the abscess. Its cause was wholly a matter of conjecture and speculation without evidence to support a finding of negligence on the part of the nurse." 

In Vannah v. Hart Private Hospital, 228 Mass. 132, the defendant conducted a private hospital and agreed for a stipulated pecuniary compensation, that the plaintiff, a woman patient, who was about to have an operation performed there by her own surgeon after being etherized by her family physician, that it would give her a room in its hospital before and after the operation and would allow her surgeon and family physician to use the operating room and would give her services of such nurses as might be necessary for care before, after and during the operation. The operation was performed and while the patient was still unconscious under the influence of ether, one of the two hospital nurses, who were present during the operation, and assisted in carrying her to her room, forcibly pulled off a valuable ring from the plaintiff's finger and stole it. 

It was said at pages 136, 137, 138 and 139: "If a .... nurse did steal the ring it is plain that the defendant is not liable on the ground that in stealing the ring the nurse was acting within the scope of her employment as a servant of the defendant..... "If the plaintiff had stood in the relation of a stranger to the defendant there would have been no error in the trial. But the plaintiff did not stand to the defendant in the relation of a stranger ..... If for example a stranger had burst into the operating room, attacked the plaintiff and done her bodily harm or had attacked the plaintiff while the nurses were carrying her from the operating room to her own room and the defendant's nurses had stood by and did nothing to protect the plaintiff from those attacks, it is plain in our opinion that there would be a violation of the duty owed by the defendant under its contract with the plaintiff.

HOSPITALS 

"It is equally plain in our opinion that the duty owed by the defendant under its contract with the plaintiff extended to the care of the rings on her fingers while she was unconscious from the effects of ether as well as to the security of her person, and finally it is equally plain in our opinion that there is as much a violation of the duty owed by the defendant under the contract where the attack upon the person or larceny of the ring is committed by one of the defendant's own nurses (whose duty it was to protect the plaintiff) as well as in the case where the attack is made by a stranger and the nurses do not undertake to protect her from the attack. "The doctrine of Bryant v. Rich, 106 Mass. 180 applies where there is a contract between the plaintiff and defendant by force of which the defendant is to furnish for the plaintiff's comfort the services of its, the defendant's employees. Where the injury is caused by the act of the defendant's servants done in the course of their employment an action may be brought on negligence of the defendant's servants for which the defendant is liable because the act took place in the course of his servants' employment, or an action may be brought in the case based on violation of the duty owed by the defendant to the plaintiff under the contract between the defendant and the plaintiff. "But where (as was the case in Bryant v. Rich and in the case at bar) the injury done the plaintiff is caused by an act of the defendant's servants outside of the servants' duty as employees of the defendant but by an act of the defendant's servants which while not in the course of the servants' employment is none the less a violation of the duty owed by the defendant under the defendant's contract with the plaintiff, the only action that can be brought is an action founded upon the duty arising out of the contract. ....'for a violation of such a contract either by force or negligence, the plaintiff may bring an action of tort, or an action of contract'. "What has been said leaves open the defence which arises out of the testimony that the plaintiff when received into the hospital was asked to put into the custody of the defendant corporation all her 'valuables'. The defendant's agent who received the plaintiff when she came to the hospital testified that that request was made to her at

HOSPITALS 

that time. The plaintiff on the other hand testified that she was asked to put her money into the custudy of the hospital but that she was not asked to put anything else into its custody. If the defendant's evidence is believed, a defence is made out. On the other hand if the plaintiff's evidence on this matter is believed, her rights depend upon the rule of Bryant v. Rich, 106 Mass. 180." 

2. Public 

A corporation, the object of which is to provide a general hospital for sick and insane persons, having no capital stock nor provision for making dividends or profits, deriving its funds mainly from public and private charity, and holding them in trust for the object of sustaining the hospital, conducting its affairs for the purpose of administering to the comfort of the sick, without expectation or right on the part of those immediately interested in the corporation to receive compensation for their own benefit, is a public charitable institution.

McDonald v. Mass. General Hospital, 120 Mass. 432 

The facts that a corporation, established for the maintenance of a public hospital, by its rules requires of its patients payment for their board, according to their circumstances and the accommodation they receive; that no person has individually a right to demand admission; and that the trustees of the hospital determine who are to be received; do not render it the less a public charity.

McDonald v. Mass. General Hospital, 120 Mass. 432 

A corporation, established for the maintenance of a public charitable hospital, which has exercised due care in the selection of its agents, is not liable for injury to a patient caused by their negligence, nor for the unauthorized assumption of one of the hospital attendants to act as a surgeon. 

McDonald v. Mass. General Hospital, 120 Mass. 432 

An action of tort cannot be maintained against a public charitable hospital corporation to recover for personal injuries caused by negligence of the hospital servants or agents. 

Kidd v. Mass. Homoeopathic Hospital, 237 Mass. 500

An action of tort cannot be maintained to recover for injuries caused by the negligence of the servants or agents of a public charity, because it has no funds which can be chargeable with any judgment the plaintiff might recover, except those held subject to the trust of maintaining the charity.

2. Public 

A corporation, the object of which is to provide a general hospital for sick and insane persons, having no capital stock nor provision for making dividends or profits, deriving its funds mainly from public and private charity, and holding them in trust for the object of sustaining the hospital, conducting its affairs for the purpose of administering to the comfort of the sick, without expectation or right on the part of those immediately interested in the corporation to receive compensation for their own benefit, is a public charitable institution.

McDonald v. Mass. General Hospital, 120 Mass. 432 

The facts that a corporation, established for the maintenance of a public hospital, by its rules requires of its patients payment for their board, according to their circumstances and the accommodation they receive; that no person has individually a right to demand admission; and that the trustees of the hospital determine who are to be received; do not render it the less a public charity.

McDonald v. Mass. General Hospital, 120 Mass. 432 

A corporation, established for the maintenance of a public charitable hospital, which has exercised due care in the selection of its agents, is not liable for injury to a patient caused by their negligence, nor for the unauthorized assumption of one of the hospital attendants to act as a surgeon. 

McDonald v. Mass. General Hospital, 120 Mass. 432 

An action of tort cannot be maintained against a public charitable hospital corporation to recover for personal injuries caused by negligence of the hospital servants or agents. 

Kidd v. Mass. Homoeopathic Hospital, 237 Mass. 500

An action of tort cannot be maintained to recover for injuries caused by the negligence of the servants or agents of a public charity, because it has no funds which can be chargeable with any judgment the plaintiff might recover, except those held subject to the trust of maintaining the charity.

HOSPITALS 

Kidd v. Mass. Homoeo. Hos., 237 Mass. 500 at 501 

Farrigan v. Pevear, 193 Mass. 147

The fact that a hospital corporation receives compensation from some of its patients does not affect in any respect its character or liability as a public charity. 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hos., 235 Mass. 66, at 67 

New England Sanitarium v. Stoneham, 205 Mass. 335, at 342 and cases cited

Funds of a public hospital are devoted to a charitable trust and to subject them to the payment of a judgment for negligence of its servants would be an unlawful diversion of the trust. 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hos., 235 Mass. 66, at 69

A private charity stands in respect of liability for negligence of its servants on the same footing as a public charity. 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hos., 235 Mass. 66, at 67

A public hospital is relieved from liability for negligence of its managers in selecting incompetent subordinate agents, as well as for negligence of such subordinate agents selected with care. 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hos., 235 Mass. 66, at 72

A corporation organized and maintained solely for the treatment of the sick as a public charity cannot be held liable for injuries to a patient caused by the negligence either of its managers or its employees; the basis of decision being that trusts for charities cannot thus be diverted and the benevolent designs of the donors thus be thwarted, and in some instances on general grounds of public policy. 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hos., 235 Mass. 66, at 72

A public hospital is exonerated from liability to patients injured through negligence of servants or employees. That result has been reached in some instances on the ground that one who accepts the benefactions of a public or private charity enters into such a relation as to exempt his benefactor from liability for negligence of his servants in administering the charity whether money is paid for the treatment or not. This ground of exemption is adopted by decisions of courts of several jurisdictions. 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hos., 235 Mass. 66, at 74 

Benton v. Boston City Hospital, 140 Mass. 13, at 17

HOSPITALS 

Among the reasons given for this exemption it has been said, that being a charitable institution rendering services to the public without pecuniary profit, if the property of the charity was depleted by the payment of damages its usefulness might be either impaired or wholly destroyed, the object of the founder or donors defeated, and charitable gifts discouraged; or that if an individual accepts the benefit of a public charity he thereby enters into a relation which exempts his benefactor from liability for the negligence of servants who are employed in its administration, provided due care has been used in their selection. 

Farrigan v. Pevear, 193 Mass. 147, at 149

It never has been held in this Commonwealth that a charitable institution was liable for negligence; on the other hand, it has been expressly held that such institutions are not liable for the negligence of their servants or agents. 

Nor is there liability in contract based upon an agreement, expressed or implied, for careful treatment; 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hos., 235 Mass. 66, at 75 also the death statute (Gen. Laws, c. 229, s. 5) imposes no liability upon a hospital toward a patient under the circumstances here alleged. That statute imposes a liability when “a person or corporation by his or its negligence, or by the negligence of his or its agents or servants while engaged in his or its business, causes the death of a person who is in the exercise of due care." 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hospital, 235 Mass. 66, at 75 and 76 The reasons already stated show that the terms of that statute are not applicable to a case where, from the nature of the corporation as a public charitable hospital, it cannot be guilty of negligence in respect of the treatment of its patients pursuant to the great charitable purpose for which it was established. 

Roosen v. Peter Bent Brigham Hos., 235 Mass. 66, at 76

An action of tort cannot be maintained against a public charitable hospital corporation for personal injuries received by a traveller upon a public highway by reason of negligence of an employee of the hospital who was driving an ambulance for it.

Foley v. Wesson Memorial Hospital, 246 Mass. 363 

نا

HOSPITALS 

In the last cited case the court said at page 365: "It is forcibly urged by counsel for the plaintiffs that this exemption of a charitable institution from liability for negligence of its servants does not extend to cases where the injury is inflicted on a stranger. 

See 5 R. C. L. 378 and cases cited “But under the Massachusetts doctrine, that these trust funds cannot be used to compensate wrongs committed by agents of those administering the funds, there is no ground for distinction between liability to a patient and liability to a stranger."

The provisions of the workmen compensation act do not apply to a corporation organized for and carrying on a public charitable hospital.

Zoulalian v. New England Sanatorium, 230 Mass. 102 

An action of tort cannot be maintained against a municipality for personal injuries resulting from gross negligence of the municipality or its servants, or agents in carrying on a hospital. B. 

Young v. Worcester, 253 Mass. 481

It was said in the last cited case at page 483: "The maintenance of the Worcester City Hospital by the defendant [city], while permissive, is a matter of public service conducted exclusively and purely for the general and common good. In some cases the statutes enjoin such service upon cities and towns, and in others permit it. When such service has been entered upon, there is no good reason why a liability to private action should be imposed when a town or city voluntarily enters upon such a beneficial work, and withheld when it performs the service under the requirements of an imperative law."

NUISANCES CREATED BY 

The operation of a hospital of itself is not a nuisance. 

Prest v. Ross, 245 Mass. 342

So the use of a dwelling house as a private hospital when properly equipped and efficiently conducted is in the interest

HOSPITALS 

of public welfare and does not create a private nuisance even though some inconvenience, discomfort and annoyance are caused to the neighborhood where these incidents are not unusual or extraordinary or substantially necessarily present in the operation of a hospital. 

Prest v. Ross, 245 Mass. 342

A valid license from a city to conduct a lying-in hospital is subject to the qualification that the business must be conducted without negligence or unnecessary disturbance of the rights of others. 

Prest v. Ross, 245 Mass. 342

In the case of Cook v. Fall River, 239 Mass. 90 a bill was filed to enjoin a Municipality from erecting a tuberculosis hospital because it would constitute a nuisance. A public hospital for the treatment of tuberculosis is not as a matter of law a nuisance. The court said at pages 93 and 94: "Hospitals for contagious diseases must be established and maintained for the protection of the general public; and it is not to be assumed in advance that such hospital, well equipped and managed under the supervision of public health boards will be a nuisance. "Without going so far as to say that purely mental discomfort cannot constitute a nuisance, certainly the law will not enjoin the erection of a municipal hospital in order to protect the plaintiffs from dangers which are found to be unreal. "The fears of mankind, though they may be reasonable ones, will not create a nuisance. "Depreciation of the market value of the plaintiffs' land, assuming it to be proved, would not be decisive in their favor." 

In Barry v. Smith, 191 Mass. 78. Where a hospital was a nuisance in that it had caused cases of smallpox to break out in the neighboring house of the plaintiff.

By Statutes 1905, Chapter 330, records of public hospitals were made admissible as evidence as to all matters therein contained; ....

Under the statute as thus amended, it was held in Raymond v. Flint, 225 Mass. 521, that records of the date of 1896 were admissible in a proceeding which involved the mental capacity of a deceased patient, for the purpose of showing her treatment and medical history while at the hospital. 

The Legislature felt that entries were made which ought not to be taken in evidence, and so enacted Statutes 1912, Chapter 442 which amended the earlier statutes of 1905 and 1908 by limiting the requirement to keeping "records of the treatment of the cases under their care and the medical history of the same" (inserting the words here underlined); and by striking out from the enactment giving the records admissibility in evidence the words "as to all matters therein contained" and inserting in their place "so far as such records relate to the treatment and medical history of such cases; but nothing therein contained shall be admissible as evidence which has reference to the question of liability."

In practice "the liability" referred to in the statute is liability for damage caused by the happenings which occasioned or attended the patient's presence in the hospital. 

A distinction is, therefore, made between (a) entries which record details of diagnosis, treatment and prognosis with mention of facts helpful to the understanding of the medical or surgical case and (b) those which narrate events or state facts connected with the patient or the occasion for his resort to the hospital but having no reference to his treatment or medical history in the hospital. 

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co., 271 Mass. 27, at 30

b. As Public Records

In Kelley v. Jordan Marsh Company, 1932 A. S. 27, the defendant without objection introduced in evidence the hospital record of the intestate, which contained this statement: "Patient was leaving department store through revolving door when door was rapidly revolved by crowd behind her. 

Patient was thrown to sidewalk and was unable to get up." 

The defendant also called as a witness the hospital doctor, who testified that the statement just quoted was made to him by the intestate.

In view of these two facts the plaintiff requested a ruling in substance that the statement in the hospital record as to the cause of the injury constituted original and primary evidence of the facts thus stated because it was a public record, and that the weight and competency of that evidence did not depend upon General Laws, c. 233, s. 65, as to declarations of deceased persons. The plaintiff contended that in substance this request required the ruling that the entry in the hospital record quoted above constituted prima facie evidence that the fact so stated was true. 

The court said at pages 34 and 35: "It is apparent from the statement already quoted from the exceptions as to the course of the trial that the hospital record was offered solely in aid of the judge in determining how to perform the duty resting on him under General Laws, c. 233, s. 65. It was not proffered or admitted generally, or as bearing on liability. It had pertinency to that duty and the defendant cannot be charged with failure to object to it on other grounds. "It is provided by General Laws c. 233, s. 79, that records kept by certain hospitals "shall be admissible as evidence.. so far as such records relate to the treatment and medical history of such cases; but nothing therein contained shall be admissible as evidence which has reference to the question of liability." 

Sullivan v. Morse, 271 Mass. 501, at 504 

Clark v. Beacon Oil Co. 271 Mass. 27 

Inangelo v. Petterson, 236 Mass. 439

This statute by its true construction does not give probative force to entries in hospital records which as to their admissibility 14a

HOSPITALS 

and evidentiary value depend upon other provisions of the statutes. 

It was not intended thereby to clothe entries in hospital records with a competency to any other extent or in any other way than that provided by General Laws, c. 233, s. 65. The two sections are in the same chapter. They must be interpreted, if reasonably practicable, so as to constitute an harmonious and consistent body of law. 

Tillson v. Springfield, 258 Mass. 72 

Brooks v. Fitch. & Leominster St. Ry., 200 Mass. 8, at 18

The final clause of s. 79, to the effect that entries in such hospital records shall not be competent upon the question of liability, forbids the use of declarations of deceased persons in the way here urged. Hospital records do not become admissible as general public records to any greater or other extent than permitted by said s. 79.

Incompetent evidence introduced in evidence without objection is entitled to its probative force. 

Ferris v. Ray Taxi Service Co. 259 Mass. 401 

That principle does not aid the plaintiff in the circumstances here disclosed.

As already pointed out, this hospital record and the supporting testimony of the hospital physician were offered and received for consideration by the trial judge under said s. 65. They have no further scope or effect.

The defendant was not bound by this evidence merely because it introduced the hospital record. A party calling witnesses or offering evidence does not become fettered thereby. It was at ilberty thereafter to take any position with respect to the facts as its view of the weight of the evidence required. 

Haun v. LeGrand, 268 Mass. 582, at 584, and cases there collected 

Newman v. Levinson, 266 Mass. 264, at 267

G. ACTIONS 2. Rights of Action b. By Husband or Wife or Both (II) For Torts (B) Personal Injuries to Wife  

An injury to the person of a married woman creates two causes of action: one in favor of the wife, for damages suffered by her personally; another in favor of her husband alone, for the loss of her services, companionship and conjugal society, and for medical expenses incurred by him in effecting her cure. 

Erickson v. Buckley, 230 Mass. 467 

Driscoll v. Gaffey, 207 Mass. 102

Duffee v. Boston El. Ry. Co., 191 Mass. 563 

As was said in Erickson v. Buckley, 230 Mass. 467, at pages 

470 and 471: "The common law right of the plaintiff to recover for the expense to which he had been put by reason of the injury to the wife resulting from the negligence of the defendant, is indisputable. 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283 

Kelley v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 168 Mass. 308 "His right is not consequential upon the right of the wife because it once belonged to her and has been transferred to him. Her rights to damage for injury to person and property under the statutes are independent of his rights to compensation for like injuries, although their individual rights may have a common origin. In the prosecution of their several and independent rights there is not privity in the assertion of their demands; and a judgment in favor of a defendant in an action brought by either of them is not a bar to an action by the other. 

McCarthy v. Wood Lumber Co., 219 Mass. 566, at 570 

Mulvey v. Boston, 197 Mass. 178 

Duffee v. Boston Elevated Railway, 191 Mass. 563 

Kelley v. N. Y., N. H. & H. R. R., 168 Mass. 308 "The actions are as independent of each other as are two actions founded on a collision of two teams, caused by the negligence of the defendant, one brought by the driver, a servant of the owner of the team, to recover for his personal injuries, and the other by the owner, to recover for damages to his horses and wagon. The defendant's liability for the damages in the two cases depends upon the same facts, but Actions [ a ]

there is no privity between the plaintiffs. Each is enforcing an independent right.'

Duffee v. Boston El. Rlwy., 191 Mass. 563 (2) Damage Personal to Wife 

Crudo v. Milton, 233 Mass. 229 (Plff. as the wife of the tenant and a member of his family, may recover for negligence of the landlord.) 

Millmore v. Boston Elevated Rlwy., 198 Mass. 370

Texas & Pacific Rlwy. v. Humble, 181 U. S. 57 

The wife can recover for hospital and medical expenses where she bound herself to pay for them. 

Kenyon v. Vogel, 250 Mass. 341, at 344

(a) Medical Expenses 

The wife only, not the husband, is entitled to recover damages based on future probable medical expenses. 

Cassidy v. Constantine, 269 Mass. 56

In the last cited case the court said at page 59: "We think that on a fair interpretation of General Laws, c. 209, s. 6, the wife is entitled to recover damages based on proved future probable medical expenses, and that she is denied recovery of such expenses in the past unless she can prove that the payment therefor has been made by her or that the liability therefor rests on her." (3) Damage to Husband 

(a) General Statement 

In Jackson v. Boston El. Rlwy., 217 Mass. 515, at 516, the court said: "The plaintiff [husband] in the second action is not entitled to consequential damages unless his wife, the plaintiff in the first action, can recover for personal injuries suffered while she was a passenger on the defendant's railway." 

Bolger v. Boston El. Rlwy., 205 Mass. 420 

Gardner v. Boston El. Rlwy., 204 Mass. 213 

Feneff v. N. Y. Cent. & H. R. R. R., 203 Mass. 278

While the wife may recover for an injury which impairs her right to her own business and her own earnings, Harmon v. Old Colony R. Co., 165 Mass. 100 as was said in Jordan v. Middlesex R. R. Co., 138 Mass. 425, at 426: "... the plaintiff's capacity to earn is her own, and, if entitled to recover for any diminution of her capacity to labor Actions [b]

that is shown to have resulted from the injury; and this is to be determined upon the whole evidence, and not by any special theory of computation suggested by counsel," she is not permitted to recover damages because she has been rendered less capable of attending to her ordinary duties as a housewife. Such incapacity affects the husband's right to services and the action for an injury to that right remains in him. 

Dennis v. Clark, 2 Cush. 347

Husband must sue in separate suit in his own name. 

Tozier v. Haverhill St. Rlwy., 187 Mass. 179

While the gist of the husband's cause of action is not the injury itself, yet consequential damages are directly referable to the personal injuries suffered by the wife. 

Hey v. Prime, 197 Mass. 474 (Suit because the disability arising from the tort has deprived him of either his wife's services or matrimonial companionship, his right to recover rests upon the ground that the wrong suffered by him, while personal in effect, is regarded as purely consequential in character, held that under the statute such an injury cannot be classed as "damage to the person.")

So, the husband cannot recover for the damage to himself unless the wife can recover for her own injury. 

Jackson v. Boston El. Rlwy., 217 Mass. 515, at 516

Gardner v. Boston El. Rlwy., 204 Mass. 213 

But when a wife is entitled to go to the jury the case of her husband should also be submitted to the jury. 

Karsokas v. Universal Motor Sales Co., 1931 A. S. 2061 

But a judgment for the defendant in an action by the wife for her personal injury is not res judicata as to the husband's action for loss of services, because the parties are not the same. 

Duffee v. Boston El. Rlwy., 191 Mass. 563 

(b) Particular Considerations 

1. Loss of Consortium

The term consortium includes not only the affection, solace, comfort, companionship and society incidental to the marital relation, but also the services of the wife. 

The wife can not maintain an action for a similar injury to her husband, since under the theory of husband and wife she could not bring an action in her own name. 

Gearing v. Berkson, 223 Mass. 257 

Whitcomb v. N. Y. etc. R. Co., 215 Mass. 440

In Kelley v. New York etc. R. Co., 168 Mass. 308, it was said at 311: "By common law it is quite clear that a husband might maintain an action in his own name alone for an injury to his wife which resulted in his loss of consortium with her; as, for example, for an injury caused by an assault and battery upon her, by medical or surgical malpractice, or by other negligence."

(5) Abatement or Survival of Action 

General Laws, c. 228, s. 1, provides: "In addition to the actions which survive by the common law, the following shall survive; actions of replevin, tort for assault, battery, imprisonment or other damage to the person, for goods taken and carried away or converted, or for damage to real or personal property, and actions against sheriffs for the misconduct or negligence of themselves or their deputies."

The nature of the damages sued for is the test for determining whether a cause of action comes within the language of the survival statute, General Laws, c. 228, s. 1.

The words "or other damage to the person" include such damages only as result from direct bodily injury, but exclude consequential damages suffered by those who are injured from a wrongful interference with their rights arising from an injury to the person of another. The action for loss of services and medical expenses being consequential in character, therefore does not survive. 

Keating v. Boston El. Rlwy., 209 Mass. 278 

Hey v. Prime, 197 Mass. 474

So, in the event the husband or the tortfeasor dies, the action abates. 

See cases just cited above. 

(6) Time Within Which Actions Must Be 

Commenced General Laws, c. 260, s. 4, as amended, provides: "Actions for assault and battery, false imprisonment, slander, actions against sheriffs, deputy sheriffs, constables or assignees in insolvency for the taking or conversion of personal property, actions of tort for injuries to the person against counties, cities and towns, and actions of contract or tort for malpractice, error or mistake against physicians, surgeons, dentists, optometrists, hospitals and sanitaria, shall be commenced only within two years next after the cause of action accrues; and action for libel and actions of tort for bodily injuries or for death the payment of judgments in which is required to be secured by chapter ninety, suits by judgment creditors in such actions of tort under section one hundred and thirteen of chapter one hundred and seventy-five and clause (10) of section three of chapter two hundred and fourteen and suits on motor vehicle Actions [e]

liability bonds under section thirty-four G of said chapter ninety shall be commenced only within one year next after the cause of action accrues."

In Mulvey v. Boston, 197 Mass. 178, it was held that the husband's action for loss of services is within this statute as being "injuries to the person" because it arises or grows out of a personal injury. (C) Personal Injuries to Husband

It is well settled at common law that no action arises in favor of the wife for personal injuries to a husband. 

Kelley v. New York etc. R. Co., 168 Mass. 308

Thus, where a husband was injured by the defendant's negligence, the wife could not recover on account of suffering and anxiety which she sustained, nor because she was obliged to assume heavy and arduous duties, which she was not required to perform before the injury. 

Feneff v. New York Cent, etc. R. Co., 203 Mass. 278 

The reason why she ought not to recover is (1) that double compensation might thereby be enacted for the same damages from the same defendant, for in an action by the husband he could recover "for being incapacitated to care for, associate with and protect her, as well as being deprived of his right to consort with her."" (2) A negligent injury to the husband, however, affects the wife or widow only indirectly or collaterally calling for mere compensatory damages, which the husband while living, or his personal representatives after his death, may collect, thus settling the grievance once for all. 

Gearing v. Berkson, 223 Mass. 257 

Feneff v. New York Cent, etc. R. Co., 203 Mass. 278 

Nolin v. Pearson, 191 Mass. 283

A right may exist in the husband, which, notwithstanding the statute, is without a correlative right in the wife. 

See cases just cited above.

The married woman's act confers no new right of action upon married women, so that a wife cannot now, any more than previously, recover for a loss of consortium due to injuries negligently inflicted upon her husband. 

See cases just cited above.
